headline: Kenny Dillingham thinks he can turn ASU football into the Clemson or Oregon of this era
fullText:
Arizona State football head coach Kenny Dillingham thinks he can turn ASU into the next Clemson and Oregon this decade.

“You have Clemson this last cycle, from 2010 to 2020," Dillingham told Pete Nakos of On3. "They just showed up. People think they’ve been around forever. You have Oregon from 2000 to 2010... There hasn’t been a team in this era, in the 2020s. The lifestyle you have in Arizona, if we can create some staff consistency, and then we’re in a league where we can continually compete to win.”

Clemson has won three national championships and 24 conference championships, but they have not "been around forever." They had just one national championship (only one more than ASU has) and 15 conference championships (two fewer than ASU had entering the 2020s) before 2010.

Clemson won two national championships and seven conference championships from 2010-2020, but they were not as successful before that.

As for Oregon; ASU has never won a national championship, but neither have the Ducks. Oregon has four Rose Bowls compared to ASU's one, but ASU also has 18 conference championships, including the Western Athletic and Border conferences, compared to Oregon's 14, including the Pacific Coast Conference.

ASU came into the 2020s with 17 conference championships, while Oregon came into 2000 with five. Dillingham and ASU have more than enough reasons to believe they could be the team of this era that Oregon was from 2000-2010.

This is especially true considering "the lifestyle you have in Arizona," as Dillingham mentions. Few schools can flex the quality of weather that Arizona State has during the school year. The school also has a reputation for a fun college campus experience and is located in a top 11 television market nationally.

The program is also located just a six-hour drive from one of the top recruiting hotbeds in the country in Southern California. Dillingham can sell Southern California families on parents being able to watch their kids play most Saturdays, without needing a plane ride.

ASU finished seventh in the final AP Poll for the 2024 season.

ASU does not have as successful a resume as Clemson. They do not have as strong a brand as Oregon. However, history proves that Dillingham's goals for ASU to be the 2010 to 2020 Clemson or the 2000 to 2010 Oregon are attainable.

Dillingham also obtained "some staff consistency" he wanted heading into 2025, and ASU is coming off a conference championship in their first year in the Big 12 he mentioned that the Sun Devils "can continually compete to win."

headline: Reader Q&A: What's up with Arizona's special gasoline blends and are they worth the cost?
fullText:
This is part of a monthly series answering readers' climate-related questions and highlighting Arizona's unsung climate leaders. The stories aim to help connect and inspire Arizonans who care about protecting a livable climate and may be struggling to find hope in that effort. You can ask a question or nominate an unsung Arizona climate leader by filling out this form at https://forms.gle/QCCxBPSHGy1bUJQ99 or by emailing climate reporter Joan Meiners at joan.meiners@arizonarepublic.com.

The price of gasoline is a frequent hot topic of conversation around the water cooler, er, gas pump. It also comes up like clockwork every four years during the run-up to the presidential election when it is, incorrectly, used to blame or praise candidates for their economic approach (turns out gasoline prices have very little to do with short-term domestic policies and are largely out of any sitting president's control, according to energy analysts).

In Arizona, gasoline tends to be a bit more expensive than the national average, as my colleague Russ Wiles reported recently in advance of Memorial Day weekend travel.

One reason could be that a state law requires the summertime use of a special blend designed to help control ozone and other air pollutants that peak during hot months in metro Phoenix, which consistently ranks among the regions with the worst air quality in the country. After Wiles' story was published, he received questions from readers about whether that requirement is still in place and, if so, whether it's worth the added cost.

More: What to expect with Arizona gas prices as Memorial Day, summer travel season nears

"Russ, unfortunately, you didn't mention the exotic blend of gasoline only Arizona is required to use to supposedly lower the ozone levels, which costs tons more than similar blends that could supposedly have the same effect on pollution and are cheaper," one reader wrote.

"You didn’t mention the special blend that is required by the consent order locally signed," another reader pointed out. "Is it no longer in effect?"

Arizona's cleaner-burning gasoline blend was not the focus of Wiles' story last month. But since burning fossil fuels like gasoline for transportation is a top contributor to the emission of greenhouse gases causing the climate to warm and destabilize, and because ozone is an indirect part of that larger equation, it is the focus of this story — part of our monthly series answering reader's climate-related questions or highlighting a local climate leader. (Submit your question here: https://forms.gle/QCCxBPSHGy1bUJQ99.)

AZ climate leader: These 'great old broads' are serious about science, wolves and reversing climate change

The concept of cleaner-burning gasoline is fairly simple

The most basic difference with cleaner-burning gasoline is the addition of oxygen-containing compounds, or oxygenates, that help gasoline burn more completely in fuel tanks and not evaporate from vehicles. This makes for better fuel efficiency (with some minor mpg tradeoffs) while minimizing toxins that end up in the air.

CBG blends also reduce the amount of benzene, a known human carcinogen, by half and the amount of sulfur, which facilitates better emissions controls on vehicles, by up to 80%. And they typically cut back on the use of other smog-forming hydrocarbons once thought to improve vehicle performance. Extensive testing with millions of miles driven on CBG blends since 1996, however, has shown no negative effects on vehicles or in other types of gasoline-burning engines. The fuel types can be used interchangeably without any modifications.

The estimated effect is a 15% reduction in smog for a 5- to 15-cent per gallon cost increase. (These stats are for California, which has a slightly different blend. Arizona officials declined to comment for The Arizona Republic on how the local CBG blend differs or might affect prices.)

It's tough to translate that added cost at the pump into health care savings related to air pollution's links to higher incidences of asthma, heart disease, lung cancer, stroke and more. But since children can be especially vulnerable to air pollutants, the value of reducing them now can pay dividends for society further into the future, with incoming generations that are able to be more productive in the workforce and less reliant on the health care system.

More: Reader Q&A: How can I protect my kids from climate pollution and advocate for clean air?

Jeremy Martin, a chemist who directs fuels policy for the Union of Concerned Scientists' Clean Transportation Program, said it's important to look at vehicles and fuels as an interconnected system shifting with gasoline markets and vehicle efficiency improvements, and also with societal health outcomes and concerns.

"One important piece of context is that federal fuel regulations have been changing as well," Martin said. "Vehicle regulations and fuel regulations go hand in hand, and together they result in reduced air pollution and reduced health impacts from that pollution."

The American Lung Association reported in 2025 that Arizona ranked fourth in the number of unhealthy ozone days and that 84% of Arizonans live in communities with unhealthy air.

Another AZ climate leader: Rhonda Bannard believes women are the changemakers for climate action and Mother Earth

The story of how Arizona came to require CBG is more convoluted

Arizona's struggle with unhealthy air goes back decades, and so does its history of trying to contain it using cleaner-burning gasoline, one of several tools in the air quality arsenal.

It all started in 1997, when the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency extended its reformulated gasoline program to the Phoenix area to bring it into compliance with air quality regulations established by the Clean Air Act. Then-Gov. Fife Symington supported this solution and asked in January 1997 that the EPA require refiners to supply local retailers with the reformulated gasoline blend by June.

But in September of that year, Symington resigned from office over bank fraud convictions that were eventually overturned. His successor, Gov. Jane Dee Hull, requested an exemption from the EPA program just one week later. Although Phoenix was still considered a "serious ozone non-attainment area," the EPA granted this removal as of June 1998, one year after it had started, because Arizona had developed its own clean fuel program to reduce emissions of particulates and volatile organic compounds that contribute to ozone formation.

The specifics of that state program have shifted and been revised over the years, with some efforts to increase its benefits for air quality and other introduced legislation, including in the current legislative session, aimed at expanding what types of fuel can be considered clean enough or loosening regulations.

Vince Wolpert, who manages CBG compliance for the Arizona Department of Agriculture, said the current supply is sourced from refineries in California, New Mexico and Texas and brought into the state primarily by two pipelines, one from California and the other from New Mexico. 

"As for how the Department of Agriculture became involved, the Office of Weights and Measures already regulated fuel quality and quantity," Wolpert said. "Therefore, the state legislature tasked our agency as the enforcement agency for the CBG program."

Read our climate series: The latest from Joan Meiners at azcentral: climate coverage from Arizona and the Southwest

Cleaner-burning gasoline, cooler climate? Yes, and ...

Beyond the cost-saving benefits of slowing destructive atmospheric warming by reducing tailpipe emissions that increase greenhouse gas concentrations and worsen storms, the climate issue becomes involved in gasoline pricing when demand for CBG intersects with Arizona's growing electric vehicle industry.

"Of course, our best bet would be to invest more in transit and electric vehicles to make a difference for our air," said Sandy Bahr, director of the Grand Canyon chapter of the Sierra Club.

Since 2022, Arizona has become an "EV battery manufacturing powerhouse," with several large new facilities incentivized by clean energy tax credits tied to former President Joe Biden's Inflation Reduction Act. Hundreds of millions of investment dollars and thousands of jobs have flowed to the state as a result.

But the Trump administration's budget proposal currently under consideration by the U.S. Senate would repeal most of those funds, as well as a program offering average Americans up to $7,500 back on electric vehicle purchases. Advocates say this would devastate Arizona's clean energy economy and have hazardous consequences for energy access, air quality and health.

Some analysts further predict that a slowing of the American electric vehicle industry — one that forces more people into internal combustion vehicles despite globally increasing market demand for EVs — could put more pressure on gasoline supply chains, causing a greater increase in prices at the pump than any version of a cleaner-burning fuel program.

Joan Meiners is the climate news and storytelling reporter at The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. Her award-winning work has also appeared in Discover Magazine, National Geographic, ProPublica and the Washington Post Magazine. Before becoming a journalist, she completed a doctorate in ecology. Follow Joan on Twitter at @beecycles, on Bluesky @joanmeiners.bsky.social or email her at joan.meiners@arizonarepublic.com.

headline: Arizona Diamondbacks lookahead: On the road to Atlanta, Cincinnati to open June
fullText:
The Diamondbacks finish up a six-game homestand on Sunday, June 1, with the final game of three against the Washington Nationals at 1:10 p.m. at Chase Field.

The Diamondbacks lost two of three to the Braves April 25-27 at Chase Field.

From Atlanta, the Diamondbacks head north to Cincinnati to play the Reds for the first time this season. The Reds, like Atlanta, have managed to remain in the wild-card conversation, as they found themselves in the middle of the pack in the NL Central earlier in the week.

Cincinnati's most exciting player is 23-year-old Elly De La Cruz, a base-stealing machine who can hit for power and can have an impact on the game in multiple ways. Former Dodgers infielder Gavin Lux has been adept at extra-base hits this season and is hitting well in a slightly more than part-time role.

The Diamondbacks are 13-14 on the road this season, having lost five straight away from home.

headline: Cheap flights from Phoenix: 15 fun places to fly for under $150 in June
fullText:
Bargain hunters in metro Phoenix might find more cities to fly to at lower prices in June.

Average round-trip airfares for June 2025 will cost $293, according to new data from travel website Hopper. That's down from $320 in May.

Higher fares are one more thing air travelers will notice this summer, along with airlines experiencing a slowdown in domestic travel reservations and Southwest Airlines updating its baggage policy to eliminate Bags Fly Free and add fees for checked luggage. Open seating on Southwest is ending soon too.

Fifteen cities offer base fares below $150 from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in June, three more destinations than last month.

Do flights get cheaper in June?

June is generally less expensive to fly than May, particularly early June just before many schools break for the summer. Hopper found the average round-trip ticket cost about $293 for flights in June 2025.

In a summer 2025 travel forecast, Berg said travelers can expect lower domestic airfares this year, citing Americans facing many economic pressures.

"While 64% of Americans say they plan to maintain or expand their discretionary spending this year, many households are looking to get more for their travel budgets this summer," she said in her outlook.

Fifteen U.S. cities have base airfares below $150 round trip in June from Phoenix and two are below $100: Las Vegas and Los Angeles, according to Hopper.

headline: How an Apache language teacher found herself on a Kevin Costner film set
fullText:
FORT THOMAS, Ariz. — Sixteen kids bent over worksheets, laboriously writing out words in Ndee biyátiʹ — Apache — as their teacher recited them in English.

"Scorpion," she said. Tsédag histasí.

"Tarantula," she said. Biganłané.

A group of bright purple posters displayed the numbers one through 10 in Apache with common items to spur memories.

Data’a — one San Carlos Apache Tribe flag. Naki — two moccasins. Tąągi — three cradleboards.

Colorful posters sporting other common Apache terms lined the classroom walls. There were even terms for television and TV table.

It was another day in Aurelia Bullis' fourth grade Apache language class.

Bullis has spent most of her life in the Fort Thomas school district. A native of Bylas, a nearby community, Bullis attended school in the district and now teaches the Apache language to pre-kindergarten through high school students. Lately, she's also been instructing actors to speak her native tongue and filmmakers how to avoid stereotypical syntax.

Summer job leads to career

Bullis started working over the summer after graduating from Fort Thomas High School.

"There was a program where you could work during the summers or just to make a little bit of money," she said. Bullis worked at the local Head Start, where she moved up from volunteer to supervisor. After a short time as both a bus driver and teacher, Bullis saw a sign recruiting for an Apache language teacher.

"I said, 'Oh, I might as well try,'" said Bullis, whose first language is Apache.

Bullis beat out two older ladies for the job because she was willing to create lesson plans for kids from kindergarten through sixth grade.

But then she had second thoughts. "What did I get myself into? How am I gonna do this?" She had never taught older kids before and felt intimidated.

Hubby Buz came to the rescue. "He took us to the Twin Arrows Casino for the weekend, just to get away," Bullis said.

Soon she hit upon a method to do the job.

"I think I know what to do now," she said. "I'm going to do this lesson for this class, this lesson for the older ones, and then it all just came to me and I started putting it together."

Bullis sat up all night typing up lesson plans for her new job.

Eventually, Bullis' position grew to include junior and senior high classes. She also sponsored the school's culture club, which includes running school royalty pageants.

She's never looked back after nine years of teaching both spoken and written Apache in the dialect common to the eastern San Carlos and White Mountain Apache peoples.

Family connection leads to movie gig

Hollywood came calling for Bullis through one of Indian Country's time-honored methods: family.

Bullis' younger sister, Beverly, lives in the La Jolla Reservation in north San Diego County with her husband, a relative of famed designer and fellow La Jolla Band of Luiseño Indians tribal member Jamie Okuma.

Okuma's son, Bodhi Okuma Linton, is an actor who has appeared in film and television shows, including "Reservation Dogs" and "Dark Winds." Linton was also featured in the 2024 film "Horizon: An American Saga — Chapter 1." During the 2022 production, staff from Kevin Costner's production company were searching for a fluent Apache speaker to instruct the Native actors cast for the film, none of whom spoke Apache.

"So Jamie asked her nephew, Melvin Nelson to ask my sister." But Beverly can only understand Apache after being barred from speaking the language while attending a religious school.

Beverly gave her older sister, Aurelia, a call. "I was teaching a summer class in San Carlos," Bullis said. "She asked if I wanted a job for the summer? It's for a movie."

And not just any movie — "Horizon" was created by the Oscar-winning Costner.

"You're kidding right?" Bullis said.

It was no joke.

Bullis was hired to translate the actors' lines into Apache.

Next came the call to teach the cast their lines on location in Moab, Utah. "My husband was excited because I told him he's coming along."

Bullis said her most thrilling, yet scary day was when Costner himself came to the set.

"I couldn't say anything. I was just too scared and in shock." She started digging in her bag just so she wouldn't pass out.

"But then he came around, and we got to shake his hand."

After several weeks, though, Bullis had to return to Fort Thomas as the school year had started. They created a workaround for that, too.

"We used Zoom to teach each actor," she said.

Bullis has more movie work in progress. She's working with at least one other filmmaker on a new project. For this job, Bullis' work is more than just translating.

"The lines are kind of generic," she said. The writer didn't know how Apache people talked. "It was like, 'Oh spirit, you gave me the mountains' and this and that.

"My husband and I both thought it was cheesy."

Bullis is now busy rewriting lines to more accurately reflect how Apache people really talk. And she said that when she arrives on the set, the actors had best be dressed properly, "like the real deal that Costner had with their regalia, no generic feathers, that sort of thing."

Another film producer is already working to become familiar with Apache culture and the language that expresses that culture. "He's been wanting to come down and see Sunrise Dances and those sorts of things," Bullis said. "We've been talking on Zoom.'

Looking forward, Bullis is hard at work teaching younger generations about their culture and language.

It was difficult, however, to make Apache her kids' first language. Bullis' husband was also forbidden to speak Apache at school and thus can only understand it, as can her four kids.

"I speak to them in Apache and they understand. They'll say a little bit of this and that, but other than that, they just go back to speaking English," she said.

Bullis is working to bridge that gap with her four grandchildren. "I teach them here," she said. "It's like Apache is their second language." Her fellow Apache teacher is also teaching her third-grade granddaughter.

But her 11-month-old grandson is another matter. "We watch him when I'm not working, and really getting him to 'say this one, say this.' So he's slowly picking up that language."

Debra Krol reports on Indigenous communities at the confluence of climate, culture and commerce in Arizona and the Intermountain West. Reach Krol at debra.krol@azcentral.com. Follow her on X, formerly known as Twitter, @debkrol and on Bluesky at @debkrol.bsky.social‬.

headline: Indigenous students at odds with UA over changes to Native program, loss of director
fullText:
Indigenous students at the University of Arizona have signed a letter to the school's president and the state Board of Regents expressing concern over the deteriorating relationship between the university and its Indigenous student community, asking that the school "reverse course and preserve the Cultural Resource Centers," which include the Native American Student Affairs program.

The letter, signed by about 30 Native American students from various tribes, was dated May 25 and sent to President Suresh Garimella, Provost Patricia Prelock, the state Board of Regents, Levi Esquerra, senior vice president for Native American advancement and tribal engagement, and Tessa Dysart, assistant vice provost for Native American initiatives.

In the letter, the students said the university "stands at a crossroads: one path leads toward continued partnership with the Indigenous people whose lands it occupies, and the other toward a betrayal of the commitments enshrined in its public promises and acknowledgment.

Two days after the letter was sent, the UA announced plans to merge its cultural affairs programs into one hub and shift the Native American student program to another office.

The university also dismissed Julian Juan, who had been director of the school's Native American Student Affairs program. He had highlighted the tension between Indigenous students and school administrators during an April event, where students expressed their uneasiness with an administrator they didn’t trust.

The students' letter argued that, as a land-grant university built on tribal lands that were taken and funded through the sale of those lands, the UA holds “a lasting obligation to not only recognize but serve Indigenous communities.” The letter cited the UA's land acknowledgment:

"We respectfully acknowledge the University of Arizona is on the land and territories of Indigenous peoples. Today, Arizona is home to 22 federally recognized tribes, with Tucson being home to the O’odham and the Yaqui. The university strives to build sustainable relationships with sovereign Native Nations and Indigenous communities through education offerings, partnerships, and community service."

The letter said the statement implies that the UA, by adopting such language, "will work with tribal nations and their students to create a more welcoming space for Native American students who both attend now and in the future."

Higher education: Colleges cancel Native convocations to comply with Trump order, disappointing students

Tensions rise over Trump's DEI policies

Three months ago, Indigenous students spoke out during the Fourth Annual Tribal Leaders Summit student meet and greet after the university appeared to align with President Donald Trump’s stance against diversity, equity, and inclusion.

The incident, posted on Instagram, showed students addressing the quiet removal of DEI and access language from the university’s website, including the phrase “committed to diversity and inclusion” from its land acknowledgment.

The May 25 letter said Garimella and the provost intended to eliminate the Native American Student Affairs program and all other cultural resource centers.

The university announced its plans on May 27 to combine its cultural resource centers into one hub, with the Native American Student Affairs operations moved to the Office of Native American Initiatives.

In their letter, the Native students said the state's university system "has long failed our Native communities and Tribal Nations."

Among the failures listed:

  • Theft of data
  • Low scholarship support
  • Failure to hire Native faculty
  • Failure to provide a space for Native students to learn to be strong citizens of their respective Tribal Nations

"Despite these failures, we remain," the letter said. "Not only are we still here, but we are here in larger numbers then at any point in the recorded history of the university."

New policies: Tribal leaders to feds: DEI memo raises concerns over sovereignty and race issues

Native American Student Affairs director terminated

On May 27, Juan posted news of his firing to the Native American Student Affairs Instagram account. He described what happened in a 15-minute video and talked about what the position had meant to him.

"This work, being able to support students, our Native students, to help them achieve their goals, to help them feel like they belong on this campus, has been the most rewarding and beautiful work I've ever had the privilege of being a part of," Juan said in the video.

In their letter, the students said that under Juan's direction, the number of Native American student organizations at the college has increased.

"Under Julian's leadership, there are more large- and small-scale events at the university to support our Native students and ensure our retention and graduation in the degrees we seek," stated the letter.

Working with the Native American Student Affairs since 2019, Juan said he started as a coordinator. In his post, he noted that it would be a difficult video to make and explained the events leading to his termination.

He recalled an event in April where students appeared visibly distressed upon seeing a university official in attendance. Since the incident at the Tribal Leaders Summit, students have expressed concern about certain members of university leadership. Juan asked the official to leave the event, "due to student safety concerns."

"Leading up to this, I've had so many students come up to me with so many concerns for their emotional safety, physical safety, their mistrust in the institution, their mistrust in some of these administrators," said Juan. "Students should not feel unsafe at their school. Students should just be allowed to be students, especially our Native students. They should not be afraid that they're going to be physically silenced by senior administrators."

Juan said the official ultimately left the event, but the incident unfolded in front of two tribal leaders, to whom he immediately apologized and explained the situation. He emphasized that his actions were in direct response to the students’ visible distress and that ensuring their sense of safety was his top priority.

At a meeting after the incident, Juan was directed to apologize to the tribal leaders who had witnessed the exchange — an apology he had already offered on the day it occurred, but was still willing to repeat.

Also, during the meeting, he was told he could bring someone he trusted, and he immediately requested the presence of his tribal leaders. The school offered to accommodate the leaders' schedules.

Juan said he was unable to respond to an email from the university's leadership that arrived during the busy graduation period. After apologizing for the delay, he said he was coordinating with his tribal leaders to find a suitable time to meet with university leadership. He also sent a draft of the requested apology.

Then, while he was out of the office, he said an urgent meeting was added to his calendar without any prior notice, with no one but himself copied on the email.

"When I got to MLK (the Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Student Center) this morning, I was notified that I was being discharged from my duties because I had not completed the requested apology or still did not have the meeting set up," said Juan. "I brought up the May 5 meeting, where I was allowed to invite tribal leaders, and if we cannot meet them in the mid-May deadline, they could push it back and we could work around their availability."

He said after the April event where he asked the provost to leave, he expressed concern over retaliation. He also told his direct supervisor that he was "afraid for the safety of these students, and I am also afraid of my professional safety and I fear I am going to be retaliated against for speaking up."

UA: Change will 'increase collaboration'

The Arizona Republic reached out to Juan, students, Tohono O'odham leadership and an Indigenous faculty member for comment, but there has been no response.

A University of Arizona spokesperson emailed this statement after The Republic reached out for comment.

"As Arizona’s land-grant university, we are committed to engaging communities throughout our state to help meet their evolving needs. In our engagement, we embrace Indigenous knowledge through collaborative relationships with Native Nations, and we will integrate local insights to co-create solutions that respect our region’s cultural traditions. This commitment is reflected in the university's strategic imperatives and guides our work throughout the institution.

"Native American Student Affairs, becoming part of the Office of Native American Initiatives, under the oversight of Tessa Dysart, Assistant Vice Provost for Native American Initiatives, recognizes and respects the sovereign status of tribal nations. Professor Dysart, a member of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, will work closely with U of A Provost Patricia Prelock and Senior Vice President for Native American Advancement and Tribal Engagement Levi Esquerra to engage Native American students and support their success.

"While we value and appreciate engaging and hearing their opinions, we believe this change will increase collaboration and strengthen support for Native students, faculty, and tribal partners," the UA spokesperson wrote in an email to The Arizona Republic.

Arlyssa D. Becenti covers Indigenous affairs for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. Send ideas and tips to arlyssa.becenti@arizonarepublic.com.

headline: 100 years ago an Irish immigrant founded this Arizona dairy. His family still runs it today
fullText:
When Shamrock Farms started in the 1920s, a gallon of milk cost just 35 cents.

In the past 100 years, so much has changed in Arizona, least of all the price of milk. But Shamrock Farms is still producing milk for Arizonans just as it has for generations, showing that some things will always be the same.

Shamrock Farms was founded by W.T. McClelland in the 1920s and has been run by the McClelland family continuously ever since. Today, father and son Kent and Devon McClelland run the business.

"When you look at everything that's changed over the past 100 years, I think it's really a testament ... of a real commitment to the state, to our community, to our business," Shamrock Farms President Devon McClelland said.

He added that "despite everything that's happened over the course of Arizona's history, we're still fundamentally the same dairy that we were when we started."

Shamrock Farms started 103 years ago with just 20 cows

Shamrock Farms began as a small Tucson operation doling milk out of 5-gallon buckets in the 1920s.

At the helm was W.T. McClelland, a man his grandson, Shamrock Foods Co. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Kent McClelland describes as a modest "hardworking dairy guy."

W.T. McClelland emigrated from Ireland and followed family ties to Arizona. He did a variety of jobs before serving in World War I. After the war, he returned to the Grand Canyon State to pursue opportunities he knew were not available to him anywhere else, Kent said.

"We always came back to Arizona, for some reason it resonated with him," Kent McClelland said. "Even his wife, when she came out eight years later, it resonated with her as well."

W.T. and Winifred McClelland, affectionately called Mr. and Mrs. Mac, purchased 20 cows and a Model T delivery truck to start delivering milk to their 40-50 customers.

This is how Shamrock Farms took shape and began to influence Arizona for generations to come — with W.T. running the dairy, Winifred handling the numbers, and her brother, William Parker, managing sales.

"They just got embedded in the community, got to know people, and began to grow their business," Kent McClelland said.

Seeing the vision for Shamrock Farms' future

When Shamrock Farms was young, there were 15 dairies in Tucson and 30 in Phoenix, Kent McClelland said. Now, just a few remain.

Shamrock Farms owes its longevity to W.T. McClelland's vision. He made the choice to move the business out of Phoenix, Kent McClelland said. He also made the visionary move to begin pasteurizing milk, becoming one of the first big dairies in the U.S. to do so.

The company also expanded its product offerings to include coffee, meat, seafood, and more, operating under the name Shamrock Foods, leveraging its expertise to reach an even broader audience.

This long history and the many bumps the company has endured — wars, pandemics and major industry changes — have helped the McClellands see that they can weather the business's difficult moments, no matter what they may be.

"It builds up a history and an understanding that crises come and go, but you can work through them," Kent McClelland said.

Their family-run company allows them to "control your own destiny, it gives you a lot of security," Devon McClelland said.

It also provides comfort in continuity for its more than 6,100 employees and all the businesses and restaurants the company distributes to.

A beloved Arizona business at heart

Though Shamrock has made its mark on Arizona, the state has left an indelible impression on the company, too.

"The future looks a lot like the past for Shamrock," Kent McClelland told Eller Magazine in 2022. "Arizona is ingrained in who we are and what we do. And while much has changed, some things will always remain the same."

And Shamrock Farms is focused on helping the Arizonans who have long helped them thrive.

"I want all the communities that we're in to be better off for having Shamrock in them," Devon McClelland said.

The company has long focused on giving back, through a long-running connection with food banks in the state and helping with any other needs the community has. This also includes donating land next to the Tucson dairy for a Little League baseball field and ensuring the 20,000-cow dairy in Stanfield can accommodate field trips for children.

The future of Shamrock Farms

Now, as Kent and Devon McClelland prepare Shamrock to last another 100 years, they are looking to the future.

They've reinvested in their facilities and continue to invest in the business, its ties in the community, and its employees. All of these moves help them prepare for the company's (and Arizona's) future.

"Arizona is a fantastic place to do business, because it continues to grow, it continues to expand," Kent said. "It's kind of a go-to place for business coming in. ... There is so much going on here that keeps us excited."

One of the opportunities the McClellands see ahead is automation. However, the goal would be to "enhance rather than replace," Devon McClelland said. A lot of the dairy work is hard manual labor, and they'd like to see how they can make those jobs easier.

"We'd like to take those folks (working hard physical jobs) and have them do something more meaningful," Kent McClelland added.

From its humble beginnings as one of many dairies in the state, Shamrock Farms has become the top dairy brand in Arizona.

As Devon McClelland, in his sixth year formally working for Shamrock Foods, goes about his regular work and interacts with employees, he is reminded how vital the work they do is.

"It really puts things in perspective when you go to a grocery store or sit down at a restaurant, just how difficult it was to actually get that plate of food on the table," he said.

headline: Vote in our poll: The Republic's 10 best Arizona high school quarterbacks in 2025
fullText:
Summer is about to start, and before you know it, the 2025 Arizona high school football season will be here. To get through another hot summer, The Arizona Republic examines a position each week with a top-10 list. We will also include polls along the way asking you to vote for the player you think is top gun at each position ahead of the season (the poll appears after the list; print readers can find it with this story online at azcentral/sports/high-schools).

We start it off with what this state is best known for: producing top quarterbacks. The year in school listed for each quarterback is for the 2025 season.

The Republic's Top 10 quarterbacks for 2025

1. Brady Goodman, Mesa Mountain View, 6-4, 215, Sr.

The multi-sport athlete really elevated himself last season as a dual threat, leading the Toros to the 6A championship game. But in the semifinals and final, he was playing on one good ankle. Under head coach Andy Litten, Goodman will keep thriving. He's coming off a season in which he passed for 3,087 yards and 43 TDs and ran for 435 yards and 11 scores.

2. Gunner Fagrell, Gilbert Higley, 6-1, 190, Sr.

Now that he will be QB1 on a full-time basis, Fagrell is set to break out like he did his sophomore season, when he led the Knights to a second straight 5A state championship, putting up video numbers. He can run well enough to keep defenses honest. And his ability to find receivers in small windows sets him apart. And he's got a swagger that makes him a natural leader.

3. Britt DeWitt, ALA Queen Creek, 6-2, 195, Sr.

He wasn't eligible until midway through his junior year. But he came of age in an Open semifinal thriller against Chandler Basha, throwing for 377 yards and five touchdowns, and nearly willing a victory with his 34-yard run in the final seconds, only to get sacked on the next play, clinching Basha's ticket to the final. College coaches aren't scrambling for him, but he could be Brock Purdy 2.0.

4. Kael Snyder, Gilbert Perry, 6-3, 215, Jr.

Maybe the most highly recruited quarterback for the 2025 season, Snyder has big-time potential with his size, arm strength and accuracy. He still is fine-tuning everything, but is set to have a huge junior season for the Pumas, looking to get them into the Open Division playoffs.

5. Donivan Dixon, Cave Creek Cactus Shadows, 5-10, 185, Sr.

He might be the most electrifying quarterback in the state thanks to his speed, moves and ability to throw on the run. He's as fun to watch as any playmaker in the state. And, with his work ethic and desire to be the best, expect an even greater version of himself this fall.

6. Brodie Vehrs, Chandler Basha, 6-0, 195, Sr.

He was terrific in his first season as QB1, following one of the state's all-time greats in Demond Williams Jr. Watch what he does in his second full season directing what could be the state's most explosive offense, surrounded by playmakers. He is so good at finding the right guy to get the ball to. Poised, big arm, accurate, confident.

7. Blake Roskopf, Goodyear Desert Edge, 6-5, 225, Jr.

He's got nine major-college offers already. He's a Ben Roethlisberger-type QB with a big arm. He's not afraid to take big shots down the field. He led the Scorpions to the 5A state title as a sophomore. His potential is through the roof.

8. Marcel Jones, Scottsdale Saguaro, 6-2, 190, Sr.

This will be his first full varsity season in his career. And, with offensive coordinator Noel Mazzone fine-tuning his game and putting him in positions to succeed, this could be a big breakout season for the dual-threat QB. Improved arm strength and accuracy will be on display.

9. Colten Meyer, Marana, 6-1, 180, Sr.

He finished third in the state in passing last year with 3,687 yards. He passed for 30 TDs and completed 74% of his passes. He won't have Player of the Year Dezmen Roebuck to get the ball to. But Roebuck's little brother, Sean, is back to find the end zone for a team that went 10-0 in the regular season.

10. Will Mencl, Chandler, 6-4, 205

He became QB1 halfway through last season after alternating series, but a late-season injury derailed his sophomore season. Expect him to emerge this season under coach Ty Wisdom.

headline: These are the last stories from Arizona Republic reporter Don Bolles before a bomb exploded
fullText:
They are stories chronicling the Arizona political scene during the final weeks of the 1976 legislative session, noteworthy because they were the final stories written by Arizona Republic reporter Don Bolles before a bomb exploded under his car and killed him.

On June 2, 1976, Bolles left the state Capitol in Phoenix to meet a source at the Clarendon Hotel. It was a ruse. After Bolles parked and walked to the lobby, a man placed dynamite under his car. As Bolles backed out of the parking space a bit later, another man detonated it.

Though Bolles previously was an investigative reporter who looked at mafia influence in Phoenix, by 1976, he had settled into the role of covering the state Legislature.

Bolles’s final weeks of stories show the work of a deeply sourced reporter who knew the ins and outs of the Capitol and had gained the trust of lawmakers from both parties.

Bolles last dispacthes

A May 12, 1976, article described a potential legislative compromise regarding a requirement that motorists in Phoenix and Tucson have their vehicles tested for emissions. Republicans and some Democrats wanted to junk the requirement. Other Democrats, including Gov. Raul Castro, wanted to preserve it.

Bolles’s article said that The Republic — undoubtedly meaning Bolles — was told about five secret meetings among legislative leaders and Castro hammering out a plan. The result: the emissions tests would stay, with some modifications.

A May 13, 1976, article predicted who would be named to the five remaining spots in the Arizona delegation headed to the Democratic National Convention. Bolles reported that one spot would be filled by a Native American and another by an African American, calling it a “relative certainty.” That weekend, Bolles’s prediction came true.

Two days later, Bolles published an article about the Department of Public Safety getting a boost in its budget. Bolles reported on an unadvertised meeting the night before the vote with the DPS director, giving what an unnamed lawmaker described as an “eye-opener” description of the growing crime problem in Arizona.

Bolles wrote on May 19, 1976, about an oral report about projected tax revenue that a legislative budget analyst gave to the chairs of the Senate and House budget committees. Bolles talked to the analyst who told him revenue would be millions more than projected.

A May 21, 1976, article told the tale of how a Tucson lawmaker was flown to Phoenix in a DPS helicopter out of fears he would be late for a crucial vote. The Democratic leader of the state Senate, Alfredo Gutierrez, told Bolles he simply wanted the DPS to escort Sen. Frank Felix to the Tucson airport so he could get a commercial flight to Phoenix, but the agency overreacted.

Felix landed on the DPS helicopter pad and was in his seat in the Senate an hour before the vote. Though Bolles noted, his vote wasn’t crucial. The measure in question sailed through 18-9.

Bolles reported on a May 27, 1976, agreement to delay implementation of the Medicaid program in Arizona for at least a year. The federal government created the program in 1965, but Arizona still had not implemented it.

In an article that ran on Saturday, May 29, 1976, Bolles said that with the Medicaid agreement firmed up, it “opened the door to adjournment of this lengthy 1976 legislative session.”

Lawmakers would return after Memorial Day, Bolles wrote, to mop up the remaining issues: How much to spend on flood control dams and school buses.

On Memorial Day in 1976, a Bolles article ran that was labeled a “news analysis.”

Bolles explained to readers that lawmakers couldn’t agree on when to start Medicaid, so they moved the potential start date past the next elections, hoping voters would put one party in charge of both legislative chambers.

If Republicans won, “they probably will vote to abandon the Medicaid program." If Democrats won, they would “vote to begin the program.” If the chambers were still split, Bolles wrote, “the impasse could continue.”

Bolles quoted a state health department administrator who said 82,000 people would be helped by the program. That expert said those people are likely relying on charity care, free clinics or going without medical help.

Bolles quoted a Republican lawmaker who chaired the House Health Committee who doubted that figure. “I don’t know where these 82,000 people are,” Rep. Diane McCarthy told Bolles. “I find it hard to believe there are that many people who are not receiving care.”

Arizona would not join the Medicaid program until 1981, when it created the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System. Today, more than 2 million Arizonans use the program.

Legislative hearing on dog racing, then a bomb explodes

On June 2, 1976, Bolles covered a legislative hearing on a bill that would ensure one company could not dominate the state’s dog racing tracks. It was an issue Bolles had long covered and had taken personally.

Bolles had written articles that detailed mafia ties of Emprise, the company that co-operated Arizona’s dog racing tracks. Bolles was told the Funk family, who, along with Emprise, owned the tracks, had hired someone to tap his home phone, hoping to get dirt on him.

It was a story that haunted Bolles, even after The Republic took him off the investigative beat and off stories about the Funk family and Emprise.

Later that day, as he lay on the asphalt after the bombing, Bolles mentioned Emprise and the mafia, figuring those entities were to blame for his death.

Authorities would quickly zero in on a man named John Adamson, who was the source Bolles was set to meet at the hotel. Adamson told police he was hired by a man named Max Dunlap to kill Bolles. Adamson enlisted a man named James Robson to build the dynamite bomb and detonate it.

Dunlap ordered the killing, police said, to gain favor with liquor magnate Kemper Marley, who was upset that a Bolles article resulted in him losing a spot on the state racing commission. Police could never definitively connect Marley to the bombing. He was never charged.

Marley had had discussions about becoming a partner in a racetrack, a relationship that was not allowed if he were on the racing commission — unless it was kept secret.

The article that cost Marley the spot on the racing commission was fairly routine, one Bolles likely wrote after combing The Republic's archives for previous stories involving Marley's misdeeds.

But Republic reporters investigating possible motives for the assassination made that Marley connection. In an internal memo, found in a filing cabinet in The Republic's newsroom, a staffer theorized that Marley could have wanted to land a seat on the racing commission while being a silent partner on a greyhound track, now that the Funk monopoly was broken up. The note, which included other possible threads to pursue, said Marley would have hidden control of a racetrack and a seat on the board that oversaw it.

“Great theory," a reporter wrote in an internal memo to his colleagues. "Now all we gotta do is prove it."

Bolles covered the legislative hearing that saw passage of the bill breaking up the Funk monopoly. Then, he went back to the press room in the state Senate building and wrote it up. He then left a note on his typewriter that gave the details of his meeting at the Clarendon Hotel.

The story about the racing monopoly bill appeared in the June 3 edition of The Arizona Republic, tucked inside a paper heavy with coverage of the “gang-style” car bombing of Bolles.

That story, his last, carried no byline.

headline: Top 5 events to watch for this summer in Arizona high school sports
fullText:
The Arizona Interscholastic Association sports year is over, but that doesn't mean high school athletes stop competing. June figures to be a big month for activities.

Here are five things to look forward to this summer:

Section 7

A lot of high schools from across the state like to go to college camps, where they compete. But most eyes will be on Section 7, a platform that helps basketball players with their recruiting in front of college coaches who attend the games.

This year it's being held at the Arizona Athletic Grounds in Mesa, moving from State Farm Stadium in Glendale. The girls' weekend is June 13-14, the boys' qualifier is June 17-18 and the boys' weekend is June 20-22. Boys qualifiers are for teams that didn't get official invitations to the weekend, which is the only time Division I college coaches are allowed to watch the games.

More than 400 high schools and 5,000 players, along with an estimated 900 college coaches, attend this annual recruiting event.

Gilbert Perry's basketball team will draw much attention, mainly to see if 6-foot-7 2027 wing Bruce Branch III will be playing. Branch is a four-star recruit with 19 Division I offers.

There's been speculation that Branch might leave for a prep academy. He's the main player left from Perry's fourth straight state championship team.

Koa Peat, D'Andre Harrison and NoNo Brown have all graduated. And Sam Duane Jr. has stepped down as coach to pursue an opportunity with Mesa Public Schools. If new coach Justin Collard, former Anthem Boulder Creek coach, can keep Branch at Perry, that's huge for a program seeking to continue its dynasty.

A lot of attention will be given to Goodyear Millennium to see dynamic 6-5 2026 swingman Cameron Holmes, who had a great AAU spring season playing for Arizona Unity. He'll be the biggest senior recruit out of Arizona next season.

Lady X

Marc Beasley and Monarch Sports always run great June tournaments for boys and girls basketball. On May 30 and 31, the top girls teams in the Valley take center court at Phoenix Sunnyslope High with the 12th Lady Extravaganza, where the two teams that met last season in the Open final are the Nos. 1 and 2 seeds -- Millennium (the 2025 Open champion) and Surprise Valley Vista.

No. 3 Phoenix Xavier Prep and No. 4 Chandler Hamilton are also part of the eight-team field, along with No. 5 Gilbert, No. 6 Sunnyslope, No. 7 Glendale Raymond S Kellis and No. 8 Gilbert Perry. The championship game is May 31 at 1 p.m.

PrimeTime

June 6 and 7 is The Sizzle at Surprise Willow Canyon and June 13 and 14 is PrimeTime at Phoenix Brophy Prep for the boys. They are both run by Beasley and Monarch Sports.

The PrimeTime will give fans their first look at Perry and Millennium. Perry is the 5 seed, so that shows you how much the Pumas are trying to rebuild from the Koa Peat/Sam Duane Jr. era.

Sunnyslope and Basha are the top two seeds with Millennium No. 3. Brophy Prep is 4, Phoenix St. Mary's is 6.

No. 7 Sandra Day O'Connor and No. 8 Boulder Creek round out the PrimeTime bracket.

St. Mary's will be intriguing with the return of 6-11 forward Cameron Williams, who is rated as the 15th top prospect in the 2026 class by 247Sports with offers from Arizona and Indiana among his eight.

7-on-7s, Big man

High school football will be on display throughout June, with 7-on-7 football passing tournaments and Big Man competitions at Arizona State, Arizona, Northern Arizona, San Diego State and hosted by the Just Chilly Flight Club.

Some of the more intriguing story lines:

  • The emergence of ALA Queen Creek 2026 QB Britt DeWitt, who has only an Idaho offer.
  • The transition from 2A to Open title team Peoria Liberty for running back/linebacker Thomas Fo’ilefutu, who has transferred from Tonopah Valley.
  • Chandler AZ Compass Prep defensive lineman Keytrin Harris, who has 20 Division I offers, and transferred to the Canyon Athletic Association school from national power Las Vegas Bishop Gorman.

Going to Omaha

Casteel baseball coach Matt Denny will be leading an Arizona all-star team to Omaha, Nebraska, July 4-6 for the Stinger High School Baseball National Championship Series at Charles Schwab Field, the same place where the College World Series is played.

Arizona is represented, along with California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nebraska and Texas.

Expect to see top Arizona players Jet Berry (Queen Creek), Baylor Denny (Casteel), Ryan Harwood (Casteel), Colton Raetzman (Tucson Salpointe), Jackson Weber (Horizon), Manny Hoyos (Queen Creek) and Abram Sherrin (Peoria Liberty).

headline: Roadworks: What is the work on Loop 202 between Chandler and Gilbert?
fullText:
What is the construction? The $200 million construction project along Santan Freeway portion of Loop 202 between Loop 101 and Val Vista Drive aims to improve traffic capacity and relieve congestion in the southeast Valley.

The project includes:

  • Adding two general purpose lanes in each direction from Loop 101 to Gilbert Road
  • Adding one general purpose lane in each direction from Gilbert Road to Val Vista Drive
  • Widening exit ramps from one to two lanes
  • Adding soundwalls
  • Widening overpass bridges
  • Reconstructing the eastbound Arizona Avenue on-ramp and bridge
  • Improving pavement conditions

Where is the construction? Construction stretches across about eight miles of roadway on Loop 202 between Loop 101 and Val Vista Drive in Chandler and Gilbert.

Separate pavement improvements are planned between Val Vista Drive and Williams Field Road.

How many drivers will be affected? The area sees nearly 100,000 drivers daily, according to 2023 estimates from the Arizona Department of Transportation. That number is only expected to increase as the Valley continues to grow.

How long will construction take? Construction began in August 2024 and is expected to take two and a half years to complete. It is slated to open in late 2026.

Will there be closures? Some on-ramp closures will last for 60 days with staggered start dates. These closures include the westbound Loop 202 on-ramp at McQueen Road, eastbound Loop 202 on-ramp at Price Road, eastbound Loop 202 on-ramp at Gilbert Road, and eastbound Loop 202 on-ramp at Arizona Avenue.

Drivers should also expect weekend closures.

Sources: The Arizona Department of Transportation, City of Chandler

headline: Demands for bathroom renovations and more: Metro Phoenix housing now a 'buyer's market'
fullText:
Metro Phoenix’s housing market is finally giving buyers a break.

The number of Valley homes for sale has soared, prices have dipped, and the deals sellers are offering are getting sweeter.

“We are in a buyers’ market,” said Tina Tamboer, senior housing analyst with The Cromford Report. “Don’t look for prices to plummet, but they could slip 3% to 5%.”

She said buyers are getting their revenge from years of sellers having the upper hand, and are asking homeowners for a lot more than mortgage buydowns and basic repairs to close a deal.

Tamboer heard from a real estate agent that a buyer asked for the repainting of the interior of a house. Another agent said a buyer asked for the replacement of a working air conditioner — and one even asked for a bathroom renovation.

In one case, a seller said no to a pricey renovation, and the buyer walked, she said.

Real estate: Former Arizona Coyotes owner sells Paradise Valley mansion. The price tag was massive

More houses to choose from

Listings of houses for sale shot up almost 53% during the past year, according to the Arizona Regional Multiple Listing Service.

That increase comes after listings shrunk between late 2020 and mid-2022 as buyers flooded the Valley and the housing market to tap ultra-low mortgage rates. But listings started to climb and sales dipped in late 2022 when the average 30-year mortgage rate climbed above 6%.

The are currently about 26,000 houses for sale in metro Phoenix.

“Buyers have more leverage now, and listings need to stand out to move quickly,” Paridhi Saboo, a real estate data analyst with ARMLS, said. “Sellers can no longer expect quick sales or premium pricing without strong preparation and marketing.”

People are buying despite mortgage rates hovering around 6.8%. In April, 7,164 Phoenix-area houses sold, up by almost 400 since March.

But the Valley’s median home price dipped by $10,000 to $445,000 in April from March, likely due to the higher supply of houses for sale.

It’s also taking longer for houses to sell, with the average days on the market hovering around 78 during the past few months, up from 67 days in April 2024.

Will sales and prices fall in May?

“Don’t expect any big, bold movements in prices anytime soon,” Tamboer said.

She said the big employers the Valley has recently drawn will continue to fuel the area’s growth, and many of those jobs are high paying. So, their employees are in better shape to buy houses.

May will have about 7,860 home sales based on homebuying contracts, according to ARMLS.

Tamboer said if mortgage rates drop, the housing market could get a fast boost.

Still, mortgage rates are difficult to predict.

“Bond yields and the mortgage rates that tend to follow them remain elevated, thanks to ongoing concerns over budget deficits and tariffs,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow Home Loans.

The median home price per square foot of sales under contract in April was slightly less than in March, according to ARMLS. That likely signals a small decline in the Valley’s median home price for May.

“Homes are selling, just not as quickly or easily as before,” Saboo said.

headline: Massive bird flu outbreak hits Hickman's in Arizona: What's next for the egg supplier
fullText:
Hickman’s Family Farms' hen population in Arizona has been decimated by avian flu, forcing the euthanasia of 95% of the company's birds in Arizona.

The egg supplier is still operating out of its facilities in Maricopa and Grand Junction, Colorado, where it has about 300,000 birds each. But Hickman's has lost roughly 6 million hens.

The company's large-scale farms in the West Valley are all closed.

Hickman's plans to lay off hundreds of its 850 workers and end its inmate labor program, Glenn Hickman, company president and CEO, said.

Hickman said at a May 30 news conference he did not expect the outbreak at Hickman’s to impact overall egg prices significantly.

Here's what to know about the flu outbreak and its impact.

Will the outbreak affect egg prices?

Egg prices around the country have dropped since reaching a high in January, Hickman said, but he expects that downward price trend to stop.

What is Hickman's Family Farms?

Hickman’s Family Farms is family-owned and operated. Founded in 1944, it is the largest egg company in the Southwest and among the top 20 nationwide, according to the company. Its headquarters are in Buckeye.

Glenn Hickman is the company president and CEO, and several third- and fourth-generation family members are active in the company.

What is bird flu, sometimes called avian flu?

H5N1 bird flu is widespread in wild birds worldwide and is causing outbreaks in poultry and U.S. dairy cows with several recent human cases in U.S. dairy and poultry workers, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It has been detected in wild birds and commercial poultry since January 2022.More than 173 million birds have been affected.

Find information about the spread of bird flu in poultry at www.cdc.gov/bird-flu.

Can humans get bird flu?

Yes, but the number of cases in the U.S. is small. And there is no known person-to-person spread at this time, the CDC said.

What are bird flu symptoms?

Birds with bird flu may show signs like lethargy, decreased appetite, ruffled feathers, reduced egg production or coughing or sneezing. Some birds may experience neurological symptoms like tremors or seizures or sudden death.

When did this outbreak at Hickman's start?

The current outbreak has killed or forced the euthanasia of 95% of Hickman’s Family Farms’ Arizona hen population, totaling about 6 million dead birds in the past two weeks, Glenn Hickman said.

Efforts to contain the disease to one of the company's farm location were unsuccessful, he said. When some birds tested positive, the company shut down travel between the farms, but it did not stop the spread.

Once a chicken is infected, the bird dies quickly, Hickman said. But based on the contagious nature of the disease, other birds contained in the same barn must also be euthanized.

What is the effect on the company and its employees?

The outbreak and loss of egg-laying hens means, for the first time in 81 years, the company will not be able to fulfill all of its customer demand, Hickman said.

Hundreds of employees are expected to lose their jobs, though Hickman said he is unsure of what the final headcount decrease will be.

The company is also ending its inmate labor program, which used inmates to help staff the farm, he said.

What measures has the company taken to prevent bird flu?

People must shower and wear company-laundered clothes to enter a Hickman’s facility, he said, and vehicles are cleaned when driving into it. There are measures, like lasers, in place to scare away wild birds and other animals that can carry the disease.

“This virus is airborne and that is our gap,” he said.

How will Hickman's move ahead?

It will take about two years to regain the size of the flock, he said. Once the barns are depopulated and disinfected, the company can move baby chicks into the space, at a rate of about 300,000 per month.

The company is still operating out of its facilities in Maricopa and Grand Junction, Colorado, where they have about 300,000 birds each. The company's large-scale farms in the West Valley are all closed.

Is there a flu vaccine for chickens?

Chickens are not routinely vaccinated against bird flu.

Hickman pointed squarely at the meat bird industry’s lobbying efforts against an avian flu vaccine for the nationwide outbreak.

The meat industry, which supplies meat to foreign countries as well as the United States, has opposed the use of an avian flu vaccine for birds because some foreign countries will not buy vaccinated meat, he said.

“The federal government knows that vaccination works,” Hickman said. “Some European countries are already vaccinating their poultry.”

If Hickman’s chickens had been vaccinated when the company had been lobbying for it in January, the effect of the outbreak would have been significantly decreased, Hickman said. The Arizona Department of Agriculture has been lobbying the federal government to begin a vaccination pilot program, he said, but the ultimate decision will be made by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Hickman’s vaccinates chickens already for other diseases like chicken pox, so adding another vaccination wouldn’t change procedures, Hickman said.

Is Hickman's Family Farms insured against its livestock deaths?

The USDA has a livestock indemnity program that compensates farmers for livestock deaths in excess of normal mortality.

According to the department, for an egg-laying hen, the payment rate is $12.17 per bird. If all 6 million birds qualify for that compensation, it would total about $73 million.

Hickman declined to discuss the financial hit that the loss of the flock would have on the business.

What was the euthanasia process? Tactics criticized by animal rights group

Animal rights organization Animal Outlook said the most commonly used method of depopulation of chickens is called ventilation shutdown plus. That involves sealing a barn’s ventilation and heating the building, which Ben Williamson, executive director of Animal Outlook, described as “cooking these birds to death,” which can take hours.

When the group became aware of the avian flu outbreak at Hickman’s, it sent an investigator to observe the barns. That person took videos of piles of dead birds being loaded into dump trucks and saw a propane company truck arriving at the facility, leading them to believe that Hickman’s was using the ventilation shutdown plus method to euthanize the chickens, Williamson said.

Hickman did not describe the company’s method of euthanasia, but said when birds are depopulated, they are “humanely euthanized.”

“I don’t think anyone who raises animals as part of their living would say they do anything but what is best for the birds,” Hickman said.

Williamson said his group advocates for carbon dioxide gas to be used instead of ventilation shutdown plus, which he said is faster and more humane, as chickens become unconscious very quickly in high concentrations of carbon dioxide, but it can be more expensive.

About two-thirds of chicken depopulation nationwide is done by ventilation shutdown plus and the other third is with carbon dioxide, he said.

headline: Arizona is probably not going to make it easier to buy a house this year. Here's why
fullText:
High hopes that this would be the year Arizona lawmakers find ways to make housing affordable have collapsed like a poorly built roof. 

Instead, as the Legislature heads into what is likely to be its final weeks of work, the prospects for the “Starter Homes Act” are dim. It’s a step back from a year ago, when a similar bill passed the Legislature with bipartisan support, but was vetoed by Gov. Katie Hobbs. 

This year’s version, Senate Bill 1229, hasn’t even been able to clear the full Legislature. While the bill passed the Senate, it is stalled in the House. Both sides of the debate say there is still some degree of negotiation, but there’s not much optimism for the most wide-ranging housing legislation of 2025. 

The key hang-up, as it was in past years, revolves around zoning.

Supporters of the bill say the control that local zoning ordinances exact on home construction is the biggest obstacle to building smaller homes. They want a state law that would supersede local rules and allow smaller homes on smaller lots, arguing that will drive down prices.

“We should support people, not cities,” said Sen. Shawnna Bolick, a Phoenix Republican and the sponsor of the “Arizona Starter Homes Act.”

The bill would bar cities from imposing minimum lot sizes in order to allow denser home construction. It also would prevent cities from requiring certain design standards, such as garages or screening walls, which add to the cost of a home. 

Critics, led by local governments statewide, say the bill would remove the community input that zoning allows. Besides, smaller does not necessarily mean “affordable,” they argue, noting there are no definitions or guarantees of what is affordable. 

Nick Ponder, who represents the League of Arizona Cities and Towns, said it's become clear to local officials and neighborhood groups that developers want "a complete deregulation of single-family zoning."

Their proposal, he said, "isn't the camel's nose under the tent; they're setting the tent on fire."

The debate has echoes of another attempted housing solution that died earlier this year. House Bill 2191 would have allowed churches to build housing on excess church property. But the “Yes in God’s Back Yard” bill got a “no” vote that stopped it in its tracks. 

Opponents worried the legislation could crowd housing units into church parking lots in neighborhoods where less-dense housing was the norm. 

Other efforts aimed at easing housing costs have also stalled.  Lawmakers took no action on a bill that proposed a five-year extension of the Low Income Housing Tax Credit, which is set to expire at the end of this year. It is unlikely to get much traction in ongoing budget talks, as lawmakers have signaled state finances are tight.

For her part, Hobbs has pushed for a provision that would ensure that half of new starter homes must be owner-occupied for the first five years. That would keep investors at bay and give Arizona residents a chance at homeownership.

But the governor on May 29 said the prospect of a compromise bill emerging this year is unlikely.

GOP lawmakers also attempted to raid $38 million from the state’s Housing Trust Fund earlier this session to help pay for increased costs in the state's disability services budget. The effort failed as Hobbs balked at taking money from one of her key priorities. She has requested a $15 million increase to bring the fund up to $165 million over two years, but that proposal faces an uncertain fate in budget talks.

Rep. David Livingston, who sponsored the "Yes in God's Back Yard" legislation, said he's already looking to next year for movement on housing, given the faint hopes for the "Starter Homes Act."

He's asked the cities' lobbyists to come up with ideas for 2026.

"We need smaller homes," the Peoria Republican said.

'Give them something they want to buy'

The lack of movement on an issue that voters have repeatedly said is a key concern has frustrated people who argue that housing prices statewide are out of reach for first-time homebuyers. 

The debate has spawned unlikely coalitions, with the libertarian-leaning Americans for Prosperity aligning with progressive Democrats to push for zoning restrictions while grassroots conservatives have sided with cities to defend the protections that zoning allows.

Rep. Cesar Aguilar, D-Phoenix, said he can’t afford to buy in the Arcadia neighborhood where he grew up. A proponent of the Starter Homes Act, he said young people don’t need all the extras that local zoning laws require, and that the bill seeks to preclude. 

“Give them something they want to buy,” he said of first-time buyers.  Many young people would be happy with a two-bedroom home with no garage, Aguilar said. 

Sen. Analise Ortiz, a Phoenix Democrat who is arguably the most passionate advocate for the legislation, said the bill opens up options that aren’t available today. Current zoning laws don’t permit the 3,000 square-foot lots that the bill proposes. Most stand-alone single family homes are on 6,000 square-foot lots. 

She dismissed critics who say this could ruin existing neighborhoods. The bill limits the denser development to vacant parcels of five acres or more that are already zoned for single family construction.

In Tempe, there are no such lots, she said, citing research done by bill proponents. In Phoenix, there are a few such properties. But most of the vacant lots are on the outskirts of the urban area, in the southeast, southwest and northwest Valley, the research shows. 

“This is about single family homes and the American Dream of home ownership,” Ortiz said. That’s a dream she wants for herself: She’s a renter, living in a 1,300 square foot home and sharing a $2,1000 monthly bill with her partner.  

The high rental price makes it impossible to save enough for a down payment in the current market, leaving her stuck, she said. 

“No opportunity to gain equity like previous generations,” she said in a text message.  

The “Starter Homes Act” would allow people to get into a starter home, build equity and move up the economic ladder, much as previous generations have done, argued Bolick, the bill's sponsor.

In the current market, that's nearly impossible, she said, noting Arizonans rate housing affordability as their top concern.

She was in her mid-20s when she first bought a home, she said in a hearing earlier this year. Today, the average first-time home buyer is 38 years old, she said. 

Bolick's support for the bill drew a censure from the Republicans in her north Phoenix district. They also censured her seatmate, Rep. Justin Wilmeth, R-Phoenix. 

The censures follow a resolution from the Maricopa County Republican Committee’s board urging lawmakers to vote against the “Starter Homes Act.”

The committee members wrote they would oppose “all bills that preempt local city government planning and zoning, strip cities of their sovereignty to govern at the local level, and silence the voice of 'We the People' in our communities."

News alerts in your inbox: Don't miss the important news of the day. Sign up for azcentral newsletter alerts to be in the know.

Opponents cite local control, fear of 'shanty towns'

The resolution highlighted the odd political alignment on the legislation. There is no party line on this matter: Republicans and Democrats alike are lining up both for and against the legislation. 

Rep. Jeff Weninger, R-Chandler and a former city councilman, announced his opposition to the bill in April. 

“I believe in both private property rights and local control,” he wrote on social media. “This tilts too much against local control of zoning and the voters having their say in the general plan.” 

State law requires cities to develop general plans to guide development and then present the plan to the public for approval every 10 years. 

Sen. Jake Hoffman, R-Queen Creek, said the bill stacks up too many limits on local control. 

By preempting local zoning, limiting design standards and barring the creation of a homeowners’ association to govern and protect homes, the bill would open the door to construction that may look good today, but could turn into “shanty towns” with time, he said. 

Online videos of tiny homes in the San Antonio, Texas suburbs also amped up concerns in some corners about what the legislation could lead to: Cookie cutter homes with only one entrance, ladders instead of staircases and cramped rooms. 

But where some see gloom, others see a potential solution to an affordable housing crisis that has hit cities nationwide.

The divided reactions reflect the stalemate in legislative action.

Wilmeth, who supports the Starter Homes Act, said the tiny home portrayals may have spurred some opposition to the bill.

“That’s not a home —  that’s a closet," he said of one prototype.

But, he added, if people want to buy a very small home, why would he want to stop them?
