headline: Offense lets Vanderbilt baseball down, with regional elimination game vs Wright State next
fullText:
No. 1 overall seed Vanderbilt baseball lost to Louisville 3-2 on May 31 amid a hapless offensive performance and will drop to the losers bracket in the NCAA Nashville Regional at Hawkins Field.

Like in the opener against Wright State, the Commodores did very little offensively. Their first run scored on a wild pitch, and the second scored after a sequence of two errors. They had just five hits, all of them singles.

Cody Bowker pitched relatively well but took the loss as he gave up all three Louisville runs. Levi Huesman and Connor Fennell held the Cardinals in check through the middle and late innings.

In the bottom of the ninth, Colin Barczi was hit by a pitch and RJ Hamilton came in to pinch-run. But Jonathan Vastine and Jacob Humphrey promptly struck out. Mike Mancini singled to put runners at the corners but Rustan Rigdon grounded into a force-out to end the game.

Louisville advances directly to the June 1 regional final at 8 p.m. CT, while Vanderbilt will face an elimination game against Wright State at 2 p.m. (ESPN2). Should the Commodores win that game, they would have to defeat the Cardinals twice to advance to the super regionals.

Cody Bowker pitches well but leaves trailing

Bowker gave up a solo home run to Matt Klein in the first inning but settled in after that. He allowed one single in the second inning and hit a batter in the fourth, but that batter was erased by a strike-em-out, throw-em-out double play.

Zion Rose homered to lead off the fifth inning and Tague Davis doubled, later scoring on an error.

Bowker was pulled with one out in the sixth inning. He finished with 5⅓ innings pitched, three runs allowed (two earned), no walks and six strikeouts.

Vanderbilt turns to Connor Fennell

Vanderbilt, trailing by one, turned to Fennell in the seventh inning. He has started games this season, including throwing a shutout against Ole Miss, but he also has frequently piggybacked with Bowker. However, the usage of Fennell leaves the Commodores with just one more available starter for the remainder of the regional, Austin Nye.

Vanderbilt's offense struggles

Vanderbilt got little going the first time through the order, including stranding a runner at third with one out in the bottom of the first. It finally got on the board in the third inning as Mancini walked, went to second on a wild pitch and scored on another wild pitch.

Vanderbilt manufactured another run in the fifth inning when two errors by Louisville allowed a run to score.

In the sixth inning, the Commodores couldn't score despite getting runners on second and third with nobody out.

headline: Why Dale Earnhardt Jr. was proud of Nashville Xfinity winner Justin Allgaier
fullText:
LEBANON — Dale Earnhardt Jr. spent May 31 in victory lane, a day before returning to the Amazon Prime Video broadcast booth for the NASCAR Cup Cracker Barrel 400 at Nashville Superspeedway.

The former Cup Series driver and current owner of JR Motorsports joined his driver Justin Allgaier, who won the Xfinity Series Tennessee Lottery 250. Making the moment even more enjoyable for Earnhardt was that Allgaier passed another JR Motorsports driver, Connor Zilisch, for the win. Zilisch finished second.

"This is a great racetrack for Justin. He always runs good here," Earnhardt said. "Jim Pohlman (Allgaier's crew chief) puts a really great race car on every single racetrack we go to for Justin. Justin's coming off an (Xfinity Series) championship. He's chased that for so many years and I feel like now that he has that out of the way, his race craft is as good as it's ever been."

It was the third win this season for Allgaier, who won back-to-back at Las Vegas and Miami in March, and he is coming off a fourth-place finish last week at Charlotte.

Allgaier has 10 top-5 finishes this season.

Zilisch took the lead on Lap 123. After pole setter William Sawalich spun out, Allgaier passed Zilisch on the restart on Lap 141 and stayed in the lead the rest of the way.

Allgaier was joined in his No. 7 Chevrolet to victory lane for the first time by his daughters, Harper and Willow.

Earnhardt said Allgaier's ability to stay calm through races like the Tennessee Lottery 250 has been the key to his success.

"He makes way, way less mistakes (than earlier in his career)," Earnhardt said. "He's put great races together. He's really dangerous for the rest of the competition at this point, I think, in his career."

Allgaier said winning the championship changed the perspective on his career.

"I always thought I was pretty calm," he said. "But winning the championship for me was an incredible eye-opening moment. That changed my mentality for how these races go. I used to think it's got to be the perfect night (to win).

"We sort of had that tonight. But five years ago I probably would have driven myself into the fence trying to get back to the clean air. I would have maybe made a mistake on one of those restarts, put myself in a really bad position and wrecked myself or somebody else."

Zilisch, 18, made his Cup debut in the 2025 Daytona 500. He won the Xfinity race at the Circuit of the Americas two weeks later and finished second last week at Charlotte.

"Zilisch was just really strong (on May 31)," Earnhardt said. "He's still got a lot to gain and grow and understand and he's already pushing Justin for a win tonight. As he continues to develop, he's going to be sensational."

JR Motosports' other three entries also ran well, with Ross Chastain finishing fifth, Carson Kvapil ninth and Sammy Smith 10th.

Dale Earnhardt Jr. looks forward to second Amazon Prime NASCAR Cup race broadcast

Earnhardt was happy with the first Amazon Prime Video broadcast for the Coca-Cola 600 at Charlotte. It exceeded his expectations, which were high.

"That was a fun race. The 600 has been one of the best races. A lot of people say it might be the best race in the series," Earnhardt said. "So we had a really good race to kick off our coverage. We have a lot of flexibilities on a streaming platform that allow us to do things a little differently the networks don't have. We were in a position to succeed and I'm glad people enjoyed what they saw."

The pressure is now on for Earnhardt and the rest of the Amazon crew, which includes Carl Edwards, Adam Alexander, Steve Letarte, Trevor Bayne and Kim Coon, to produce another strong broadcast.

"We have an incredible team of people, some that I've known very briefly, some that I've known for years," Earnhardt said. "It's weird, it's like a race team with that same competitive spirit, the same want-to, the get-up-and-go, the hustle. All of that is present in the TV compound just like it is in a race shop or garage."

headline: What Dale Earnhardt Jr. said about NASCAR career, celebrating wins with daughters
fullText:
LEBANON — Dale Earnhardt Jr. might not be done racing in NASCAR — at least in the Xfinity Series.

Earnhardt, who will be part of the Amazon Prime broadcast team on June 1 for the Cracker Barrel 400, said he may drive at least a couple more Xfinity race before he completely ends his NASCAR racing career.

"I might not be done Xfinity cars just yet," Earnhardt said. "I only got a couple left in me, if any."

Earnhardt, 50, retired as a full-time NASCAR driver in 2017, but he has raced at least once in the Xfinity Series every year since.

Earnhardt's race team, JR Motorsports, had drivers finish first and second on May 31 at the Tennessee Lottery 250 at Nashville Superspeedway. Earnhardt said he was home in North Carolina in the morning before the race to attend his daughters' dance recital, then flew to Middle Tennessee.

There, his winning driver, Justin Allgaier, celebrated the Nashville win by putting his own daughters, Harper and Willow, in the winning car after the race and driving them to victory lane.

"It's kind of this new trend where drivers are encouraged to have their kids be a part of that front stretch interview (after winning)," Earnhardt said. "It's a great moment, it really is if you are a father.

"It's touching and emotional."

headline: How is Nashville real estate doing? Steady rates, rising prices make their mark
fullText:
Last week, Greater Nashville Realtors hosted its annual economic summit, Nashonomics, bringing together business leaders, economists and real estate professionals to discuss the latest trends shaping our region’s housing market and economic landscape.

Laurel Graefe, regional executive of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s Nashville Branch, provided a timely update on interest rates. As of this week, the national average for a 30-year mortgage has remained below 7% for the 17th consecutive week. While that stability is welcome, Graefe noted that elevated rates — combined with rising home prices — continue to pose affordability challenges, especially for first-time buyers and middle-income households.

Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist and vice president of research at the National Association of Realtors, shared an in-depth look at housing affordability across the region. With the median sales price now hovering around $500,000, she pointed out a growing generational gap in homeownership. Today, the median age of a first-time buyer is 38 — up from 28 just four decades ago — while baby boomers accounted for 42% of all home purchases between July 2023 and June 2024.

On the broader economic front, Jeff Hite, chief economic development officer at the Nashville Area Chamber of Commerce, emphasized that while Nashville’s economy remains strong, it trails peer cities like Charlotte, North Carolina, Austin, and Atlanta in some key indicators. Hite focuses on four primary metrics to assess economic health: job growth, population growth, GDP growth, and cost of living. Nashville’s cost-of-living index sits just below the national average at 98.7, but lags behind cities like Charlotte (91.2) and Tampa, Florida, (97.6), indicating some room for improvement in regional affordability and competitiveness.

Despite these challenges, the outlook for Greater Nashville remains optimistic. Job growth, population expansion, and sustained housing demand continue to position our region for long-term success. However, to meet that future head-on, ongoing collaboration is essential.

As realtors, we play a critical role in shaping the housing conversation and driving solutions forward. That’s why our association is committed to working closely with local leaders — like Mayor Freddie O’Connell and Metro government — on initiatives such as the new Unified Housing Strategy. And next week, we’ll take our advocacy to the national level during the Realtors Legislative Meetings in Washington, D.C., where we’ll join colleagues from across the country to champion real estate policies that support homeownership, fair housing, and vibrant communities nationwide.

When Realtors are at the table, we help turn insight into action — and ensure that our region continues to thrive for years to come.

headline: New York to Franklin: charity's $1B mission to solve global water crisis comes to life
fullText:
Scott Harrison was a promoter at a night club for 10 years before he took a volunteer trip that changed his life. He spent several weeks at a hospital ship stationed off the coast of Liberia and saw hundreds of people who were battling illnesses due to consuming unsafe water, he said.

After he returned to New York City, he decided to do something about it. Nineteen years later, charity: water has raised $1 billion and funded over 186,000 water projects in 29 countries, organizers say.

The nonprofit's latest project, a free, permanent exhibit at The Factory at Franklin takes visitors through the lives of those who don't have access to clean water through the use of virtual reality and other hands-on activities.

“It's so hard to get people to focus on a problem that they've never experienced,” said Harrison, who now lives in Williamson County. “ You've never experienced it because of the privilege you were born into. But 10% of the world has never known what you know, which is clean water. It's a completely solvable problem down to the last person.”

Across the globe, more than 703 billion people do not have access to clean drinking water, the charity estimates, noting that as a last resort, many consume water from swamps, ponds, streams and rivers that are contaminated with bacteria

“It's impossible to have health without clean water,” Harrison said. “I think there's a terrible irony, and sadness, when you realize how easy the problem is to solve. You have thousands of people living on top of the resource, which is only 150 feet beneath them."

charity: water uses pumps to access that water and provide it to communities.

From materials to paying for local labor, each water pump costs about $10,000 to be installed in a community, officials estimate.

"The issue is they don’t have $10,000 to tap into that resource, and as a result, they are dying,” Harrison said. The search for clean water has taken the charity from Nepal to Niger and everywhere in between.

When they find a community in need, the nonprofit connects with local partners to fund water, sanitation and hygiene programs. 

The Franklin exhibit is the next phase in the charity's fundraising efforts. The immersive space, called the Experience Lab, shows visitors what a lack of clean water does to a community. It follows a Ugandan family, highlighting the issues they face without water and how their lives drastically change when they are able to receive it.

“In a way, this is a bid for attention,” Harrison said. “We are asking people to give an hour of their time to go through an experience to learn about an issue that faces 10% of the world. We want people to know how their lives would be drastically different.”

From VR headsets that transport visitors to communities halfway around the world to a 4D room where they carry jugs as they walk on a treadmill in 90-degree weather and a working water spout, the exhibit uses real life experience as a teaching tool.

"I doubt people are going to come to Franklin solely for this, but having a location in a place like the Factory, where there is so much traffic, hopefully we can get more interest in lending a helping hand," Harrison said.

And efforts are already paying off.

An 11-year-old who originally came in as workers were finalizing plans was recently celebrated for a large donation.

“He took one of the piggy banks we gave to kids and came back weeks later with $10,000,” Experience Lab Director Brian Seay said of the boy.  "We've been a little overwhelmed but pleasantly surprised by how much we've resonated with people and families here."

Not only are 100% of the charity's public donations sent directly to water projects, an interactive map shows people where it goes down to the geotag location. 

“We believe that when people truly understand the need for clean water around the world, they’ll be inspired to engage,” Harrison said. “In today's world, with so much competition for attention, we're making a bet on in-real-life experiences. The Experience Lab is more than an exhibition, it’s a call to action.”

The exhibit is on the second floor of the Factory at Franklin.

While it is free to attend, reservations are required. Hours are noon-5 p.m. on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. More information can be found at www.charitywater.org/experience.

headline: Hundreds of performances over 10 days in June: How we cover CMA Fest and Bonnaroo
fullText:
Never is Nashville's Music City moniker more on display than in June.

By day, tunes blare from the city's sun-splashed honky-tonk district while families and fans gather on blankets in Centennial Park for the annual Musicians Corner music series. By night, music pours out of venues as large as the Ascend and First Bank amphitheaters and as small as the patio stage at any given neighborhood bar. (For more on this, check out music writer Melonee Hurt's guide to outdoor music).

But during the 10 days beginning on June 5, the volume gets turned up with the arrival of two massive music festivals: CMA Fest from June 5-8 and Bonnaroo from June 12-15. Together, the events are expected to bring more than 150,000 people from all over the world to Middle Tennessee to see hundreds of bands and performers from virtually every musical genre.

Covering these events is no easy feat, and it requires a newsroom-wide effort. CMA Fest is one of Nashville's signature events and, with music throughout the day on several free stages, even The Tennessean's award-winning five-person music team needs help. Reporters from other beats jump into the fray, patrolling Lower Broadway and surrounds for news alongside hordes of sunburnt, cowboy-booted tourists. In addition to covering the music, the team must monitor the weather, potential medical and crime issues and all that comes with adding tens of thousands of people to a neighborhood that is bustling on its quietest days.

In the evenings, the action moves across the Cumberland to Nissan Stadium, where country music's biggest names hit the stage in four consecutive nights. We'll have journalists in a box, writing in real time high above the crowd; deep in the belly of the stadium, interviewing stars moments before they take the stage and, of course, in the pit at the front of the stage capturing images to add to The Tennessean's extensive photographic archives.

In nearly a decade covering the festival, moments that standout for me include Miranda Lambert's 2016 cover of Little Feat's classic "Willin,'" the 2019 collaboration between Lil Nas X, Billy Ray Cyrus and Keith Urban on the viral hit of that year "Old Town Road" and Jelly Roll's emotional 2023 performance from a stage on the 50-yard line at Nissan, a stone's throw from the detention center where his younger self had been incarcerated.

Covering Bonnaroo is even more of a logistical challenge. Our team of as many as 10 reporters, photographers and editors spend four days on 'The Farm" in usually quiet Manchester, which, for the duration of the festival, becomes one of Tennessee's most populous cities. Some sleep in a large RV that doubles as an office during daylight hours. Others camp. In either case, Bonnaroo is a grueling assignment. It's hot, either muddy or dusty (pick your poison) and the media camping area seems to always be adjacent to the endless thumping of the EDM tent, making ear plugs a must.

Still, I've never had a shortage of staffers volunteering to make the trek. As with CMA Fest, our coverage goes beyond the music to include public safety issues, human interest features and economic impact analysis. But also like CMA Fest, the music is center stage. Personal favorites over the years have included U2's 2017 performance of the album "The Joshua Tree," the antics of artist Chance the Rapper that same year and watching from side stage in 2019 as John Prine performed an epic version of his summertime standard "Lake Marie."

Over the course of 10 days, The Tennessean will publish scores of articles, photo galleries and videos, giving our audience a front-row seat to the festivities. The content is always popular with fans who were unable to make it to their preferred festival or those wishing to relive the experience.

This editor is just glad they no longer take place during the same week.

headline: CMA Fest showcases surge in country music's popularity fueled by social media, streaming
fullText:
Nearly one million people have been drawn to downtown Nashville for a weekend in June each year for the past decade, as the Country Music Association Fest has evolved into a major event.

CMA Fest's popularity has surged alongside the rise of online music streaming. Emerging artists with large streaming audiences are propelled onto CMA Fest stages.

This year, the event takes place from June 5 to 8. Headliners include Jason Aldean, Luke Bryan, Dierks Bentley, Brooks & Dunn, Rascal Flatts, Darius Rucker and Keith Urban.

Over the past three years, country music has transformed from what Country Music Association CEO Sarah Trahern describes as an expanding "biggest tent" of a musical genre into an epicenter of emerging popular culture, particularly evident at events like CMA Fest.

👉 Don't miss out! Your guide to must-see events and concerts at CMA Fest 2025

Music streaming platforms gained dominance during the COVID-19 pandemic, as artists found vast audiences on social media. Interest in these artists peaked at major festivals like CMA Fest, where fans could finally gather en masse and engage with them in real time.

"Long-lasting careers and supercharged success can exist (simultaneously). Social media and streaming's growth has caused the music industry overall to evolve (to a place where) both of these types of artists are relevant," said Warner Music Vice President of Digital Marketing Brooke Hardesty. "In country, where the genre has existed for 100 years, we have 50 years of both kinds of artists — that makes things more exciting than ever."

According to surveys after the 2024 CMA Fest, the Country Music Association found that 82% of attendees use streaming services to discover new artists.

Festival events that have helped launch artists' careers include pre-planned moments that sometimes exceed expectations, such as breakout stars Lil Nas X or Post Malone performing at Ole Red's Spotify House installation, or massive crowds drawn to free CMA Fest stages to see Shaboozey and Tucker Wetmore near Bridgestone Arena and the Hard Rock Cafe.

Performers like Gabby Barrett, Jelly Roll and Bailey Zimmerman quickly achieved pinnacle stage recognition at Nissan Stadium after attaining breakout success.

Ultimately, the power of social media and streaming platforms' increasing grip on the music industry and its fans is showcased from digital screens to Nashville stages.

From the archives: Take a look back at decades of iconic performances from CMA Fest, Fan Fair

'Beatlemania'-level excitement for country's breakout stars on Nashville's streets

Streaming platforms and the country music industry have formed a strong partnership, significantly influencing the American music scene.

Streaming platform plays earned nearly nine out of every ten dollars in the music industry, according to 2024 Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) data. One-fifth of 2024 gold and platinum-selling albums and singles claimed Music City roots in 2024, the data shows.

Sometimes, watching popular acts on social media and streaming at festivals like CMA Fest is reminiscent of the first time The Beatles hit America's shores.

Shaboozey's "A Bar Song (Tipsy)" saw the performer gain a 1,600% increase his monthly listenership. When he performed at CMA Fest, during a daytime set, the rush of fans to Bridgestone Arena forced the gates to be closed. "There hasn’t been anyone else this big on this stage (before)," a Metropolitan Nashville Police Department officer told a Tennessean reporter.

One day later, with his songs "Wine Into Whiskey" and "Wind Up Missin' You" only massive on social media and streaming platforms, Tucker Wetmore, like Shaboozey, drew over 5,000 fans to a stage outside Lower Broadway's Hard Rock Cafe.

Emily Cohen Belote has been a curator at Amazon Music for eight years and currently serves as the platform's principal curator for country music.

She has seen at least two dozen artists break out on playlists including Country Heat, and Americana and rootsy pop-leaning "Bonfire" over the past five years.

They include 2025 Amazon Breakthrough program artist Dasha, Breland, Ella Langley, Megan Moroney, Jelly Roll and the previously mentioned Wetmore and Zimmerman. Between 2023 and 2025, all six acts suddenly emerged as star talent, based mainly on social and streaming interest, and who performed at Nissan Stadium during CMA Fest.

Our favorite pictures: A look back at Fan Fair and CMA Music Fest through the years

"These are artists who have a great work ethic are unquestionably self-aware and (savvy) at building a culture around their point of view on social media. Plus, their music is excellent and reflects who they appear to be online (and in real-time)," Belote said.

After the COVID-19 pandemic, social media and streaming platforms initially boosted interest in music, she said. Platforms like Amazon Music can now adopt strategies that stand out, as access to audiences is more democratized and visibility has increased.

"Once those factors blend with these artists having their reach grow, then having more music people want to listen to and engage with equates to popularity everywhere, from festivals to radio and more," Belote said. "We can't do everything to support an artist, but with their lead, we can amplify their vision."

Social media, streaming create stars faster than radio

Since 2019, there has been a more than 700% jump in monthly American streams for country music, according to Spotify data.

Lil Nas X's “Old Town Road” earned nearly 25% more streams than Drake’s then-year-old single-week song streaming record for “In My Feelings” in 2019.

Two months later, Lil Nas X and Billy Ray Cyrus performed the hit song on the Ole Red rooftop as part of the pop-up Spotify House at CMA Fest. The Tennessean described "a sea of cell phone cameras and shouts of "can't nobody tell me nothing" during their performance.

Like Lil Nas X and Billy Ray Cyrus, Post Malone and his "Pour Me A Drink" partner, Blake Shelton, performed at Ole Red in 2024.

It's become a trend.

Spotify Country editor Claire Heinichen said the accessibility and round-the-clock online news cycle has allowed more artists, like Ella Langley, find fame faster.

"In previous decades, country music moved slower as a whole, relying on traditional album release cycles and working singles to radio for a long period of time. Albums and radio are still important to the genre, of course, but social media and streaming have allowed artists to feed their fan bases with more music in a much shorter time period," Heinichen said.

"For example, Ella Langley knew she had something special with (her 2024 hit) 'You Look Like You Love Me.' I distinctly remember the day she posted the first video of that talking chorus. That song became an instant hit on streaming, and fans have gobbled up every song she’s put out since."

The incredible two-year journey of Gabby Barrett's 'I Hope'

The interruption to business during the COVID-19 pandemic fundamentally transformed numerous industries, including music.

EMarketer data shows that TikTok usage grew by 20% in the first nine months of the COVID-19 pandemic, during which half of the world's population became social media users. On average, people spent 90 minutes per day scrolling through social media platforms.

Notably, as well, country music’s popularity on streaming services spiked five times greater than the entire music industry during the first nine months of COVID-19 interruptions, according to MRC Data/Nielsen Music.

For acts like American Idol finalist Gabby Barrett, an unprecedented number of eyes and ears were captivated. Barrett's single "I Hope" became the first female-sung song to top Billboard's Country Streaming chart. Six months later, it reached No. 1 on country radio. By November, it was a top-five all-genre Hot 100 pop hit that had sat atop country's sales charts for five months. The song ended 2021 having achieved 5-time platinum-selling status.

But, in 2020 and 2021, CMA Fest was cancelled due to COVID-19 regulations.

By the 2022 return of CMA Fest, Barrett had evolved from a Sunday afternoon free stage performer to an artist spotlighted on Friday night on the big Nissan Stadium stage.

"A song that is real, raw and, years later, stands the test of time, reflected what my fans from social media and absolutely crazy streaming numbers grew to trust about me," Barrett said.

Bailey Zimmerman surges from 'A Rock and a Hard Place' to CMA Fest's biggest stage

In Oct. 2020, then 20-year-old rural Illinois native Bailey Zimmerman was working on a natural gas pipeline and singing rock covers on TikTok to a growing throng of 300,000 followers.

Four years later, Zimmerman released No. 1 country hits like "Fall In Love" and "Rock In A Hard Place," leading to becoming a main stage participant at Nissan Stadium during the 2024 CMA Fest.

Returning to Nissan Stadium in 2025, his success now includes 10 times as many TikTok followers. It represents a new era of artists growing on social media, hitting on streaming and maintaining that impact in real time.

"Bailey's growth from a star in social media's lifted truck sub-culture to an artist capable of being in tune with his fans and himself is nothing short of amazing," Warner Music Nashville Vice President of A&R Rohan Kohli said. "An artist who can rise to the occasion and channel crazy on-stage energy into being an incredibly smart and astute musician, successfully learning how to be comfortable as an artist with a huge following, is rare.

Hardesty added: "Bailey's success at bridging social media, streaming and (well-received) live performances makes him an artist of consequence now capable of reaching far beyond the country industry to reveal many more untapped audiences."

Social and streaming pushing live country engagement creates 'an ideal world'

For the first time in recent memory, this year's headlining performers at CMA Fest on Nissan Stadium's mainstage feature a whopping 40% of artists whose growth can be tied to five years of social media and streaming interest, keying increased fan intrigue.

"In an ideal world, at Nissan Stadium this June, there's a Bailey Zimmerman fan who watches Brooks & Dunn sing 'Neon Moon' and becomes a fan of theirs and a Brooks & Dunn fan who hears Bailey sing 'Rock and A Hard Place' and becomes a fan of his," Hardesty said.

Kohli added: "All of the lanes are open at a time when a rising tide is lifting all boats."

headline: Your guide to CMA Fest 2025: Must-see performances and events
fullText:
CMA Fest 2025 will take over downtown Nashville's Lower Broadway corridor and surrounding areas from June 5 to 8.

Now in its 52nd year, the event has drawn nearly one million revelers to Nashville over the past decade. As 2023 CMA Entertainer of the Year Lainey Wilson sings, "country's cool again."

Artists with over 200 No. 1 singles on country radio in the past 25 years will headline the nighttime activities at Nissan Stadium. During the day, stages like the free one at Riverside Park along the Cumberland River will feature breakout performances from rising country stars.

🎶 Country's cool again: CMA Fest 2025 thrives on social media and streaming buzz

Those attending the ticketed events at Nissan Stadium will enjoy performances from longtime and current superstars like Luke Bryan and Darius Rucker. Those who prefer the free stages on Lower Broadway can catch favorites like Gabby Barrett, Colbie Caillat, Dasha, Brandon Lake, Midland, Megan Moroney, and Tucker Wetmore.

CMA Fest on Nissan Stadium stage draws world's eyes to Nashville

The event at Nissan Stadium is recorded for an annual CMA Fest special that airs at the end of summer on ABC and Hulu.

How popular is this program? Festival organizers emphasize its global reach, which has been crucial in growing the festival to welcome 20 times as many country music fans to the genre's longest-running festival worldwide. This includes thousands of fans from all 50 states and nearly 50 countries.

Notably, 2025 award-winners and country and pop chart-toppers like Jason Aldean, Brooks & Dunn, Riley Green, Cody Johnson, Ella Langley, the Red Clay Strays, Shaboozey, Blake Shelton, Zach Top, Keith Urban, and Bailey Zimmerman will be featured at Nissan Stadium.

Tickets for one or all four nights of the festival and country music's ultimate stage are available via CMAfest.com/tickets.

From the archives: Take a look back at decades of iconic performances from CMA Fest, Fan Fair

Our favorite pictures: A look back at Fan Fair and CMA Music Fest through the years

CMA Fest free stages and other experiences

Free daytime performances and events are key to the CMA Fest experience.

Hundreds of artists perform throughout downtown Nashville on five outdoor stages — no ticket is required. These concerts are free to attend and showcase emerging talent and well-established stars.

In 2024, breakout stars Shaboozey and Tucker Wetmore each attracted crowds of over 5,000 fest attendees to performances in front of Bridgestone Arena and the Hard Rock Cafe.

Also, to mimic what CMA Fest was for three decades before moving to downtown Nashville, the Fan Fair X indoor exhibition offers exclusive artist meet-and-greets, shopping for festival merchandise and various indoor activities at Music City Center.

CMA Fest 2025 performers: Who to watch

  • Riverfront Stage: Georgia native Gavin Adcock is a hard-living countrified rock favorite gaining in streaming renown. Also, Tanner Adell is a streaming-to-real-time favorite, gaining love from everyone from Beyoncé to Shaquille O'Neal and seemingly every pop cultural touchstone in between.
  • Dr Pepper Amp Stage at Ascend Park: Texas traditionalist Jake Worthington will bring his syrupy drawl to the stage. Many may also know Tiera Kennedy from her performance on Beyoncé's "Cowboy Carter" track "Blackbiird."
  • The Chevy Vibes Stage at Walk of Fame Park: Graham Barham is a singer-songwriter whose track "Oil Money" is a countrified trap-soul song turning heads. Kashus Culpepper also melds Otis Redding's soul with gospel-honed and countrified sounds.
  • The Good Molecules Reverb Stage at Bridgestone Plaza: Willow Avalon and Carter Faith lead a class of female singer-songwriters bringing a blend of vintage aesthetics and modern heartbreak. Chapel Hart also brings a multitude of country music harmony-driven, time-honored traditions to any live performance.
  • The Hard Rock Stage in front of 1st and Broadway's Hard Rock Cafe: Chandler Walters is a singer-songwriter and currently the pedal steel guitarist in Post Malone's live band. He's also co-signed by his Deville Records label boss, Ernest, plus has a classic-rock-meets-traditional-country approach to his music that could gain support quickly.

CMA Fest Ascend Amphitheater events to see

Four decades of Nashville favorites — including Country Music Hall of Famer Wynonna Judd, chart-topping performer Jake Owen, and the renowned Whiskey Jam performance series — will be highlighted during nighttime concerts at the downtown riverfront Ascend Amphitheater during CMA Fest 2025.

From June 5 to 7, three nights of live music will feature CMA joining forces with Whiskey Jam, a “Jake Owen and Friends" show with the "Barefoot Blue Jean Night" vocalist joined by Carter Faith, Max McNown, Lukas Nelson, Wynn Williams, and more.

On Saturday evening, Hall of Famer Judd's “Wynonna Judd’s Girls Night Out” will feature Grand Ole Opry member Sara Evans, award-winning duo The War and Treaty, rising star Madeline Edwards, and Noah Cyrus, among many others.

Tickets start at $17 and are on sale to the public beginning April 18 at 10 a.m. CT. Tickets can be purchased at CMAfest.com/tickets.

headline: From the Archives: CMA Fest memorable performances over 50 years in Nashville
fullText:
Nashville's four-day blitz of boot stompin', honky-tonkin' country music is back again — it's time for one of Music City's biggest events, CMA Fest.

This year, the Country Music Association's festival will take place from June 5-8, bringing over 300 country music artists to multiple stages across Downtown Nashville.

In its 52nd year, CMA Fest has become the prolific fête it is today through decades of memorable performances and events, bringing over 90,000 attendees to Nashville in 2024.

🎶 Country's cool again: CMA Fest 2025 thrives on social media and streaming buzz

CMA Fest memorable moments: From 1972 to 2025

CMA Fest includes four jam-packed days of live music, autograph signings and fan club parties.

At its core, CMA Fest is the ultimate country music fan experience, celebrating the crowds who continue to champion the genre.

The festival began in 1972 as Fan Fair when 5,000 people visited Nashville's Municipal Auditorium to see their favorite artists. Now, it's become the longest-running country music festival in the world.

All of the festival's artists perform for free to support the CMA Foundation, sending a portion of the proceeds to support music education since 2006.

And over the years, CMA Fest has continually solidified its place in Nashville history with some iconic moments.

Back in 1985, a pre-fame Patty Loveless scored a meet-and-greet with Vince Gill. Years later, the "Timber, I'm Falling in Love" singer would become more than just a fan of Gill's; instead, a frequent collaborator.

👉 Don't miss out! Your guide to must-see events and concerts at CMA Fest 2025

In 1988, a power outage caused George Strait and Reba McEntire to sign autographs in the dark for one evening. Reportedly, Strait signed 1,500 autographs during the technical difficulties.

There was the time in 1996, the festival's 25th anniversary, when Garth Brooks signed autographs for 23 hours straight.

After hunkering down in a vacant area near a livestock building, Brooks spent nearly a full day chatting with fans as he posed for pictures — rumor has it he never even took a bathroom break. The day has become country music lore.

Taylor Swift hosted a 13-hour meet-and-greet in 2010 — yes, based on her lucky number, 13.

In 2013, Jason Aldean invited Lenny Kravitz to the stage with him at Nissan Stadium to duet on "American Woman." After leading into a solo set from Kravitz, the audience didn't respond like he hoped, and Kravitz flipped off the crowd.

Back in 2017, Miranda Lambert led a memorable march for her charity, MuttNation. Alongside her own rescue pups, Lambert walked through downtown Nashville with fans and their dogs, advocating for the adoption of shelter pets.

In 2019, Joan Jett surprised the crowd, performing alongside Carrie Underwood at Nissan Stadium and duetting on iconic tracks including “I Hate Myself For Loving You" and “I Love Rock and Roll.”

And at last year's CMA Fest, Dolly Parton announced that a musical based on her life, "Dolly: An Original Musical," would soon be headed to Broadway.

What country music history will be made at CMA Fest in 2025?

You'll just have to show up, boots and all, to see.

Audrey Gibbs is a music journalist at The Tennessean. You can reach her at agibbs@tennessean.com.

headline: Vanderbilt baseball's pitching depth will be tested in regional elimination game vs Wright State
fullText:
Vanderbilt baseball has prided itself on its pitching depth all season.

The Commodores have had tons of options and a deep bullpen. They have the No. 1 strikeout rate in the country, and that doesn't come from just one player. They have pieced innings together from a multitude of pitchers.

But just how far does that pitching depth go? They're about to find out.

Vanderbilt lost to Louisville 3-2 on May 31 to drop to the losers bracket in the Nashville Regional and will face Wright State in an elimination game June 1 (2 p.m. CT, ESPN2).

The pitching wasn't the problem against the Cardinals. It was the offense that put up just five singles and scored its two runs on a wild pitch and an error. Worse still, the Commodores burned their best weapon in Connor Fennell, who pitched the final three innings and didn't allow a run. He has plenty of experience starting games this season and could have been a key piece to a run through the losers bracket.

Instead, No. 1 overall seed Vanderbilt (43-17) will have Austin Nye as its only reliable starting option while also needing to win three games to break a three-year streak of losing in regionals.

"He was the right guy," Vanderbilt coach Tim Corbin said of going to Fennell. "He could keep the game there. We knew that, and we were going to score a run, so there wasn't a doubt in the mind whether or not we were going to score another runner or two, but he was the right guy just to hold the game right where it was, not thinking about Game 3 when playing Game 2, and know we're going to win Game 2, so we'll take care of Game 3 tomorrow."

At the point Fennell went into the game, the Commodores were coming off an inning in which they had gotten runners to second and third with nobody out, still down one run, yet could not score. They also had failed to score a runner from third with one out in the first inning.

But from this point forward, they won't have any pitching options as good as Fennell and Cody Bowker, who started against Louisville and pitched 5⅓ innings, his longest outing in more than two months. He allowed all three runs (two earned) with no walks and six strikeouts.

"We just couldn't get the timely hit," Corbin said. "Little bit of balls hit hard right at them a couple times . . . But when you play that close to the vest, you know it can back up on you. We pitched well. We really did play hard, pitched well, played good defense, ran the bases well.

"But as far as timely hitting, no, they have to give credit to Louisville. They pitch well, and that was the tough part for us."

Vanderbilt didn't tip its hand as to who would start against Wright State (39-20). Nye is an option; so could some who have pitched in multi-inning relief this season, like Brennan Seiber and Alex Kranzler.

In 2022, when the Commodores were in a similar situation, they turned to Nick Maldonado to start an elimination game while holding back then-freshman Devin Futrell for the nightcap against Oregon State. Nye could be the pitcher in Futrell's situation this time, but Vanderbilt already almost lost to Wright State once.

Regardless of the configuration, pitchers who have been relatively low on the depth chart will have to step up if Vanderbilt hopes to advance. Pitching depth has been the strength all season; now that pitching depth will have to keep the season alive.

Aria Gerson covers Vanderbilt athletics for The Tennessean. Contact her at agerson@gannett.com or on X @aria_gerson.

headline: Tim McGraw closes Music City Rodeo with timeless hits at Bridgestone Arena
fullText:
Tim McGraw closed out the inaugural edition of Nashville's Music City Rodeo with a 90-minute set showcasing the country superstar's time-tested brand of country rock, power ballads and more than three decades of hits.

The "I Like It, I Love It," vocalist, now 58, was charming, gracious and, to borrow a quote from one of his three-dozen crossover hits, "Humble and Kind" onstage at downtown's Bridgestone Arena. His live set felt like a celebration of his 35-year Nashville legacy, chosen and served like a delightful, metaphorical smorgasbord of powerful emotions.

"We're going to be here every year as long as you keep coming out," McGraw said, in a nod to the well-attended three-day event becoming a Music City staple.

'King Rodeo'

The seller of 50 million-plus albums performed a set that was light on songs from his 2023-released 17th studio album "Standing Room Only." However, he did perform "King Rodeo," a song from a yet-to-be officially announced album, on which he's currently working.

McGraw collaborated on the Music City Rodeo with Bryan Kaplan, co-founder and chief strategy officer of his Down Home social media development venture, and Nashville-based commercial real estate developer Patrick Humes. Down Home is also developing a May 2024 greenlit scripted Netflix rodeo drama series that, according to a press statement, "follows a legendary bull-riding champion facing a life-altering crossroads upon the arrival of a fearless young rider, whose presence challenges his ways and uncovers a sinister underbelly in the sport."

"King Rodeo," a piano ballad straight from the Billy Joel and Lionel Richie school of adult contemporary splendor, feels like a title track for the forthcoming project.

McGraw and The Dancehall Doctors deliver rocking country anthems

In this chapter of his career, McGraw's set marries together rock guitars, stunning arrangements and earnest songwriting.

"I Like It, I Love It" turns 30 next month, and its jazzy honky-tonk piano and swinging rhythms still hold the weight of rock guitars and foot-stomping sing-alongs.

The same can be said for "Southern Voice," a gold-selling country chart-topper 15 years older than the previously mentioned classic. Live, the rootsy rocker benefits from McGraw and his live band forming at the front of the stage in a manner mimicking legendary Southern rockers Lynyrd Skynyrd.

In a throwback to when his daughters were aged 6, 9, and 11, he brought out Gracie, Maggie, and Audrey McGraw (along with the track's producer, Byron Gallimore's daughters, Sophia, Ella Rose and Evangeline Gallimore) to perform the final chorus on 2007's "Last Dollar (Fly Away)." As the trio now sings in an entirely different key than the two-decade-old backing track, the singer poignantly smiled and joked, "they're not as young as they used to be."

For 2002's "Real Good Man," McGraw's band The Dancehall Doctors hammered into a groove that, along with McGraw's tenor, worked the crowd into a frenzy.

'Live Like You Were Dying'

With McGraw, however, one comes for the rock, but stays for the pop ballads.

The night opened with the crooner self-effacingly calling himself "Tim, better known as Faith's husband" and ended with “The Cowboy in Me,” “Humble and Kind," “Where the Green Grass Grows" and “Live Like You Were Dying."

Few stylists in any genre embody McGraw's ability to excel as both the lead vocalist of a song and the lead character in the cinematic imagery that the song aims to evoke.

"Live Like You're Dying" is linked to his Major League Baseball star pitcher father, Tug McGraw, who was hospitalized with a brain tumor on March 12, 2003, and died nine months later. McGraw's voice and the song's arrangement are driven by the power of the moment, allowing fans to find their own story in the anthem.

It made sense as a closer to the 2025 Music City Rodeo because, it's a song about drawing friends close, staying in the moment and making a memory defined by time spent together.

headline: Tennessee gave out $1.5B in tax refunds to corporations: Here's who benefitted
fullText:
The Tennessee Department of Revenue released a list of every company receiving a franchise tax refund on May 31. The state of Tennessee is paying out a total of $1.5 billion in refunds to more than 58,000 entities, many of which are subsidiaries of larger companies, as approved by state lawmakers in 2024.

Some of the biggest businesses in Tennessee benefited, including Nissan, Dollar General, and Amazon. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee's 81-year-old family business, Lee Company, also received a significant refund.

Lee championed the plan for refunds, and it was the largest new item in his 2024 budget.

The deal restructured how the state charges franchise taxes and allowed companies that paid franchise taxes based on their property taxes over the last three years to receive a refund.

Approximately 81% of the estimated 100,000 businesses determined eligible for refunds are located in Tennessee. However, the revenue department estimated that 53% of refund dollars were headed out of state, according to documents The Tennessean obtained last year through a records request.

15 notable recipients of massive refunds

The Department of Revenue's list is broken down based on the size of the refund. The category with the most significant amount is "greater than $10,000." It does not specify the exact value received by each company. Still, the advocacy group Tennessee for All estimated that the average refund for the "over $10,000" group could be as high as $75,000.

Here are some of the most prominent companies that received refunds of over $10,000:

  • Nissan
  • Tesla
  • Nike
  • Dollar General
  • Fujifilm
  • Vanderbilt University
  • Amazon
  • Autozone
  • Hankook
  • Tractor Supply Company
  • FedEx
  • Lee Company
  • International Paper Company
  • Papa John's
  • Pilot Flying J

For the full list of businesses that received refunds, visit the Tennessee Department of Revenue. The list will only be publicly available on the Department of Revenue's website for one month.

Why Republicans said the refunds were necessary

Republican lawmakers said in 2024 that legal issues made the $1.5 billion in refunds unavoidable, though no state agency has publicly provided evidence of a legal threat.

Senate Finance Chairman Bo Watson, R-Hixson, defended the action, saying it helped the state avoid a lawsuit that would have cost the state more money than the refunds will.

“Because of the way we've managed the budget over the past 15 years, we could take on a really significant financial hit,” Watson said to reporters earlier this year.

He was among 17 senators who disclosed a personal interest in the bill.

“The most important thing is that we were able to mitigate hundreds of millions of dollars in legal fees,” Senate Republican Caucus Chair Ken Yager, R-Kingston, previously told The Tennessean. “There were going to be hundreds of attorneys involved in this. It’s in the best interest of the state to do this.” 

Democrats respond: 'This is the real cost of trickle-down economics'

Critics of the refunds said the plan is an example of lawmakers prioritizing corporations over individual Tennesseans.

"Corporate tax collections have cratered, and Tennessee families are still paying sky-high grocery taxes, while our schools, roads, and healthcare remain among the worst funded in the nation," Sen. Heidi Campbell, D-Nashville, said in a statement. "This is the real cost of trickle-down economics: corporate handouts while working families get left behind. It’s fiscally irresponsible and morally indefensible."

Tennessee House Democrats said the legal threats Lee and the GOP leveraged to pass the bill were based on the "dormant commerce clause," which implies from the U.S. Constitution that states may not unduly burden interstate commerce.

“As I travel the state, the most common question I’m asked is, ‘Where has all our money gone?’” Rep. John Ray Clemmons, D-Nashville, said in a statement. “The sad reality is that working families’ hard-earned money is being enjoyed in boardrooms around the world rather than in living rooms across Tennessee.”

Vivian Jones contributed reporting to this story. She covers state government and politics for The Tennessean. Reach her atvjones@tennessean.com.

headline: Tennessee zebra on the loose: Pet escapes, shuts down Rutherford County interstate traffic
fullText:
A Rutherford County resident's pet zebra broke free on Saturday, May 31, and made its way to the interstate — causing an afternoon of chaos before escaping into the woods.

Drivers took to social media to report narrowly dodging the animal as it was weaving in and out of traffic. Rutherford County Sheriff's deputies quickly closed a section of I-24 eastbound and westbound in Christiana, but they were unable to capture the zebra.

Corporal Zach Campbell met with the owners of the zebra, who said they obtained the animal less than 24 hours before it fled their property.

On Sunday morning, the sheriff's office reported that the zebra had still not been caught. Other official social media pages, including the Rutherford County EMA, continued to update the situation into the afternoon.

The zebra was last spotted heading into the wooded area between Joe B. Jackson Parkway and the Epps Mill Road exit late Saturday afternoon, according to the Rutherford County Sheriff's Office. Some reports Saturday evening falsely stated that the animal had been captured.

"Initial reports stating the zebra was contained were mistaken," Rutherford County Commissioner Jonathan Beverly said in a statement.

Can zebras be pets in Tennessee?

While the Library of Congress says zebras’ "unpredictable nature and tendency to attack preclude them from being good candidates for domestication," it is legal to own one in Tennessee.

Tennessee categorizes zebras as Class III animals— along with llamas, camels, and giraffes — which means they do not require any special permits or paperwork to be kept as pets.

Found the zebra? Call the sheriff

The Rutherford County Sheriff's Office asks anyone who spots the zebra to call 615-898-7770 and report the location.

Individuals should not approach the zebra if found, officials said.

headline: Two people killed in Maury County shooting; Columbia police charge suspect
fullText:
Two people are dead, and a suspect has been charged in a shooting in Maury County.

Around 3 p.m. on May 31, shots rang out on Somerset Lane.

The Columbia Police Department arrived at the scene by 3:07 p.m. to find three people who had sustained gunshot wounds. Officers pronounced John Bidle, 46, dead at the scene, and emergency responders transferred the other two victims to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville for treatment.

Stacie Wright, 51, died later Saturday evening during surgery at VUMC. The third victim's injuries were not life-threatening, according to Columbia Police.

Law enforcement did not release the suspect's name or provide a reason for withholding the information. Still, CPD officials said a 46-year-old male is being charged with two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted first-degree murder.

There may be additional charges for the unnamed suspect, according to a news release.

"Investigators are still processing the scene, conducting interviews, and combing through information. Other charges are likely at the conclusion of this investigation," CPD said in a statement.

headline: Nashville SC's Walker Zimmerman added to U.S. men's national team roster prior to CONCACAF Gold Cup
fullText:
Nashville SC defender Walker Zimmerman has been called up to the United States men's national soccer team's training camp roster ahead of this month's friendly matches against Turkey and Switzerland.

Zimmerman, Nathan Harriel and Paxten Aaronson were added to the roster as injury replacements for Folarin Balogun, DeJuan Jones and Sean Zawadzki. The USMNT is preparing for the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup, which will be held June 14-July 6 in the United States and Canada.

The USMNT faces Turkey on June 7 (2:30 p.m. CT, TNT) in East Hartford, Connecticut and will play Switzerland on June 10 at Geodis Park in Nashville (7 p.m., TNT) in its final send-off match before the Gold Cup.

Zimmerman, 31, has made 44 international appearances and scored three goals for the USMNT. He started three of the team's four matches at the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, and was the captain at the 2024 Paris Olympics as one of the under-23 squad's three overage players.

Injuries have kept Zimmerman on the fringes of the USMNT picture for the past two years. After starting the 2023 Nations League final against Canada, he didn't appear for the senior team again until a pair of friendlies in January 2025 against Venezuela and Costa Rica, his first under national team coach Mauricio Pochettino.

A two-time MLS Defender of the Year with Nashville, Zimmerman has two assists in 10 games (eight starts) in 2025 for NSC, which is in fourth place in the Eastern Conference at 8-4-5 (29 points). He suffered a concussion in an April 5 loss at Charlotte FC and missed nearly two months before returning against Toronto FC on May 24.

MORE: Nashville SC's Walker Zimmerman relished Olympics experience, now has eye on 2026 World Cup

Pochettino must submit his roster, with a minimum of 23 players and a maximum of 26, for the Gold Cup by June 4. The USMNT currently has 27 players in training camp.

The Gold Cup is the last major tournament the U.S. will play in before the 2026 World Cup in the United States, Canada and Mexico. The USMNT will be without key players Christian Pulisic, Weston McKennie, Tim Weah, Antonee Robinson, Yunus Musah and Gio Reyna for the Gold Cup.

headline: Vanderbilt baseball first No. 1 overall seed not to reach NCAA regional final with loss to Wright State
fullText:
Vanderbilt baseball became the first No. 1 overall seed to fail to reach the regional final and the fourth No. 1 seed to be eliminated in regionals with a 5-4 loss to Wright State on June 1 in the NCAA tournament.

Vanderbilt's Austin Nye gave up four runs in the first inning. Vanderbilt's only hit until the ninth inning was a solo home run by Brodie Johnston in the second inning.

Mike Mancini hit a two-run single in the ninth inning to make the score 5-3. Rustan Rigdon hit a ground rule double to score one runner. RJ Austin then flew out to end the game.

The Commodores did draw eight walks and reached on an error.

Vanderbilt (43-18) has been eliminated in regionals four straight seasons, tying the program high under Tim Corbin, and has not advanced to the regional final in any of the last three seasons.

Vanderbilt's Austin Nye has a shaky start

Vanderbilt opted to start Austin Nye, its lone remaining pitcher who has seen significant time in the rotation this season. But Nye wasn't sharp, giving up four runs in the first inning including two home runs.

After that one inning, Nye was pulled from the game and replaced by Alex Kranzler. Kranzler hit as high as 98 mph with his fastball, according to the stadium gun. He largely held Wright State at bay. He allowed one unearned run in his four innings of work, walked one and struck out five.

Miller Green came in for the sixth inning and escaped a jam with the bases loaded and nobody out as he got a strikeout and then induced a double play. Green recorded four strikeouts and did not allow a run in his three innings of work.

Vanderbilt's offense struggles again

Brodie Johnston hit his 15th home run of the season in the second inning, the most single-season home runs for a Vanderbilt player since 2021. But outside of Johnston, the offense largely no-showed the same way it had in the first two games.

Across the three games of the regional, the Commodores recorded just 12 hits, four of which were home runs. Johnston had three of those 12 hits.

Aria Gerson covers Vanderbilt athletics for The Tennessean. Contact her at agerson@gannett.com or on X @aria_gerson.

headline: What a weak and embarrassing end to a strong Vanderbilt baseball season | Estes
fullText:
If you happen to see the Vanderbilt baseball team from the past few weeks, the one that won an epic series in Knoxville, swept through the SEC Tournament and earned the NCAA Tournament’s No. 1 overall seed, please notify someone on campus. People are looking for those Commodores.

Most of them weren’t at the NCAA Regional at Hawkins Field.

Most of the Commodores hitters who did show up in their uniforms to lose two games in three days, ending a strong season in the weakest of fashions, were strangers.

They didn’t just play poorly. They played tight and timid and terrified of the moment. The opposite of this season’s famously clutch performances, these Commodores wanted zero smoke. They wilted in the hazy pressure, and it only got worse as that pressure increased.

A weekend that started alarming, with a close call in a 4-3 comeback victory over Wright State, turned disappointing with a 3-2 loss to Louisville, dropping Vanderbilt into the losers’ bracket. Then it just got embarrassing the next afternoon, with Wright State plating four runs in the first inning and withstanding a late rally to hold on for a 5-4 victory in an elimination game, putting Vanderbilt out of its misery.

And, truly, this was misery for any Vanderbilt fan unfortunate enough to be there to witness it.

The top-seeded Commodores played 27 innings, and they trailed in all but one. Their pitching and defense, for the most part, was solid enough.

But offensively? Haha.

In the opener, the Commodores were no-hit for six innings by a Wright State pitcher, Cam Allen, with an ERA above 5. Against Louisville, they didn’t have an extra-base hit or an RBI. Then, in the saddest of them all, Vanderbilt was silenced by another Raiders pitcher, Griffen Paige, who opened the game with an ERA of 8.90. Paige allowed one hit – ONE! – in eight innings.

For the regional, Vanderbilt batted .132 and didn't get its first hit of the regional with a runner in scoring position until down to its final out in the final game. Prior to that, Vanderbilt started the regional 0-for-14 with runners in scoring position.

Bad luck. Bad at-bats. Bad swings. Bad everything.

Such a thorough humbling for the tournament’s No. 1 overall seed, while stunning, would’ve been even more so if it didn’t continue a rough narrative for the home team.

This NCAA Tournament is no longer the Commodores’ playground. It’s now their house of horrors.

Since losing in the College World Series’ final game in 2021, Vanderbilt has failed to make it out of an opening regional for four consecutive years and counting. Its record in NCAA games the past three years is 2-6 (four losses were at Hawkins Field) and there are losses to Xavier, High Point and Wright State.

Last season’s 0-for-2 showing in an NCAA regional (including that High Point loss) seemed a turning point for a declining Vanderbilt program that appeared to get its act together in 2025.

These Commodores were a good team that had some good moments. Most notably, they regained control of the in-state rivalry against Tennessee, punctuating it with a blowout win over the Vols in the SEC Tournament. The No. 1 seed was a nice, surprise bonus, too.

But in college baseball, none of it means much without success at the end of the season. And that is when Vanderbilt’s baseball program has picked up a habit of shrinking from the challenge.

This was a priceless opportunity to change the narrative by proving otherwise.

Instead, with Vanderbilt's regional embarrassment of 2025, that narrative is stronger than ever. And it's impossible to dispute.

headline: NASCAR Nashville race's Cracker Barrel 400 sold out
fullText:
For the fourth time in five years the NASCAR Cup Series race at Nashville Superspeedway has sold out according to Nashville Superspeedway director of communications Alan George.

The fifth-annual race, the Cracker Barrel 400, reached capacity at 38,000 before the 7 p.m. CT. start. It was the third time in the last four years to race sold out ahead of the start. A sellout was announced during the second stage of the 2024 race after a rain delay.

The 2023 race, formerly known as the Ally 400, sold out a week in advance along with the inaugural race in 2021, which was the first NASCAR Cup race in the Nashville area in 37 years.

The only year the race failed to sell out was in 2022 when attendance was slightly over 30,000.

Fans attending the race have come from all 50 states and 11 countries, according to Nashville Superspeedway officials.

Nashville Superspeedway has 25,000 permanent seats. Temporary grandstands are brought in each year for the NASCAR tripleheader weekend to expand the capacity to 38,000.

Nashville Superspeedway opened in 2001 without a NASCAR Cup race. It closed in 2011 after attendances for NASCAR Xfinity, truck series and IndyCar races steadily declined.

headline: How Vanderbilt baseball's fourth straight season ended in regional for a reason no one expected
fullText:
In past years, there were various reasons that could be blamed for Vanderbilt baseball's postseason failures. NIL, the transfer portal, assistant coaching hires and more came under fire amid the Commodores' regional losses in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

But the 2025 season was perhaps the most shocking of all.

After Vanderbilt made staffing changes in the offseason and was more active in the transfer portal, it seemingly had the exact result the Commodores had hoped for: the No. 1 overall seed, an SEC tournament championship, a home regional.

Instead, the season ended in heartbreak once again as Vanderbilt was eliminated June 1 with a 5-4 loss to Wright State, becoming the first No. 1 overall seed to fail to reach the regional final.

This time the talk turned to the mental side of the game, the pressure that came with being No. 1 and how Vanderbilt couldn't recapture the same mentality that led it to comeback win after comeback win in the regular season.

"It felt tough. It felt heavy," Vanderbilt coach Tim Corbin said. "The guys were trying. I feel like I didn't equip them properly in some way. Having done this a lot of times, I just feel like I didn't equip them for this this moment, but they were trying, and we could feel like we were going to pull it out."

The Commodores were pressing. It showed when they were no-hit through six innings in the opener against Wright State, when they recorded just five singles against Louisville and when they had just one hit until the ninth inning in the elimination game against Wright State.

Even the Raiders could see what was happening in the other dugout.

"Vanderbilt, really good team, outstanding team," Wright State coach Alex Sogard said. "I think there's extra pressure being the No. 1, right? On a smaller scale, we know from our league, we've won our league seven years in a row, so there's a bigger target on your back, right? And so we understand that a little bit. But yeah, I think there's a lot of pressure, and it can be a mental game, right? The human behind it, that's a big piece of it."

Corbin said the team felt it was close to breaking through despite it all. In the ninth inning of game 3, the Commodores loaded the bases with three walks. Mike Mancini hit a two-run single, then Rustan Rigdon sent a ball into the gap that would've tied the game − but it hopped over the fence for a ground rule double, leaving Mancini on third.

"We were trailing all season," Mancini said. "We needed to win to, get this seed, or we needed to win because all the SEC was in the middle of the pack, and we found a way to do it. And it sucks one game, an elimination game, doesn't go your way. But it could easily look the other way. That ground-rule double, how many times have we had a ground-rule double all year? I would have scored, but just didn't."

There were a few players who consistently came up with clutch hits. Brodie Johnston hit home runs in both the first and third games, bringing his total to 15 on the season. Riley Nelson had the deciding two-run home run in the opener. Mancini scored from second on a wild pitch in the second game and had the two-run single in the third. But the Commodores as a whole recorded just 12 hits in the three games.

Vanderbilt's offense still lagged behind many of its SEC peers in 2025, but there were some signs of moving in the right direction in the six weeks leading up to the postseason. Braden Holcomb and Colin Barczi showed power surges while Rigdon proved an offensive catalyst at the top of the order. That all evaporated in the regional, though.

"When you've got a group of guys that ... really care about each other, then that too can play into trying to finish something, because everyone wants it for one another, and when you want it for one another, and it doesn't work out," Corbin said. "Sometimes you're trying harder, and I could feel that. And there's no magic words, magic dust for that moment, but you could sense that these kids really, really wanted this for each other, and sometimes when that happens, it's squeezing the bird too hard."
