headline: Fever backup point guard 'progressing really quickly' from upper leg injury
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS — Fever coach Stephanie White is already encouraged by Sydney Colson’s progress after her upper left leg injury Friday night.

Colson injured her leg in the first quarter of Friday’s loss to the Connecticut Sun. She got tangled up with Sun guard Jacy Sheldon near the Fever bench, and Sheldon landed on her leg as they both fell.

Sheldon was able to get up without incident, but Colson stayed on the ground, holding her leg. White called a timeout for trainers to be able to attend to Colson, who got up after a few moments. She stayed in the huddle through the timeout, then walked without assistance, albeit gingerly, back to the locker room. 

She never returned to the bench, and she was ruled out for the game at halftime.

Colson and teammate Sophie Cunningham, who was injured in the fourth quarter, both got MRIs following the game, and it delivered encouraging results.

“I think we got good news from both of their MRIs, as good of news as you can get,” White said. “And so right now, it's a day-to-day thing. We're looking forward to hopefully them returning at some point sooner rather than later, but at the same time, it's how each of them progresses in their rehab.”

Colson was on a stationary bike for a portion of practice that was open to media Sunday afternoon, talking with longtime Fever trainer Todd Champlin and shouting out encouragement to her teammates as they went through drills.

“Syd’s been progressing really quickly, she's gonna get out there and get some shots up too,” White said. “So we'll see where she sits when she comes back after her recovery from today, make sure we don't have any setbacks.”

Colson put some shots up following practice with player development coach Keith Porter, running actions without any kind of noticeable wrap on her left leg.

The Fever are hoping to sign a hardship player ahead of Tuesday’s game — Indiana is able to get an emergency hardship exception as long as they’re under 10 players, meaning at least one of Colson or Cunningham (or both) will be out on Tuesday.

headline: With 8 healthy players, no Caitlin Clark, who might Fever sign for hardship exception?
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS — The injury bug has hit the Indiana Fever, and they are potentially down to eight available players for the time being.

Starting point guard Caitlin Clark is out at least until June 9, a two-week minimum, because of a quadriceps strain. She will miss at least the next two games (vs. Washington on Tuesday, at Chicago on Saturday) before she is reevaluated on a potential return to play.

That already put the Fever down to 10 available players. Then, both backup point guard Sydney Colson and emergency point guard Sophie Cunningham got injured in Friday’s game against the Connecticut Sun, leaving the Fever with no true point guards and just two healthy guards: Kelsey Mitchell and Lexie Hull.

In the two days since, the Fever front office and coaching staff have been mulling their options, from adding new players on hardship contracts to using their players in a different way.

Using some of their frontcourt players, like Aliyah Boston or DeWanna Bonner, to bring the ball up the floor, isn’t out of the question — especially against Washington on Tuesday.

“It's been trying to figure out all of our options, from potential hardship contracts and players and who's available to you know, with our coaches really like how we reimagine, you know, how we're using our players,” Fever coach Stephanie White said Sunday. “... We anticipate Washington coming with a lot of pressure, so we've got to have our bigs be able to bring the ball down the floor.”

Hardship explainer: Fever may be down to 8 available players. Here's how Indiana can go over cap to sign another

Cunningham and Colson’s MRIs were encouraging, and White said they are “day to day.” Neither participated in practice, but Colson was on the stationary bike during it and put up some shots after. Cunningham didn’t practice at any portion, wearing slides as she came up to the court after practice was over.

It seems like they’ll be out for some time — enough that the Fever are hoping to sign a hardship player ahead of Tuesday’s game against Washington.

What is a hardship exception in WNBA?

The Fever are eligible for an emergency hardship exception from the league, meaning they can go over the cap to sign a player to a hardship contract, as long as they are under 10 available players. These three injuries put the Fever at eight available.

The replacement players can play as long as the original injured players are unavailable, but must be released as the Fever get back up to 10 available players.

“We’re down in numbers, but we’re looking at adding another player, a replacement player, to help us with our numbers, and we’ll try to get people healthy and try to get back to a full roster together,” Fever president Kelly Krauskopf said. “I mean, games are still coming, so it’s gonna be an adjustment, but we have a good group, and we have good depth, thankfully.”

Who can Indiana Fever sign with hardship exception?

The Fever have already been looking at available players to sign, prioritizing a ball-handling guard. 

There are multiple players available, including Jaelyn Brown, who the Fever cut on the final day of training camp; Serena Sundell, who was drafted by the Storm then cut in training camp; Deja Kelly, who was drafted by the Aces then cut in training camp; and Aari McDonald, who has four years of experience in the league but was cut by the Sparks in training camp ahead of this season.

White said they’re not necessarily looking for someone who already knows her or the Fever’s system; with all these injuries, anyway, the system has been shifting. They want the best available player that will fit with their needs.

“I think best player available at that position who can add value on both ends,” White said. “Certainly, we need to have someone who can add value on the defensive end. We got to have somebody who can help us navigate and get into offense, will handle the ball since we're down to what, two healthy guards. The goal would be to get everybody kind of back to their natural positions if we can.”

The Fever will be the third team to add a hardship player to their rosters just two weeks into the season. The Los Angeles Sparks signed a hardship player May 20 as they had two injuries already on their roster, and the Phoenix Mercury just added a hardship contract in the wake of their multiple injuries on Sunday.

Will the WNBA expand rosters?

Roster expansion, or some way of having a taxi squad or development players available for WNBA teams, has been a point of contention for the league for multiple years now. Rosters are limited at 12, and multiple teams (including the Fever) only roster 11 because of salary cap limits — meaning even two or three injuries can derail rosters, force teams to bring in new players mid-season, and put more wear on the available players. 

“More bodies would be good,” Krauskopf said.

headline: 'Hunt for beef': Scott McLaughlin, Tony Kanaan's yearlong IndyCar feud renewed by crash
fullText:
DETROIT — McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown said Saturday he thinks IndyCar drivers "go to each others' birthday parties too often" in reference to a racing series that rarely features public spats once drivers hop out of the cockpit and get a second to cool off.

But drivers and rival team principals? That's another story.

A year-old social media feud between Arrow McLaren team principal Tony Kanaan and Team Penske driver Scott McLaughlin was stoked again Sunday afternoon in the wake of McLaughlin's role in spinning second-year Arrow McLaren driver Nolan Siegel early in Sunday's Detroit Grand Prix.

The incident, which McLaughlin was given a stop-and-go penalty for avoidable contact, was captured on the Fox broadcast, a clip of which circulated on Twitter, and which Kanaan quote-tweeted mid-race with a simple message of: "Oh ok then..."

Following the race, McLaughlin, who managed to finish 12th despite the penalty after starting seventh, quoted the same video clip of the incident and wrote: "Misjudged this one. Ol' mate broke quite a bit earlier than I anticipated. Good to see McLaren team principals are still on the hunt for beef... @GoodRanchers (a McLaughlin sponsor) has loads for ya. Use code #BrakeLater for 0% off."

Insider: Fewer cars, bigger cities, more risks part of McLaren Racing CEO's advice for IndyCar's future

Kanaan quickly took issue and quoted McLaughlin's post-race post, both making reference to McLaughlin's Indy 500 warmup lap crash and Roger Penske firing his entire IndyCar leadership team amidst Team Penske's 500 qualifying tech infractions: "Misjudged last week, misjudged this week, at least you get a weekend off to square that away. I came looking for your team principal to have a chat but I couldn't find him. Oh wait..."

At the time of writing, McLaughlin has had the last word, writing back: "Our team principals aren't usually on Twitter during the race, but you've got my phone number mate (with a laughling emoji at the end for good measure)."

Here's the entire exchange:

Scott McLaughlin, Tony Kanaan beef started June 2024

Nearly a year ago, the pair went back-and-forth a couple times in the wake of Arrow McLaren releasing Theo Pourchaire midseason, just over a month after committing to the young French driver for the remainder of the 2024 IndyCar season post-Indy 500 in the No. 6 Chevy as a medium-term replacement for David Malukas, who injured his wrist in a preseason mountain biking accident and then was fired four races into the campaign through a clause in the deal that gave Arrow McLaren the ability to sever ties without issue. Pourchaire had made his IndyCar debut at Long Beach as a Malukas stand-in before also tackling Barber and the IMS road course. Callum Ilott took the reins for the 500, but a runway had been cleared for Pourchaire for the final 12 races of 2024.

And then Siegel, an Indy NXT title contender at the time who missed Road America while filling in for Juncos Hollinger Racing's Agustin Canapino, made clear to IndyCar teams his wishes to hop in an Indy car midseason if possible, and in the wake of the young American driver assisting in a 24 Hours of Le Mans class win for the Brown-owned United Autosports team, Brown, Kanaan and then-Arrow McLaren team principal Gavin Ward opted to hire Siegel as the team's long-term Malukas replacement.

Insider: Alex Palou's crash in Detroit Grand Prix continues streak of Indy 500 winner not winning next race

The unrelenting, multi-month game of musical chairs — started by Alex Palou signing a contract with the team in the fall of 2022 for 2024-2026, and then deciding late in the season to stay with Chip Ganassi Racing — made the team a popular punching bag both publicly and privately in the paddock. And no one leaned into it more than McLaughlin, who wrote on Twitter in the wake of Pourchaire's release: "Let's take a moment of silence for all the trees sacrificed for McLaren contracts."

Kanaan then made light of Team Penske's much-maligned push-to-pass scandal earlier that year, writing: "A shame Push to Pass didn't have a moment of silence in St. Pete... but we can take one together if you like." McLaughlin then made the witty reference to his car's frequent primary sponsor: "TK, if you're looking for beef, you won't find any better than @GoodRanchers. I can send ya a box this weekend."

headline: Cincinnati Bearcats lose to Tennessee Volunteers in NCAA Knoxville Regional
fullText:
KNOXVILLE, TN – When they saw "Cincinnati" flash across the screen on Selection Sunday, the University of Cincinnati Bearcats baseball team had this matchup in mind.

But, they couldn't pull off the dream scenario. Tennessee plated two runs in the first inning against starter Kellen O'Connor and never trailed in a 10-6 victory.

At a jam-packed Lindsey Nelson Stadium Saturday night, May 31, UC was able to throw down against the 2024 national champion Tennessee Volunteers but they couldn't match the firepower. Tennessee pulled away with a four-run sixth inning and the closest UC got was 3-2 in the third inning when Jack Natili singled in a run and Cal Sefcik hit a sacrifice fly.

With the orange Vols fans living and dying on each pitch, Cincinnati struggled against Tennessee's No. 2 pitcher Marcus Phillips and reliever A.J. Russell.

"We definitely took our walks, we struck out a little bit too much," UC's Kerrington Cross said of Phillips. "Overall he's a good pitcher. He beat us today, plain and simple."

The Bearcats did put a scare in the Vols in the ninth on run-scoring hits from Quinton Coats and Cal Sefcik. Reliever Russell had pitched two scoreless, hitless frames. Tennessee brought in Brandon Arvidson who struck out pinch-hitter Kory Klingenbeck to end the contest.

"Embrace the chaos," Tennessee coach Tony Vitello said. "It's that time of year. I don't know that this game was more chaotic than the one before us but both were kind of what you'd expect."

Tennessee goes to 45-16 with the win while UC drops to 33-25.

Tennessee MLB arms

A recent ESPN mock MLB draft had Saturday night's starter Marcus Phillips as a late, first-round pick of the Mets. The sophomore touched 98 mph against the Bearcats. Christian Mitchelle's home run to left forced his exit in the seventh inning. Phillips threw 98 pitches, allowing just four hits and striking out eight through six innings.

At 6-foot-4 and 246 pounds he has tight end size but hasn't played football since the seventh grade. UC coach Jordan Bischel noted how Phillips has improved with men on base. The Bearcats swiped three bags, but only one against Phillips (Donovan Ford) and the big guy picked off UC's Cross.

"When it takes less time to deliver the baseball it's less time to steal the base," Bischel said.

For what it's worth, Tennessee's Friday starter Liam Doyle, who beat Wake Forest with 11 strikeouts in 6.2 innings, is projected to be the No. 2 pick overall to the Angels.

UC starter Kellen O'Connor was chased from the game in the sixth inning and finished allowing eight hits and seven runs with five walks and four strikeouts. Adam Buczkowski was off-target with three consecutive walks and Brandon Scheurer had to finish the sixth.

O'Connor went 5.1 innings allowing eight hits and seven runs with five walks and four strikeouts. Brandon Scheurer finished the game for UC going the final 3.2 innings allowing four hits and striking out two.

Cincinnati Bearcats lineup changes

Most notably, Landyn Vidourek who delivered two hits and two steals in the Wake Forest win Friday was out of the lineup. Vidourek had just returned from an oblique injury.

Bischel inserted Tommy O'Connor as the designated hitter vs. the Vols and put Christian Mitchelle at second base. Both have been regulars in their UC careers and both last played in the Big 12 tournament vs. West Virginia.

While an injury to Vidourek wasn't divulged before the game, it was after the game.

"He's hurt," Bischel said. "Day-to-day like he's been for two weeks. Hopefully, he can get back out there tomorrow but when you're dealing with a middle body injury in a sport that requires a lot of rotation, it's tough."

Cincinnati Bearcats, Tennessee Volunteers runs

Top 1st – With UC as the home team under NCAA tourney rules, Tennessee hit first. The Vols loaded the bases with no outs. Curley's single plated Kilen and Fischer. A diving catch by UC's Pitts saved multiple runs to end the frame. Tennessee 2, Cincinnati 0

Top 3rd – Tennessee's Curley homered to center. Tennessee 3, Cincinnati 0

Bottom 3rd – After walks to UC's Ford and Cross, Natili singled in Ford. Cross scored on a sacrifice fly by Cal Sefcik. Tennessee 3, Cincinnati 2

Top 4th – Tennessee's Kilen with a bloop triple then scores on Fischer's ground out. Tennessee 4, Cincinnati 2

Top 6th – Tennessee's Peebles doubled, Kilen singled, Fischer drove in both with a double. After Kellen O'Connor exited. Tennessee drew three straight walks against Buczkowski to score Fischer. Scheurer relieved Buczkowski. Chapman's sac fly scored Ensley. Tennessee 8, Cincinnati 2

Bottom 7th – UC's Mitchelle homered to left. Niehaus walked, stole second and third and scored on a passed ball. Tennessee 8, Cincinnati 4

Top 9th – Tennessee's Cannon Peebles hit a two-run double. Tennessee 10, Cincinnati 4

Bottom 9th – Quentin Coats and Cal Sefcik had run-scoring hits. FINAL: Tennesee 10, Cincinnati 6

It's on to Sunday

Wake Forest now awaits the rematch with the Bearcats as the teams will reconvene Sunday at noon at Lindsey Nelson Stadium. The Demon Deacons held on against the Miami RedHawks 14-13 in a squeaker Saturday afternoon. A veteran of many leagues, UC's Bischel wasn't concerned about the quick turnaround.

"I grew up playing and coaching Division III ball," Bischel said. "Fourteen hours between games, you usually get 25 minutes (in DIII). This is a long rest. If we're not excited to play baseball in the NCAA tournament we've got a lot bigger problem than how many hours we slept."

The Bearcats will have to win Sunday afternoon to keep playing. Should they down Wake Forest again, it will be a doubleheader as they'll have to square off again with Tennessee at 6 p.m. Sunday. If they win both games Sunday, they would have to return Monday June 2 at a time to be determined since NCAA regionals are double elimination.

The Bearcats will start Carson Marsh who is 3-5 with a 7.03 ERA with 46 strikeouts in 39.2 innings. Of his 23 appearances, he has started eight times.

"All hands on deck once you get to elimination day," Bischel said.

Added Cross, "If you treat it like an elimination game then you're going to get nervous. I think the goal is to tell them (teammates) it's another day. Keep the energy high. If we just play our style and want to be there you're going to see the results in the end. If you treat it like an elimination game you're cooked from the start."

headline: 'Tough night.' FC Cincinnati suffers 1st home defeat of the season in loss to D.C. United
fullText:
FC Cincinnati entered its match against D.C. United Saturday, May 31 hoping to return to form as one of the top teams in Major League Soccer in its final contest before the halfway point of the regular season. 

Instead, an inconsistent FC Cincinnati theme dubiously continued, and the Orange and Blue dropped points to a third consecutive team below the playoff line in a 2-1 loss at TQL Stadium in front of a sellout crowd of 25,513.

It's FC Cincinnati's first home loss of the season.

"Tough night, tough stretch, tough week for us results-wise and performance-wise," FC Cincinnati head coach Pat Noonan said.

FC Cincinnati’s defensive issues persist against D.C. United 

If D.C. United’s offense was struggling heading into the final match of the first half, you wouldn’t have known it after the opening 20 minutes. 

FC Cincinnati has conceded seven goals over its last two matches and its struggles on the defensive end continued right away Saturday as D.C. United tallied a pair of deflating goals that took the collective air out of the building.

The icebreaker came in the second minute from wing Gabriel Pirani, who was left unattended at the top of the box off a set piece created by a questionable penalty by FC Cincinnati centre back Teenage Hadebe. 

Less than four minutes after FC Cincinnati tied it 1-1, D.C. United took its second lead of the match when Gabriel Pirani lofted a crosser deep in the box off another set piece and met a leaping Conner Antley for a header. 

"There's so many things from experienced players that could be eliminated," Noonan said of the set-piece defense that has plagued FC Cincinnati lately.

D.C. United entered TQL Stadium with the second-fewest goals in the Eastern Conference, with six of its goals from forward Christian Benteke, who has been out with an ankle injury since May 14. 

D.C. United had scored just one goal in its last four matches and Saturday marked its first multi-goal game in MLS play since a 2-1 win over Colorado May 3. 

Kevin Denkey scores 10th goal of season in loss to D.C. United

FC Cincinnati found an equalizer early in the first half when Evander dribbled through traffic and fed Kevin Denkey for a point-blank tally from the box.

It was Denkey's team-high 10th goal of the season and Evander's club-best sixth assist, but the celebration was short-lived after D.C. United took a 2-1 lead moments later, which would hold until full-time.

What the FC Cincinnati faithful were booing about as the first half came to an end was a mystery, but they had plenty to pick from.

In what seemed to be a get-right spot for the Orange & Blue turned ugly as the hosts conceded a pair of early goals, were outshot 10-4 over the first 40 minutes and were unstable on both sides of the ball.

"In the first half, I think they outworked us and were more physical," Noonan said. "They're a good pressing team. There were moments that I thought we handled it well. It's gonna be like that all game and you have to be prepared for it. If you're not, then the game becomes transition."

FC Cincinnati’s best moment in transition came in the 37th minute with Gerardo Valenzuela dribbling into the box. He hit the deck after being met by D.C. United’s Matti Peltola, then DeAndre Yedlin was taken to the turf while trying to corral the rebound. 

"I felt like definitely on Dado (Valenzuela) there was (a foul)," Yedlin said. "At the end of the day, it's the ref's call and there's nothing we can do about it."

FC Cincinnati pleaded for a foul that would’ve warranted a penalty shot but play resumed and the Orange and Blue went into the locker room with a one-goal deficit.

FC Cincinnati's defense did not concede a shot on goal in the second half, but its offense came up empty against the heavy-pressing D.C. United defense.

"It's been tough. It's the way it goes. Sometimes, things don't fall your way, sometimes you don't do things great, and they do fall your way. We've had a couple games like that this year," Yedlin said. "We gotta figure it out."

Kei Kamara, searching for his first goal in an FC Cincinnati kit, came up just high on a header off a crosser from Evander in the 56th minute. Evander had a solid look in the 81st minute but D.C. United goalkeeper Luis Barraza made a diving stop before swatting away the ensuing penalty kick.

What’s next for FC Cincinnati? 

It will be over a month before FC Cincinnati hits the pitch at its home venue (Saturday, July 5 vs. Chicago Fire FC) as TQL Stadium is set to host four matches in the FIFA Club World Cup 2025, beginning with Bayern Munich vs. Auckland City FC on Saturday, June 15. 

FC Cincinnati has two weeks off before it begins a three-match road streak, beginning Saturday, June 14 as the Orange and Blue will try to sweep the regular-season series against the New England Revolution.

FC Cincinnati won the first meeting at home, 1-0, April 5.

"Maybe the break will come at a good time to reset, try to come out of it in a better way than we went into it," Noonan said.

headline: Q&A with Jim Obergefell on the future of Supreme Court's gay marriage ruling, LGBTQ rights
fullText:
In 2013, Ohioans Jim Obergefell and John Arthur flew on a medical jet to exchange vows in Maryland where same-sex marriage was legal at the time.

With Arthur in hospice care for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, time was slipping away for the Cincinnati couple and their home state of Ohio prohibited same-sex marriage.

Days after their tarmac wedding, civil rights attorney Al Gerhardstein showed them a blank Ohio death certificate.

More: After 775K gay marriages, Americans are still fighting for rights 10 years later

"Do you guys understand that when John dies, his last record as a person will be wrong here, where it says marital status at the time of death?" Gerhardstein told them. "Ohio will say John was unmarried. And Jim, your name will not be here, where it says surviving spouse name."

Brokenhearted and angry at the idea of not being recognized by Ohio, Arthur and Obergefell told Gerhardstein, yes, they wanted to do something about it.

Arthur didn't live to see the fruits of that decision: On June 26, 2015, in a 5-4 decision in Obergefell v. Hodges, the U.S. Supreme Court decided states must allow for same-sex marriages and must recognize those solemnized in other states.

Arthur died in October 2013 at the age of 48.

Obergefell, now 58, splits his time on multiple projects: a wine business, speaking engagements, promotion of a new book, helping a local equality nonprofit and more. He lives in his childhood hometown of Sandusky.

The following is a question and answer session with Obergefell, reflecting on the 10-year anniversary of the same-sex marriage ruling and the state of LGBTQ+ rights today. It has been edited for clarity and brevity.

Question: Ten years ago, you were in the courtroom on June 26 when U.S. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy read the decision summary. What was your reaction?

Obergefell: Initially I thought ‘we won’ but it’s legal writing, which isn’t incredibly clear to non-lawyers, but then it sunk in, "Yeah, Jim, you won." And I burst into tears, and I could hear people around the courtroom sobbing. My first thought was, "John, I wish you were here. I wish you could experience this. I wish you could know that our marriage cannot be erased." What I wasn’t expecting to feel was this realization that for the first time in my life as an out gay man, I felt like an equal American.

The decision changed the lives of millions of Americans. How do you feel about that now, 10 years later?

Being part of the plaintiffs who took the fight to marriage equality to the Supreme Court has been an amazing experience. When people find out who I am or recognize me, they’ll stop and hug me, shake my hand, tell me stories, show me photos of their loved ones. I’ve had people come out to me. One woman told me if it weren’t for the decision, she would’ve committed suicide because she never saw a future for herself. I’ve had the joy of officiating almost 30 weddings since decision day. And John’s been gone almost 12 years but I get to talk about him again and again.

You’ve experienced an outpouring of love and support. Have you also encountered hate?

I have not been subjected to outright hate in public but I’m worried that may change. Other plaintiffs in the case have had bad experiences. I have not. The only explanation I can give is that our story is one of love and loss and most people can relate to losing someone they loved. I also made the decision early on to never read comments on the internet.

Do you feel like a historic figure or hero?

My name is on a landmark Supreme Court decision, so I know I’m part of history. I still remember when my niece texted me a photo of her high school textbook with the story of "Obergefell v Hodges." I don’t feel like a hero. John and I simply found ourselves facing a simple question: Were we willing to fight for what we believed in and to fight to exist? And to me, that wasn’t a brave decision. That was an obvious decision. John deserved to die with an accurate death certificate, and we deserved to be seen by the state we call home.

How do you feel about same-sex marriage in America now, given the current political climate?

Ten years after the decision, I never thought I would be worried about marriage equality continuing as a right in our nation. We have two sitting Supreme Court justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, who said they want to overturn Obergefell. And Clarence Thomas mentioned other cases that are important to the queer community, including Lawrence versus Texas, which overturned anti-sodomy laws. We have state legislatures passing resolutions urging the court to overturn the case. So, 10 years later, I’m worried about marriage equality because there are people who refuse to let it lie. I just honestly don’t understand why. How has any queer marriage ever impacted a straight marriage? It hasn’t.

Ohio’s defense of marriage act remains in state law and the state constitution. Why do you think Ohio lawmakers never removed those?

It’s understandable that a lot of people think the court decision invalidated those laws. But we live in a time when the Supreme Court no longer believes in the bedrock principle of precedence. They overturned Roe versus Wade, which had been precedent for 49 years. Marriage equality has been here for 10 years. It is at risk.

Rick Hodges served as the Ohio Department of Health director at the time during Gov. John Kasich’s administration. His name is on the other side of Obergefell v. Hodges. What is your relationship with Hodges?

People assume that the person on the other side of a case is an adversary. I love sharing the fact that Rick Hodges and I are friends. We do events together, speak together, do press conferences together. We met in 2016 over coffee and one of the first things he said was "I’ve never been happier to lose something." As health director, he took an oath to uphold Ohio law but he was on our side the entire time.

After you won at the federal district court, then-Gov. Kasich and then-Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine appealed the case to the 6th District Court of Appeals. How do you feel about Kasich and DeWine?

It’s fair to say that there is no love lost between John Kasich, Mike DeWine and myself. DeWine as governor has done some things I’ve approved of but then he does other things that harm the LGBTQ+ community.

What is your message to Gov. DeWine today?

I’d like to remind you that everyone in our community are human beings, deserving of the same human rights and civil rights as any other person in this state. I ask you to push back against the hateful legislation that arrives on your desk. It’s your duty to look out for all of us, and that includes people you might not personally like. We deserve to live our lives on equal footing with others in the state. Stop bowing down to the extremists in the state Legislature, push back on the harmful, hateful legislation that comes from that body. Stand up. Have some principles and actually make decisions that are based on facts, reality and science instead of lies and half truths made up to target and marginalize communities. That is your duty as a governor.

There is a backlash against diversity, equity and inclusion, LGBTQ rights and against transgender Americans. Where do you think it’s leading?

It’s leading this nation to a White Christian fascist state. We are heading backward in time instead of forward. We are going back to a time when people of color and queer people weren’t considered human beings. You’re passing laws and doing things that tell us we are not human beings. That is not what this nation is about. Our founding documents starts with "we the people." And the people means all of us, not just White, straight Christians.

Following the Obergefell decision, polls showed increased support for same sex marriage but then opponents of LGBTQ rights seemed to shift their focus to transgender Americans. Why?

Over those first few years, marriage equality became a normal part of life for millions of people across the country. Their neighbors, their friends, their family members, their coworkers, they were seeing queer marriages happen. People opposed to marriage equality realized they lost that fight but still didn’t like the queer community. So they decided to attack the most vulnerable part of the LGBTQ+ community, the trans community. They’ve been successful in turning trans people into the boogeyman, into these dangerous people when nothing could be further from the truth. They just want to live their lives without fearing for their lives.

Do you see any turning point for the trans community in the next five to 10 years, either positive or negative?

Every part of our community needs to fight for our trans family. We are all considered outsiders by straight society. The thing that would have an impact is if the entire LGBTQ+ community, with one voice, says the trans community is part of our family. We support them. We fight for them. They deserve every right that we enjoy, every right that the rest of society enjoys.

What will the future look like for LGBTQ+ Ohioans and Americans 10 years from now?

I’m going to go with optimism. The future depends on people across the country, across Ohio, realizing that hate is not the way for this country to operate. It will take people understanding that our nation was founded on religious freedom – that doesn’t mean making your particular interpretation of your particular faith foremost in everything that happens in our country. It doesn’t mean you get to use your faith as a weapon or to dictate how people live their lives. So that national realization has to happen and there has to be pushback against that dangerous path that we’re heading down. We also need people to vote.

Having your name on the Supreme Court ruling has given you a big platform. Have you been intentional about how to use it or did your approach just evolve into what we hear from you today?

I used to say I’m an accidental activist. But then I realized John and I were quiet activists because we were open about who we are. I think because of John’s health and our decision to get married, I became an activist. That really did change me profoundly. I have to keep fighting to make the world a better place for people who come after me, because, honestly, I owe it to the people who came before me, people like Edie Windsor, Frank Kameny, Harvey Milk. I want a future where a queer kid doesn’t have to be afraid or wonder, well what kind of future do I have? They don’t have to be terrified about being authentically themselves. So that’s what I have to keep fighting for.

headline: Cincinnati tennis courts succumb to an invasive species: Pickleball players
fullText:
Tennis players face habitat loss.

Historic tennis courts are morphing into courts for their smaller racket sport cousin, pickleball. There's room for both, say tennis clubs and stores. But for now, it looks bleak for tennis.

Tennis players will lose another landmark court this summer with the closing of the Eastern Hills Indoor Tennis Club. After 54 years of tennis in Linwood, the club served its last volley in May. Last tennis volley, that is. Like others in the area, it will become a pickleball club.

Eastern Hills was the last indoor tennis facility in the city limits.

"It’s meaningful," said Cincinnati Tennis Foundation Founder and Chief Executive Officer Matthew Detkas. "It’s the last one standing in the city."

The Enquirer asked pickleball and tennis players about the future of their sport.

What's a tennis player to do?

Tennis players like Lila Logan have resorted to pickleball. She can't find other tennis players, she said. When she lived in Vermont three years ago, Logan had vaguely heard of pickleball. This spring, she reluctantly picked up a pickleball paddle.

"I had kind of heard of it on the periphery maybe three years ago, and then all of a sudden, it seems like it's everywhere," said Logan, 47, of Springfield Township.

On a warm March evening, she gripped a pickleball paddle on courts in Wyoming, a Cincinnati suburb. It was just the third time she's played the smaller racket sport.

Her impression so far? She'd rather be playing tennis.

"It's like a ping-pong ball, so it feels a little silly somehow, you know, like a bar game instead of like a sport," Logan said with a laugh. "That's what it kind of feels like. You could drink beer and play pickleball. You don't drink beer and play tennis."

For many, that is the draw of pickleball. It's both exercise and social activity. That's why pickleball has spread over tennis courts across not just the region but the country, players say.

Is tennis an endangered species of sport in Cincinnati?

For the Eastern Hills Indoor Tennis Club, it seemed like only a matter of time before the 54-year-old complex became a pickleball facility.

People for the last few years have approached the owner Brian Clark about buying the club to turn it into a pickleball facility, Clark told The Enquirer. He finally relented this year when the owner of West Chester's Pickle Lodge approached him. It was the right time and a competitive offer, Clark said.

"Is pickleball invading tennis?" Clark said. "Some would argue yes. I think it complements it ... I try to tell people, if you want to learn how to play pickleball, learn how to play tennis, because tennis translates into pickleball."

Cincinnati Tennis Foundation: 'They can coexist'

Tennis organizations, actually, are embracing pickleball. The Cincinnati Tennis Foundation in the past year has added pickleball as part of its outreach programs in schools, the foundation's CEO, Detkas, said. The foundation is dedicated to growing the sport of tennis among youth. Pickleball isn't the enemy, he said.

"We love pickleball," Detkas said. "We want to be inclusive. They can coexist."

He agrees that one of the biggest impediments for tennis players is finding other people to play with. Unlike pickleball, you can't just show up to a court and find people to play. For tennis players who don't want to play pickleball, he recommends finding a club or community. Detkas said people can reach out to the tennis foundation for help. The city still has a variety of tennis clubs, including the 145-year-old Cincinnati Tennis Club, the Club at Harper's Point, Hyde Park Tennis Club and Carmargo Racquet Club.

By the end of next year, the Cincinnati Tennis Foundation hopes to open an indoor tennis facility within the city limits to replace the loss of Eastern Hills.

Detkas and others don't see the current clubs going away, though some have already started offering pickleball next to tennis. That's the future, Detkas said. Pickleball courts alongside tennis courts, he said.

"We want racket sports to work together," Detkas said. "They are great lifelong sports, and pickleball is a lifelong sport."

Pickleball bursting at the seams

Two years earlier, Pickle Lodge owner Mitch Dunn bought an a tennis club in West Chester and converted it into the first Pickle Lodge. Within six months of the lodge opening in 2024, the membership reached capacity, Dunn said.

That's when he approached Eastern Hills.

"I think pickleball's growth is not going to stop in Cincinnati," Dunn said. "You’re going to see other franchised brands come into town."

Indeed, Arizona-based Pickleball Kingdom announced in February that it will open a 33,000-square-foot pickleball facility with 12 indoor courts in Mason.

How many tennis courts are we losing?

While many municipalities and clubs have opened pickleball courts alongside tennis courts, a growing list of tennis courts are turning into pickleball courts.

According to Dunn, 56 tennis courts across 14 local facilities have been converted, or will be this year, into pickleball courts. There are now 141 total pickleball courts, and 49 tennis courts, across those sites.

It's happening across the country, too.

A Wall Street Journal article said the United States Tennis Association in 2024 estimated 10% of the nation's tennis courts had become pickleball courts. A spokesperson for the tennis association, though, told The Enquirer it doesn't track the number of tennis courts converted to pickleball.

Those in the tennis industry are reluctant to characterize the struggle for turf as a war between tennis and pickleball. Like Clark, they say there's room for everyone to get along.

Where did Sawyer Point's tennis courts go?

A pivotal moment in the battle between tennis and pickleball happened three years ago at Sawyer Point along Cincinnati's riverfront.

At the behest of a large group of pickleballers, the city of Cincinnati in 2022 spent $509,000 to resurface the eight tennis courts into 24 pickleball courts. Three tennis courts remain, and those are overlaid with pickleball courts. The rest became 18 permanent pickleball courts.

The result: Tennis courts built there in 1988 for Cincinnati's bicentennial as part of Sawyer Point park are now part of a premier pickleball facility, one that has hosted professional tournaments.

The remaining tennis courts are rarely used, said Gary Lessis, founder of Pickleball at Sawyer Point. He keeps meticulous spreadsheets and records of how many people use the pickleball and tennis courts. It's how he helped convince the city to convert most of the courts to pickleball.

Last year, 40,076 pickleball players played on the Sawyer Point courts compared to 432 tennis players, Lessis' records showed.

Tennis players are quick to point out that their numbers are growing, just not at the rate of their pickleball counterparts.

The U.S. Tennis Association, in its 2024 U.S. Tennis Participation Report, said tennis participation nationwide grew 34% since 2019, going from 17.7 million players to 23.8 million. It also notes that pickleball during that same period grew 289% going from 3.5 million players to 13.6 million.

USA Pickleball recorded 4,000 new courts last year in its court database, bringing the total number of courts to 15,910 nationwide.

Pickleball paddles, shoes and accessories have taken more shelf space in recent years at Midwest Racquet Sports, formerly known as Tennis-Point and Midwest Sports. The Sharonville-based company has become a nationally renowned tennis supply store.

Tennis still makes up a bulk of the business, said Colleen Leonard, the store's chief brand officer. While Leonard wouldn't share specific sales figures, she did say pickleball is a fast-growing part of the business.

Can't we all just get along?

All racket sports ‒ tennis, pickleball and even the emerging padel ‒ can help each other, Leonard said. They can co-exist.

"Tennis will always be there, growing slower than pickleball," Leonard said. "But pickleball opens up racket sports to a whole new group of people."

And people often play both. Alan Cooper is also a dual pickleball/tennis player. The 38-year-old from Finneytown said he and his wife were introduced to pickleball three years ago on a trip to Florida. He still plays both but finds himself playing pickleball more often. It's easier, more accessible and takes less time, he said. He plays pickleball twice a month, tennis once a month.

"I still play tennis," Cooper said. "That is the sport that makes me curse the most. Pickleball, a little less cursing. Tennis, way more cursing."

headline: My pickleball journey: How a tennis player learned to stop worrying and love pickleball
fullText:
The impending conversion of Eastern Hills Indoor Tennis Club into a pickleball facility seemed another in a long list of harbingers for the demise of tennis in Greater Cincinnati.

After the announcement of the Eastern Hills sale to the Pickle Lodge, my editors looked to me to find the future of both tennis and pickleball in Cincinnati.

I found out, in an increasingly divided world, at least tennis and pickleball players can get along.

That mirrors my own racket-sport journey.

While I play both, it took me a while to warm up to pickleball.

I felt displaced by the hordes of paddle-wielding interlopers. They didn't just come in groups of twos and fours. They came by the dozens.

They didn't just want one court. They wanted them all.

I get why pickleball is the fastest-growing sport in America.

Tennis is hard.

I've played for decades and still am not good at it.

When the weather is above 50 degrees, I'm usually on the tennis court with my buddy every Saturday morning. We've called various public courts in Cincinnati and Northern Kentucky home.

A few years ago we started noticing new people on the courts. They weren't playing tennis. They were playing a hybrid game of tennis and ping-pong called pickleball. A few years ago, a group of more than 30 pickleball players began renting an entire public court in Erlanger, Kentucky, on Saturday mornings where I played with my friend. So we had to move.

It took us a while to find a safe haven, one where pickleball courts and tennis courts exists side-by-side. Then I played pickleball with my dad. And what do you know? It's pretty fun.

Tennis players I've talked to see more hybrid tennis/pickleball facilities, both public and private, in the future. Both sports have grown, though nowhere near to the level of pickleball.

Both see a future for tennis and pickleball.

And hey, at least it's not racquetball.

Joking. Only joking.

headline: Just Askin': What are Ohio's official state symbols?
fullText:
The Enquirer's Just Askin' series aims to answer the questions that no one seems to have an answer for, except maybe Google.

Fellow Ohioans could probably tell you the nickname of their state (the Buckeye State) or even the official bird (the cardinal). But could they tell you the official insect or the official artifact?

Since the early 1900s, lawmakers in the U.S. have designated specific symbols to represent the unique characteristics of their state.

Question: What are Ohio's official state symbols?

Here's Ohio's list, according to Ohio.gov:

  • State Flag: The Ohio Burgee, adopted in 1902.
  • Coat of Arms: Depicts a sunrise over mountains, a river and a field, adopted in 1996.
  • State Seal: Consists of the coat of arms within a circle with the words "THE GREAT SEAL OF THE STATE OF OHIO," adopted in 1996.
  • State Motto: “With God All Things Are Possible," adopted in 1959.
  • State Slogan: "Ohio, The Heart of it All," adopted in 1984, reinstated in 2023.
  • State Capital and Capital Building: The Ohio Statehouse, located in Ohio's capital of Columbus, designated in 1816.
  • State Nickname: The Buckeye State, adopted in 1953.
  • State Bird: The cardinal, adopted in 1933.
  • State Insect: The ladybug, adopted in 1975.
  • State Mammal: The white-tailed deer, adopted in 1988.
  • State Reptile: The black racer snake, adopted in 1995.
  • State Amphibian: The spotted salamander, adopted in 2010.
  • State Frog: The American bullfrog, adopted in 2010.
  • State Pet: The shelter dog, adopted in 2019.
  • State Flower: The red carnation, adopted in 1904.
  • State Tree: The Ohio buckeye, adopted in 1953.
  • State Wild Flower: The white trillium, adopted in 1986.
  • State Fruit: The tomato, adopted in 2009.
  • State Native Fruit: The pawpaw, adopted in 2009.
  • State Beverage: Tomato juice, adopted in 1965.
  • State Song: "Beautiful Ohio," adopted in 1969.
  • State Rock Song: "Hang On Sloopy," adopted in 1985.
  • State Bicentennial Bridge: Blaine Hill Bridge, adopted in 2002.
  • State Prehistoric Monument: Newark Earthworks, adopted in 2006.
  • State Artifact: Adena Pipe, adopted in 2003.
  • State Historical Architectural Structure: Barn, adopted in 2019.
  • State Airplane: 1905 Wright Flyer III, adopted in 2025.
  • State Gemstone: Flint, adopted in 1965.
  • State Fossil: Isotelus trilobite, adopted in 1985.
  • State Fossil Fish: The Placoderm Fish, adopted in 2021.

Do you have a question for Just Askin'? Send it to us at justaskin@enquirer.com.

headline: What a 1958 Cincinnati newspaper says: Cold War, Play-Doh and a Ruth Lyons fashion line
fullText:
The Enquirer used to run a feature called “20 Years Ago in Cincinnati” with brief summaries of articles from that day in history. Sometimes it was 50 years or 100 years. It was an interesting exercise to see what was important, how far we’ve come and what hasn’t changed all that much.

We can learn a lot by a single day in history – or in this case, a single newspaper.

So, I decided to look back at an old Enquirer to see what it tells us. I asked Random.org for a random date in the 20th century, and it spit out Sept. 3, 1958.

Let’s see what random history we find.

Front page news in 1958: Cold War, Space Race, desegregation

The front page of the newspaper of record contained 12 stories, a standalone photo and a cartoon. Compare that to today, when The Enquirer features two or three longer stories on the front that jump inside.

Those 1958 headlines were mostly national and international. With no internet or 24-hour news coverage on TV, newspapers were the main source of information from all over the world.

That day, Enquirer readers found out about:

  • The Cold War – Who had the mightiest military, the U.S. or Russia?
  • The Space Race – One year after Russia reached outer space first with the Sputnik 1 satellite, the United States was offering a “space plan for peace.”
  • Chinese Communists blockading the island of Taiwan (then called Formosa) – Back then, Communists were routinely called Reds in print. That’s why the Cincinnati Reds became the Redlegs in 1953 (the name was restored in 1959).
  • More attempts to thwart integration of schools in the South.

The previous September, nine courageous Black students attended the previously all-white Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. But Gov. Orval Faubus had called in the National Guard to block the students from entering the school. The photo of an angry white student shouting at 15-year-old Elizabeth Echford was shown in The Enquirer and other newspapers across the country. President Dwight Eisenhower then sent Army troops to escort the students to class.

But a year later, Gov. Faubus was back claiming he would fight any U.S. marshals or federal troops trying to force integration of Arkansas schools.

Yet, we often characterize the 1950s as a period of stability and conformity. Not so much.

Getting the best of the competition

A cartoon of two neighbors talking about The Enquirer: “You’re so right … The Enquirer has so many of the best features of the old Times-Star it’s just like getting both of them now – in the morning!”

The Enquirer’s jab at its defunct competition has a back story.

In 1952, the Cincinnati Times-Star, an afternoon newspaper, attempted to purchase The Enquirer for $7.5 million. But the Enquirer staff, led by reporter James H. Ratliff, didn’t like the idea and raised a counteroffer of $7.6 million to buy the Enquirer themselves.

Instead, E.W. Scripps, owners of the Cincinnati Post, bought out the Times-Star in 1958, and shut it down. The Post then added Times-Star to its masthead. No love lost among competitors.

Ruth Lyons debuted her own line of dresses

The Enquirer ran ads for both Gidding’s and Jenny clothing stores before they merged, radio station WZIP 1050 AM (“Greater Cincinnati’s Only ‘GOOD MUSIC’ Station,” which banned rock ’n’ roll), plus Four Roses whiskey and Tareyton cigarettes.

You could pick up a classic ’57 Chevy Bel Air with chrome and fins for $1,897 at Schott-Lippert Buick. That may be $21,000 in 2025, but the same car today from a collector would cost you $75,000.

Sept. 3 was the grand debut of the queen of Cincinnati television’s own fashion line under the label Ruth Lyons Autograph.

Lyons worked with international designer Joset Walker on the designs. “The candor and thoroughness Ruth shows on her TV program were manifest in her selection of fabrics, suggestions about design, and approval of individual creations by Mme. Walker,” The Enquirer reported.

The dresses sold from $22.95 to $49.95 ($250-$550 in 2025).

One last story: Small company had record year in 1958

The Enquirer editorial page quoted a recent Wall Street Journal front-page article on “the simple tale of a small company whose principal product fell victim to the march of technology … but as a result of its tussle for survival the company’s sales in 1957 were 167 per cent higher than its previous best year, and this year are expected to climb another 123 per cent.”

That company was Kutol Products of Cincinnati, which sold wallpaper cleaner. It was a big seller in the days of coal-burning stoves, when walls needed to be cleaned of soot. But with gas stoves and painted walls, the market for the product was hit hard.

Until Kutol’s Joseph McVicker got the idea from his sister-in-law to use the dough-like cleaner as “creative play material” and add some bright colors. “And thus ‘Play-Doh’ was born,” The Enquirer wrote.

headline: North College Hill police chief fired, adding new wrinkle to city's year of instability
fullText:
(This story was updated to add comments from the police chief's attorney.)

North College Hill city officials have fired Police Chief Ryan Schrand after being on administrative leave for more than a year.

In a letter of termination that The Enquirer obtained, North College Hill city administrator Arious Dukes-Dean informed Schrand he was being removed as the city's police chief effective May 21. Dukes-Dean cites in the letter that her decision was "based on my lack of confidence in your ability to effectively lead the department."

Schrand's firing is the latest shakeup in an unstable year for North College Hill's city government. Since March 2024, 75% of the city's firefighters resigned and then rescinded their resignations, city officials placed Fire Chief Brian Fels and the longest-serving cop, Lt. Frank Petrocelli, on administrative leave, and the city's former administrator resigned.

The Enquirer has also sued the Cincinnati suburb for not fulfilling numerous public record's request in accordance with Ohio's public records law. This includes a records request for Schrand's personnel file.

The Enquirer contacted Schrand, who declined to comment. However, his attorney, Mark Byrne, said they don't understand how Dukes-Dean, who was hired nine months after Schrnad was placed on leave, could lack confidence in his ability to lead the department when he never reported to her while she's been the city manager.

More: Mysterious resignations, city secrets: What's happening in North College Hill?

Complaints allege Schrand 'created a hostile work environment'

Before the city fired Schrand, Mayor Tracie Nichols had placed him on leave on March 19, 2024. In a letter to Schrand, Nichols wrote she received multiple reports and complaints claiming Schrand "created a hostile work environment."

In one complaint, an officer, whose name was redacted, alleges that Schrand and other supervisors subjected her to "unfair treatment and harassment." The supervisors included Petrocelli, who resigned in February in light of allegations of theft and fraud.

The officer said inaccurate rumors had spread about her having an intimate relationship with another officer. Schrand repeatedly questioned her for it, even after she informed him that she and the other officer did not have anything beyond a close friendship.

She alleges Schrand had a "fixation" over the rumored relationship and would regularly ask other officers about it. In one instance outlined in her complaint, another officer had told her that Schrand said if he ever found out she lied about her relationship, he would "bury me, fire me immediately and go to the extent of putting me on the Brady list." The Brady list is a compilation of law enforcement officers and other staff who have credibility issues.

The officer said she was frustrated with the issues at the police department, so she resigned and started working at the Lebanon Police Department. However, she didn't think the new job was a good fit for her and asked Schrand to rescind her resignation.

Schrand accepted to bring her back, but two months later, the officer said she was placed under investigation for her "performance and activity, or lack thereof."

According to the complaint, Schrand assigned Lt. Emily Englebert to conduct the investigation but the officer filing the claims said that assignment represented a conflict of interest because Schrand had previously told her that Englebert called her the "anti-Christ."

The officer filed a grievance regarding the disciplinary write-up she received as a result of the investigation but said Schrand denied it without any further conversation. However, Schrand attached a letter to the grievance in which he said she had begged for her job back and he reluctantly took her back, the officer's complaint states.

The officer's complaint goes on to claim that Schrand would have "emotional outbursts" where he spoke disparagingly about the officer who filed the complaint and other employees.

"I feel unsafe, uncomfortable, and embarrassed going to work because of the assassination of my character and obvious mistreatment by the people who are supposed to lead this department," the officer wrote in the complaint.

Another complaint from a different officer states that Schrand would also let his anger affect working relationships with other agencies, harshly discipline some officers while giving a "free pass" to others, and threaten to fire officers when they underperformed instead of coaching and training them.

The second officer also said in the complaint that Schrand had a "golden rule," which was that "He wears the Eagles." If someone disagreed with him about complaints or morale, the second officer alleges, he would say, "I wear the Eagles and they have been serving since breakfast."

In regards to these complaints, Byrne said "a number of those statements are false, and they will be the subject of litigation shortly in the future."

Schrand sued after Taser death of man in 2013

In 2013, when Schrand was still a sergeant with North College Hill police, the family of Corey McGinnis, a man who died after Schrand shocked him with a Taser, sued him, according to a report by Enquirer media partner Fox19.

The suit alleged Schrand unreasonably shocked McGinnis with a Taser on June 26, 2012, following an altercation during a basketball game. The lawsuit sought compensation for McGinnis' eight children, as well as Taser policy reforms.

A year later, the city of North College Hill and the McGinnis family settled a wrongful death lawsuit for $650,000 and agreed to a few changes to the city's Taser policy, Fox19 reported.
