headline: When Columbus boychoir left, its women's board refocused on creation of The Buckeye Ranch
fullText:
The Boychoir Women’s Board was organized in 1945 to support the Columbus Boychoir School, founded eight years earlier, with event planning and fundraising. But the school’s founder, Herbert Huffman, decided to move the school in 1950 to Princeton, New Jersey — becoming the world-renowned American Boychoir School, which finally had to close due to financial problems in 2017.

When the boychoir school left Columbus, the local women's board pivoted to become the Women’s Juvenile Service Board (WJSB) to support child welfare and juvenile services in Franklin County.

Within a few years of redirecting their efforts, they began planning to create their own home facility for troubled boys. The group’s plan was to create an interracial residential treatment center for troubled boys ages 12 to 16 who would benefit from care outside of their current home environment to help them avoid juvenile delinquency.

Creating a rehabilitation facility such as this in Franklin County was considered a preventative measure that would combat the number of children being sent to the Industrial School for Boys. The WJSB looked at similar facilities in Ohio, such as the Starr Commonwealth for Boys Van Wert home and the Boys’ Village in Smithville, as models for their home.

The WJSB raised more than $145,000 to purchase 75 acres of farmland in Grove City at 5665 Hoover Road and announced their plans to build the “Buckeye Ranch for Boys” in 1958. The women continued their fundraising efforts by selling boutonnieres, corsages, hats, and event tickets.

By November 1960, Ohio State University head football coach Woody Hayes, and Grove City Mayor Anton Patzer were shoveling dirt at the groundbreaking ceremony for the ranch. Construction was completed and the dedication took place less than a year later in summer 1961.

The Buckeye Boys Ranch opened with a single cottage that could house 8-12 boys. The original unit was named the Argo House in honor of Dorothy M. Argo, who was instrumental in acquiring the land and establishing the facility. The plan was to build four more units so the ranch could provide a temporary home for up to 50 boys at a time.

By 1979, 48 boys lived at Buckeye Boys Ranch. There was a fully accredited high school on the property, and they had a vocational program that provided the youths with career education and work experience.

The boys would learn landscaping, create products like cat litter and wooden toys, and market the products to local businesses. These entrepreneurial skills would hopefully help the boys long after they left the ranch.

Buckeye Ranch has continued to expand and grow since its 1961 beginnings and is still active today. The organization helps several thousand of young people and families every year with a variety of mental health and child welfare services. Buckeye Ranch now has six locations in Ohio, including the original 5665 Hoover Road location.

In 2023, The Buckeye Ranch and Nationwide Children's Hospital partnered to begin construction of Ohio's first psychiatric residential treatment facility for children at its Grove City campus. The $35-million project, which includes a new 57,000-square-foot residential mental health treatment facility and the renovation of two existing buildings on campus, will serve up to 48 youths who fall into a current gap in care in the state between needed hospitalization, going back home or going out of state for treatment. It is expected to open this summer 2025.

The founding members of the Women’s Juvenile Service Board would be amazed at what their efforts had achieved.

Nicole D. Sutton is Black Heritage Special Collections Librarian with the Columbus Metropolitan Library.

headline: After saving drowning infant, Sunbury native was named USO Coast Guardsman of the Year
fullText:
Logan Boyd said that when he graduated from Wittenberg University, he felt stuck and wanted to find a way to give back.

The Sunbury native and Big Walnut graduate said a family friend inspired him to join the United States Coast Guard.

"I thought that the service would help open some doors for me, and it has done way more than that. It's given me a lot of really great experiences and, you know, put me in touch with a lot of great people that are going to be friends for life," Boyd said.

Years later, from that place of feeling stuck and now a U.S. Coast Guard Boatswain's Mate 3rd Class stationed in Destin, Florida, Petty Officer Boyd was just named the 2025 USO Coast Guardsman of the Year.

On what would have otherwise been a normal evening in the fall of 2024, when the day was winding down, Boyd and some teammates were on an AOR, or Area of Responsibility, run.

They got a call notifying them that someone might be drowning and in need of emergency help.

While responding to the call, Boyd identified a person clinging to what looked like a lifeless infant on the shore.

'Right place, right time'

Boyd immediately began administering CPR and continued working to save the child's life, resuscitating the baby girl before handing her over to the care of emergency medical services.

"Me and another crew member jumped off the boat and ran over, and I started doing compressions on the baby while we talked to the family and tried to get some more information that we could pass along," Boyd said. 

"We took the baby on board, and I continued to do CPR."

Petty Officer Garrett Goodbread was one of Boyd's crew mates during the life-saving moment.

Uplifting the community: Carter Kindness is 'sprinkling' love across central Ohio

Reflecting on the situation, Goodbread said they didn't have any idea of the severity of the situation when the crew arrived, but Boyd sprang into action without any instruction once they realized it was an infant in dire need of life-saving resuscitation.

While Boyd and the crew didn't keep in touch with the child's family, he said he was glad he was there in that moment and the child survived.

"It was kind of right place, right time. (I'm) just happy that I could help," Boyd said.

"We just hope that when we get those situations to help and give back that we can take advantage of those things and get the outcome that we want."

Goodbread said the entire crew is excited for Boyd, who is a presence of humor and levity for their team.

Creating change: Dance therapy research for cancer survivors extended 5 years

"A lot of the things we do out here don't really get that much recognition, but the fact that this one is good, we're pretty excited for him," Goodbread said.

"He's just an all-around good guy."

Nominated by their command leadership for going above and beyond normal duties to perform heroic and selfless acts of bravery, Boyd and seven other military personnel were recognized at the 2025 USO Gala in Washington, D.C. on May 29.

"He's super happy all the time. He makes a lot of light (through) a lot of bad things we have around here. We see a lot of bad stuff, and he finds a way to take our minds off of it by making jokes. He's just good to have around," Goodbread said.

headline: Dr. Kube: Patient learns about peer pressure with an explosive injury
fullText:
As the weather started warming up and people became more active doing outdoor activities, we were seeing more people with traumatic injuries.

We refer to this as “trauma season,” as this is a seasonal occurrence. I was working in the Emergency Department (ED) on the first really warm summer weekend, and I saw numerous patients with traumatic injuries in the first few hours of my shift.

Some were involved in car and motorcycle accidents, and one young patient was injured when an ATV he was riding in rolled over. Thankfully none of these patients had life-threatening injuries and all ended up being OK.

I was walking by the charge nurse desk in the ED when I heard a paramedic calling to advise us of a patient they were bringing in. He was speaking quickly and sounded excited when he called in, which got my attention. They told us that they had an 18-year-old male, Thomas, who was injured when a firework exploded in his hand. He had sustained burns to his hands, chest and face.

Their report stated that the patient’s heart rate was elevated, but his blood pressure was normal. They had given the patient pain medications, yet you could still hear him shouting out in pain in the background. I alerted our trauma team that the patient would be arriving soon, and our team was assembled and ready in our trauma room a few minutes before the patient arrived.

Thomas was brought in the ED, directly to our trauma room. After we received report from the paramedics, we quickly moved him from the ambulance cot to the bed and rapidly began to assess him.

Dr. Kube: Mental health a priority to check with patients

One nurse placed an intravenous (IV) line in his arm so we could give him more pain medications. Another nurse placed stickers on Thomas' chest, arms and legs and attached him to our cardiac monitor. We began our focused trauma assessment that begins with the ABCs — airway, breathing and circulation.

I assessed Thomas’ airway and breathing by looking in his mouth and nose with a small light and checking for any signs of burns or swelling. I listened to his lungs with my stethoscope and made sure his lungs were symmetric and clear.

To assess his circulation, we felt Thomas’ pulses in his wrists and ankles. As we were assessing Thomas’ ABCs, we undressed him so we could visualize his body to check for injuries.

We also quickly evaluated his mental status by asking him to follow commands and asked him simple questions — like his name, the date and where he was. He told me that he did not have any drug allergies and said his pain level was “off the charts” in his hands, where he had sustained the greatest injury. I ordered Thomas more pain medications as we turned our attention to his hands.

He had very significant tissue loss to his right hand — which involved his index finger and middle finger. You could clearly see the bones of those digits because the tissue and skin was burned away. His thumb was burned but thankfully was much less affected than the other fingers. He had just superficial burns to his left hand.

After we fully assessed Thomas and gave him adequate pain medications, we moved him out of our trauma room and into a quieter room, where his parents came to see him. A short time later, the hand surgeon evaluated Thomas and discussed the plan for surgery to unfortunately amputate the end portions of his index and middle fingers, as there was no way they could be saved due to the severity of the tissue loss.

He planned to remove the burned tissue and skin to the thumb and make all attempts to preserve the function of the thumb as it is vital to allowing your hand to grasp and manipulate.

Thomas then had the opportunity to tell us what had happened. He was at a Memorial Day party with several friends, and a few guys had snuck in some alcohol. After several hours of drinking, another friend arrived to the party with fireworks and dared Thomas to hold onto the firework until the very last second before it exploded.

He was crying as he said he tried to throw the firework away from himself in time because he knew he was making a big mistake. That obviously did not happen, and the firework exploded while he was still holding it.

Research does suggest that males engage in higher risk-seeking behavior than females, however, this is a complex science that stems from a complex interaction of environmental and biological factors that can be difficult to separate.

Some studies have suggested that men tend to take more risks when under stress, while women take fewer risks when stressed, which may be in part due to hormonal differences affecting brain activity.

Dr. Kube: Young woman prioritizes her own health

While it is culturally accepted that women take less risks than men, a study showed no difference in risks between men and women when faced with the same consequences. Ultimately your risk-taking behavior depends on multiple factors, such as your upbringing, genes and personality traits.

Alcohol use is often associated with a change in an individual’s threshold for taking risks and frequently results in people taking chances in engaging in activities or behaviors they otherwise may not engage in.

Alcohol use may have contributed to Thomas’ accident, but he also succumbed to peer pressure, even though he knew he was taking a serious risk.

Thomas’ surgery went well, and the hand surgeon expected an uncomplicated post-operative course. Thomas, however, had a long course ahead of him. He would go through physical therapy to adjust to the loss of portions of his index and middle fingers.

Because the surgeon did not have to amputate any portion of Thomas’ thumb, he would be able to maintain a significant portion of the function of his right hand after going through physical therapy.

While Thomas had a bad injury and would suffer permanent consequences for his bad decision, things could have been much worse for him, and he was grateful this injury did not take his life.

Dr. Erika Kube is an emergency physician who works for Mid-Ohio Emergency Services and OhioHealth. She can be reached at: drerikakubemd@gmail.com.

headline: Central Ohio kids to participate in The Great Ladybug Hunt in June
fullText:
Grab your magnifying glass because it's time for a ladybug hunt.

For the first time, central Ohio kids can participate in a monthlong event to scout for rocks painted as ladybugs and even take part in painting the ladybug rocks themselves.

The Hous Foundation, a local nonprofit organization with a mission to remove financial barriers that prevent kids from participating in nonschool activities, will kick off its first-ever Great Ladybug Hunt for the entire month of June.

Why ladybugs in June? The 3-year-old organization was founded in honor of Annie Niewenhous and her two children, Izzy and Parker, who were killed in an act of domestic violence.

The event takes place during their memorial and is a remembrance for Niewenhous' love for nature and crafts — like painting ladybug rocks with her daughter.

Kids are encouraged to enjoy the summer weather outdoors by searching for hidden ladybugs and uploading photos of them to social media with #Housladybug to be entered into weekly drawings for raffle prizes.

"We hope that all of central Ohio will participate," said Sonya Thesing, executive director of The Hous Foundation. "I hope that it's a good beginning-of-the-summer activity for kids."

The event will end with a Jeni's Splendid Ice Creams fundraiser at the Columbus Commons on June 30 from 3-6 p.m.

Supporting activities for kids

Recreational activities that aren't associated with school are not accessible to every kid, but they should be. At least that's The Hous Foundation's mission.

Since getting its start, the foundation has helped 30 youths participate in activities. Thesing said they plan to surpass 50 this year.

"We are working with families to pay the cost of participation," Thesing said.

One single mother, Janae Walker, said she's especially grateful for The Hous Foundation for helping get her 8-year-old daughter, Naeyerie, into gymnastics in February.

"It's been a really positive impact on her; she seems happier and she looks forward to going on every session," Walker said. "Being a single mom, it can be expensive to pay for activities like gymnastics, but I think every kids deserves an opportunity to do something they enjoy."

Whether it be gymnastics, piano lessons and other sports, these activities instill long-lasting skills such as team building, improved self-esteem, confidence, higher grades in school and better attendance, Thesing said.

Math and science scores also increase when children engage in recreation.

"Part of our mission is to make sure all kids have access not only to participate in the activity, but also those long-term benefits," Thesing said.

Trending features reporter Amani Bayo can be reached at abayo@dispatch.com.

headline: Five years after George Floyd protests, activists, Columbus officials say more work needed
fullText:
When Columbus activist Aramis Sundiata first heard of George Floyd's death at the hands of a then-Minneapolis police officer in May of 2020, he brushed off the news.

"OK, another Black man got killed," Sundiata said. He was jaded after years of such deaths and little accountability for the officers responsible.

But sitting in his Linden bedroom as the news replayed Floyd’s death over and over again, Sundiata heard Floyd call out for his mother. He knew then something was coming. His phone was blowing up.

Starting May 28, three days after Floyd’s death, thousands of outraged protesters would flood Downtown Columbus, mirroring demonstrations across the country. The demonstrations lasted through the summer during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Columbus Division of Police wasn't prepared.

Officers fired pepper spray, flash grenades and wooden bullets into the crowds. Mounted officers, bicycle officers and cops in riot gear worked to disperse protesters. Some protesters damaged downtown Columbus storefronts.

Columbus Mayor Andrew J. Ginther declared a state of emergency and set a city-wide 10 p.m. curfew. Brian Steel, now president of the Fraternal Order of Police Capital Lodge No. 9, said the protests caught the city off guard, and police weren't adequately trained.

On May 28 of this year, while he stood outside OhioHealth Grant Medical Center after a shooting that injured two Mifflin Township police officers, Steel said that being a police officer is “one of the most impossible jobs."

In an interview for this story prior to the shooting, Steel said he believes Columbus needs leadership committed to reform that does not come at the expense of those who risk their lives every day to protect our communities.

"We must reject politicized approaches and instead embrace a path that protects community voices and the rights of officers alike," Steel said.

Officials describe the spring and summer of 2020 as a watershed moment for the city that exposed a need for police reform. A judge’s ruling and an independent review into the police response pointed to failures in leadership and divisions between the police and the community.

In the five years since, the city has ushered in several reforms. A Civilian Police Review Board was formed. The division revamped its responses to protests, founding a “dialogue team” to work with demonstrators. The city brought in Police Chief Elaine Bryant, a former Detroit Police Department deputy chief and the first Black woman to hold the post, to reform the division in 2021. The city offered 100 senior police officers buyouts so more reform-minded officers could take the lead.

More: Four ways policing in Columbus has changed five years after the death of George Floyd

But activists interviewed by the Dispatch say the changes aren't enough — they are glad to see some reform, but don't believe police are more accountable than they were five years ago, or that citizens are safe from wrongful uses of force.

The Columbus Division of Police declined to make Bryant or any other division members available for an interview for this story. Bryant provided a written statement detailing reforms that have taken place.

“In a very short time, these leadership initiatives have ushered in a cultural shift within our agency — a change I am extremely proud to highlight as Chief,” Bryant said in part. “As we look to the future, we remain committed to building on this strong foundation, striving for a Columbus that is safer, stronger, and more united.”

City officials say these changes are successful, but reform is a continuous, ongoing project.

“Sometimes the things that make us the most uncomfortable force us to grow, adapt and transform more than had we not been put in those positions or faced those times,” Ginther said.

Columbus City Council President Shannon Hardin said a lot of raw emotions and generations of pain came to a head at one time during the protests, and pressure from the community forced officials to act.

“It was hard, it was hurtful, but looking back five years, it was necessary because it allowed us to do things policy-wise that we had not and could not and would not have done,” Hardin said.

"Because we created the Civilian Review Board, because we instituted the body worn cameras on all of our officers, because we did Andre's Law, those things cumulatively create a level of the public knowing there is accountability."

Andre's law requires officers to activate body-worn cameras during encounters and requires them to call for medical help and render first aid following a use of force.

Steel pointed to other positive progress in the Columbus Division of Police, such as Columbus police liaison officers and youth outreach efforts.

'Out of control’ 

People disagree on what to call the weeks of demonstrations that followed Floyd’s death in Columbus. Sundiata calls it a “rebellion.” Steel said, “There were protests, and then there were riots.”

The demonstrations were largely peaceful by day, but devolved at night to include acts of vandalism and physical confrontations between police and protesters, according to an independent report released in April 2021. The review was headed by former U.S. Attorney Carter Stewart and Trevor Brown, dean of the John Glenn College of Public Affairs at Ohio State University.

Steel said the city was unprepared for the weeks of demonstrations. Officers worked 12-hour shifts in riot gear in sweltering heat with little training, he said. Many were also distraught by the footage of Floyd’s death, but the protesters appeared to blame them, Steel added.

He said they were face-to-face with shouting protesters during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, with minimal training on managing crowds and inconsistent communication.

From late May to mid-July, the Columbus Division of Police deployed about 1,400 officers, arresting 147 protesters and using 1,370 rounds of less-lethal munitions, according to the independent review.

Researchers said the city was unprepared for the protests of that size and energy. Communication within the police division was inconsistent, and officers received conflicting orders. Interviews showed “a large rift” between officers and the community, and Black communities in particular were distrustful, angry, and fearful of police.

Many protesters believed the use of force was unfair and indiscriminate. Some moments of police use of force were recorded on video.

On the morning of May 30, 2020, Hardin, Congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Franklin County Commissioner Kevin Boyce went to the corner of High and Broad Streets to stand with the demonstrators and encourage peaceful protesting.

Hardin said they witnessed a police force “that was out of control.” The police and community didn't trust each other, he said.

Boyce said officers were trying to get people to stay out of the street, and Boyce, Beatty and Hardin were trying to help. They saw police pepper-spray a woman and slam a man to the ground. Everyone started screaming, and Beatty started "going off, (saying) 'why would you do that?'" Boyce said.

Police pepper-sprayed the crowd and all three officials.

Later that day, Hardin attended his nephew’s kindergarten graduation. There, an older Black woman approached Hardin and told him she was terrified — if the police could do that to some of Columbus’ most powerful elected officials, what would they do to her family?

“That hurt me," Hardin said. "It was that sentiment that made it so that I had to turn this moment into policy ... I wasn't going to be quiet about the need for a civilian review board."

Beatty declined to be interviewed for this story, but said in a video statement at the time, "Too much force is not the answer to this."

Steel said officers did the best they could with the resources they had.

“Someone’s in your face for eight hours, screaming every word to you, and our officers of color had it the worst. And then you wonder why an officer might have a bad reaction?”

City Attorney Zach Klein also told the Dispatch that "our officers were thirsty for leadership" from the top brass and were not getting it.

The city received more than 800 complaints related to police actions during the protests. The city hired a local law firm, BakerHostetler, to investigate the complaints.

One officer received counseling for not filling out the proper paperwork. Three officers were charged with misdemeanor offenses. None were convicted.

“I was disappointed that there weren't more tools available to hold those officers accountable that we have now put in place that will help us do that in the future,” Ginther said.

The city did pay out at least $5.8 million in settlements to protesters injured in the protests.

The most visible move to hold officers accountable in the future came in November 2020, when voters approved the creation of the Columbus Civilian Police Review Board. The board reviews investigations into allegations of misconduct by Columbus police officers and recommends discipline. Early feedback has been mixed. Steel said the board makes police look more accountable, but exonerates officers at roughly the same rate.

In another reform effort, Klein’s office and the police developed immersion training for recruits that partners with neighborhood leaders to help officers better understand the communities they'll patrol. Many officers do not live in Columbus.

A different approach 

After the independent review and a ruling by federal Judge Algenon L. Marbley that favored injured protesters who sued the police, Columbus police Commander Duane Mabry was tasked with reworking the division’s crowd management tactics. He contacted Clifford Stott, a professor of social psychology at Keele University in England, who studies crowd psychology.

Stott and Mabry helped build the Columbus police dialogue team. Stott said he worked to teach Columbus police officers that the protests and the aftermath weren't an attack on police, but a learning opportunity.

“Approaching 2,500 locations across the United States experienced demonstrations,” Stott said. “But in only less than 10% of those locations did violence and property damage occur.”

In areas where violence did occur, like Columbus, police escalated the situation, Stott said. Columbus police were working from outdated crowd psychology theories and overusing force rather than communicating with people in the crowd, causing an escalating cycle of violence from the protesters and police, Stott said.

Today, dialogue team officers wear bright blue vests and speak with demonstrators. Their goal is to ensure people can safely express their free speech rights.

Related reading: After disgraceful 2020 protest response, Columbus police team now model for doing it right

The dialogue unit has gone on to train other departments, and Stott called them a “world leader” in responding to protests.

But Stott said that policing in America has changed very little since 2020.

“There’s only really one truism in public order and policing, and that is that change follows disaster,” Stott said. “The big problem in this area is that policing doesn’t really reform until something’s already gone badly wrong.”

Five years later 

Despite the reforms, many activists don’t believe enough has changed at the Columbus Division of Police. They are still jarred by what they witnessed that spring and summer.

DeJuan Sharp said police pepper-sprayed him and shot him with wooden bullets even though he followed directions. These days, police monitor traffic and block roads when protesters march, he said.

“They have evolved from being combative to a little bit helpful,” Sharp said. “That’s the best I can say.”

Trenae Williams, 44, a Columbus Realtor, attended the protests for weeks and said officers provoked the demonstrators.

“To actually see a police force or national guard, seemingly there to protect and serve, actually be the agitators or aggressors was kind of wild in real time,” Williams said.

Williams doesn’t think the police have changed for the better, though she wasn’t aware of the Civilian Review Board or the dialogue team. She said nationally, officers continue to use excessive or deadly force, particularly against Black people, and she wants them held accountable.

Columbus police shot and killed nine people in 2024. The shootings have sparked intermittent, smaller protests.

A jury convicted ex-officer Adam Coy in November of murdering Andre Hill, an unarmed Black man, in December 2020. As of this writing, a county judge is deciding whether Coy deserves another trial.

Former K-9 officer Ricky Anderson is pending trial on a murder charge for fatally shooting Donovan Lewis in his bed while attempting to serve a warrant. No date has been set for trial while the U.S. Supreme Court decides a Texas case that could have implications for police use of force cases nationally.

More reforms sought

Some activists aren’t satisfied with reforms because they oppose the idea of the police themselves.

Sundiata said the police are an oppressive force, less concerned with fighting crime than ensuring submission from the public. He said people locally, especially families of Black citizens killed by police, have made “righteous efforts” toward reform, but he would like to see a radically different approach to justice in which police don’t exist and people in communities work amongst themselves to right wrongs like theft.

“The state is an antagonistic force to the people always,” Sundiata said.

Other activists, like the Columbus Safety Collective, would like to reduce police involvement in situations like mental health and drug addiction crises. They say police aren’t well equipped to handle those calls, so sending a social worker or counselor instead could free up police resources and prevent police from using force against someone who is having a crisis, not committing a crime.

Since 2020, Columbus has established four alternative crisis response teams. They usually pair social workers or clinicians with police and other emergency responders to connect people to longer-term support services, such as mental health or substance abuse treatment.

But the city’s alternative response teams have limited hours and typically still involve police.

Chana Wiley, co-chair of the  Columbus Safety Collective executive committee, said city leaders have been receptive to alternative crisis response, but they've had years of discussion and still haven't fully funded a robust program.

For Wiley, it's personal. She has been advocating for police accountability and reform since her brother Jaron Thomas died in January 2017 after he called 911 in a mental crisis, and responding police restrained him. Federal courts struck down the family’s lawsuits against the police. But Wiley believes her brother might be alive today if a mental health professional, not an officer, had shown up in 2017.

The Columbus Safety Collective is collecting signatures to put the Community Crisis Response Amendment on the November ballot.

“We did tell them a couple of years ago if the funds aren’t used appropriately, you will see us at the ballot, and we just wanted to keep our word,” Wiley said.

headline: Columbus Jazz Orchestra to heat up Hinson Amphitheater with summer series
fullText:
Columbus Jazz Orchestra’s (CJO) 2025-26 season doesn’t begin until October, but you don’t have to wait until then to get into the swing of things.

With band leader Byron Stripling at the helm, CJO is heading into its summer series at the Hinson Amphitheater, 170 E. Dublin Granville Road in New Albany.

“There is no better way to spend summer nights than listening to jazz outside amongst Mother Nature and loved ones,” Katy Coy, CEO of Jazz Arts Group, said in a press release.

“This concert series is the definition of pure summer fun and extraordinary talent.”

Featuring a trio of high-energy al fresco performances, the series will get underway on June 7 with “Best of Broadway.” Attendees will hear showstopping Broadway numbers popularized by Ella Fitzgerald, Cole Porter, Irving Berlin and others.

In observation of Independence Day, “Red White & Blues” will offer Americana favorites and patriotic songs on July 5. The special guest band leader for this Fourth of July celebration will be Zach Compston, vice president of education and community engagement for Jazz Arts Group.

CJO will wind down the summer series with a big band dance party on Aug. 23.

All of the concerts will begin at 8 p.m. Doors for tables and premium admission will open at 6 p.m. Doors for general admission (lawn seating) will open at 6:30 p.m.

Tickets for front tables start at $94.80, rear tables at $71.60 and lawn seating at $47.40. Tickets can be purchased at jazzartsgroup.org or by calling the CAPA Ticket Center at 614-469-0939.

If you’re still jonesing for jazz after the series ends, the band will perform a free concert as a send-off to summer on Sept. 12 in Bicentennial Park. A special opener will appear at 5:30 p.m., followed by CJO at 7 p.m.

headline: Music Notes: June concerts include Buckeye Country Superfest, Rick Ross, Hozier
fullText:
Welcome to June, the month with the longest daylight hours of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. Those extra rays of sunshine will come in handy when Vampire Weekend kicks off this month’s concert lineup on June 2 at KEMBA Live!, 405 Neil Ave.

Despite their name, they won’t erupt into flames or crumble to ashes if exposed to sunlight, so cross your fingers and wish for summery weather because the show is outdoors, rain or shine.

Fun fact: Vampire Weekend’s name comes from a short film that frontman Ezra Koenig worked on while attending Columbia University.

Doors open at 6 p.m. The band Geese will be the opening act.

Get tickets for Vampire Weekend

Whether you prefer pop or hip-hop, new wave or new country, the list of concerts below offers a musical feast to satisfy assorted appetites!

All Out Music Festival

3 p.m. June 14, KEMBA Live!

Rebecca Black sang about “Friday” more than a decade ago, but she’ll be performing on a Saturday at this event supporting and celebrating members and allies of the LGBTQ+ community.

Started four years ago in Pittsburgh, All Out is making its Columbus debut with local celebrity Nina West as the host. In addition to Black, mainstage performers include Tinashe, Betty Who, Kaleena Zanders, VINCINT, Molly Grace, Jaesyun, Crystal Envy and Luxx Noir London. Local talent will appear on the Queertopia stage.

Part of the proceeds from the fest will go to the Nina West Foundation, which supports local nonprofits serving LGBTQ+ youth and families in Columbus.

Get tickets for All Out Music Fest

Santigold

7 p.m. June 16, Newport Music Hall, 1722 N. High St. 

The boundary-breaking Santigold grew up listening to reggae, jazz, Nigerian music, soul, punk and new wave, which influenced her genre-straddling style, which has received praise from critics for its innovativeness.

"The songs get better and weirder as she goes on," NPR’s John Morrison said of the Philly native’s music. "That ain't always an easy thing to pull off, to grow and make better music that's also more forward thinking, more experimental."

Get tickets for Santigold

Queens of the Stone Age

6 p.m. June 17, KEMBA Live!

Queens of the Stone Age formed after the breakup of frontman Josh Homme's previous band Kyuss. Fun fact: The band's name came from a nickname their producer Chris Goss had bestowed upon Kyuss.

In a 2000 Ozzfest interview, Homme said the band wanted to strike a balance between masculine and feminine in the rock world, and "Kings of the Stone Age" would have been too macho.

"Rock should be heavy enough for the boys and sweet enough for the girls. That way, everyone's happy and it's more of a party. Kings of the Stone Age is too lopsided," Homme said.

Get tickets for Queens of the Stone Age

Hozier

7:30 p.m. June 18, Historic Crew Stadium, 1 Black and Gold Blvd. 

Before we go any further, let’s get one thing straight: Hozier rhymes with “cozier,” not “closure.”

That said, Andrew Hozier-Byrne is quite the dichotomy. On one hand, he’s a lyrical poet who writes songs that often convey his social and political beliefs — e.g., "Take Me to Church," "Eat Your Young" and "Nobody's Soldier.” On the other hand, he’s practically a TikTok deity — some fans adoringly call him “Forest Daddy.”

Get tickets for Hozier

DEVO

7 p.m. June 20, KEMBA Live!

The Ohio band is probably best-known for their headgear, called energy domes, which have been mistaken for flowerpots, dog bowls and lampshades, and their biggest hit, "Whip It." Fun fact: The Top 20 hit was penned as an anthem of encouragement for former President Jimmy Carter.

Get tickets for DEVO

Buckeye Country Superfest

3 p.m. June 21, Ohio Stadium, 411 Woody Hayes Drive 

This year’s megaconcert will feature double headliners Kane Brown, who first turned heads with his songs on social media, and Jelly Roll, who promoted his music the old-school way: By selling mixtapes out of his car.

Openers Megan Moroney, Treaty Oak Revival, Dasha and Conner Smith will warm up the crowd.

Wanna do a little Superfest pregaming? Head across from the stadium to Fan Fest, a free and open-to-all-ages tailgate party where fans can hang out from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. In addition to performances by Austin Snell, Lanie Gardner, George Pippen and Ian Harrison, the event will offer food, beverages, official festival and artist merch and more. No tickets are required!

Get tickets for Buckeye Country Superfest

Modest Mouse

6:30 p.m. June 21, KEMBA Live!

If this catchy, darkly humorous Pacific Northwest band is ever looking for a moonlighting gig, they're the perfect fit for television advertising. Their song "Gravity Rides Everything" was featured in a commercial for the Nissan Quest minivan, while their Grammy-nominated hit, "Float On," was used to hawk American Express Platinum. (The latter is also fun to play in "Guitar Hero.")

Get tickets for Modest Mouse

Nationwide Picnic with the Pops: Rick Ross

8 p.m. June 21, Columbus Commons, 160 S. High St. (Gates open at 6 p.m.)

Performing at the Columbus Bicentennial Pavilion, the Columbus Symphony will usher in the annual summer concert series with “A Night of Symphonic Hip Hop,” with rapper Rick Ross, known for songs such as "Mafia Music," "Money in the Grave" and "Hustlin'."

Before his career blew up, Ross was a correctional officer for 18 months — not exactly the best way to earn street cred … and it gives a whole new meaning to the title of his song “Usual Suspects.”

headline: Four ways policing in Columbus has changed five years after the death of George Floyd
fullText:
In the spring and summer of 2020, protests and demonstrations in response to the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis rocked Columbus.

Since then, the city and the Columbus Division of Police have ushered in a variety of reforms and changes designed to increase police accountability and change the way police handle situations from protests to mental health crises.

More: Five years after George Floyd protests, activists, Columbus officials say more work needed

Here are four of the key changes:

Columbus Civilian Police Review Board

In November 2020, Columbus voters approved an independent civilian board to review accusations of misconduct. Voters also approved the creation of the Department of the Inspector General, which investigates police misconduct and excessive use of force.

Today, the Civilian Police Review board has 11 members.

Jacqueline Hendricks, a retired Detroit police officer and former investigator for the Detroit Office of Inspector General, was appointed Columbus’ first inspector general in Feb. 2022.

Citizens can file complaints to the Department of Inspector General in person, online and by phone.

Columbus Division of Police buyouts

In 2022, the city selected 100 senior Columbus police officers with 25 or more years of experience for $200,000 retirement incentive buyouts. The city said these buyouts would offer officers resistant to change and reform a way out.

Four commanders, nine lieutenants, 28 sergeants and 59 officers were selected. They came from a variety of units, including the SWAT, basic training and community service unit, as well as the chief’s office.

Most or all of the officers in the mounted unit were included in the list. The unit had come under criticism during crowd control for the George Floyd demonstrations.

The 100 officers came from 217 who applied for the buyouts. About 500 were eligible to apply.

Dialogue Team and crowd response changes

After a $5.75 million settlement with injured protestors who sued police and an independent post-incident analysis that found flaws in Columbus’ protest response, Columbus police sought to revamp its response to protests.

Working with international crowd psychology experts, Columbus police founded a Dialogue Team. Its officers wear bright blue vests and appear at protests. They say they work with protestors and demonstrators to find ways they can safely express their First Amendment rights.

Columbus also restricted officers from using tear gas, pepper spray and other “control agents” against nonviolent protestors and set limits to use of “less lethal” weapons like wooden bullets in a City Council ordinance passed in June 2022.

The ordinance codified a preliminary injunction restricting the use of those weapons by Chief U.S. District Judge Algenon L. Marbley in the lawsuit from injured demonstrators.

Alternative Response Teams

Columbus has adopted several programs combining healthcare and social workers with emergency workers to better respond to certain non-criminal incidents, including crises that arise from untreated mental illnesses or addiction.

Today, Columbus has four Alternative Crisis Response Teams: the Rapid Response Emergency and Addiction Crisis Team, the Right Response Unit, the Specialized Program Assessing Resource Connectivity and the Mobile Crisis Response Unit.

The teams generally work by pairing social workers or healthcare workers with police to triage and respond to incidents, and by linking people suffering from crises to longer term resources to address their underlying conditions.

Other steps

In addition, Mayor Andrew J. Ginther hired Chief Elaine Bryant in 2021 as the first person to be hired as chief from outside the department's current ranks.

Following the December 2020 death of Andre Hill, City Council passed Andre's Law, which requires officers to have their body cameras turned on and provide medical aid. Columbus also funded an upgrade to the department's body worn cameras.

headline: Replay: Scottie Scheffler wins by 4 strokes to repeat as Memorial Tournament champion
fullText:
Scottie Scheffler shot a final-round 2-under-par 70 to win the Memorial Tournament on June 1.

He is the second player to win consecutive Memorials. Tiger Woods is the other, having won three in a row from 1999-2001.

Scheffler had one bogey in the final round, his only bogey in this year's tournament.

This was Scheffler’s third win in his past four starts.

Scheffler finished at 10 under for the tournament, and was followed by Ben Griffin, who shot 1 over in the final round to finish at 6 under for the tournament.

Sepp Straka was third at 5 under, followed by Nick Taylor at 4 under. Maverick McNealy and Russell Henley tied for fifth at 2 under.

Scottie Scheffler in position to win

Ben Griffin’s drive on the par-4 No. 17 hit a spectator, leaving a red ball mark on his back. Griffin stopped and autographed his glove and gave it to the fan, then proceeded to double-bogey the hole.

Meanwhile, Scottie Scheffler remained steady and parred the hole to stretch his lead to three strokes with one hole to play.

Scheffler is at 10 under. Griffin is at 6 under. Sepp Straka is third at 5 under.

Live scores: Who is leading the Memorial Tournament?

For up-to-the-minute scoring, see our scoreboard powered by USA Today here.

Memorial Tournament names Aussie David Graham as 2026 honoree

Australian David Graham, who from a certain perspective became the first and only left-handed golfer to win the Memorial Tournament, has been selected by the Captains Club to be the tournament's 2026 honoree.

Graham, 79, first learned to golf left-handed before switching sides at age 14 when a co-worker in the pro shop where he was employed convinced him to make the change. He quickly became proficient at the game, and in 1968 turned professional, honing his craft on the Australian and Asian Tours. He earned his PGA Tour card in 1971 and collected his first win in 1972 at the Cleveland Open.

Graham won eight times on tour, including two majors -- the 1979 PGA Championship and 1981 U.S. Open. He also won the 1980 Memorial. He has 36 career tour wins that came on six different continents, and won five times on the Champions Tour before retiring in 2004.

Ben Griffin is alive! Bridies No. 16 to cut Scottie Scheffler lead to 2

Ben Griffin followed his eagle on No. 15 with a birdie on the par-3 No. 16. Scottie Scheffler parred the hole, so he now leads Griffin by two strokes.

Scheffler is at 10 under while Griffin is at 8 under. Next is Sepp Straka at 5 under.

Ben Griffin eagles No. 15 to retain hope

Scottie Scheffler birdied the par-5 15th but was outdone by Ben Griffin's eagle on the same hole.

Scheffler is at 10 under while Griffin is at 7 under. Next is Sepp Straka at 5 under.

Scottie Scheffler leads by 4 strokes with 4 holes to play

On the hole the leaders were warned for slow play, Ben Griffin bogeyed the par-4 13th to fall four strokes behind Scottie Scheffler.

Each parred No. 14.

Scheffler is at 9 under while Griffin and Sepp Straka are at 5 under. Next is Nick Taylor at 3 under.

Scottie Scheffler, Ben Griffin given warning for slow play

The leading twosome of Scottie Scheffler and Ben Griffin received a warning for slow play, according to the CBS telecast.

Scheffler leads Griffin by 3 strokes.

Another bogey by Ben Griffin stretches Scottie Scheffler's lead to 3

Ben Griffin bogeyed the par-3 12th hole while Scottie Scheffler parred.

Scheffler is at 9 under, three strokes ahead of Griffin.

Trailing Griffin by one at 5 under are Sepp Straka and Nick Taylor.

Scottie Scheffler birdies No. 11 to stretch lead to 2 strokes

Both Scottie Scheffler and Ben Griffin went for the green on the tough par-5 11th hole. Both carried the water but missed left. While Griffin’s landed in deep rough, Scheffler’s was in trampled grass and in a better position.

Griffin asked for a rules judgment because his left foot was close to a sprinkler cap. He played it anyway and chipped close to the hole.

Scheffler made a 14-foot birdie putt to go to 9 under. Griffin then missed from 5 feet to fall two strokes behind Scheffler.

Rare Scottie Scheffler bogey trims lead over Ben Griffin’s to 1 stroke

Scottie Scheffler hit his tee shot near a tree on the par-4 10th and had to chip out onto the fairway. He then hit onto the green and two-putted for his first bogey of the tournament. He is at 8 under, one stroke ahead of Ben Griffin.

Nick Taylor is in third at 5 under, with Russell Henley and Sepp Straka next at 4 under.

Scottie Scheffler birdies No. 7, extends lead over Ben Griffin to 2 strokes

Scottie Scheffler broke his string of pars with a birdie on the par-5 No. 7. He is at 9 under and leads Ben Griffin by two strokes and Nick Taylor by three.

Brandt Snedeker makes most of sponsor exemption

Brandt Snedeker, ranked 430th in the world, got into the Memorial only because of a sponsor exemption. The 44-year-old has an endorsement deal with tournament presenter Workday. He turned the special invitation into a chance to prove himself, which he accomplished by shooting a final-round 65 that puts him in a tie for ninth at the moment.

Ben Griffin birdies No. 5, cutting Scottie Scheffler lead to 1 stroke

Scottie Scheffler missed a short birdie putt on No. 5, and Ben Griffin followed with a birdie putt of his own.

Scheffler has parred every hole on June 1 and is at 8 under and leads Griffin by one stroke. Nick Taylor and Sepp Straka are three back at 5 under.

Ben Griffin bogeys No. 4, moving Scottie Scheffler's lead to 2 shots

Scottie Scheffler has not hit a green in regulation in the final round, but he is even par and at 8 uunder has a two-shot lead over Ben Griffin and Nick Taylor.

Griffin has two bogeys and a birdie and is 1 over for the round. Taylor is 1 under for the round with two birdies and a bogey.

What's with Ben Griffin's sunglasses?

Ben Griffin has worn aviator sunglasses this weekend that don't look like customary sporting eyewear.

Golfweek's Adam Schupak provided details about why Griffin wears them.

Griffin has been wearing sunglasses on the course since the 2024 RBC Canadian Open last June, where he finished second, due to seeing floaters. Since that first week with a designer knockoff brand he happened to have in his bag, he’s relied on U Swing sunglasses. “It hasn’t affected my vision – I still see floaters – but they darken things and make the floaters less defined,” he said. “I think they also help me with reading greens and seeing slopes better.”

Originally, he wore a pair of designer knockoffs that he found in his house that he had purchased a year earlier with no significance to golf. But before long he admired a model of aviator-style glasses worn by and endorsed by fellow Tour pro C.T. Pan and they've become Griffin's super power — he's won twice this season sporting them.

“I Venmo-ed him $20 and he shipped me a pair,” Griffin recalled. “I’ve been wearing them ever since.”

He added: “Sunglasses are solely just to make it darker and, honestly, it helps with the floaters because the floaters are dark, and so when it's really bright they're way more defined, especially on a golf course where there's not much shade. So, when I have the sunglasses on I don't see 'em quite as much. That's really the only benefit.”

Here comes Sepp Straka

Sepp Straka is 2 under after three holes and is three shots behind leader Scottie Scheffler.

This comes after he shot a 66 on May 31 to move close to contention.

Watch the Memorial Tournament with a Fubo free trial

Ben Griffin birdies No. 2 to get to within 1 shot of lead

After bogeying the first hole to drop two shots behind leader Scottie Scheffler, Ben Griffin birdied No. 2 with a 5-foot putt to get to 7 under. Scheffler has opened with two pars.

Brandt Snedeker moves into top 10 as strong round continues

After opening the day at 6 over par, Snedeker continues to climb as his final round comes to a close. Through 16 holes, Snedeker is 7 under, putting him on pace to tie for the best individual round of the 2025 Memorial Tournament.

Snedeker is now tied for 10th at 1 under. He shot 75, 73 and 74, respectively, on each of the first three days.

Scottie Scheffler extends lead on Ben Griffin after first hole

Scheffler sunk a 7-foot putt to shoot par on his first hole of the day, but things didn't go as easily for Griffin, who missed a similar putt by six inches and settled for a bogey.

Scheffler now drops to 8 under, two strokes ahead of Griffin who is alone in second place.

Scottie Scheffler, Ben Griffin get final rounds underway

Scheffler opened the final round one stroke ahead of Griffin at a tournament-best 8 under, and the two have now teed off on the first hole. Scheffler is vying to be the first golfer to win consecutive Memorial Tournament titles since Tiger Woods did some from 1999-2001.

Watch as Jordan Spieth just misses hitting fan with shot

Spieth opened the day tied for fourth at 3 under, and while he managed to shoot par on the first hole his day got off to an inauspicious start. The television broadcast captured a shot from Spieth that flew just over the heads of a crowd of spectators, and you can see it below.

Shane Lowry, Sam Burns move up in top 10

Lowry entered the final day at 2 under, tied for seventh overall, but has already gained a stroke by birdieing the opening hole to improve to 3 under and a four-way tie for fourth. Burns, meanwhile, started at par and birdied his third hole when he sunk a 7-foot putt and is now tied for 10th at 1 under.

Ludvig Aberg finishes third-best round of entire tournament

After shooting a 77 in the third round, Ludvig Aberg had the fifth-earliest tee time for the final day of the 2025 Memorial Tournament. He opened Round 4 at 7 over par, but he closed with one of the best rounds of the entire tournament.

Aberg had six birdies and shot par on the other 12 holes, finishing the day with a 66. Only two other golfers have bested that number so far in this year's event: Sam Burns shot 65 in the second round and Ben Griffin did so on the first day.

Top 10 on leaderboard getting final rounds underway

Russell Henley entered the final day of the tournament at 1 under par, tied for 10th in the standings. He began Round 4 around 1:10 p.m. and opened the day with a bogey, dropping him back to par for the tournament and a tie for 11th place.

Scottie Scheffler leads Ben Griffin by one stroke. They tee off at 2:05 p.m.

Ludvig Aberg, Brandt Snedeker sharing lead for best Round 4

Aberg is through 13 holes and Snedeker through eight, but both are 5 under while going through their final rounds at this year's tournament. Both Aberg and Snedeker have five birdies apiece as the latter opened the day finishing under par on his first three holes.

Snedeker is 1 over for the tournament, currently tied for 15th, while Aberg is tied for 21st at 2 over.

Austin Eckroat first golfer to finish his round

Austin Eckroat has finished his solo round and is the first player to make the cut to be done at the 2025 Memorial. Eckroat teed off alone at 8:55 a.m. and finished the day right around 12:10 p.m., shooting 6 over to finish the tournament at 17 over. After shooting 73 on each of the first two days, Eckroat finished at 81 in Round 3 and 78 in Round 4.

Five collegiate golfers presented with 2025 Jack Nicklaus Award

As the final day of competition gets underway, five golfers were recognized as national players of the year for their respective collegiate divisions.

David Lee of North Carolina (Division I), Adam Duncan of Colorado Christian (Division II), Jonathan McEwen of Washington & Lee (Division III), Jack Whaley of Dalton State (NAIA) and Adam Bresnu of Odessa (NJCAA) were all recognized during the morning at Muirfield Village Golf Club.

"This year's group of winners once again puts on display the incredible depth of talent in the collegiate game that has led to parity at every level, evident by our Division I, II and III recipients being the first Nicklaus Award recipient in their school's history," Nicklaus said in a statement.

Watch: leader Scottie Scheffler hears advice from fan after standout Round 3

The 2024 Memorial Tournament champion enjoyed the first bogey-free round he's ever played at Muirfield Village Golf Club when he climbed to first place at 8 under par. After finishing Round 3, Scheffler got some friendly advice from one of his fans.

Matt Fitzpatrick enjoying best start so far

After entering the final day of the tournament shooting 9 over par, the native of Sheffield, England, has had a better go of things through the front nine. Although he bogeyed the opening hole, Fitzpatrick recovered with a birdie on No. 2 and another on No. 8, but the highlight was an eagle on 7 when he hit his second shot 275 yards and finished with a putt from about 4 feet.

headline: New retail development proposed near downtown Dublin features walkability, town square
fullText:
A developer is seeking to make a “walkable, high-quality shopping destination” in Dublin’s Bridge Street District.

Columbus-based Wood Cos. is proposing a 94,000 square foot development near West Bridge Street and Monterey Drive, according to a concept plan submitted to the Dublin Planning and Zoning Commission.

This is the first project for Wood Cos. outside of the Short North Arts District in Columbus, where the company owns several apartments and commercial buildings for longtime establishments such as Northstar Café, Brassica, Jeni’s and some Cameron Mitchell restaurants.

Wood Cos. President Tyler Puhl emphasized in an interview with The Dispatch that the project is still in early stages — the land remains under contract, and the project would require multiple additional presentations to the zoning board — but the company is looking forward to applying its experience of “creating unique and treasured experiences” in the Short North to the suburbs.

“We’re still in the early innings of this project, and nothing's set in stone, but our team is excited to do what we do best: Deliver top-of-market buildings with lasting materials and a standout mix of retailers that create wonderful experiences. We are long-term holders with a long-term vision to create community value,” Puhl said.

The developer is aiming for the majority of the space to be non-food and beverage retail. Puhl said he couldn't comment on what specific stores could go into the development but noted the western part of central Ohio "could use more apparel shopping."

The development is across the street from John Sells Middle School and next to the Dublin Cemetery, a few hundred feet west of historic downtown Dublin. A Shell gas station on the lot stands to be demolished if the project moves forward, as the plan includes reworking most of the space.

Dublin Development LLC, based in Delaware, owns most of the parcels. However, the city has owned one of the parcels at Bridge Street and Monterey Drive since 2005, auditor records show.

The development emphasizes pedestrian accessibility and accessible open space, which would link the businesses with a 15,000 square foot “town square” at the center of the development that could host community events. The plan also calls for linking the development to the existing Monterey Park, just south of the lot. There are 470 parking spots included in the development, mostly in a new two-story garage on the eastern side of the lot, which meets the minimum number of spots that city code requires.

Dublin’s future land use plan designates the area as a “mixed-use village,” which specifies a “small-scale, pedestrian-oriented district preserved and developed with respect to historic building context and character.”

Palisades Village in Los Angeles inspired the design for the project in Dublin, as both feature “small-scale, high-quality buildings with diverse rooflines and carefully selected materials,” according to the project narrative, which will compliment the surrounding neighborhood.

The Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to review the concept plan at its June 5 meeting.

Anna Lynn Winfrey covers the western suburbs for The Columbus Dispatch. She can be reached at awinfrey@dispatch.com.

headline: How did Memorial Tournament, Muirfield Village get their names? Jack Nicklaus explains
fullText:
The heavens have a way of dropping seas of liquid sunshine on the Memorial Tournament, so it makes sense Muirfield Village Golf Club was birthed in mud after being conceived by a Golden Bear.

The light bulb first went off to build a Columbus-area championship golf course and accompanying PGA Tour event in 1964, after the PGA Championship at Columbus Country Club drew a big crowd. But the idea did not germinate until 1966 at Augusta National Golf Club, where a 26-year-old Jack Nicklaus and friend Ivor Young began to dream a few days before Nicklaus won his sixth major championship.   

“What if…?”

The friends from Columbus envisioned something akin to the Masters coming to their hometown, though Nicklaus insists there was never any intent to turn the Memorial into a carbon copy of the Masters, or become a fifth major championship.

It took another 10 years for the Memorial to come into existence, and during the lead-up to the first tournament in 1976 Nicklaus sent Young to find a site worthy of a world-class course. 

Finding perfect piece of golf course property was group effort

Nicklaus and Young joined with former Ohio State quarterback Pandel Savic and businessmen Robert Hoag and David Sherman, with help from golf course architect Pete Dye, to zero in on farm acreage in Dublin, which then had a population of about 700, and the work began. PGA Tour commissioner Joe Dey visited the site early in the process.

“Joe came out here and walked in the mud with me,” Nicklaus said.

Construction began in 1972, and while traipsing through muck up to their ankles, Nicklaus and Dey kicked around names for the new golf course, including “The New Course.”

Luckily, that one didn’t win out. 

“We named the area Muirfield Village. I didn’t want to name it directly Muirfield because I didn’t want it to be a dead copy,” Nicklaus said, referencing the Scottish course where he won the 1966 British Open. “I was so happy with what happened with me at Muirfield, winning the British Open at a place where I wasn’t supposed to win. It was a golf course with very narrow fairways, very high rough, not typical Jack Nicklaus, they thought in 1966, could win at. I was so proud of that, this place became Muirfield Village.”

Nicklaus, from Upper Arlington, emphasized that “Village” has always followed “Muirfield.”

“It’s never been Muirfield,” he said. "Always Muirfield Village, and then we finally just settled on Muirfield Village Golf Club."

As for naming the Memorial Tournament, which early on had a working title of the Memorial at Muirfield Village, that credit goes to Dey.

“We’re walking through the mud, which is what it was when we first got here, and trying to figure out what kind of concept we want for the tournament,” Nicklaus said. “Joe came up with the idea of, he says, ‘It’s Memorial Day. And around Memorial time why don’t we honor the past people who have contributed to the game of golf in the past?

“I said, ‘Fantastic,’ … but I don’t want to be selecting those people. I don’t think that’s the right way to do it.” 

Dey offered another idea, of creating a Captains Club of golf dignitaries who would “take the pressure off you and your shoulders,” Nicklaus said, adding the Captains Club not only would select the annual honoree but serve as the tournament’s “guiding light.”

Jack Nicklaus modeled the Memorial loosely on the Masters

Among the first captains was Clifford Roberts, chairman of Augusta National, who told Nicklaus “You’ve got an opportunity to do here in 10 years what it’s taken us 40 to do at Augusta.”

Roberts opened his books to Nicklaus, offering support and guidance for “whatever you want to know.”

Nearly 50 years later, and Nicklaus takes great pride in what the Memorial has become, and how it helped Dublin grow from a sleepy bedroom community into a 1980s hot spot for growth in Franklin County.

“You look back at what happened and where it went and how it started from a very small, humble beginning,” Nicklaus said. “The whole idea of the Memorial Tournament was to bring golf back to Columbus, a place where I grew up, to thank the people in central Ohio for the support they gave me through all my career.”

As for Muirfield Village's initial design, Nicklaus would do it differently today.

“From a design standpoint, I wouldn’t have designed the golf course this way,” he said. “What I mean by that is I designed it basically for a tournament, and spent the next 50 years trying to ease it enough so the average member can play it. I would have done it the other way around, would have had it a little more user friendly to start with, which is what I do now, and if I want to lengthen a hole here or there to handle a tournament, I would do it that way.”

Live and learn. 

Watch the Memorial Tournament with a Fubu free trial

“In those days, that’s what the (golf course) owner wanted, but most owners today want a golf course for their membership, and if they want to have an event to be able to stretch it to handle that event. I think that’s a much more practical way of playing golf for 51 weeks of the year.”

But for that 52nd week? Muirfield Village, especially when the heavens open the floodgates, is a beast of a test for the world’s best golfers. The player who wins at Jack’s Place deserves a toast, whether with a famous clubhouse milkshake or something stronger.

Here’s mud in your eye. And everywhere else, too. After all, it’s the Memorial.

headline: With few natural lakes, central Ohio's waters require infusions of fish
fullText:
Ohio wasn’t exactly steeped in water after the crushing weight of glacial ice covered much of it.

The melting did leave behind an abounding Lake Erie, some picturesque streams prone to flooding and drying, and about 110 natural ponds, generously known as lakes, of 5 acres or larger.

However, historical dwellers in what became Franklin County had no lakes of 5 acres or larger. Marshes were not uncommon, but water needs were met mostly by two rivers, known today as the Scioto and the Olentangy, and three creeks, Big Darby, Big Walnut and Alum.

The great outdoors: More on central Ohio hunting and fishing

Fishing wasn't a big part of village life. A few small, natural watering holes were available to anyone willing to take a long walk toward what became Pickaway and Licking counties.

These days much is taken for granted, such as the fact most of Ohio’s important recreational waters wouldn’t exist had they not been constructed to feed canals, to control floods or to supply people with water.

Ohio's artificial lakes outnumber natural lakes by about 20 to one. Artificial impoundments cover about 30 times more surface area than do natural lakes and ponds not counting Lake Erie, according to the Ohio Department of Natural Resources.

That which is made by hand assuredly requires tending lest it revert to a more natural state.

Take, for example, fish life.

Most inland lakes require regular infusions of saugeyes, yellow perch, muskellunge, catfish and bluegills.

The visible hand also adds ingredients to the ecological recipe, such as bacteria-nurturing agricultural runoff.

Here we are, then, and it’s doubtful many people would trade what is now for what was then.

One of the state’s artificial lakes, its largest at almost 12,900 acres, received for the first time last week about 217,000 artificially grown saugeyes measuring 1 to 2 inches.

The plan is to replenish the saugeye stock annually at Grand Lake St. Marys, a popular attraction that spans part of Mercer and Auglaize counties near Celina. When built in the mid-19th century to feed a canal linking Lake Erie and the Ohio River, Grand Lake was the largest man-made impoundment in the world.

Despite its expansive footprint, the lake is shallow at only 5 to 7 feet on average.

Saugeyes, a hybrid offspring of the native sauger and walleye, are far more tolerant of heat and shallow water than their parent species. That makes saugeyes a good fit with many Ohio impoundments, including Alum Creek, Hoover and Buckeye lakes.

Buckeye, another canal lake, is shallow, aging and has needed costly maintenance. It requires yearly fish infusions of millions of saugeyes, hybrid striped bass and yellow perch.

One separator between Buckeye and Grand lakes is that chances are next to nil that an escaping stocked hybrid from Buckeye is going to get where it can mess with local fish communities. Nor is a saugeye let loose in Grand Lake likely to mingle with Lake Erie walleye, but as a safeguard, the fish are treated at the hatchery to ensure they are sterile when released.

Another separator is blue-green algae, actually cyanobacteria, which have largely spared Buckeye but have been a persistent summer problem at Grand Lake St. Marys for more than a decade. Cyanobacteria produce a toxin that has been associated with human health problems.

Eating fish taken from water rife with cyanobacteria comes with cautions. The cyanobacteria outbreaks at Grand Lake St. Marys have been linked to nutrient overload wrought from animal farms.

Biofilters designed to reduce cyanobacteria are reportedly operating as intended this year. That hopefully will continue.

headline: 'They were better than us': Columbus Crew reflect on 5-1 loss vs Lionel Messi, Inter Miami
fullText:
In over two seasons under Wilfried Nancy, the Crew had never conceded more than four goals in a game. That changed with their 5-1 loss at Inter Miami on May 31.

The Crew entered their meeting with Miami, which marked their seventh game in a 28-day span, already dealing with uncharacteristic defensive struggles. After allowing just 13 goals through the first 14 games of the regular season, Columbus gave up a combined five in their two most recent matchups against Charlotte FC and Nashville SC.

Replay: Lionel Messi scores twice, Columbus Crew handed 5-1 loss vs Inter Miami

Miami took little time figuring out the holes in the Crew's defense and took advantage in the 13th minute when forward Tadeo Allende received a pass from Lionel Messi on a run to score the first goal of the game.

"They were better than us," Nancy said. "We were reactive, not proactive. We were slow a bit, not only physically but also mentally. After that, they did what the team wanted to do in terms of playing the ball in behind, and we were reactive. ... This season we've been good, but today, we were not good – simple as that."

Miami scored again when Messi capitalized on an error from Crew goalkeeper Nicholas Hagen to record the first of two goals. Messi's second goal occurred 11 minutes after Allende's.

The Crew went into halftime down 3-0 but showed their only bit of life in the 58th minute when defender Cesar Ruvalcaba scored his first MLS goal with a header off a corner kick.

Scoring failed to boosted the Crew's momentum as they went back down three goals six minutes later when striker Luis Suarez scored. Substitution Fafa Picault sent the final dagger with a goal at the 89-minute mark.

The Crew finished this 28-day span with a 1-2-4 record, putting their record at 7-3-7 and dropping their ranking from as high as first in the Eastern Conference on May 10 to fifth.

"It's hard mentally, but it's not the end of the world," Crew midfielder Mo Farsi said. "We're still in the playoffs spot. ... It’s a bit of a tough moment, but we have to stay positive and keep working. That's it, just don't forget the beginning of the season that we had. It’s not because right now it's hard that we have to have to panic."

Without 2 key defenders, Columbus Crew backline woes reach a low vs Inter Miami

There have been teams that have attempted to break through the Crew's backline with long passes during counterattacks, but no team had as much success as Miami.

Of Miami's five goals, three were assisted by long up-field passes.

"Usually, we always have pressure on the ball to read that, and if we don't have pressure, we drop and we adjust," Nancy said. "We didn't do it. When the ball was in the air, it was too late, and we should have reacted before. This is something that we didn't do. That's why we got punished."

The Crew were without defender Sean Zawadzki, who was credited with containing Messi in Columbus' 1-0 loss to Miami on April 19, due to a knee injury. Ten minutes into this Miami matchup, the backline also lost Malte Amundsen to a leg injury.

Columbus Crew unable to comeback from first-half collapse vs Inter Miami

The Crew's entire lineup went into halftime knowing they'd been outplayed by Miami.

Along with the defense allowing two long balls that led to goals, Hagen showed his first signs of struggle since taking over in goal for an injured Patrick Schulte two games earlier. On Messi's first goal, Hagen sent the pass directly to Messi, leading to the shot.

The Crew only took three shots, none on goal.

"You can imagine at halftime I was not happy," Nancy said. "They were not happy, too. … This is rare that we are like this. That's why I was not happy and I felt it at halftime, I had to ask myself - and also my staff - to think about why we had a lack of personality. Usually, this is not us. This was my message. We had a kind of reaction in the second half, but still the same."

Columbus Crew go into FIFA international break following Inter Miami loss

Due to the FIFA international break, the Crew have nearly two weeks to regroup before returning to the field on June 14 to face the league's top team, the Vancouver Whitecaps.

Nancy, however, is ready to turn the corner on this loss and Columbus' winless streak.

"I don't want a break," Nancy said. "I want to go back and to work. At the same time, they need a break and everybody needs a break. That's why we're going to take the time to analyze this game. It won't be difficult, to be honest, to analyze this game because we got punished on the same situation."

The Crew host the Whitecaps at Lower.com Field, with kickoff set for 7:30 p.m.

headline: Woman charged in connection with Mifflin Township police shooting
fullText:
A woman with a connection to Daveonte Dixon, the 21-year-old man who allegedly shot two Mifflin Township police officers after fleeing from a traffic stop, was charged with two felonies Saturday.

Jayla Call, 31, is facing two class-3 felony charges for obstructing justice and tampering with evidence by attempting to alter, destroy, damage or conceal records, according to Franklin County Municipal Court records.

Officers arrested Call May 31. Her address in court records, an apartment in Obetz, is the same as where officers found Dixon May 30, court records show.

Call is currently being held at the Franklin County Corrections Center. She has an arraignment scheduled for 9 a.m. June 2. No bond has been set for her case, according to court records.

Dixon was transported to Grant Medical Center on May 30 after he shot himself at the Obetz apartment while deputies arrived with a warrant.

headline: Memorial host Jack Nicklaus golfed three times on his honeymoon and lived to tell about it
fullText:
Jack Nicklaus played golf three times on his honeymoon – and lived to tell about it.

During the June 1 presentation of the Jack Nicklaus Award, given to the nation’s best college golfers, Division II recipient Adam Duncan, who is about to be married, asked the Golden Bear what advice he would give to a new husband who will be traveling the country playing golf.

“Is Barbara here?” Nicklaus asked the crowd. Upon learning his wife of 64 years, who is the 2025 Memorial Tournament honoree, was not yet in the media room, he added, “OK, good, I can talk.”

Laughter all around.

Nicklaus, who met Barbara at Ohio State when both were freshmen, shared how she wanted to see New York City following the couple’s wedding in 1960.

“She had never been out of Ohio and she wanted to go to New York City for her honeymoon,” he said.

'There's no golf in New York City.' − Jack Nicklaus

Jack’s immediate thought: “New York City for a honeymoon? There’s no golf in New York City.”

A lot of guys would get “the look,” or worse, after a comment like that, but instead of taking a swing, Barbara got in the swing of things when her husband agreed to visit the Big Apple.

“We got married on a Saturday and drove over (to NYC) on a Monday and spent the night in Hershey, Pennsylvania,” Jack said. “The fellow who was the head pro at Hershey was an assistant where I grew up at Scioto, and I called him and played golf at Hershey and Barbara walked around with me.”

Nicklaus was just getting started.

“We went into New York and went to a couple shows and the second night we were there we went down to a little (jazz club) called Eddie Condon’s,” he said.

Nicklaus bumped into an acquaintance who wondered if “Nick”, as he was known, was planning to play at the famed Winged Foot Golf Club, located just north of the city.

“I thought you’d never ask,” Nicklaus said, with a wink. “Anyway, the next day I go to Winged Foot and it’s pouring rain, I mean buckets. Barbara went with me and a caddie and we were the only three people on the 36 holes of Winged Foot that day.”

The next day, Barbara admitted she didn’t want to spend two weeks in New York, so she suggested heading to Atlantic City, where she wanted to see the boardwalk.

“Of course you go right by Clementon, New Jersey, to get there,” Nicklaus said, eyes brightening. Clementon is the home of Pine Valley, among the most prestigious private golf courses in the world.

 “So we go to Clementon and I walk into the clubhouse and … I say ‘I’m here with my wife.’ They go, ‘Your wife? Jack, this is a stag club, women are not allowed on the property.”

Uh-oh.

The club asked if he still wanted to play golf

“I said, ‘Oh yeah, I’d love to play golf.’ I was a 20-year-old kid,” he said.

The Golden Bear lives a charmed, nine-lives life

Clearly, the Golden Bear has nine lives, because he was still breathing after explaining to Barbara that she could not accompany him around the golf course.

Watch the Memorial Tournament with a fubo free trial

“They took her around the outside and she had to peer through the fence and see me play golf,” he said. “That basically was our honeymoon. We went to Atlantic City, looked at the boardwalk and said, ‘Let’s go home.’ So we did.” 

Tongue firmly in cheek, Nicklaus added, “How many women get to see Hershey, Winged Foot and Pine Valley on their honeymoon?”

The epilogue?

“I’ll tell you what, Barbara never complained one time about any of that,” Nicklaus said. “She laughed and loves it and has been a great supporter. She’s been my partner for 65 years now. A pretty good deal.”
