headline: Memorial Tournament to honor two-time major winner, 1980 Memorial champ David Graham
fullText:
Australian David Graham, who from a certain perspective became the first and only left-handed golfer to win the Memorial Tournament, has been selected by the Captains Club to be the tournament's 2026 honoree.

Graham, 79, first learned to golf left-handed before switching sides at age 14 when a co-worker in the pro shop where he was employed convinced him to make the change. He quickly became proficient at the game, and in 1968 turned professional, honing his craft on the Australian and Asian Tours. He earned his PGA Tour card in 1971 and collected his first win in 1972 at the Cleveland Open.

Graham won eight times on tour, including two majors -- the 1979 PGA Championship and 1981 U.S. Open. He also won the 1980 Memorial. He has 36 career tour wins that came on six different continents, and won five times on the Champions Tour before retiring in 2004.

Watch the Memorial Tournament with a Fubo free trial

"This is one of the greatest honors I have received," said Graham, who was inducted into the World Golf Hall of Fame in 2015. "I'm just tickled to death as a past winner of the Memorial and proud Muirfield Village Golf Club member to have been selected by the Captains Club."

His victory at the Memorial remains one of the most memorable finishes in tournament history. He holed a 20-foot eagle putt at No. 15 to pull within one shot of Tom Watson, and went to the 18th hole tied with Watson. Staring at a 30-foot downhill birdie putt for the win, Graham hit a slow roller that found the cup. Graham finished at 8-under 280, breaking by one stroke the tournament record set by Memorial host Jack Nicklaus in 1977.

"Without a doubt, David was one the toughest competitors on the tour when I was playing," Watson said "He was strong mentally."

Graham and Nicklaus have a strong friendship developed both inside and outside the ropes.

"David has been a great friend for a very long time," Nicklaus said. "David worked at one time for MacGregor, the company I owned for awhile, and actually helped me make clubs. David was a very good player when he (arrived) in the United States, but he really learned how to win once he was here."

headline: Yankees' rookie Will Warren gets a harsh lesson vs. the world champion Dodgers' lineup
fullText:
LOS ANGELES – Win, lose or no-decision, Will Warren would gain something by facing the defending world champs.

“Whatever happens, I feel like we’re continuing to see the emergence of a really good pitcher,’’ Yankees manager Aaron Boone said of his rookie right-hander, prior to Saturday’s start.

About two hours later, before 51,746 fans at Dodger Stadium, Warren received perhaps the harshest lesson of his young, big-league career.

Warren retired just four batters, and the Dodgers scored seven runs against him, on the way to a stunning 18-2 late afternoon victory.

"Left balls over the heart of the plate, didn’t get ahead and they capitalized,'' said a dejected Warren, whose ERA soared from 4.09 to 5.19.

Warren faced 10 batters in a 39-pitch first inning, and his six-hit, four-walk outing put the Yanks on an express toward ending their streak of seven straight series wins.

"I mean, they’re good,'' said Warren, but "if we execute and attack in the zone, get ahead,'' he would've anticipated a better outcome against a potent Dodger lineup, without Mookie Betts - day-to-day with a left big toe injury.

Still, "I’m going to let it soak in. It hurts. It (stinks),'' said Warren. "I let the team down, but (I'll) learn from it and move on.''

It’ll be lefty Ryan Yarbrough on Sunday for the Yanks (35-22) against Yoshinobu Yamamoto as the Dodgers (36-22) try for a three-game sweep, which could echo into October.

Shohei Ohtani on the pitching comeback trail

And if there’s to be a true 2024 World Series rematch this fall, Shohei Ohtani could be a full-fledged weapon on the Dodger pitching staff.

Continuing his gradual buildup from Tommy John surgery rehab, Ohtani tossed two simulated innings against live batters earlier Saturday, drawing plenty of media attention.

At the plate Saturday, Ohtani went 2-for-4 with two singles and was lifted for a pinch-hitter in the sixth inning of this lopsided affair.

That helped Aaron Judge to win their personal in-game Home Run Derby, as Judge launched Nos. 20 and 21 of the year, accounting for all of the Yankees' Saturday scoring.

Entering Sunday's series finale, Judge has three homers this weekend to Ohtani's two - giving Ohtani an MLB-leading 22 homers, tied with Seattle's Cal Raleigh.

Will Warren's on-the-job training

Over his first six starts this season, Warren’s 5.65 ERA in 24 innings, with 26 strikeouts and 12 walks, was a window into the Yanks’ pitching reality.

Ace Gerrit Cole (elbow surgery), Luis Gil (lat strain) and eventually Marcus Stroman (knee inflammation) were missing from the rotation, necessitating Warren’s presence.

But Warren had a solid spring training and his five starts prior to Saturday – 2.70 ERA, 41 strikeouts, 8 walks in 26.2 innings – reflected more than just promise.

Finding “ways to contribute any way I can,’’ Cole spoke at length with Warren, a few weeks ago, about “executing pitches at a high level.

Warren’s recent success was “partially him becoming more comfortable with the weapons that he has,’’ said Cole, and Boone saw a pitcher with "more answers for lefty hitters'' with a good mix of fastballs, sinkers, curves and changeups.

And then the roof caved in Saturday afternoon, capped by Max Muncy's three-run homer - giving the Dodgers a 7-0 lead and starting a carousel of Yankees pitchers that ended with middle infielder Pablo Reyes.

"(Warren) has all the equipment to move right through this one,'' said Boone. "It's no fun going through it...but it's part of the game sometimes.''

Yankees' bullpen could get a boost; Carlos Rodon's updated schedule

Before Reyes pitched the eighth and yielded a three-run homer to Dalton Rushing, Boone was forced to use six relievers, including Devin Williams and Luke Weaver.

Boone avoided using Jonathan Loaisiga and Tim Hill, but the bullpen might need a fresh arm for Sunday's game.

By Tuesday or Wednesday, the Yankees expect to have Fernando Cruz (shoulder inflammation) off the injured list and back in the bullpen.

Cruz threw a simulated inning Saturday at Dodger Stadium and came away feeling "really good...the velocity is there. No discomfort.''

Sunday is Carlos Rodon's normal rotation turn, but Boone elected to start Yarbrough - with a 2.25 ERA in four straight starts - to provide Rodon extra rest following Tuesday's seven shutout innings at Anaheim.

Rodon is now due to open the Yanks' homestand Tuesday against Cleveland and finish it next Sunday against Boston.

headline: Takeaways: Knicks' playoff run ends as they come up short in Game 6 loss to Pacers
fullText:
Game 6 between the Knicks and Pacers reflected exactly what was at stake for both teams.

The Knicks were fighting to keep their season alive. The Pacers were fighting to put the Knicks away and advance to the NBA Finals.

From the opening tip the game was fast paced, intense, physical. There were bodies hitting the floor for loose balls, tough fouls, big defensive stops.

But in the end, it was the Pacers who won out.

The Knicks couldn’t keep up in the second half and saw their season come to an end with a 125-108 loss to the Pacers Saturday night in the Eastern Conference Finals at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis.

The Pacers moved on to play the Oklahoma City Thunder in the Finals, which begins Thursday at Oklahoma City.

Game 6 capped a wild series, which saw the Knicks fall into an 0-2 series hole before fighting back enough to force a Game 6.

But Tom Thibodeau’s team ultimately couldn’t keep up with the Pacers.

OG Anunoby led the Knicks with 24 points, while Karl-Anthony Towns had 22 and Jalen Brunson had 19.

The Pacers held a four-point lead at halftime but started pulling away in the third quarter, during which they outscored the Knicks 34-23.

Pascal Siakam had 31 points for Indiana, which shot 54.1 percent from the field, including 51.5 percent from three-point range.

Three takeaways

Way too many turnovers by the Knicks

The Pacers are tough enough to beat as it is.

Beating them by turning the ball over – again and again and again?

Practically impossible.

The Knicks committed far too many turnovers Saturday night and Indiana capitalized, scoring a staggering 34 points off 18 New York turnovers.

Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges each had five of their own.

The Knicks failed to take care of the basketball, which is inexcusable in a game of this magnitude.

Great defense by the Pacers

Indiana clamped down on the defensive end from the start, a stark contrast from the way it played on the end of the floor in Game 5.

The Pacers were extremely physical, they pressed, they hounded the Knicks’ ball-handlers, they made shots difficult.

Simply put, they played the type of defense that’s required at this stage of the playoffs and made it extremely difficult for the Knicks to get anything going consistently on offense.

Andrew Nembhard’s defense on Brunson, specifically, made a huge difference in this game.

Now what for the Knicks?

Tom Thibodeau has overall done a great job coaching the Knicks, but does the front office believe it’s time for a change?

It’s a question that’ll linger at least for a few days until any definitive answers become public.

But what about roster changes?

The Knicks need to improve their depth in the offseason. And whether they put together some type of package to acquire a star also remains to be seen, though might be unlikely.

headline: Feds to remove asbestos and lead from Paterson factory ruins near Great Falls
fullText:
PATERSON — Workers for the Environmental Protection Agency are ready to start removing asbestos and lead contamination from factory ruins at the Great Falls national park on June 2.

Federal officials acknowledged the risks involved in the $4 million environmental cleanup project in notices the EPA distributed during the last week of May for people who live near the site.

“These contaminants have the potential to spread as the structures break down and material becomes airborne,” the federal agency warned.

The EPA included in the notices details of its safety plan. But some community leaders and activists said the agency should have told residents what steps they should take to protect themselves.

Story continues below photo gallery.

David Soo, a historic preservation activist who lives close to the contamination, said residents have received no information on whether it’s safe to keep the windows in their homes open during the work or whether residents need to wear masks when they go outside.

“I have a 6-month-old baby in the house, and she doesn’t need to be exposed to asbestos,” Soo said.

EPA will take air samples

The EPA said it would be taking air samples around the perimeter of the site as the work takes place and directed residents to an agency webpage where they can view that data: response.epa.gov/AlliedTextilePrintingRV3.

“I would like the EPA to do a better job of community outreach,” said Bob Guarasci, head of the New Jersey Community Development Corporation nonprofit organization, based near the Great Falls. “I think residents have reason to be concerned when they receive notices saying they could be exposed to hazardous substances.”

The first step in the project is the removal of a portion of a 118-foot-high smokestack, which the EPA says is “unstable, leaning, and at risk of collapsing.” The smokestack danger needs to be addressed, officials said, before anyone can go among the ground-level ruins and remove the contamination.

The plan is for a worker wearing a protective suit and respirator to rise to the top of the smokestack in a “manlift,” or aerial platform, to remove the bricks, one by one.

The bricks will be taken to ground level through a fabric chute to prevent dust from spreading in the air, the EPA said. The bricks will then be stacked at the site and tested multiple times to see if they are contaminated or safe enough to remain at the ruins.

Throughout that work, federal officials said the crew will spray the smokestack and surrounding area with water to prevent contamination from going airborne.

Once the top half of the smokestack is removed, an engineer will check the remaining portion to determine whether it’s stable enough to remain in place or also needs to be taken down, officials said.

The EPA has not released a time frame for the cleanup. The contamination has delayed the opening of a $7.9 million expansion of the Great Falls national park because the new recreation area is directly next to the tainted ruins. The park expansion was finished last September.

The focus on the June 10 primary will be the gubernatorial election, but there are lots of local contested races in Bergen, Passaic, Essex and Morris counties.

This is New Jersey's first primary where all 21 counties will use a black ballot design for both parties instead of the "county-line." The line traditionally gave candidates who were endorsed by the county party a preferred ballot placement, but it was dismantled by a federal judge last year.

As of May 1, New Jersey had 6,565,285 total registered voters, which includes 2,449,526 Democrats and 1,621,669 Republicans. More than 691,000 vote-by-mail ballots were sent out across the state and about 234,000 have been returned, according to state officials.

Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked by June 10.

Primary races to watch in Bergen County

One of the top contested local primary races to watch is that of the Bergen County commissioners. The contested Democratic primary will see former Palisades Park Mayor Chris Chung, former Bergen County Democratic Organization state Senate candidate John Vitale and former Closter Councilwoman Dolores Witko face off against incumbents and party-endorsed candidates Democratic Commissioners Tom Sullivan, Mary Amoroso and Germaine Ortiz.

Other top local races to watch include the Rutherford Council, where six Democratic candidates are running for two seats, and Cresskill, where a two-year unexpired mayor term is up for grabs after Mayor Benedict Romeo, who had been in the post since 1999, died in February.

Primary races to watch in Morris County

headline: 50 fascinating facts about 'Jaws' as it celebrates 50
fullText:
Oh the shark has pretty teeth, dear. And he showed them, pearly white, exactly 50 years ago this June — when the movie "Jaws" made its sensational splash. Remember the screams in the theater as Chrissy (Susan Backlinie) was dragged under the water in that harrowing first sequence? Remember the banter of those three men in a boat (Roy Scheider, Robert Shaw, Richard Dreyfuss) as they track down the monster responsible for destroying the tourist season on the fictional Amity Island?

"Jaws," released June 20, 1975, is often cited as the film that launched modern Hollywood: the pioneer "summer blockbuster," the first major film to have a "wide" opening, the film that established Steven Spielberg as one of the twin peaks of the new Hollywood (George Lucas' "Star Wars" would come out two years later), the film that made "high concept" a buzzword and lowest common denominator the goal.

But "Jaws" could just as easily be called the last hurrah of the old Hollywood. It was one of the last big films of the pre-CGI era: The special effects had to be welded, hammered and bolted together. And that led directly to the happiest accident of the film. The mechanical shark, nicknamed "Bruce," turned out to be such an unwieldy, unconvincing Edsel of a contraption that Spielberg was obliged to keep it offscreen for most of "Jaws."

That, as it turned out, was the making of the movie. The scary John Williams DUH-duh-DUH-duh music, the underwater "shark's eye" shots and the audience's imagination provided a far more fearsome shark than Spielberg, with 1974 technology, could have shown onscreen.

50 facts about the film 'Jaws' for its 50th anniversary

"Jaws" has also gotten the blame for making America shark-crazy — as phenomena like Discovery Channel's annual "Shark Week" and the "Sharknado" TV movies attest. The late "Jaws" author Peter Benchley, an amateur oceanographer, came to regret his share in the vilification of the great white shark, an animal now on the endangered species list.

"I couldn't possibly write 'Jaws' today, because you can't demonize an animal," Benchley told The Record in 1999.

"What people forget is that, 25 years ago, nobody knew anything about great white sharks. The concept of a rogue shark that has a taste for human flesh — people believed it."

Here's a mouthful of "Jaws" facts — 50 in all — for the 50th anniversary of "Jaws":

  1. The mechanical shark Bruce was named after Spielberg's lawyer, Bruce Raimer.
  2. "Jaws" was nominated for four Oscars and won three: best sound, best score, best editing.
  3. Backlinie, who played the shark's first victim, was harnessed to two ropes that dragged her back and forth in the water to simulate the attack.
  4. There are six shark victims in the movie (including — implied — a dog).
  5. Spielberg was only 28 when "Jaws" was released.
  6. Benchley plays a TV reporter in one movie scene.
  7. Benchley (originally hired to write the screenplay) and Spielberg publicly sniped at each other in the months leading up to the release.
  8. "Jaws" was filmed mostly on Martha's Vineyard: Islanders will recognize Edgartown, Gay Head, the Chappaquiddick ferry and Menemsha, among other locations.
  9. In the original novel, the mafia puts pressure on the mayor to keep the beaches open.
  10. Composer John Williams, whose career got a huge boost from this movie, was known as "Johnny Williams" back when he wrote scores for TV shows like "Lost in Space."
  11. Carl Gottlieb, the primary author of the screenplay, plays the newspaper editor Meadows.
  12. "Jaws" opened simultaneously on more than 450 screens in North America.
  13. Murray Hamilton, who played the sleazy mayor of Amity, was chosen according to one source partly for his resemblance to Richard Nixon.
  14. In 2001, "Jaws" was declared "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant" by the U.S. National Film Registry, Library of Congress.
  15. There were three "Jaws" sequels.
  16. Quint's monologue about the U.S.S. Indianapolis — supposedly an uncredited contribution by screenwriter John Milius— was based on a real incident.
  17. The film was originally scheduled for a 55-day shoot; it took 159 days.
  18. Charlton Heston lobbied hard for the Brody role.
  19. "Jaws" was based on an actual 1916 incident at the Jersey Shore: A rogue shark killed four bathers, two of them in an estuary (there is a similar scene in the movie).
  20. In the original novel, Hooper (Dreyfuss) and Mrs. Brody (Lorraine Gary) have an affair.
  21. Scott Joplin's ragtime is heard from the band shell during the "beach panic" sequence; "The Sting," the 1973 hit movie that sparked the ragtime revival, co-starred Robert Shaw of "Jaws."
  22. The "shock" moment when Ben Gardner's disfigured head pops out of the boat was an 11th-hour addition; after test screenings, Spielberg decided the movie needed one more big scream.
  23. Besides "Moby-Dick," "Jaws" may owe something to Henrik Ibsen's play "An Enemy of the People," in which a doctor tries to warn townspeople that their resort is contaminated.
  24. At one point, a disgruntled Hooper drawls, "I'm not going to stand this abuse much longer" — a parody of Clark Gable in "Mutiny on the Bounty."
  25. Universal Studios spent $1.8 million promoting "Jaws."
  26. "Jaws" was first shown on TV in 1979.
  27.  "You're gonna need a bigger boat," the film's most famous catchphrase, was an improvised line.
  28. Reduced beach-going and increased shark-sightings in 1975 were both attributed to "Jaws."
  29. In the original novel, Hooper dies.
  30. Benchley followed up the monster shark with a monster eel ("The Deep," 1976) and a monster squid ("Beast," 1991).
  31. Quint's boat is the Orca. A "Jaws" movie rip-off, "Orca," about a killer whale, came out in 1977.
  32. "Jaws" lost the Oscar for best picture to "One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest."
  33. Movie rights for "Jaws" were purchased for about $175,000.
  34. Lorraine Gary (Ellen Brody) was the wife of Sid Sheinberg, the then-president of MCA/Universal, which distributed the film.
  35. Shaw based his Quint characterization on Craig Kingsbury, a Martha's Vineyard fisherman, who played Ben Gardner in the film.
  36. The striking shot of Brody's (Scheider) reaction to the beach attack was achieved by simultaneously zooming in and trucking out, a technique Spielberg borrowed from Hitchcock's "Vertigo."
  37. Dick Richards, an earlier director considered for the project, was dropped by irritated producers Richard D. Zanuck and David Brown when he kept referring to the shark as "the whale" in story conferences.
  38. The film had a legendarily difficult shoot, with many delays and problems; the crew took to calling it "Flaws." Until it opened, many thought "Jaws" would be a colossal flop.
  39. Spielberg skipped the final day of shooting; he was afraid disgruntled crewmen would throw him in the water. He later made it a tradition to be absent from his sets on the last day of the shoot.
  40. "Jaws" cost $12 million to make; it ultimately grossed $260 million domestically.
  41. A 2008 documentary about the making of "Jaws" was called "The Shark is still Working." A 2019 play about the making of "Jaws," written by Ian Shaw (Robert Shaw's son) and Joseph Nixon, is called "The Shark is Broken."
  42. "Jaws" has been rightly accused of creating shark phobia. It has also been rightly credited with creating more awareness of and concern for sharks.
  43. Richard Dreyfuss is the only one of the three principal actors still alive.
  44. Amity Island the fictional locale of Peter Benchley's book, appears to be modeled on Long Island. Most viewers of the film, which was shot on Martha's Vineyard, assume it's somewhere in New England.
  45. Peter Benchley had never set foot on Martha's Vineyard before filming began.
  46. Hooper, in the originally screenplay, was supposed to die in the shark cage, as he had in Benchley's book. However, footage of a live shark mauling the empty cage was so exciting that Spielberg wanted to incorporate it in the film. In order to explain the empty cage, they devised the twist where Hooper escapes and hides on the ocean floor.
  47. A scene of Quint laughing at the 1956 movie version of "Moby Dick" was nixed when Gregory Peck — who played Ahab in that film — refused to grant permission.
  48. Jeff Bridges, Jon Voight, and Timothy Bottoms were all considered for the role of Hooper.
  49. "Show Me the Way to Go Home," the 1925 English music hall song that Brody, Hooper and Quint sing in drunken fellowship, has also been quoted in dozens of books, including George Orwell's "Burmese Days" (1934), Norman Mailer's "Naked and the Dead" (1948), Truman Capote's "A Christmas Memory" (1956), and films including "The Crowd" (1928; it was rendered as subtitles), "Beauty for Sale" (1933), "Hell Below"(1938) "Husbands" (1970), "A River Runs Through It" (1992), and Woody Allen's "Cassandra's Dream" (2007). In 1932, it was the centerpiece of a Max Fleischer "bouncing ball" cartoon.
  50. Benchley thought the film's ending, where the shark was blown up by firing shots into a scuba tank, would strike audiences as ridiculous. Spielberg argued that the audience has suspended so much disbelief by that point that they would accept that as well. He was right.

headline: Bet you don't know these 5 Jersey connections to 'Jaws,' celebrating its 50th this month
fullText:
Amity Island, in the late Peter Benchley's 1974 bestseller "Jaws," appears to be a thinly-disguised Long Island.

In the 1975 movie, celebrating its 50th anniversary June 20, Amity would seem to be somewhere in New England. Not just because Steven Spielberg shot his $260 million-grossing blockbuster on Martha's Vineyard, but because of certain lines of dialogue that paint police chief Brody (Roy Scheider) as a New York fish out of water. "They're in the yahd not to fah from the cah," he says at one point, mimicking the local accent.

But the place that "Jaws" has the closest connection is neither of these two.

New Jersey can justly claim "Jaws" as its own — for the following five excellent reasons.

1. The real shark attacks happened here

There was a real-life "Jaws." The actual shark attacks that inspired Benchley's story began on July 1, 1916, on Beach Haven, on Long Beach Island. Vacationer Charles E. Vansant went out for a before-dinner swim. Soon he began screaming, and his dog came running out of the water. His master's legs were being bitten off.

Five days later, bellhop Charles Bruder of Spring Lake, 45 miles to the north, went into the surf and also had his legs bitten off. The story became front page news; shark panic swept the Jersey shore.

Then on July 12 the shark cruised up Matawan creek, a brackish inland waterway that was a popular swimming hole for kids — the last place you'd ever expect to see a shark.

It killed 11-year-old Lester Stillwell, and then killed local businessman Stanley Fisher, who dove in to recover Stillwell's corpse. It also severely injured another boy, 12-year-old Joseph Dunn. Two days later, on July 14, an eight-foot great white was caught in Raritan Bay, off South Amboy. There were no more attacks.

Much of this is "Jaws" in embryo: the great white, the July 4 setting, the panic at the beach, the shark swimming up the estuary, the hunt by local fishermen. Whether the shark they killed was the shark — and if it was, why it attacked — is still hotly debated. But Benchley knew a good story when he heard one.

2. Peter Benchley lived in Princeton

Peter Benchley, who died in 2006, was the descendent of two famous Benchleys. His father was novelist Nathaniel Benchley, author of "Sail a Crooked Ship," "Welcome to Xanadu" and "The Off-Islanders" (adapted by Hollywood as "The Russians are Coming, the Russians are Coming").

His grandfather was humorist Robert Benchley: Algonquin Round Table wit, Hollywood character actor, author of "From Bed to Worse" and "My Ten Years in a Quandary and How They Grew." Once, a drunken Benchley staggered out of a hotel and ordered a man in uniform to "get me a taxi." The outraged man replied that he was not the doorman, but a four-star admiral. "Then get me a battleship," Benchley replied.

The Benchley family had New England connections: young Peter spent his boyhood fishing and boating in Nantucket, in the same waters where the movie "Jaws" was filmed. But he never set foot on Martha's Vineyard, Nantucket's sister island, until the first day of shooting (he had a walk-on role as a TV reporter). "I'd never had occasion to be there," Benchley told the Record 26 years ago.

Benchley had been a speechwriter for L.B.J. in the 1960s; after that gig ended in 1969, he settled down in Princeton's tony west side.

That's where he wrote "Jaws." That's where he lived for the rest of his life — much of it devoted to ecology and oceanography. And that's where The Record caught up with him in 1999. He regretted the part that "Jaws" had played in demonizing sharks, he told us. But he didn't have any illusions about the animal kingdom. "I don't think nature is particularly benign," he said.

3. Steven Spielberg came from Camden County

Spielberg, Hollywood's ace of aces, director of "E.T. The Extra-Terrestrial," "Schindler's List" and "Saving Private Ryan," hit the big time with "Jaws." He was born in Cincinnati — but at age 6 the family moved to Haddon Township, N.J., where he lived until age 11.

Which is significant, not in relation to "Jaws," but to another blockbuster that Spielberg made 18 years later.

Hadrosaurus, the first dinosaur discovered and named in America, was unearthed in Haddonfield, Haddon Township, in 1858. Unlike some of the more truculent creatures in "Jurassic Park," Hadrosaurus was a vegetarian. Well, it is the Garden State.

4. The nation's oldest shark science institution is in central Jersey

The Shark Research Institute was founded in 1991 in Princeton, but it has field offices as far away as India and Mozambique. A great part of its work involves undoing the reputational harm done to sharks by their neighbor, Princeton's Peter Benchley (who also regretted it later in life).

“Sharks are animals that maintain the health of the ocean,” Marie Levine, founder of the Institute, told The Record in 2016. “They keep the ecosystem stable. We want sharks there.”

5. Roy Scheider was from Orange

Roy Scheider typically played a cop. That's what he was in "The French Connection," "The Seven-Ups," "Last Embrace," "Blue Thunder" and in "Jaws" — twice (he returned as Chief Brody in the first sequel, "Jaws 2," in 1978).

Likely, this was because of his lean physique, developed as a young welterweight boxer who competed in, among other events, in the Diamond Gloves Boxing Tournament in Elizabeth.

Scheider, who grew up the son of an auto mechanic in Orange, attended Columbia High School in Maplewood and studied drama at Rutgers.

Belying his rough-hewn looks, the Oscar-nominated Scheider, who died in 2008, appears to have been a sensitive soul who marched for peace and, in 2003, joined anti-war protesters is laying down in the middle of the Montauk Highway in Long Island.

You know — where "Jaws" is set.

headline: Fifty summers ago, 'Jaws' kept us all out of the water
fullText:
In June, 1975, Americans made a shocking discovery.

There are sharks in the ocean.

The news wasn't the sharks. It was the discovery.

Hundreds of thousands who happily swam in the ocean, unthinking, before the release of the movie "Jaws" 50 years ago this month — June 20, 1975 — were now suddenly aware that they had company. Dum-DUM-dum-DUM-dum-DUM-dum-DUM-dum-DUM.

It was 1975 — The Summer of the Shark. And it was murder.

Don't go in the water!

Not so much for swimmers. The year saw 49 shark attacks worldwide and, in the U.S., one fatality — statistically the high end of the normal range (there were 36 attacks in 1974; 38 in 1976).

But it was murder on the tourist industry. And murder on the sharks themselves.

"There were shark tournaments, and they were 'Jaws' generated," said David McGuire, founder and director of Shark Stewards, a California non-profit dedicated to saving sharks and their ocean habitat.

"People were fishing for sharks for prizes," McGuire said. "This was vendetta killing."

People were behaving, in other words, very much like Quint (Robert Shaw) — the old salt who, with police chief Brody (Roy Scheider) and shark expert Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss), sets out to hunt the great white shark that, in the unforgettable first scene of "Jaws," zeroed in on the naked lady (Susan Backlinie) and dragged her, screaming, down under the water.

An unforgettable moment

It still ranks as one of the most terrifying moments in the movies. And "Jaws," the first of the ultra-blockbusters, raking in $260 million domestically and opening (a first, for Hollywood) in 400 theaters simultaneously, had an influence that went beyond the box office. It changed real-world behavior.

"The film generated a lot of irrational hysteria around sharks," said McGuire who, in addition to being a shark aficionado, is also a seasoned surfer. He well remembers the summer of 1975.

"I remember being in the water and somebody yelled out 'shark!' and everybody scrambled," he said. "It turned out to be just a little leopard shark, which is harmless."

Perhaps only the Martian scare of 1938, generated by the radio broadcast of "War of the Worlds," is more notorious than the shark scare that was unleashed by "Jaws" in the summer months of 1975.

"[It] has resulted in thousands of unconfirmed sightings of sharks." wrote Los Angeles Times reporter Robert E. Dallos in a July 1975 article that was reprinted nationwide.

"It has veteran swimmers scared of deep water and novices and children afraid to stick their big toe in the water at all."

A lasting impression

One child who found the movie life-changing was Gautam Barua. He was 3.

When the shark gets his choppers around the old shark-hunter himself — Robert Shaw, bitten in half by what, even in 1975, savvy film fans knew to be a robotic F/X contraption named "Bruce" — Barua lost it.

"I was screaming by the time we got to the scene where the shark eats the fisherman," Barua said. His parents (he was raised in Connecticut), hadn't pre-screened the movie. They just took their son, in good faith, to the film he had been pestering them to see.

"My dad said, 'Stick your head in the seat,' " Barua said. " I think he didn't know what to tell me."

Far from being traumatized for life, Barua was hooked. From then on, sharks were an obsession. He, too, now volunteers with Shark Stewards (he's currently chair of the organization). "It created this deep visceral interest in sharks," he said.

For most viewers in 1975, however, the visceral reaction was of a different sort. Fear.

Beaches closed until further notice

At Menemsha, Martha's Vineyard, where part of "Jaws" was filmed (Quint's fishing shack was specially built on the waterfront) there had only been six reports of sharks the entire previous summer. By July 4, 1975, two weeks after "Jaws" was released, there were already 20, Dallos reported.

"Any fish in the water now becomes a shark," said Jim Holland, chief lifeguard for Dade County beaches in Florida, in the same article.

"People are staying closer to shore; no long distance swimming at all this year," Holland said.

In Long Island, the actual inspiration for the film's Amity Island (though the movie was filmed in Martha's Vineyard), beaches were closed for the first time in 10 years.

" 'No question about it — they were sharks,' said officer John A. Stein, who saw three triangular fins slicing through the water about 100 yards off Dolphin Beach." This, according to an unsigned AP story in early August, 1975, that reported on the beach closings. Scores of swimmers, it continued, "made an 'orderly' rush to shore."

"Jaws" was nothing less than a national emergency, according to the Pleasure Island Tourist Board, which held a hasty "tourism forum" in North Carolina in August.

In fact, there had been only two documented cases of shark attacks in the state in the previous 50 years. But that didn't stop Steven Spielberg's blockbuster movie from killing off summer tourism in the tidewater region, the group claimed. Perhaps government compensation was in order?

"The effect on the minds of the vacationing public of the movie 'Jaws' is having a telling effect on the tourist economy of coastal resort areas from Maine to Florida," read the board's official statement. "Unfortunately, this is not a passing phenomenon."

Solutions, they said, could include "legal relief."

"Hopefully, this rather bizarre flap will run its course in due time," wrote Lee Hamilton of The Robesonian (Lumberton, North Carolina), commenting on the commotion in his Aug. 6, 1975 "Sights and Sounds" column.

"We suggest that, at least for the most part, the sharks would like to forget it too," he added.

Even lifeguards were scared

It was not just casual tourists who were spooked by "finnyphobia," as the New York Times called it (the clinical name is galeophobia). Experienced lifeguards were freaked, too.

"I had to force myself back in the water after seeing the movie," said Bob Burnside, deputy director of Los Angeles County Department of Beaches. "So have my lifeguards."

The county, he told Dallos in his Los Angeles Times article, had 500 lifeguards. And they were naturally worried. What if they had to actually rescue someone from a shark attack?

After seeing "Jaws," Burnside said, "I went right home and called a meeting of all my captains and chief lifeguards for the next morning." They prepared memos and talking points for the public — including the fact that there had not been a shark attack in LA for at least 30 years. Even so, on the July 4 holiday lifeguards got 500 inquiries about sharks, Burnside said.

There were even reports — though McGuire says he finds this unlikely — of ichthyologists themselves suddenly becoming shark-shy.

"A shark research program at Wayne State University in the Midwest is at a standstill because divers aren't supplying sharks anymore," wrote Jan Campbell in the Post Standard (Syracuse N.Y.) on August 23, 1975.

"Researchers at the university say shark hunters have lost their nerve since the release of the film," Campbell wrote. Biology professor Walter Chavin was quoted as saying, "We never used to have a problem, but now we can't get anyone to catch them. Ever since that damn movie came out."

Best advice

Newspapers, all through that fearful summer, hastened to assure readers that shark attacks are statistically rare, that people had a greater chance of winning the lottery than being attacked by a shark, that sharks had more reason to be afraid of humans than vice versa.

They printed edifying charts distinguishing Makos from Hammerheads, and listed helpful hints for bathers: don't swim at dawn or dusk, don't wear shiny jewelry, don't swim if you have an open wound.

It made little difference. The statistics might sound reassuring. But no one wanted to be one.

"Afraid that a Great White Shark will make you his afternoon snack?" quipped an unsigned article in the Bridgeport (Conn.) Post on Monday, July 21.

Don't be, the article continued. Fairfield County beaches are perfectly safe.

This despite a five-foot blue shark that had been captured by "enterprising fishermen" Saturday evening. And despite the fact that Peter Gilman, of the Norwalk Park and Recreation Committee, admitted that the closest he's been to water after seeing "Jaws" was "a water fountain."

Even as they reassured, the newspapers just couldn't resist pressing those buttons.

Companies that sold shark repellent gear had a field day. A shark dart, made by Farallon Industries Inc. ($30 to $150) doubled in sales after "Jaws" was released, Dallos reported.

Making a killing

Nor were neighborhood merchants shy about hitching their wagon to a shark.

Locally, Willner's Apparel Shop on Main Street in Hackensack put a sign in their window in July. "Shark Sale," it read.

"With 'Jaws' — the tale of a menacing shark — pulling in the crowds at the neighboring movie theater, [the store] decided to add a little adventure to its annual swimwear sale," ran the caption of a photo than ran in The Record on July 17.

"A portion of the window display...extolls the shop's 'shark-proof fitting rooms,' " the Record continued.

By the end of the year, the early terror had begun to subside. Now people were having fun with sharks. On Oct. 11, a new show called "Saturday Night Live" made its debut on NBC. One of its earliest sketches, on episode 4, was "Landshark." Chevy Chase played a diabolical Great White who knocks on doors in the suburbs. "Plumber!" he'd say. Or "Candygram!" "Candygram, my foot!" says Laraine Newman through the locked door. "You're the shark, and you know it!"

Even so, The Great Shark Scare of 1975 lingered in memory. Enough so that "Jaws 2" (1978) could be advertised with the unforgettable slogan: "Just when you thought it was safe to go back in the water."

Taking the shark's side

But even 50 years ago, not everyone reacted to "Jaws" with terror.

"Oh, poor old shark," yelled one little boy at a local Jersey screening, according to The Record's John De Canio on June 29, when the first harpoon struck.

It was a telling moment. An early indication of the pro-shark pushback that is one of the most interesting legacies of "Jaws."

Because in the last 50 years, sharks have morphed from pop culture villains into objects of veneration, respect — even love. Who doesn't cherish the peerlessly inept Left Shark from the Katy Perry halftime show? What child doesn't love "Baby Shark doo doo doo doo doo doo"?

" 'Jaws' unleashed this lasting fascination with these animals," Barua said. "They became 'charismatic megafauna.' That's a term in conservation. That's a bright spot in all this. It created awareness."

"Jaws" pushed sharks onto center stage. As a monster, initially, no question.

But it was just this popular interest that gave oceanographers a platform to talk about shark endangerment, and point out the difference between shark fact and shark fiction. "Shark Week," the Discovery channel's ratings monster that began airing in 1988, unquestionably wouldn't exist without "Jaws." But it has also done its part to undermine some of the movie's more outlandish ideas.

Even "Jaws" author Peter Benchley, who based his 1974 bestseller on the real 1916 New Jersey shark attacks at Beach Haven, Matawan and Spring Lake, later devoted himself to clearing up the misconceptions that his 20-million-selling gold mine had unleashed.

 "I couldn't possibly write 'Jaws' today, because you can't demonize an animal," the late Benchley, a Princeton resident, told The Record in 1999.

"What people forget is that, 25 years ago, nobody knew anything about great white sharks," said Benchley, himself an oceanographer. "The concept of a rogue shark that has a taste for human flesh — people believed it."

OK, Boomer

Today, Barua notes, there is an interesting generational divide between the older people who grew up with "Jaws," and the younger ones for whom it was not a formative experience.

Older folks, he's noticed, still tend to fear sharks. Younger ones, not so much.

"Boomers are generally very anti-shark, and the X'ers like me, there's a pretty broad mix, but it tends to lean toward negative," he said. Millennials and Alphas, meanwhile, tend to have a much more benign view of the toothsome critters, he said. And that may have to do with the fact that they never saw "Jaws" — or if they did, they tend to take a dim view of it as a Boomer artifact.

"At this point, the production values and the staging and everything is so dated," he said. "What was suspenseful at the time isn't really landing now. So 'Jaws' made its mark, but that mark is fading away with the change of generations."

Many, of course, still regard "Jaws" as a classic film. There's no doubt it was a game-changing one.

Because of it, Steven Spielberg became Hollywood's fair-haired boy. And because of it, and "Star Wars" two years later, the "summer blockbuster" phenomenon completely remade the movie industry — for better or worse.

"We're going to show it on the anniversary, as an educational exercise," said McGuire of Shark Stewards. "It is a good story, I think."

Meanwhile, for the record: "Jaws" didn't scare everyone from the beach, in that long-ago summer of 1975.

Surfers, McGuire recalls, regarded it as a windfall. For the most part, they've always taken sharks in stride. And they were delighted, for one summer, to have the waves to themselves.

"I was one of those," McGuire said. "The fewer people in the water, the better."

headline: With season over, here are 3 questions facing the Knicks heading into the offseason
fullText:
The Knicks’ season ended with a thud Saturday night as they suffered a blowout loss to the Indiana Pacers in Game 6 of the Eastern Conference Finals.

The 125-108 defeat ended what had been a wild run through the NBA Playoffs for Tom Thibodeau’s team, which went 51-31 during the regular season to earn the No. 3 seed in the conference.

The Knicks beat the Detroit Pistons in the first round, upset the defending champion Boston Celtics in the second, then fell to the NBA Finals-bound Pacers.

There was plenty of good this season for the Knicks – they were one of the best offensive teams in the NBA, they added another star right before training camp began in Karl-Anthony Towns, they managed to rise to the occasion several times in the playoffs.

But there was also some bad – they struggled during the regular season against some of the league’s elite teams, their defense was far too inconsistent and their depth was an issue.

With all that being said, here are three questions facing the Knicks this offseason:

Will the Knicks move away from Tom Thibodeau?

Overall Thibodeau has done a great job in his five seasons with the Knicks. He’s helped oversee the Knicks through an organizational turnaround, taking them from an NBA doormat to the cusp of the Finals.

They made the playoffs in four of his five seasons at the helm.

That being said, sometimes things at Madison Square Garden are a bit unpredictable. So while the prevailing belief is that the Knicks will stick with Thibodeau, it’s not out of the realm of possibility they could make a change, either.

Perhaps there’s an argument that Thibodeau is too stubborn. Perhaps there’s an argument that he didn’t use his bench well enough during the season – though he certainly did that well in the conference finals.

Still, given the overall success Thibodeau has had, it’s hard to see a move being made.

But it has to at least be a question heading into the offseason.

Can the Knicks improve their depth?

This needs to be a top priority.

They traded away a lot of their depth last off-season to acquire Bridges and Towns – mostly in the Towns trade, which included parting with Donte DiVincenzo.

The Knicks weren’t deep enough this year and it showed in the playoffs – their bench players like Cam Payne and Landry Shamet and Delon Wright had their moments, but they didn’t provide enough of the quality depth the Knicks need to win the whole thing.

Adding three-point shooting should be a priority.

Will the Knicks look to add another star?

Again, anything is possible.

The Knicks don’t necessarily have a ton of assets – they traded a lot of those away too in the Towns deal.

But they do have pieces, and if a player like Giannis Antetokounmpo becomes available, the Knicks are almost certainly going to be linked to those conversations.

Other big-name players could be made available.

Of course, acquiring a star will almost certainly mean parting with a star already on the roster, so no deal will be easy to pull off.

Regardless anything is a possibility.

headline: Track: Highlights from Day 2 of Group 2 and 3 state championships
fullText:
SOUTH PLAINFIELD - Demarest made history look easy as it comfortably won its third straight boys’ Group 2 Championship 83-52 over Bernards to become the first North Jersey public school to achieve a three-peat at groups.

Rumson-Fair Haven beat Willingboro 77-64 ½ for its third girls’ Group 2 Championship in four years, while Winslow Township swept Group 3 with a combined 203 points 

Here are some observations from the final day of the NJSIAA Groups 2&3 Championships at South Plainfield’s Frank Jost Field:

Demarest becomes the first North Jersey public school to win three straight boys’ group championships 

You can’t have peanut butter without jelly, salt but no pepper and hot chocolate with no mini marshmallows. The same has become true for Demarest and the Group 2 boys’ state championship. A 44-point barrage during the second day of groups secured the Norsemen's third-straight title, marking the first time a North Jersey public school won the group championship back-to-back-to-back in track and field.

“The Norsemen have had a great tradition going back to the four Norsemen (winners of the 1960 Penn Relays 4-x-400 Championship of America). It’s surprising that they hadn’t won a group championship in the past, so for us to do three in a row is amazing for a program that’s been so good for so long,” boys head coach Mike Theuerkauf said. 

Demarest held a six-point advantage over Bernards entering the second day. Twenty-three of its 39 points came in the jumps, with Liam Paneque winning the long jump for the third straight year being the highlight. But there was still work to be done. 

“The message this morning was we knew where they were coming, but they were going to run out of points,” Theuerkauf said. “We needed to step up and be ourselves, but we all had to be really good and just be within our talent and not do anything stupid to maximize our points.” 

The lead grew to 18 after Noah Chang and Paneque finished second and fourth in the 110 hurdles, respectively. The Norsemen itched closer to a third straight title after its 4x800 squad – Adam Kaufman, Ivan Timochko, Amadeo Bonde and Luke Davis – placed first in Group 2 for the second year in a row with a time of 8:05.12, five seconds faster than second-place Haddonfield, while Bernards’ 4x800 scratched. 

“I thought it’d be a little closer. But I wouldn’t be in the position if it wasn’t for them putting me ahead by that much,” Davis said. “It made the race so much easier. It was more of a calm 800 than what I’m used to.”

With the lead at 28 points, Paneque and Brendan Alef’s 14 points in the triple jump and Chang’s third place in the 200 sealed the deal. 

“We didn’t know if we’d be able to pull through. It’s a lot of work but we got it done,” Paneque said. “I’m proud of myself and the team.”

Everton Bills continues impressive form in discus, wins Group 3 by six feet

Everton “E.J.” Bills didn’t even know what he was capable of in the discus before outthrowing state leader Benji Shue at the Bergen Meet of Champions. His throw at BMOC of 181-9 was 17 1/2 feet further than his winning throw at sectionals. Since then, he hasn’t lost a step. 

“It’s not like a fluke where I only hit 181 once. I hit 181 and then I hit 179 for my last one. Today wasn’t the best day but it was really good,” Bills said. 

During the first day, Bills placed fifth in the Group 3 shot put with a final throw of 53-8 1/2, just under two feet fewer than his throw that also won at sectionals. For Bills, it was just fuel to the fire. 

A mark of 175-4 sealed his first state championship and solidified his position as a contender to dethrone Shue, who placed second in the Non-Public A with a throw of 173-4, at the State Meet of Champions on June 4. 

“Pretty phenomenal, I guess that would be the word,” Bills said about his end of season performances.

headline: In our self-centered world, Shavuot reminds us of the power of kindness | Opinion
fullText:
Each year, during the Jewish holiday of Shavuot (celebrated this year from June 1 to 3), synagogues worldwide read a surprising text: the Book of Ruth. Shavuot marks the moment when G-d gave the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai, a foundational event in Jewish history. Yet the chosen reading is not filled with miracles or dramatic divine intervention. Instead, it tells a quiet, human story. A Moabite woman, recently widowed and newly converted, follows her also-widowed mother-in-law back to Bethlehem. There, she begins again with humility and grace.

This choice of text may seem puzzling. Why, on the very day that commemorates the giving of the Torah, a moment defined by awe and revelation, do we read a book where no explicit miracles take place, no laws are given, and no epic battles unfold?

What can we learn from the lesson of Ruth?

The ancient sages offer a profound answer. They teach that the Book of Ruth was written to highlight the value and impact of chesed, or loving-kindness. The Talmudic rabbis even asked why the book was written at all since it contains no new commandments or theological breakthroughs. Their answer was clear: to demonstrate the power of everyday acts of goodness.

This message may initially seem quaint, perhaps fitting for a religious holiday. But in truth, its relevance has only deepened. We live in an era of digital connection that often isolates people. It is a time when self-expression is constant, yet genuine community is harder to find. We are surrounded by curated identities and personal brands, yet we are increasingly hungry for something real. In a culture so focused on self, the story of Ruth offers a necessary reminder: greatness begins with care for others.

Ruth is not remembered for grand speeches or heroic status. She is remembered for her quiet, consistent acts of kindness. She leaves behind comfort and familiarity to stay with Naomi, her grieving mother-in-law. She works in the fields, gathering what others left behind so they might eat. She seeks nothing for herself. Her compassion is steady and unassuming, yet deeply transformative.

The heart of the story is a lesson about what makes life truly meaningful. It is not about dominating others or claiming status. It is about stepping outside oneself to serve. Ruth lives not by the question “What do I gain?” but by the question “Who can I help?”

That is why we read her story on Shavuot. The Torah is more than a set of laws or rituals. It is a blueprint for how we live with one another. It was given in a barren wilderness, a place that belongs to no one. That physical setting carries meaning. It teaches us that true wisdom is received only when we let go of ego and entitlement.

Among the most well-known words in Ruth’s story are these: “Where you go, I will go. Where you lodge, I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” These are not just poetic lines. They are a radical statement of devotion, of choosing solidarity over self-interest. In a world that often prioritizes autonomy above all, Ruth’s words speak of connection, loyalty and purpose.

Opinion: This lesser known Jewish holiday about agriculture teaches lessons on time

Kindness opens the door to connection, belgonging and faith

Many people today, especially young people, ask how to find meaning, how to reconnect with faith and how to feel less alone. Often, the answer begins with something small: offering a ride, sharing a meal, welcoming someone who feels left out, etc. Kindness is not only a moral choice. It opens the door to connection, belonging and even spiritual discovery.

Parents frequently ask how to teach their children to care. One simple way is to encourage generosity in everyday moments. For instance, when a child packs school supplies, include extras and say, “See if someone forgot theirs and share with them.” Teaching kindness does not begin with lectures but with habits of thought. It begins when we teach ourselves and our children to look beyond ourselves.

In an age that glorifies the individual, the story of Ruth reminds us that a life is best measured not by how high we climb, but by how deeply we care. That is the essence of Shavuot. It is not only a celebration of receiving the Torah. It is a call to become the kind of people who are worthy of it.

Kindness is not a weakness. It is a strength. It changes families, heals communities and reshapes the world. And perhaps, as Ruth’s story suggests, it is the quiet, unseen foundation on which redemption is truly built.

Rabbi Benny Berlin is the rabbi of BACH Jewish Center in Long Beach, New York. For more information, visit: www.bachlongbeach.com.

headline: In 2025, as chaos and hate swirl, we need Pride now more than ever | Opinion
fullText:
In 2009, I was researching the Stonewall uprising for a 40th-anniversary article I was writing for The Record. I was curious what The Record had reported in real time, and I found it on microfilm in the newspaper’s archive. It was a short article on the riot that ensued after a police raid on the Stonewall Inn.

Stonewall outside of New York City was news, but it was not page one with a banner headline. Like many seminal events, the moment — in the moment — was not universally seen as momentous. That Stonewall would become the exploding powder keg for the gay rights movement was not apparent on June 28, 1969, for many people. It was not for me.

In June 1969, I had just finished sixth grade. Gay rights were not top of my list, although looking back, they should have been. My childhood memories informed me later in life that I was always gay, but children of the 1960s were not talking about being gay. Gay was not even a common word for being attracted to people of the same sex.

The words for gay in the 1960s were not nice ones, and I still have trouble now, in my late 60s, with the word “queer.” Decades ago, it was not an inclusive term. It was a slur.

Wounds heal. Scars remain.

It's an unsettling time to be gay or queer

Today, young gay men refer to men of my generation as “elders.” While not “queer,” the label does not quite fit, either. Elder Doblin sounds like a doorbell-ringing man in the opening of “The Book of Mormon.” I am not an elder. But I certainly am not young.

These are unsettling times for individuals who identify as gay or queer. The pendulum is swinging hard to the right. The trans community is the primary target, but drag story hours and drag theatrical presentations are also under attack. Where will this end? 

When I was young, Anita Bryant was on a personal crusade to vilify gay men. There were not the same legal protections in place then that there are now, and outed gay men could lose their jobs and housing — and they did. Gay and straight people mobilized and successfully fought back against Bryant. But not long after, with the onset of the AIDS epidemic, homophobia spread with a new intensity.

Hate and fear always go hand in hand, and public displays of affection between this insidious couple were everywhere.

I look back at that time and I find it hard to understand how anti-gay activists ever could state that gay men were indoctrinating straight men to become gay. Exactly what was the sales pitch? Get hit with a bat in the West Village? Have random people shout homophobic slurs at you because you appear to them as gay? Go out on a date and not be sure if the person you are with is healthy?

Pride, and prejudice: What happens to marriage equality now in NJ and nation?

How will Pride look in 2025?

Fast-forward many decades and I am now this so-called elder, without a doorbell, looking at another Pride Month and hearing many of the old hateful tropes once again. Some Pride celebrations across the country are being scaled back because of politics. Even Pride celebrations in large cities, including New York City, are seeing a retreat of parade and festival sponsors. If I were a doorbell-ringing kind of elder, now would be the time to start.

We don’t recognize seminal moments in the moment they occur, and I wonder whether we have missed several. It is not an observation that brings me any comfort as I move closer to 70. As a younger man, I expected that civil liberties moved linearly, with each year moving us collectively to that elusive mountaintop. It was a naïve belief, because despite that we profess it as a God-given right, freedom is a gift that has been taken away just as often as it has been given.

I lived in Los Angeles during the Rodney King riots and remember his plaintive cry, “Can’t we all just get along?” The answer was then and still is, “No, we can’t.” We should, but we cannot. At best, we could learn that happiness is not a zero-sum proposition: Someone else having it does not mean you cannot have it as well.

Stonewall, in the moment, was about respect. It was not about many other things that came later. It was basic — people not being treated with respect. No one can understand everyone’s journey through life, but all of us should respect each person’s right to take their journey as they see it.

Lost in the cherry-picking of Scripture about homosexuality is the obvious fact that gay people have existed for thousands of years. We are not an invention of someone living in Chelsea with a million followers on TikTok. We are part of the human experience.

We want to love and be loved. We want to form families and be part of communities. We want at the end of our journey for people to say, “There was a good person, a kind person.”

It is disheartening to see our society once again at a crossroad with regard to LGBTQ rights. Do we go left? Do we go right? Do we expect a talking scarecrow to show us the way?

We should do none of the above. We should go forward on the path not as smooth; on the path that requires all of us — straight and gay — to find our way together to that elusive mountaintop where we all coexist without hate and fear.

I am not an elder gay. I am not a doorbell ringer. I am just me. And that is what Pride is all about.

Alfred P. Doblin is a former editorial page editor for NorthJersey.com and The Record. His debut book, “Tales of the Lavender Twilight,” a collection of short stories focused on older gay men, has just been published by Rattling Good Yarns Press. Follow him on X @AlfredPDoblin or on Bluesky @apdoblin.bsky.social.

headline: Move aside, Rockies: Dodgers are next for Mets following weekend sweep of MLB's worst
fullText:
NEW YORK — The Mets' performance on Sunday afternoon was probably what the team's front office envisioned when they handed out big money to both Juan Soto and Pete Alonso to fill out the heart of the team's lineup this offseason.

The ball was flying out of Citi Field as if the Mets and Rockies were playing in the thin air of Denver. The Mets' nucleus provided the game-altering explosion.

Pete Alonso, Francisco Lindor and Juan Soto powered the Mets offense with a home run apiece as the Mets swept away the Rockies with a 5-3 victory in front of a sold-out crowd of 43,224 fans on Sunday afternoon at Citi Field.

"There's three really good hitters at the top and it's fun to see them going deep in the same game," Carlos Mendoza said. "We envisioned that. When you got those three at the top, it's pretty special and we saw it today. Hopefully, they'll get going here."

It was the first time that the trio had each homered in the same game since they joined forces this season.

A successful homestand into the next challenge

The Mets did exactly what they were supposed to do against across a nine-game homestand, which featured the World Series champion Dodgers and the bottom two teams in each league — the White Sox and Rockies.

Against the Rockies, who are on pace for an MLB-record 133 losses, the Mets did not drop a game. They took two out of three from both the White Sox and Dodgers to finish 7-2 in the stretch, moving their record to a season-best 37-22.

Now, with some momentum behind them, they will travel for a rematch with the Dodgers across four games beginning on Monday at 10:10 p.m. at Dodger Stadium.

"Obviously their talent jumps off the page, and for us, we just need to stay in our area, stay locked in and really play our game," Alonso said. "That's really it. We just need to stay locked in. Every game matters. Every game counts."

Francisco Lindor, Pete Alonso power offense

The power surge continued at the top of the Mets' lineup on Sunday afternoon.

Less than 24 hours after Brandon Nimmo and Soto delivered back-to-back home runs, it was the other two members of the top four spots that came through to break through against Rockies' Carson Palmquist.

After Palmquist worked through the lineup once with six strikeouts and one hit allowed, the Mets put the pressure on in the fourth inning as Starling Marte walked and Soto was hit by a pitch. Alonso punished that lapse in command, blasting a three-run home run on an outside fastball to right field to move the Mets ahead 3-1.

"He's kind of a funky and tough release. Obviously a lot of funk coming out of that wind-up," Alonso said. "His stuff was playing up today, he had really good stuff and I'm just really happy that we were able to capitalize and make adjustments."

Alonso's home run gave him 12 home runs and 46 RBI. He's now fourth all time in Mets history with 632 career RBI.

One inning later, Francisco Lindor tagged a belt-high fastball to left field to give the Mets a 4-3 lead. It was Lindor's third home run in as many days after he homered from both sides in Friday night's 4-2 victory. He leads the Mets with 13 long balls on the season.

After going more than three weeks between home runs, Soto added his second home run in as many days, dropping to a knee to send out a splitter from Rockies reliever Zach Agnos in the bottom of the eighth inning. It was Soto's 10th home run of the season. In the series, Soto was 4-for-9 with two home runs, three RBI, four runs and two walks.

"I feel good since day one, it's just the results haven't been there," Soto said. "For me, definitely I'm finally getting some balls landing, finding some holes and some gaps. We just gotta keep working on it."

Clay Holmes delivers longest start of career

Clay Holmes did his part to help the Mets secure the sweep with his longest outing of his career.

The Mets right-hander tossed seven innings for the first time, allowing three earned runs on three hits without a walk and three strikeouts.

"I feel like I'm in a good rhythm right now, good routine, recovering well and I feel like I have the ability to kind of fill up the strike zone up right now and kind of let the defense work," said Holmes, who improved to 6-3 with the win . "When I'm doing that and trusting my pitches, hopefully I'll get deep into games."

The lone blemishes on Holmes' ledger were a solo home run to Orlando Arcia, which gave the Dodgers a brief 1-0 lead in the top of the third inning, and a two-run game-tying home run to Tyler Freeman on a hanging slider in the top of the fifth inning.

Aside from those two long balls — Holmes has now allowed two home runs in three of his last four starts — the Mets righty was fairly dominant. He faced the minimum number of batters in the other five innings when he did not surrender a long ball.

"If there was one pitch I probably could have back, it was that (slider)," Holmes said. "I think it's just being aware of that and the situation, especially days like today when I feel I have pretty good command, I can trust some balls out of the zone a little bit more in certain situations."

Holmes needed just 85 pitches to get through seven innings, saving the Mets' bullpen for this week's marquee matchup with the high-powered Dodgers offense.

headline: Bergen County high school sports advocate and WWII submariner Daniel Luciano dies at 101
fullText:
Daniel Anthony Luciano, the namesake of Bergen County’s individual golf championship and one of the region’s most influential high school coaches and athletic directors, died on May 18 at 101.

A World War II submariner and longtime Northern Valley Regional High School leader, Luciano helped shape the landscape of high school athletics in Bergen County. Across a 34-year career, he pushed for expanded opportunities for girls in sports, introduced safety equipment for athletes and built winning programs on the football field and golf course.

“He was a titan in high school golf,” said Bergen Catholic’s Jim Jacobsen, who coached Luciano’s grandson, Martin Catalioto, and recently retired after 43 seasons and a New Jersey record 1,239 wins. “He put golf on the map in Bergen County. He made sure there was a golf tournament for all the kids to participate. He also got all-county golf selections in The Record. He was quite a man.”

Luciano began his coaching career at Lodi High School. He started there as junior varsity coach in 1950 before being named head football coach the following July by athletic director Stan Piela, who had coached him at Bergen Junior College. In the offseason, he coached baseball at Wood-Ridge.

“Danny Luciano is a jack of all trades,” Joe Lovas wrote for The Record in June 1972. “He’s small in stature but packs a lot of energy in his 5-foot, 7-inch frame. And when Luciano does anything, he’s always certain to make it a No. 1 promotion.”

Born Sept. 9, 1923, in Lodi, Luciano was a standout athlete at Lodi High School, lettering in football, wrestling and baseball before graduating in 1942. He earned Diamond Gloves and Golden Gloves boxing titles in 1939 and went on to play football and baseball at Bergen Junior College, where he received the Outstanding Athlete Award.

In May 1943, Luciano was drafted into the U.S. Navy along with dozens of other, mostly Army-bound men from Garfield, Lodi, Little Ferry and Hasbrouck Heights, according to The Record's archives. He served as a sonar and radio operator aboard the USS Sea Cat, a submarine in the Pacific, before being discharged as a radioman at Mare Island, California, in March 1946.

After the war, he resumed his studies, receiving a bachelor’s degree from Springfield College and later a master’s degree from Seton Hall University in 1956, The Paterson Evening News reported in June 1956. His wife, Jean Louise Porter of Bergenfield, was a Syracuse University graduate who worked in administration for New York City's Grand Union Company when the two married in June 1951 at Tenafly Methodist Church, The Herald-News reported. 

Luciano made his debut as the head football coach for Northern Valley Regional High School in Demarest in September 1958 and quickly made his mark with a historic 25-19 upset of Pascack Valley. The team had lost 62-0 in their matchup just one year earlier.

In 1962, Luciano joined the newly opened Northern Valley Regional High School at Old Tappan, where he became the school’s first athletic director and chaired the physical education department. He held the director's role for 14 years.

While there, Luciano made his name coaching golf, with his teams winning 100 matches before losing 13. Over 23 seasons, he compiled a record of 267-58 and retired as the winningest high school golf coach in Bergen County history after a 1984 season that saw his team go 18-1 in the Northern Bergen Interscholastic League’s second division.

His teams won 10 league titles, five Bergen County championships and two New Jersey State District 1 titles, according to The Record archives. Members of the Bergen County Coaches Association picked Luciano as the first Coach of the Year in golf in 1972, when he organized the All-County Golf Selection Committee. He received Coach of the Year honors again in 1977 and 1984. 

Outside of Old Tappan, Luciano was a leading organizer in county athletics. In 1971, he persuaded Edgewood Country Club to help revive the Bergen County Scholastic Golf Tournament. He continued directing the tournament annually and in 1977 called it "the greatest thrill I’ve ever had," The Record reported. A class golfer himself, Luciano won the 1968 Bergen County Coaches Association tournament at River Vale Country Club with a round of 78.

“Danny learned the game of golf at an early age,” Lovas wrote in 1972. “He began to caddie when he was nine at Orchard Hills, Saddle River and Arcola. He plays to a 10 handicap today, scoring in the high 70s or low 80s. And, for a small guy, he hits ‘em long off the tee.”

In 1984, the Bergen County Golf Championship was renamed the Bergen County Dan Luciano Individual Championship in his honor. In local golf circles, it is known simply as the “Bergen Luciano.”

Luciano's legacy nonetheless went beyond golf. He also officiated basketball and track, coached wrestling, bowling and baseball, and was a member of the Bergen County Coaches Association, the Bergen County Directors of Athletics Association and the North Bergen Interscholastic League, where he served as secretary-treasurer. He was president of the Bergen County Interscholastic Golf League in 1967, helped organize the LPGA Chrysler Plymouth Classic in conjunction with the Youth Satellite Golf Tour and advocated for girls’ interscholastic athletics in Bergen County.

He was inducted into the New Jersey State Coaches Association Hall of Fame in 1974, received the New Jersey Director of Athletics Award in 1976 and was given the YMCA of Bergen County Service to Youth Award in 1981. He was also inducted into the Lodi High School Hall of Fame and the Northern Valley Old Tappan Hall of Fame in 1994. That same year, he was honored by the Bergen County Board of Freeholders, now called commissioners.

After he retired, Luciano and his wife moved to Hilton Head Island, South Carolina. In 2022, the National World War II Museum recognized him for his service, and his name is engraved on the National World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C.

Luciano is survived by his sister, Ann Longo of Lodi; daughters Debra Catalioto-Buzzelli, Sandra Schrettner and Amy Luciano-Heinrich; and grandchildren Martin Catalioto, Kimberly Schrettner and Daniella Castillo.

Staff Writer Greg Mattura contributed to this story.

headline: NJ officials continue to warn of scam DMV text message about unpaid traffic tickets
fullText:
Local police and state officials are warning residents of a fraudulent text message campaign using the long-defunct name “New Jersey Department of Motor Vehicles” that is warning recipients about unpaid tickets and threatening to suspend their license if they fail to pay immediately.

The messages are fake.

Officials with the state’s actual agency, the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission, said the agency uses text messages only to remind customers about appointments and has not used the DMV moniker for more than two decades. Any other texts claiming to come from the commission are not legitimate, including alleged traffic fine notices, they said.

“This is a phishing scam designed to steal your personal and financial information,” Motor Vehicle Commission officials said in a May 29 statement.

Messages cite made-up legal codes and a June 1 payment deadline. They threaten registration suspensions, toll surcharges, 30-day license holds and prosecution. One version ends with: “Please pay immediately before enforcement to avoid license suspension and further legal disputes.”

Officials with the New Jersey Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Cell, or NJCCIC, confirmed that the campaign, which is similar to those involving recent bogus E-ZPass violation messages, has picked up over the past week.

In a June 1 social media statement, members of River Edge Policemen's Benevolent Association Local 201 warned residents of the scam messages.

"The New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission and the New Jersey Court System will never request payment via text messages," they said. "If you receive one of these text messages, do not click on any links it contains, immediately delete the message, or click Report Junk."

State officials said residents should avoid clicking on links, never submit information to unverified sites and forward the texts to 7726 (SPAM). They also recommended reporting incidents to the Federal Trade Commission, the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center and NJCCIC.
