headline: What happened in UCLA, Tennessee softball game; why controversial home run counted
fullText:
In a dramatic Women’s College World Series elimination game on Sunday, June 1, UCLA and Tennessee battled in a high-stakes softball showdown that nearly ended in controversy.

With two outs in the top of the seventh inning, UCLA’s Megan Grant launched a clutch two-run home run to tie the game at four runs each. 

But as she rounded the bases, Grant appeared to miss home plate, placing her left foot in front of the plate and then skipping her right foot over to the backside of the plate.

Grant was swarmed by a throng of waiting teammates; one quickly urged her to go back and tag it.

Tennessee immediately appealed the play, arguing Grant never legally scored. 

But after an official review, umpires ruled the play non-reviewable under NCAA rules. According to the NCAA’s review guidelines (Appendix G), base-touching and runner assistance aren’t included in what can be reviewed.

Despite clear video evidence of the missed plate, the home run counted.

In NCAA softball, it’s considered runner interference if anyone other than another active runner physically helps a teammate touch the bases.

According to NCAA rules, means coaches, bench players and teammates not currently on base can’t help a runner touch a base, including home. If they do, it’s an out.

When Grant missed home, teammate Alexis Ramirez grabbed her arm to pull her away from the player swarm, and told her to touch home.

Despite that, a lengthy official review ruled the runs counted because runner assistance is not reviewable.

The game went into extra innings, with Tennessee eventually winning in the night inning.

They’ll play Texas on Monday, June 2 and need to win that first game in order to play a decisive second game later in the day.

headline: New Jersey parks launch new pet-friendly program. Here's what to know
fullText:
At these New Jersey parks, nature lovers can reconnect with the outdoors alongside their own furry friends. 

Thanks to a new pet friendly camping program, pet owners can bring up to two domestic dogs or cats to designated campsites for just an additional charge of $5 a night. 

Which NJ parks have pet-friendly campsites?

  • Allaire State Park
  • Bass River State Forest
  • Belleplain State Forest 
  • Brendan T. Byrne State Forest
  • Cheesequake State Park
  • High Point State Park
  • Jenny Jump State Forest
  • Parvin State Park
  • Round Valley Recreation Area
  • Stephens State Park
  • Stokes State Forest
  • Swartswood State Park
  • Wawayanda State Park
  • Wharton State Forest

(Parks and Forest staff will advise patrons which sites within these parks allow pets.)

What should I do before camping with my pet?

  • Permittees are required to fill out a Pet Registration and Certification Form during the check-in process.
  • Dogs and cats must have current rabies vaccinations, and owners must have written proof of the pet’s current rabies vaccine/license. 
  • Pet camping is limited to domestic dogs and cats, with a maximum of TWO pets per camping permit. 
  • Caged pets like birds, amphibians or reptiles are allowed only within camping recreational vehicles like trailers or motor homes.

Campground rules for bringing pets

  • Pets must be kept on a leash six-feet-long or less in and under its owners control at all times.
  • Pets are prohibited from all buildings, swimming beaches and swimming waters, non-designated pet friendly campsites and overnight facilities.
  • Pets cannot be left unattended unless the owner is using the restroom or visiting a park facility briefly, for which the pet must be confined to a camping unit or vehicle weather permitting. 
  • Quiet hours are from 10pm to 6pm to be observed by all visitors.
  • Excessive barking and other pet noises that may cause a disturbance to others must be controlled.
  • Any injuries must be immediately reported to the State Park Police or to the 24-hour DEP HOTLINE at 877-927-6337.
  • Owners are responsible for cleaning up after their pets and disposing of any waste. 
  • Pet food cannot be left outside, as it will attract wildlife. 
  • Pet washing in natural waterways with potable water such as lakes, rivers and streams is prohibited. 
  • If a pet is suspected of being neglected, animal control officers will be contacted. Owners are responsible for any animal control costs.

The New Jersey State Park service strongly emphasizes responsible ownership, and violators of these guidelines are subject to permit revocation and eviction from participating parks and forests.

headline: How summer began at the Shore, in the middle of WWII: From the Asbury Park Press archives
fullText:
Tuesday, June 1, 1943 — 82 Years Ago

The long shadow of World War II, now in its 18th month, looms over the Jersey Shore’s start to the 1943 summer season. As reported here, the casualties were not limited to the theater of combat.

Mrs. Enright Killed By Bus, Was 1st American ‘Wren’

SEA GIRT — Mrs. Marie F. Enright, 40, the first American woman to join the British Royal Navy’s “Wrens,” was fatally injured early yesterday when she was run down by a bus in the dimmed-out beachfront section.

Mrs. Enright, wife of Patrolman James T. Enright of Sea Girt, was dead on arrival at Fitkin Hospital, Neptune, in the Manasquan First Aid Squad ambulance. She had suffered numerous head and body injuries.

Mrs. Enright was struck by a Coast Cities Coaches bus as she peddled her bicycle along Beacon Boulevard, between First and Second avenues, where traffic travels through the dark in the overnight hours because of restrictions on automobile lights in sections adjacent to the oceanfront.

A Wren is a member of the Women’s Royal Naval Service, a branch of the Royal Navy in the United Kingdom.

Crowds Large, Hotels and Beaches Filled — Beachfront Bare of Automobiles

More than 1,000 Asbury Park men and women are now serving in the military forces of the United States, some of whom have already made the supreme sacrifice. Their service was paid tribute to Sunday in a Memorial Day dedication of the city’s honor roll, during which commemoration was also made to those who fought in previous wars.

The dedication was preceded by a parade, the highlight of a long weekend that ushered in the second wartime summer season. American soldiers, Coast Guard men and British sailors, marched with military veterans and Civilian Defense Corps volunteers.

Serving as a barometer for the impending vacation season, a large crowd of visitors to the city filled most of its hotels and relaxed on the beachfront.

Frank S. Savage, executive secretary of the Asbury Park Chamber of Commerce, said that many hotels experienced their best Memorial Day weekend since 1929. Many of them had to turn patrons away.

The boardwalk concessionaires, however, reported that while business was good this weekend, the ban on pleasure driving had definitely hurt, Mr. Savage said.

As motorists apparently heeded the warning that gasoline is to be used only for wartime needs, the beachfront was virtually barren of parked cars. Trains brought many visitors from the metropolitan areas, but a curtailment of bus operations was also a factor in holding down the crowds, he said.

Jones Is Back, His Leg Lost

POINT PLEASANT BEACH — Mr. and Mrs. David Jones, 708 New Jersey Avenue, received word last night from the most reassuring source they know that their son, Lt. Eugene Jones, who was wounded in the Battle of Tunisia, is now in this country.

The news came to them in a telephone call from Lieutenant Jones, now recuperating from his injuries, which includes the loss of one leg, in a Long Island hospital in New York.

The call came at 7:30 last night to the home of their next-door neighbors. Mr. and Mrs. Alex Henry, 706 New Jersey Avenue, immediately summoned the lieutenant’s parents, wife and sister-in-law, Mrs. Paul Jones, whose husband is a yeoman in the Navy.

During a 15-minute conversation, dotted with exclamations of joy and sprinkled with tears, Lieutenant Jones told his family that he had just returned to the United States from North Africa, where he had been wounded on March 10.

headline: Bruce Springsteen keeps pressure on Trump in France, fans wave American flags
fullText:
There was twistin', shoutin', and resistin' in Marseille.

Bruce Springsteen and the E Street Band brought their Land of Hope and Dreams Tour to the Orange Vélodrome in Marseille, France on Saturday, May 31 with a new twist.

A cover of the Isley Brothers and Beatles classic “Twist and Shout,” a first for the tour. A fan held up a sign with the word “resist” on it near the front of the stage during the song, according to a live stream from the venue. Springsteen delivered the tour's statements of democracy, which included calling the Trump administration “corrupt, incompetent and treasonous,” at the show on Saturday.

“Bruce brought the anger and the ruckus to the show and some of the band members told me they were really happy to return to perform here,” said fan Suzanne Lovett of Providence, Rhode Island, who was at the show and stayed at a hotel where band members stayed. “The message was loud and clear, with the French translation of his words put on the big screen.”

Fans cheered Springsteen's message and some waved American flags in support of the Boss. One fan wore a shirt that stated “In a world full of Donalds be a Bruce.”

The current tour began May 14 at the Co-op Live arena in Manchester, U.K. President Trump has attacked Springsteen on social media several times in response, including sharing a meme that depicts Trump hitting a golf ball and striking Springsteen, which knocks him down on stage.

Saturday's show was originally scheduled for May 25, 2024 but was postponed due to Springsteen's vocal issues at the time. The next show is Wednesday, June 4 at Anfield Stadium in Liverpool, U.K.

Below are the Springsteen statements as recorded on May 14:

Introduction to Land of Hope and Dreams

“Good Evening! It's great to be in Manchester and back in the U.K. Welcome to the Land of Hope and Dreams Tour! The mighty E Street Band is here tonight to call upon the righteous power of art, of music, of rock ‘n roll in dangerous times.

“In my home, the America I love, the America I've written about, that has been a beacon of hope and liberty for 250 years, is currently in the hands of a corrupt, incompetent and treasonous administration. Tonight we ask all who believe in democracy and the best of our American experiment to rise with us, raise your voices against authoritarianism and let freedom ring!”

Introduction to House of a Thousand Guitars

“The last check, the last check on power after the checks and balances of government have failed are the people, you and me. It’s in the union of people around a common set of values now that’s all that stands between a democracy and authoritarianism. At the end of the day, all we've got is each other.”

Introduction to My City of Ruins

“There's some very weird, strange and dangerous --- going on out there right now. In America they are persecuting people for using their right to free speech and voicing their dissent. This is happening now.

“In America the richest men are taking satisfaction in abandoning the world’s poorest children to sickness and death. This is happening now. In my country they're taking sadistic pleasure in the pain they inflict on loyal American workers. They're rolling back historic civil rights legislation that has led to a more just and plural society. They are abandoning our great allies and siding with dictators against those struggling for their freedom. They are defunding American universities that won’t bow down to their ideological demands. They are removing residents off American streets and without due process of law, are deporting them to foreign detention centers and prisons. This is all happening now.

“A majority of our elected representatives have failed to protect the American people from the abuses of an unfit president and a rogue government. They have no concern or idea for what it means to be deeply American. The America I've sung to you about for 50 years is real and regardless of its faults is a great country with a great people. So we'll survive this moment. Now, I have hope, because I believe in the truth of what the great American writer James Baldwin said, he said 'in this world there isn't as much humanity as one would like, but there's enough.' Let’s pray.”

headline: Why Palm Beach County's best baseball program of the last 25 years no longer exists
fullText:
Twenty years ago, Miguel Cuello took over the baseball program at a small private school in Lake Worth.

Cuello was lacking in facilities – Trinity Christian Academy had no baseball field – but not in talent. Over the next two decades, he won 376 games, made eight trips to the final four, posted back-to-back state titles and produced six Palm Beach Post Player of the Year winners.

By that measure, Trinity Christian has been Palm Beach County's most successful program over the past 25 years.

But now, after a stunning series of events, that's where the story ends. Cuello left Trinity Christian in 2024 after a controversial letter from the school's pastor led to an exodus of staff and students. The school did not field a baseball team in 2025. And as this past school year came to a close, officials announced that Trinity Christian will be closing after 34 years.

None of that takes away from what the Warriors, mostly under Cuello, were able to accomplish on the baseball field.

"Those memories do not fade away," said Cuello, now head coach at Atlantic Christian. "I still talk to a lot of my players – some of them have kids now."

One of the players Cuello inherited in 2005 was catcher Shawn Zarraga, a native of Aruba. Zarraga was The Post's Player of the Year for small schools in 2006 and 2007, leading the Warriors to a state runner-up finish his senior year.

Zarraga was drafted by the Brewers out of high school and spent 10 years in the minor leagues. He made it to the majors for one day, getting a call-up from the Dodgers on Aug. 25, 2016, to serve as an emergency catcher. Legendary announcer Vin Scully mentioned Zarraga on the air, Cuello said, but he did not play and was sent down the next day, joining the list of "phantom players" who suited up for an MLB game but never got on the field.

Zarraga, who also played for the Netherlands in the 2017 World Baseball Classic, was part of a Caribbean connection that helped the Warriors dominate their small-school competition – and often angered rivals who accused Trinity of recruiting. Other star players came from Curacao, the Bahamas and Puerto Rico. 

"When those kids came here, they didn't know how to play USA baseball," Cuello said. "They didn't know how to run the bases. They didn't know how to hit the ball the other way. We had to fine-tune these players."

Cuello had back-to-back Players of the Year in 2009 (pitcher Jacob Johnson) and 2010 (pitcher/shortstop Adaric Kelly, also from  Aruba). But a state title remained elusive, with the Warriors losing to Deltona-Trinity Christian in the Class 1A final in 2010.

The breakthrough came in 2016, a year after Trinity lost to Benjamin in the regional final. 

After that defeat, four players visited Cuello, including current Marlins shortstop Xavier Edwards. "They said, 'Coach, we got you next year.' That's why it was so special," he said.

Sure enough, the Warriors rolled to the Class 2A title, beating Jacksonville-Christ's Church Academy 12-1 in the final. Aldrich De Jongh, who was later drafted by the Dodgers, was named The Post's Player of the Year after a remarkable season on the mound (11-0, 0.12 ERA, three no-hitters) and at the plate (.358, three home runs, 30 RBIs).

Cuello said the 2016 team "can compare to any team at any time."

"It was like a track team," he said. "We had more walks than strikeouts. It's tough to beat a team like that."

The Warriors repeated as Class 2A champions in 2017, led by yet another Player of the Year, pitcher/first baseman Angel Tiburcio.      

Trinity made another final four appearance in 2021. In 2024, Cuello's final season, the Warriors started 1-8 with a lineup that included two eighth-graders but rebounded to win a district championship and advance to the regional semifinals.

But the demise of the program – and ultimately the school – began that spring when Trinity's lead pastor, Matt Baker, sent out a harshly worded email canceling Autism Awareness Week. 

“If Jesus Christ led Trinity, would HE have an Autism Awareness Week? Of course not!” Baker wrote. “Why? Because anything that exalts itself above the name of Christ should be brought down. Also, anything that teaches our children to have their identity in anything other than Christ is idolatry and demonic.”

The controversial message made national news and resulted in the loss of teachers, students and staff.  

"I stayed until the last month," Cuello said in February. "I saw a lot of people leave. I prayed about it. I thought, 'Why not start all over?'"

headline: Where are they now? Ex-Wellington star, MLB pitcher Sean Burnett cultivating next generation
fullText:
Sean Burnett spent 19 years in professional baseball, including nine in the major leagues, but he's never really left Wellington.

"This has always been home," he said. "The first few years after I signed (a pro contract), I still lived at home in the offseason. When I pitched In the majors, I'd go to Pittsburgh or L.A. or Washington during those months, but my offseasons were always back here. My parents still live in the house I grew up in."

Wellington is where Burnett made his name as a baseball player. 

As a high school junior, he helped Wellington win its only state championship, pitching a complete game in a 5-4 victory over Panama City-Mosley in the 1999 Class 6A final. As a senior, he shared Palm Beach Post Player of the Year honors with his catcher, Rob Orton, as the Wolverines made another run to the state tournament.

And at age 17, surrounded by friends and family at his home, he heard his name called as the Pittsburgh Pirates' first-round draft pick, No. 19 overall.

Of the Post's Players of the Year from the past quarter-century, Burnett is one of the most accomplished. Only four others have played in the majors and only two others (Jonathan India, Triston McKenzie) were first-round picks.

Burnett still keeps in touch with former high school teammates and former coach Scott Benedict, who remains active coaching youth baseball after a successful career at Wellington and Palm Beach Central. Asked what he remembers most about his high school days, Burnett answered quickly: "Scott Benedict's long practices."

"Playing for Scott Benedict was a blessing for all of us," he said. "The hard work, the time you have to put in, the sacrifices you have to make. ... From the first day of school until the baseball season started, we were in the weight room, conditioning, running the stairs on the football field. Being out there doing the fundamentals over and over and over, that was the reason why we became so dominant."

Entering his junior year, Burnett was the Wolverines' No. 2 pitcher behind right-hander Bobby Bradley, who was getting most of the attention from pro scouts.

Summer Celebration: Vote for the best Player of the Year winner from 2000-25

More: Vote for best baseball state champion of last 25 years

The Case For: Why Palm Beach County's best baseball program of the last 25 years no longer exists

"He was the ace – he could match up with anyone in the country," Burnett said. "He was signed to go to Florida State but he was going to be a high pick in the draft, so every game we played was packed with scouts. It was cool for all of us to get a chance to play in front of those guys.

"Benedict would let him pitch five or six innings and then let me throw the last in front of the scouts, to kind of give them a preview of what was coming next year. He did a great job of showcasing us, getting eyeballs on us."

Bradley, The Post's 1999 Player of the Year, set an example for his younger teammate.  

"For a big part of my career, I got to watch Bobby, to be in the shadows and see how he handled it," Burnett said. "Having Bobby there was something I fed off of. ... I got to see firsthand what was possible." 

When the Wolverines reached the state tournament, Benedict pitched Bradley in the semifinal round, then turned to Burnett in the championship game. 

"I started to struggle toward the end," Burnett recalled. "I remember Bobby coming up and making a statement to me that, uh, can't be said. He came to me in the dugout and pretty much told me to finish the job."

Bradley was the eighth overall pick in the 1999 Draft – by the Pirates – but a series of injuries prevented him from making it past Triple-A. He was out of baseball at age 24.

Burnett, meanwhile, became the Wolverines' ace as a senior. Their bid for a repeat ended in the state semifinals against South Miami, the eventual champion, with Burnett taking the loss. 

When he was drafted in the first round, he gave up a scholarship to the University of Miami to sign with the Pirates. By age 21, he was pitching in the majors, going 5-5 with a 5.02 ERA in 71 2/3 innings.

That's when a shoulder injury derailed his career. He missed the entire 2005 season and had to work his way back through the minors, finally making it back to the Pirates in 2008. He battled other injuries but managed to pitch nine seasons with the Pirates, Nationals and Angels, mostly as a situational left-hander, compiling a 15-23 record with a 3.52 ERA and 277 strikeouts in 378 1/3 innings. 

Reflecting on his MLB career, Burnett said, "It's the dream since you've been a little kid. That's the level you want to get to, but very few can do it. The biggest accomplishment was getting to stay there as long as I did. ... I had some bumps in the road – everybody deals with injuries, but I dealt with some tough ones and was able to overcome it."

Now back in Wellington full time, Burnett has turned his attention to teaching young players. He helped out with the high school team on an unofficial basis for several years, then served as pitching coach the past two seasons, with his son, Sebastian, on the staff. This past season, the Wolverines finished 18-11 and upset Jupiter to win the District 11-7A championship.  

This fall, he'll join the staff of the Wellington Sports Academy, an ambitious new venture that is offering a full-time school/baseball environment for middle school and high school players. Burnett, 42, will have a dual role as director of pitching and assistant director of player development.

"It's not a job, it's teaching kids baseball," Burnett said. "The game's given me so much; everything I've gotten is because of the game. I can maybe give it back to some of these kids, give them that little tip or secret that will make them a little bit better. 

"It's going to be cool for the community and great for any kid who wants to play baseball and have the opportunity to advance to the next level. For us, it's like Disney World."

headline: Traveling or flying with a pet? Here's what you need to know before you go
fullText:
We Americans love our pets — so much so that in 2024, we spent $150.6 billion on them. About half of us have a dog, and more than a third have a cat.

I’ve had a dog most of my life, but I never considered traveling with one until early 2024 when my husband, Otis, asked whether I wanted to spend the summer in Massachusetts.

That was a no-brainer.

“Absolutely!” I replied. I wanted to see where he had spent his summers growing up, meet his best friend, eat “lobstah” and check New England off my bucket list.

Then, reality struck. What would we do with Josie?

More from Alessi: Retiring Palm Beach County teacher reflects on cellphones, testing frenzies, tardies and more

Josie, a Morkie (Maltese/Yorkshire terrier mix), has lived with me since 2018, when my niece Hillary had her second baby and said, “Aunt Janet, I can’t take care of two kids and a dog. Would you like Josie?” I’d been dogless for six years, so that, too, was a no-brainer.

When I drove to Naples to meet Josie, she (Josie, not Hillary) wouldn’t stop barking and leaping from one piece of furniture to another. I’m pretty tranquil, so her crazy energy concerned me. Thankfully, I brought her home anyway.

After figuring out my doggie door, she burst through it like a bat out of hell to run laps around my fenced-in backyard. She only stopped long enough to dart into my house for water. Then, she bolted out to continue chasing an imaginary mechanical rabbit around what she was claiming to be her personal racetrack.

Seven years later, Josie still has that crazy puppy energy, but when she wears herself out, she squeezes between me and the armrest of my couch.

When I recline, she sprawls out on top of me and rests her head on my chest while gazing up at me with big, brown eyes that exude love and devotion. If I dare take a break from patting her head or rubbing her tummy, she squirms and whimpers.

How could I leave her for two months?

Short answer: I couldn’t. But, wouldn’t traveling with her be complicated?

Yes! Yet, after doing so last summer, I can tell you it is so worth it — as long as you're sedated.

Here are five lessons I learned:

Unless you’re filthy rich, consider the cost.

Since Josie would have been stressed without me for the two months we’d be gone, boarding wasn’t really an option. Still, I researched it. In Palm Beach County, prices range from $44 to $66 per day, with additional fees for bedtime biscuits, story time, and personal playtime. We would have spent at least $3,000 for Josie’s stay!

Driving would have been the least expensive way to travel, but a 3,000-mile, 44-hour round trip was out of the question. A previous near head-on collision had given me PTSD.

Since driving wasn’t an option, we looked into flying. Delta — which charges $95 per pet per flight — was our best choice.

But flying with a pet also meant more expenses: a vet fee (for a health certificate and sedatives) and an airline-approved pet carrier (soft-sided, ventilated, leak-proof, and 18 by 11 by 11 inches) — which I purchased from Amazon for $46. I also had to buy a dog bed in Massachusetts.

Josie stayed for free at the house we rented, but we took several short trips. One hotel didn’t charge for her, one charged $100, and another $125.

The hotels had a weight limit (for Josie, not us), barking restrictions (again, for Josie), and legal paperwork with too much small print to read — placing the financial burden on us should one of us leave fleas behind or destroy property. And if anyone complained about barking, we could be asked to leave and would not receive a refund. As we signed on the dotted lines, we begged Josie not to make us regret bringing her.

When flying with a pet, know the rules and be prepared.

Once we decided on flying, the real fun began.

Delta allows 20-pound-or-under pets to fly under the seat in front of their person. Fortunately, Josie had been dieting for a year and weighed 18 pounds.

Before purchasing airline tickets, I called Delta to reserve a spot for Josie, as they limit the number of dogs per flight. My greatest fear was that Josie wouldn’t let us stuff her into her carrier. So, Otis began Operation-Acclimate-Josie-to-Her-Kennel-by-Putting-Her-Favorite-Treat (Popcorn)-In-It on a daily basis.

My second greatest fear was that she wasn’t — as stipulated — “small enough to fit comfortably” in her carrier and didn’t have “the ability to move around without touching or sticking out from the sides.”

I wondered whether they cared that at 6-foot-2, I don’t fit comfortably in my seat, can’t move around, and stick my legs out when I can.

Have a back up plan and remember to text.

In case Josie didn’t cooperate, or Delta said she was too smooshed and wouldn’t let her fly, we came up with Plan B.

After dropping us off at the airport, my stepson would circle around waiting for a thumbs-up text. If need be, he’d take custody of Josie until he could hand her off to my daughter, who — with a baby and two dogs of her own — would be less than thrilled.

At the airport, we took Josie to the Special Service Counter, where an agent made sure she and her kennel met Delta’s requirements, and I paid the fee.

This was also where Josie demonstrated her best problem-solving skills by nudging the zipper open in a thankfully-thwarted attempted escape. With Zipper Security in place, we passed inspection.

We were so thrilled and relieved that we forgot to send a thumbs-up text. My stepson is still circling the airport.

Try to anticipate what you're getting yourself into.

At home, I walk Josie a few times a week for exercise, but she mostly takes care of her business in my backyard. With no doggie door and fenced-in yard at our place in Massachusetts, I was in charge of her potty breaks. I made a shocking discovery. Josie goes. A lot. Translation: I needed a lot more poop bags than I packed.

For future trips with Josie, before booking a hotel, I’ll check out its surrounding area. When we stayed in Boston for a few days, we had to walk three blocks to get to a grassy area. Three blocks probably seemed like 3 miles to poor Josie, who’d been holding it for hours in our hotel room.

Something else we didn’t anticipate? Finding ticks on all three of us after a hike. We responded the only way we could. We researched Lyme disease, freaked out, and bought tick spray. Oh, and removed the ticks.

On the first leg of our journey, Otis carried Josie in her carrier. But, for our return flight, Josie and I were on our own. I soon learned that carrying 18 pounds of a squirming fur baby while pulling a suitcase isn’t easy, so I now have wheels for her carrier for future trips.

At security, I felt like a single mom with a squirming infant — except my “baby” had four legs and a tail, and the rules seemed to change every five minutes.

“Take her out of the kennel. Don’t take her out. Put her on a leash but hold her. Put her down. Don’t take her through the scanner with you.” Oy vey.

Enjoy having your pet with you!

Josie may be a Florida girl, but I’d never taken her to the beach. Her reaction to her first ocean encounter in Brant Rock was priceless: Barked at the waves. Sampled the salt water. Swore off salt water. For life.

We often went on long walks along the ocean, and others almost always stopped to talk to us because of Josie. She also befriended our next door neighbors’ dog Bentley, even though he was four times her size.

Josie never had any idea where we were going in our rental car, but she always wanted to go. If begging didn’t work, she tried reverse psychology. To try to trick us into taking her, she’d lie in bed and pretend she didn’t care if we left without her. But, when we tried double reverse psychology and feigned that we didn’t care that she didn’t care, she let us know there would be consequences to pay if we left her behind. This was her vacation, too, darn it!

In the evenings, most of our neighbors sat in rockers on their front porch. We were happy to adopt this lifestyle and enjoyed watching Josie go nuts because we wouldn’t let her out of our screened-in porch to chase the bunnies hopping around our front yard.

My husband’s BFF offered to keep Josie when we went on overnighters, but the truth is we would’ve missed her. We’d learned that we enjoyed traveling with her.

Because our kids were grown when Otis and I married in 2020, his kids don’t think of me as their stepmom, and mine don’t think of him as their stepdad. This trip was the first time he and I felt as if we were co-parents.

At the end of our trip, my husband — who had only owned big dogs — said, “For a small dog, Josie’s not bad. She’s not yappy, and when I talk to her, she looks me in the eye.”

In March, he stayed with her for a week while I visited my son in Georgia. When I returned, Josie made sure I noticed that she was snuggling next to him, not me. A couple of days later, Traitor Josie — as I started calling her — must have forgiven me because, once again, she’s a mama’s girl.

Despite the challenges, traveling with Josie made our trip unforgettable. And she was so good that on both flights, the person whose seat she was under didn’t even know she was there. She will definitely be coming with us on our next adventure. After all, she’s part of our family.

Janet Meckstroth Alessi is a frequent contributor to Accent. She can be reached at jlmalessi@aol.com.

headline: Trump joined TikTok a year ago as a candidate. Now he has a hand in the platform's future
fullText:
President Donald Trump joined TikTok as a Republican presidential candidate a year ago, quickly gaining millions of followers, even though he tried to ban it in his first presidency.

His debut video was taken alongside UFC president Dana White at a fight in Newark, New Jersey.

"The President, is now on TikTok," White said. "It's my honor," Trump responded.

The app is facing an upcoming deadline for a ban after President Joe Biden signed a law forcing the Chinese parent company ByteDance to spinoff the app. Trump had unsuccessfully tried to ban TikTok through executive action in 2020. But now he's trying to save it by facilitating a buyout deal.

"I’d like to see it done," Trump previously said about the divestment, adding that he has a "little sweet spot" in his heart for TikTok, which he claims helped him win votes during the 2024 presidential election. "It’ll be protected. It’ll be very strongly protected. But if it needs an extension, I would be willing to give it an extension."

More: No, Trump did not approve $1,200 for stay-at-home moms, despite viral TikTok videos

Is TikTok getting banned? Next deadline is June 19

If ByteDance does not divest TikTok by June 19, it could be banned in the U.S. again. However, Trump has stated that if a sale is not finalized in time, he will extend the deadline.

Under federal legislation that put the ban in place, the president can implement a 90-day extension on the deadline to sell. But Trump didn't take this route in January or April, instead, he signed executive orders delaying the ban by 75 days. If Trump wishes to sign another executive order ahead of the June 19 deadline, he can.

Who might buy TikTok?

Ahead of the April 5 deadline, several buyers expressed interest in striking a deal to buy the app. A White House official previously told USA TODAY that a deal to spin off the platform to be operated in the U.S. had been reached, but it was derailed when tariffs were imposed on Chinese imports.

China and the U.S. were in an escalating trade war until May 11, when they both walked back the steep tariffs for 90 days while they ironed out a trade deal. But the talks could be stalled as Trump accused China of violating the agreement in a May 30 Truth Social post.

The White House did not comment on the latest update about the deal.

Who put their hat in to buy TikTok? Amazon, Blackstone, OnlyFans founder among the bidders

Why might TikTok get banned? How we got here

In January, TikTok went dark for a little more than 12 hours in the U.S. after the app was effectively banned under federal legislation. U.S. internet hosting services made TikTok unavailable to access, and app stores removed the app for download.

This federal legislation was signed by Biden in 2024. The legislation gave ByteDance until Jan. 19, 2025 to divest TikTok or face a ban. Some politicians see TikTok as a national security threat, expressing concern that ByteDance may be sharing U.S. user data with the Chinese government. ByteDance has denied these claims, which remain unsubstantiated.

During the short-lived January shutdown, Trump promised internet hosting services and app stores that they could restore TikTok and not face legal penalties. Under the federal legislation, companies could be fined $5,000 per user they help access TikTok. For companies like Google and Apple, this could mean a $5,000 fine for each user who downloads or updates TikTok.

Internet hosting services like Oracle didn't waste time rebooting the app, but it wasn't until Feb. 13 that TikTok became available again in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store.

Trump also tried to ban TikTok in his first presidency

Trump cited national security concerns when he signed an executive order in 2020 ordering ByteDance to sell or spin off its U.S. assets within 90 days.

The executive order was challenged in court and never came to fruition, but Congress has overwhelmingly passed a law under the Biden administration that forced ByteDance to sell its U.S. operations within a year or else face a nationwide ban.

Despite Trump's own efforts to ban the app, he has criticized Biden for doing the same, posting on Truth Social, "just so everyone knows, especially the young people, Crooked Joe Biden is responsible for banning TikTok."

headline: Late-night SpaceX rocket launch in Florida: What time is liftoff, what to know
fullText:
A rocket launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, is on the horizon — and when this “so Florida” thing occurs, it's very Instagram-worthy.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket will potentially launch a batch of Starlink satellites into low-Earth orbit.

Though rockets here blast off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center or Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, people beyond the Space Coast can sometimes see this phenomenon.

Weather permitting and depending on cloud cover, a rocket launch from Florida’s Space Coast could be visible from Jacksonville Beach and Daytona Beach to Vero Beach and West Palm Beach (see videos and photo gallery with this story). When there’s a launch window in the middle of the night or very early morning, there’s an opportunity for unique photos — the rocket lights up the dark sky and the contrail after makes for a great photo.

headline: The Palm Beach Post's Baseball Player of the Year winners: Vote for the best of 2000-25
fullText:
The Palm Beach Post is hosting a summer celebration featuring the best of Palm Beach County high school athletics from the first 25 years of the 21st century.

Starting the first week of June, The Post will roll out content highlighting every state champion and Player of the Year winner from 2000 to 2025, including photos, reader polls and premium content. A full publication schedule can be found at the bottom of this page.

There's no better place to start in the "dog days of summer" than baseball, as plenty of collegiate, professional and MLB players got their start on local diamonds.

A couple of notes regarding the historical record: The Post awarded Large and Small School Player of the Year awards until 2022, when the award was consolidated in association with the Palm Beach County High School Sports Awards Show. No award was given in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

Summer Celebration: Vote for the best baseball state champ of last 25 years

Where are they now? Ex-Wellington star, MLB pitcher Sean Burnett

More: Why Palm Beach County's best baseball program of the last 25 years no longer exists

Here's a look at The Post's Large and Small School Player of the Year winners from 2000-25:

2000: Sean Burnett, Wellington

  • Burnett led Wellington to state semifinals with 10-0 record and 0.81 ERA, striking out 97 batters in 60 innings before an upset loss to South Miami. He also hit .333 with five home runs and 16 RBIs. Burnett was selected by the Pittsburgh Pirates in the first round of the 2000 MLB Draft.

2000: Rob Orton, Wellington

  • Orton had a .481 batting average with seven home runs and 48 RBIs and left Wellington as the program's all-time hits leader. He signed with Florida Atlantic.

2000: Gator Brooks, King’s Academy

  • Brooks had an 8-2 record with a 1.86 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 56 innings. He threw four complete-game shutouts as well as a no-hitter and three one-hitters. Brooks also had a .413 batting average with seven home runs and 32 RBIs.

2001: Derek Hutton, Palm Beach Gardens

  • The son of Marlins color analyst Tommy Hutton, Derek Hutton batted .412 with 33 RBIs and played shortstop for the Gators. He was drafted by the Marlins in the 48th round and ultimately signed with Florida Atlantic.

2001: Gator Brooks, King’s Academy

  • Brooks repeated with a 15-1 record and 0.83 ERA and 110 strikeouts while batting .390 and scoring 36 runs. He pitched a one-hit shutout in the state semifinals and then scored the winning run and picked up a two-inning save in the Class 2A state championship game. Brooks signed with Rollins College.

2002: Matt Whitney, Palm Beach Gardens

  • Whitney nearly won the area triple crown with a .495 batting average and a county-best 11 home runs and 45 RBIs. He signed with Clemson but ultimately went pro after the Cleveland Indians selected him in the first round.

2002: Aaron Verrett, King’s Academy

  • Verrett had a .470 batting average, five home runs, 33 RBIs and 31 runs scored as the Lions' shortstop.

2003: Colby Coates, Wellington

  • Coates hit .487 with a .908 slugging percentage and was an area leader with six home runs, 36 RBIs and 27 runs.

2003: Braedyn Pruitt, King’s Academy

  • Pruitt enjoyed a career year with a .487 average, seven home runs and 33 RBIs leading to a 21st-round selection by the Oakland A's in the MLB Draft.

2004: Vinnie Scarduzio, Jupiter

  • Scarduzio was Jupiter's No. 2 pitcher, posting a 9-1 record with a 1.61 ERA. He also hit .443 with 29 runs and 27 RBIs.

2004: David DiNatale, King’s Academy

  • DiNatale hit .493 with a .920 slugging percentage, including four home runs with 39 RBIs and 16 stolen bases.

2005: Chris Volstad, Palm Beach Gardens

  • Volstad finished with a 0.46 ERA and 105 strikeouts while hitting .315 with 19 RBIs. He was selected by the Marlins with the 16th overall pick in the MLB Draft.

2005: Teddy Fallon, Cardinal Newman

  • Fallon was the Crusaders' ace with an 8-1 record, 1.86 ERA and 83 strikeouts. He also hit .333 with nine home runs, tying a school record, as well as 38 RBIs. He signed with Boston College.

2006: D.J. Leonard, Palm Beach Gardens

  • Leonard posted a .427 batting average and 41 RBIs along with a school-record 13 home runs.

2006: Shawn Zarraga, Trinity Christian

  • Zarrage posted a ridiculous .714 batting average along with 13 stolen bases and 30 RBIs as Trinity's full-time catcher.

2007: Mike McGee, Port St. Lucie

  • McGee posted a 9-1 record with a 1.13 ERA and 75 strikeouts in leading Port St. Lucie to the 5A state championship game, the best season in program history at the time.

2007: Shawn Zarraga, Trinity Christian

  • Zarraga repeated with a .621 average, five home runs, 47 RBIs and 49 runs scored. He also went 3-0 on the mound in the postseason with a 0.43 ERA and 32 strikeouts en route to a state championship game appearance. He signed with UNC-Greensboro.

2008: Chris Matulis, Park Vista

  • Matulis finished with an 11-0 record and 0.67 ERA with 100 strikeouts. He also posted a .361 batting average with 21 RBIs.

2008: T.J. Mullins, John Carroll Catholic

  • Mullins finished with an 11-1 record and 0.91 ERA with 97 strikeouts. He also posted a .316 batting average and played second base.

2009: Devon Travis, Palm Beach Central

  • Travis finished with a .467 batting average with 26 RBIs, 42 runs and a perfect 23-for-23 stolen base record.

2009: Jacob Johnson, Trinity Christian

  • Johnson finished with a 6-2 record and 1.63 ERA with 71 strikeouts. He also hit .486 with four home runs and 36 RBIs.

2010: Alex Hernandez, Palm Beach Central

  • Hernandez batted .402 with three home runs and 21 RBIs for the Broncos. He also struck out 27 batters.

2010: Adaric Kelly, Trinity Christian

  • Kelly overcame an ankle injury to go 6-1 and bat better than .400 for the Warriors en route to the state championship game. He also played shortstop and designated hitter.

2011: Kyle Smith, Santaluces

  • Smith went 9-1 with a 0.40 ERA and 116 strikeouts for the Chiefs. He was committed to join the Florida Gators but ultimately signed with the Kansas City Royals after being selected in the fourth round.

2011: Tim Stoops, St. Andrew’s

  • Stoops posted an 8-1 record with a 0.47 ERA and 93 strikeouts. He also drove in 23 runs for the Scots.

2012:  James Jean, Palm Beach Gardens

  • Jean was the county leader in RBIs (32) and also hit .337 while helping the Gators reach the state semifinals for the first time since 2005.

2012: Kevin Stypulkowski, King’s Academy

  • Stypulkowski hit .412 with seven doubles, three triples and 30 RBIs. His last varsity hit was a two-run home run in a 3-2 region final loss.

2013: John McCarthy, Jupiter

  • "Johnny Mac" was the cleanup hitter on a breakthrough Jupiter team, hitting .367 with six homers and 34 RBIs en route to the program's first state semifinal appearance.

2013: Matt Harris, Benjamin

  • Harris went 6-0 with a 1.19 ERA on the mound and hit .361 with 22 RBIs at the plate. He signed with Elon to play college baseball.

2014: Austin Smith, Park Vista

  • Smith dominated on the mound with a 12-1 record and 0.36 ERA and also at the plate with a .425 batting average and 20 RBIs. He signed with Florida Atlantic.

2014: Bruce Steel, Cardinal Newman

  • Steel hit .514 as a senior, scoring 31 runs with 23 RBIs and struck out just 10 times all season. He signed with Wake Forest.

2015: Triston McKenzie, Royal Palm Beach

  • McKenzie went 9-5 with a 0.62 ERA and 157 strikeouts for the Wildcats. He was drafted in the first round by the Cleveland Indians and ultimately signed with the MLB club.

2015: Jonathan India, American Heritage-Delray

  • India posted a .405 batting average with 23 RBIs en route to signing with his childhood favorite team, the Florida Gators.

2016: Brandyn Ward, Jupiter

  • Ward hit .427 with seven doubles, four triples and three home runs while roaming the outfield for the Warriors. He signed with South Carolina Upstate.

2016: Aldrich De Jongh, Trinity Christian

  • De Jongh was comprehensive in leading Trinity Christian to a historic state title, posting a perfect 11-0 record with a 0.12 ERA, allowing just a single earned run all season. He was named the 2A Player of the Year and signed with Florida Atlantic.

2017: James Marinan, Park Vista

  • Marinan, a pitcher, signed with the University of Miami but ultimately was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers and chose to forgo college.

2017: Angel Tiburcio, Trinity Christian

  • Tiburcio helped Trinity repeat as state champion, the first county team to do so since 1938-39, as the team's No. 1 starter. He went 4-1 with a 2.08 ERA and 53 strikeouts. He signed with Florida International.

2018: Jared Petronis, Santaluces

  • Petronis was a dominant pitcher for the Chiefs, posting an 8-2 record with a 0.54 ERA and 62 strikeouts. He hit .297 with 13 RBIs.

2018: Kris Armstrong, Benjamin

  • Armstrong pitched and played shortstop, posting a .411 average with four home runs and a scintillating 1.211 OPS. He switch-pitched and had a 5-2 record with a 1.80 ERA and 50 strikeouts. He signed with the Florida Gators.

2018: Isaiah Thomas, Benjamin

  • Thomas hit .490 with eight home runs, tied for the county lead, and posted a 1.442 OPS with 16 stolen bases. He signed with Vanderbilt and was drafted by the Colorado Rockies.

2019: Pablo Ruiz, Forest Hill

  • Ruiz hit .563 with 12 doubles, four triples and three home runs, leading the county in average, doubles, stolen bases. He signed with UCF.

2019: Carmine Lane, American Heritage-Delray

  • Lane hit .417 with 12 doubles, 10 home runs and 39 RBIs for the Stallions. He signed with South Florida.

2021: Griffin Hugus, Wellington

  • Hugus hit .475 with six doubles and three home runs with 18 stolen bases. He also was 4-1 as a pitcher with a 1.17 ERA and 39 strikeouts. Hugus signed with Cincinnati.

2021: Gavin Adams, St. John Paul II

  • Adams was an ace for the Eagles with a 5-2 record, 1.69 ERA and 68 strikeouts. He signed with Indian River State College.

2022: Jayden Hylton, Palm Beach Gardens

Hylton was fearsome at the plate for the Gators with a .438 average, eight doubles, five triples and four home runs. He also stole 26 bases. Hylton signed with Stetson.

2023: Ethan Mattison, Park Vista

Mattison was a dominant southpaw with a 7-1 record and 0.44 ERA. He struck out 121 batters in 63 innings. Mattison signed with Florida Gulf Coast.

2024: Jackson Miller, Dwyer

Miller was a centerpiece transfer addition in Dwyer's run to the Class 6A state championship. He batted .475 with three home runs, four triples and 25 RBIs. Miller signed with Ole Miss.

2025: Blake Anderson, Cardinal Newman

Anderson never lost when taking the mound his senior season, compiling a 10-0 record and 1.39 ERA for the Crusaders. He tossed a complete game no-hitter against rival St. John Paul II and also had a solid bat with a .333 average and 26 RBIs.

headline: Panthers' Seth Jones, son of NBA forward Popeye Jones, forged own career in NHL | D'Angelo
fullText:
FORT LAUDERDALE — Florida Panthers defenseman Seth Jones was 6-years-old when he and his younger brother, Caleb, settled in along the glass for Game 7 of the 2001 Stanley Cup Final in Denver.

The Jones family was well connected when it came to securing Avalanche tickets. Dad, Ronald 'Popeye' Jones, a former NBA forward and current Denver Nuggets assistant, played for the Nuggets and established a relationship with Avalanche center Joe Sakic, who played an important role in Seth's development as a hockey player.

Colorado's 3-1 victory over the New Jersey Devils gave Seth a front row seat to the celebration, which included the long tradition of each player circling the ice while holding the Stanley Cup above his head.

"Seeing the Cup was unbelievable," Seth said.

That is the closest Seth Jones, 30, has come to a Stanley Cup celebration. Now, all that can change. Instead of following his dad, Seth chose another path and 12 seasons into an NHL career he is in position to etch another Stanley Cup memory …

This one with him hoisting the Stanley Cup.

Recent: Florida Panthers no longer satisfied just to play in Stanley Cup Final | D'Angelo

"I'll never forget that moment," Jones said about watching the Avalanche celebration. He spoke following a Panthers practice ahead of their Stanley Cup Final that starts June 4 in Edmonton.

"It is crazy that it kind of came full circle this way. A lot's happened the last four months and I'm extremely happy where I'm at. I'm happy I'm competing for a Stanley Cup. This is what I wanted."

What happened was Panthers GM Bill Zito made two brilliant moves at the trade deadline, acquiring Jones from the Chicago Blackhawks and Brad Marchand from the Boston Bruins.

Both have played vital roles in helping the Panthers advance to their third consecutive Stanley Cup Final with hopes of going back-to-back in the rematch with the Oilers.

Seth Jones went from struggling Blackhawks to title contender Panthers

When the deal was made in March, Panthers coach Paul Maurice knew he was getting a big (6-foot-4, 213 pounds), physical, offensive defensemen who can win the battles along the boards, disrupt shooters and create offense by rushing the puck.

But while Jones was establishing himself as a four-time all-star playing in Nashville, Columbus and Chicago, his teams won just two playoff series his first 11 seasons.

"He could round the back of the net, and kick it up the ice, generate so much," Maurice said about Jones' style.

Maurice recalls how Jones excelled during the playoffs. "And then life happens. Change teams and then just play on a couple of teams that were in different development curves. Just weren't there yet."

That all changed with one deal. Jones went from a team (Blackhawks) who finished with the second fewest points in the league this season to one that will be playing well into June.

In a little more than one month he's played in more winning postseason series than he had in his career.

Jones transformed Florida's defense, took over the point on its top power play unit and was a natural fit for its physical, grind-'em-out style. Matthew Tkachuk credits newcomers like Jones, Marchand and Anton Lundell for helping put the Panthers "over the top." Without them, says Tkachuk, the Panthers would not be four wins away from a second title.

"This is the player we had hope for," Maurice said about Jones, who has three goals and four assists in the playoffs, and is among the Panthers' plus-minus leaders.

So how does the son of a man who pulled down just shy of 4,000 rebounds, averaged 7.0 points and guarded players like Karl Malone, Charles Barkley and Dennis Rodman wind up on skates?

The answer is easy.

"It just never, never happened for me," Jones said about the desire to play organized basketball as a kid.

And he's not Popeye Jones' only son in the NHL. Seth's younger brother, Caleb, also a defenseman, has been in the league for seven years, playing last season with the L.A. Kings. The Jones brothers were teammates for two years in Chicago.

Seth, though, still has a soft spot for basketball. He loves watching the NBA playoffs, he enjoys "shooting hoops" whether in the gym or on a playground, and he plays pickup games in the summer.

But he never played organized basketball. Seth says Caleb did briefly, as did their other brother, Justin. But they all preferred hockey.

Seth began playing organized hockey when he was 6. His dad was playing for the Nuggets at the time and when he saw his sons interest was on the ice and not the court, he asked Sakic, a Hall of Famer who played two decades in the NHL, for advice.

Popeye has said he does not think Sakic knew who he was when he stopped him inside the arena and said, "My kids want to play hockey, and I really don’t know anything about it."

Figuring the boys would be athletically inclined, Sakic told Popeye to make sure they knew how to skate. Seth then took lessons from a figure skating coach for a year before playing organized games.

"He was fine with it," Seth said about his dad. "I never took basketball lessons like I did skating lessons. He never pushed me to do something if I didn't want to do it.

"My parents were big into that. They never pushed me into something I didn't love."

Environment played a big part of Seth's hockey obsession. Maybe if his dad was in Miami or Phoenix, the exposure to hockey would have been different. But after three years in Dallas — Seth was born in Arlington, Texas — Popeye spent the next six seasons in Toronto, Boston, Denver and Washington.

All hockey hotbeds to varying degrees.

"The Avalanche were really good in early 2000s. I don't think I was the only kid that started playing because of that," Seth said.

"It's just funny how things kind of just line up and work. All these little things in your life kind of add up to where you are today. And one thing changes your whole life today could be different."

NBA/NHL Game 7 doubleheader for Jones family

May 18 was bitter/sweet for the Jones family.

Two Game 7s. Two lopsided results. One a downer. One reason to celebrate.

During the day, Popeye was in Oklahoma City on the Nuggets' bench as Denver was looking to eliminate the team with the best regular season record in the NBA. Any chance of an upset ended early. The Thunder eliminated the Nuggets with an easy 125-93 victory.

OKC now is headed to the NBA Finals.

Hours later, Seth set the tone for the Panthers' 6-1 beatdown of the Toronto Maple Leafs with his best game of the playoffs. He opened the scoring in the second period with a wrist shot to the far side, just over goalie Joseph Woll's blocker. He added an assist on Jonah Gadjovich's goal just more than six minutes later that made it 3-1.

And he would have had a second goal had it not been disallowed because of goaltender interference.

An historic NBA/NHL crossover day.

Seth was asked if had a chance to see any of his dad's game as he was preparing for his game in Toronto.

“I was watching a little bit of the first half before our game,” Seth said following the Panthers win. “It wasn’t pretty for him."

Although Popeye never won a title as a player, he does have a championship ring as a Nuggets assistant in 2023.

We'll know soon if Seth is able to match his Pops and come full circle from that night 24 years ago when he got to witness his only Stanley Cup celebration in person.

Tom D'Angelo is a senior sports columnist and reporter for The Palm Beach Post. He can be reached at tdangelo@pbpost.com.

headline: Memorial Tournament: Scottie Scheffler wins again after early struggles at Muirfield Village
fullText:
It took Scottie Scheffler a little time to get going this season. 

But he’s now playing golf on the level he displayed in 2024 when he won seven times and was the overwhelming choice as PGA Tour Player of the Year. 

Scheffler, who led by one shot to start the final round overcame early struggles with his iron play but recovered to birdie both par-5 holes on the back nine of the Muirfield Village Golf Club in Dublin, Ohio, on June 1 and won his second Memorial Tournament in a row at 10-under-par 278, four shots over Ben Griffin in a battle of the last two winners on the PGA Tour. 

MONEY! Memorial Tournament purse, payout: See prize money for Scottie Scheffler this week

Scheffler (70) won for the third time in four starts, a streak that began when he captured his third major championship at the PGA at Quail Hollow. He now has 16 PGA Tour titles and has won 11 of 17 when holding or sharing the 54-hole lead, including the last seven in a row. 

He is the first player to win The Memorial back-to-back since Tiger Woods in 1999 and 2000.

Scheffler's third victory in 2024 came at the Masters but he didn't play this year until Pebble Beach because of an off-season hand injury and finally broke through in the PGA. He will take this week off and will be the obvious favorite in the U.S. Open June 12-15 at the Oakmont Country Club in Oakmont, Pa.

Griffin (73) is still headed for a special year. He has won twice and recorded four top-10 finishes among his last six starts, and his runner-up check of $2.2 million vaulted him eight spots from 13th to fifth on the money list with $7,116,472. Griffin is projected to remain fifth on the FedEx Cup points list. 

Scheffler remained atop the PGA Tour FedEx Cup season race with 700 points (giving him 3,500, 834 over Rory McIlroy) and took over first on the PGA Tour money list with the $4 million first-place check in the PGA Tour Signature event.  

Scheffler now has $14,558,698, knocking McIlroy ($13,987,340) out of the spot he held since winning The Players Championship on March 18. 

Scheffler saved his round early with clutch par putts 

It wasn’t easy early in the round for the world’s No. 1-ranked player. Scheffler missed his first four greens but got up and down for par all four times, including a 7-foot putt at the first hole. 

Scheffler missed a birdie putt of nearly 4 feet at the par-5 fifth hole and had to work to nail a 7-foot putt for par at No. 6. But Griffin wasn’t putting much pressure on him by mixing two birdies and two bogeys among his first five holes. 

Scheffler made another clutch par putt from 9 feet away at No. 9 to turn with a two-shot lead over Griffin. 

Scheffler finally blinked with a bogey at the 10th hole, after being forced to lay up out of heavy rough and missing a 12-foot par attempt. That reduced his lead to one shot over Griffin. 

Again, Griffin didn’t take advantage. He bogeyed Nos. 12 and 13 after missing both greens and fell four shots behind Scheffler at one point. 

Griffin eagle gives him hope 

Griffin made a final run at Scheffler, drilling his second shot at the par-5 15th from 252 yards out to within 12 feet, and making the eagle putt, then rolling in a 27-footer for birdie at No. 16.  

But Scheffler did what he does best: refuse to make mistakes when it counts. Starting with the 12th hole he hit seven of his last eight greens, birdied No. 15 on a two-putt from 14 feet, then safely two-putted the next two holes. 

Griffin then blew his last chance when he doubled the 17th hole after hitting his tee shot into heavy rough on the left side, then blasting his second shot over the green and into thick grass behind the green. He failed to advance his third shot to the green, then two-putted from 16 feet.

Scheffler closed his day out by smacking hit tee shot into the 18th fairway and finding the putting surface. After hitting his 46-foot birdie attempt 7 feet past the hole, he drained a par putt, prompting CBS announcer Jim Nanzt to proclaim: "The man is a machine!"

No other player came close to contending other than Scheffler and Griffin. Sepp Straka (70) finished third at 5-under and Nick Taylor (73) was fourth at 4-under.

headline: Man injured after shootout with officers in North Austin, police say
fullText:
A traffic stop that turned into a shootout with police left a man hospitalized late Saturday night in North Austin, officials said.

Officers attempted to pull over a car that was suspected of being stolen but the driver fled and officers pursued him, police Chief Lisa Davis said at a news conference early Sunday. The car struck the rear of another vehicle and spun around near the 700 block of W. Anderson Lane, near N. Lamar Boulevard.

As officers approached, the driver fired at police, Davis said. The officers returned fire, she said, and the suspect was hit in the shoulder.

The man was taken into custody and then to a hospital, Davis said. She said a passenger in the car that was struck was taken to a hospital because of back pain.

"We are very fortunate tonight that we are not reporting on an officer being shot or an officer being killed," Davis said. "The officers acted very bravely in a situation where they were being fired upon and they took action."

headline: Kira Smith, Gabriella Fleming take home Iowa high school girls tennis state titles
fullText:
The 2025 Iowa high school girls tennis season wrapped up for individuals with the culmination of the state singles and doubles tournament on May 31.

The tournament brought with it elation and heartbreak, as only two individuals and two doubles teams were able to claim the title of state champion.

Here's a rundown of the action.

Ankeny's Kira Smith  claims Class 2A individual title

In Iowa City, where the Class 2A tournament was held, Kira Smith claimed the state title with a win over Clinton senior Sescie Haan. Smith earned the victory in straight sets and did not lose a single set during the tournament.

According to Bound, Smith was undefeated on the year in both doubles and singles competition.

More: Sibling rivalry: Eastern Iowa brothers make history facing off in state tennis title match

North Scott sophomore Madelyn Jepsen took home third place with a 2-1 win over Cedar Rapids Jefferson junior Lily Holland.

Dowling Catholic duo captures Class 2A doubles title

The doubles team from Dowling Catholic claimed the state title in straight sets over Waukee Northwest, winning 2-0.

The Maroons' team of Grace Frye and Juju Mauro, both seniors, took down the Wolves' duo of sophomores, Mia Deines and London Taylor.

The team of Sasha Postnikov and Marie Stier from Iowa City West finished in third, defeating Dowling's team of Payton Blume and Mady Pierron in straight sets.

Xavier's Gabriella Fleming makes run to Class 1A title

To the northwest of the action in Iowa City, the Class 1A tournament was happening out in Waterloo.

Cedar Rapids Xavier sophomore Gabriella Fleming kept the good vibes rolling for the Saints. Earlier in the week, Charlie LeGrand claimed the boys 1A individual title and the duo of Jacob Schmit and Bennett won the doubles crown for the Saints. Flemming added more hardware to Xavier's trophy case, taking down Kate Holton from Waterloo Columbus in straight sets.

It's the second-straight state title for Fleming, who did not lose a single set throughout the tournament.

Pella senior Claire Smock finished the tournament in third place with a win over St. Edmond senior Lauren Gibb.

Xavier claims 1A doubles state championship

It was one heck of a week for the Saints, sweeping the singles and doubles competition at both the boys and the girls state tennis tournaments. The senior duo of Ruby Smith and Isabel Tobin took a straight-sets victory over the Dike-New Hartford team of Izzy Norton and Aidalyn Tott. Smith and Tobin lost just one set in the tournament.

Decorah's team of Grace Huinker and Olivia Huinker finished in third, taking down a second team from Dike-New Hartford, Addy Joslin and Lauren Muller, in straight sets.
