headline: Doctor Deception: How these Iowans learned their mom's doctor was their biological father
fullText:
Barbara and Warren Steinkraus desperately wanted to have a baby. So did Marlys and Clyde Stoughton. And Donna and Bert Miller Sr., too.

The couples weren’t acquainted. They lived in different Iowa towns and grappled as if in bell jars with the persistent companions of grief and hope inherent in infertility.

But their stories collided at the University of Iowa’s Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, bound together by the doctor who helped them conceive: Dr. John H. Randall.

Unbeknownst to the couples, they would also be connected by a dark, decades-long secret.

At least five adult children have discovered through direct-to-consumer DNA testing that Randall is their biological father — and they may be far from the only ones.

Tying together past, present and future, Register senior writer and Iowa Columnist Courtney Crowder's three-part "Doctor Deception" serial examines issues of consent, medical obligations and the meaning of family in 2025.  

  • Part 1: These Iowans learned their mom's fertility doctor is their father. Now they want justice.
  • Part 2: 'My mother was violated': Did a beloved Iowa fertility doctor prey on young women?
  • Part 3: 'They just want to bury it': Iowans seek justice for moms violated by fertility doctor

About the author

Courtney Crowder, the Register's Iowa Columnist, traverses the state's 99 counties telling Iowans' stories. She endured three and a half years of infertility and two rounds of IVF to have her son, Clark. Reach her at ccrowder@dmreg.com or 515-284-8360. Follow her on Twitter @courtneycare.

headline: These Iowans learned their mom's fertility doctor is their father. Now they want justice.
fullText:
This is the first installment in the Register's three-part serial, "Doctor Deception."

Liz Bright wasn’t going to sleep until she found their connection, the one she knew would unquestionably link her to him.

She meant this literally. She was in her fifth hour of searching, skipping from family tree to family tree, the blue screen of her computer playing nightlight in the darkness of morning’s wee hours. No letting up, she told herself, until this was done.

Rest had been elusive for the past few years anyway, ever since a little spit in a tube promised to unlock more of her family’s history. A trove of documents and records and wide smiles in old pictures were ready to be found; right there, if the commercials were to be believed, just a click or two away.

More of her family’s history? What an understatement.

A collection of health issues drove Bright to take a DNA test with 23andMe, and later Ancestry.com. She wanted to know what genetic tendencies would turn up, and her kids did, too. Maybe the panacea to her ailments existed right there, in her heredity.

But her hunt for family connection revealed a cloak in her DNA, a presence like a coiled sleeping serpent. She already suffered from fears of abandonment and a tendency to self-isolate, a one-two punch of the orphan mentality she inherited like her skinny legs and cheeky smile from her mother, who lost her parents young.

That absence felt like sitting precariously on a cliff’s edge, a void she avoided by clinging with white knuckles to her father’s relatives.

Research had been her buoy against the breakers of doubt and depression that pulled at her mind like riptides. The methodical pairing of last names to obituaries to grave sites to hometowns was a life raft. So, too, was the focus required to follow the chutes and ladders of genetic lines. And both were a distraction from lingering too long in all the unknowns.

Each new connection felt like another pushpin in her metaphorical wall of red string: Iowa. Iowa City. The University of Iowa. The university hospital.

More from Courtney Crowder: After nearly 50 years, this Iowa man discovered his mother's doctor was his biological father

When a piano falls from the sky, the rope doesn’t snap in half with a clean break, she knew. The cord tears slowly, strand by strand, losing strength until the keys hit the pavement.

Closer. She was getting closer.

But the work inched as the whys and hows behind her results consumed her thoughts.

At dinner with her husband one night, Bright was talking about her research — again. And revisiting all her questions — again. She was starving for a break, or sign at least.

She pulled out her cell phone and Googled: “gynecologist” and “Iowa City” and “1950s.”

“Honestly, I felt like God was telling me what to look up,” she says, “because I was just praying for answers.”

One of the top results was an article with a title as clunky as a craggy boulder:  “Obstetrics and Gynecology at the University of Iowa: Three leaders and 51 years.” She clicked. Why hadn’t she looked this up before?

An academic feature written for the nichiest of niches, the piece tells the story of, as one can guess, the three leaders of the Iowa OB-GYN department during the middle 50 years of the 20th century, when the university became the incubator for the world’s first sperm bank and a pioneer for innovation in fertility care.  

A few pages in, one of the leader’s headshots stole the air from her chest.

Bright saw her face on top of his, transposed almost like a Magic Eye autostereogram. Her stomach churned with the unease of recognizing someone she had never met, a kind of Fun House-perverted déjà vu.

She lost her sense of balance, motion sick even though she was sitting still. The tingles of dizziness crawled around her brain and down her neck, like the physical manifestation of twinkling stars encircling a cartoon character hit in the head with a comically large mallet.

The doctor's last name, Randall, was one she had seen before.

On her Ancestry results page.

Hunkered down at her desk, she was grounded again, lost in genetics. Up a genetic chute, down a genetic ladder. Systematically going back a generation and back a generation and back a generation to find where her tree and his overlapped. She had access only to what was publicly available, to the information users had uploaded to the database and made shareable.

But she knows she’ll find it, that connection.

She stops. There. Their common ancestor, the connection between her family tree and Dr. John H. Randall.

Between her and her mother’s fertility doctor.

The truth came down like a baby grand with velocity: He's her father.

Dr. Randall is her father. 

Dizziness crawls again. Twinkling stars return. A deep sense of darkness, too, like something nefarious had lingered in all the unknowns, wrong and off. And shame, too.  

“I instantly felt like my mother had been violated,” she says.

Then, in her next thought, a dreadful question: How would she tell the others?

Three couples, one doctor and a secret lying dormant

Barbara and Warren Steinkraus desperately wanted to have a baby. So did Marlys and Clyde Stoughton. Donna and Bert Miller Sr., too.

The couples weren’t acquainted. They lived in different towns and worked different jobs with different shifts, grappling as if in bell jars with the persistent companions of grief and hope inherent in infertility.

But their stories collided at the University of Iowa’s Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, bound together by the doctor who helped them conceive:  Dr. John H. Randall. Struggling during the infancy of modern fertility medicine, these couples all sought intrauterine insemination, a procedure injecting sperm into the uterus.

Unbeknownst to the couples, they would be connected by a dark secret, too. That coiled serpent in their children’s DNA.

A secret held for decades. One that was, quite possibly, never supposed to come to light.  

Beloved by many, Dr. Randall was the head of the department. He was a scientist first, with a specialty in cervical cancer. His ethics seemed unimpeachable.

So, no one questioned why Randall didn’t have a nurse during the treatments, or why the procedures happened after hours, when the clinic was empty.

The Stoughtons welcomed their children first: Ron in 1943 and Becky in 1948. Randall happened to be the attending physician on duty the day Marlys went into her second labor, and, as he was for baby Becky’s conception, he was present for her delivery, too; his name forever inked on her birth certificate.

The Millers came next: Nancy in 1954, Bert Jay in 1956 and Randy in 1958. Randall participated in those births, too.

And finally the Steinkrauses, who had a daughter, Liz, in 1958.

Again, their stories fracture. Families move. Children grow, marry, have children of their own. Parents die. Whole lives are lived assuming their family trees are grounded in the people who’d raised them, in the stories they’d been told and retold and told again.

Six decades of bedrock, built year by year, memory by memory.

For these children — and others who’ve similarly discovered their mother’s doctor is their father —  this revelation makes Swiss cheese of their identity, that core understanding of WHO I AM dissolving like a sugar cube in rushing rapids.

Physically, too, they are left without access to half their medical history — not only wondering if they’ve inherited something but if they’ve unknowingly passed something on to their children and their children’s children; some kind of clinical buckshot blown clear into the future immemorial.

But for many the discovery also reveals a crime: Their parents, they say, neither knew nor consented to other specimens being used — definitely not their doctor’s.

They feel a deep violation of body, mind and spirit.

Medical malpractice at best. A kind of rape at worst.

After a years-long legal battle, a civil case filed by five of the six children — Ron, Becky, Nancy, Bert Jay and Liz — reached the Iowa Supreme Court this spring. In filing the suit — and in speaking out as they are now — they act as the voices for their parents, who, like Dr. Randall, are all dead.

They seek justice for a harm that can ricochet across generations like a trapped fly. Back and forth. Violently. 

And they hope to find answers to questions left lingering like wayward shrapnel since this truth took a Molotov cocktail to their sense of self.

What actually happened with Dr. Randall in that exam room?

Are there more of them — more siblings  —  waiting to be found?

And: When the tempest finally blows through, can a battered family tree regrow its bark?

Becky and Ron: ‘Genealogy is like a puzzle’

The missing branches in Becky Stoughton Myers' family tree made sense, to a certain extent.

Myers’ grandfather left his family when her mother was 2 years old, eventually remarrying and starting a new life. Her parents got divorced, too, in the 1980s after decades together.

Myers and her brother, Ron Stoughton, were grown by then with their own families, and the split was a shock. Her parents, who met in Iowa, moved east to North Carolina following a promotion for her dad.

They had designs on retiring to the West Coast when the time came. Twilight in the Golden State.

“They were on their way to California, and he told her at the airport, ‘I'm not going with you,’” Stoughton says.

He left her on the runway, suitcases and all, Stoughton adds. “She was very bitter about that.”

So, yes, Myers understands how family trees can be more like bushes, growing sideways, instead of up.

Myers is a bit of a genealogy junkie. On her desk is a three-ring binder overflowing with tabs and sticky notes and protective sheets brimming with paper, the sort of ad-hoc collection a doctoral student would have after spending too long in the stacks.

“This is my book on my dad’s side of the family,” she says, setting it down two-handed with an audible ka-thunk.

“I have one on my mom’s side that's the same size.”

She’s on Ancestry and 23andMe, joining back in the early 2010s when the data wasn’t as specific as it is today. Over the years, she’d dip in and out of her accounts, checking for new information, watching as the growing networks led to more precise results.

Sometimes people would message: How are we related?

Myers would look into their connection when she had time, opening that binder with a ka-thunk and thumb through her notes.

Genealogy is like a puzzle, she says, “because you have all these pieces that are all spread out and, little by little, you're finding a piece, and eventually you get enough where you're starting to get a picture of what's going on.”

“I'm still working on my puzzle, but I'm getting there,” she says with a hint of self-deprecation. “I've almost got a full puzzle now.”

When she signed into 23andMe in December 2018 — one of her normal check-ins, she says, just to see what, if anything, had been added to her profile — the screen lit up with a message. Well, that’s new, she thought.

In big, bold letters — “They didn’t want me to miss it,” she chuckles — a banner read: We Predict She is Your Half Sister.

There was a woman’s picture. And a name, Liz Bright.

Sister? But she didn’t have a sister.

Bert Jay and Nancy: ‘I was just curious about my ethnicity’

Bert Jay Miller had just turned 60, one of those big, round numbers that act as a fulcrum between past and future. Birthdays that prominently feature gravestones on their cards have a way of inviting recollection.

And the winter holidays were fast approaching. A season known for blowing the dust off well-worn stories and reanimating the frozen frames of good memories, sure. But a time of year that also has a way of surfacing what remains unsaid.

So with Thanksgiving leftovers still testing the limits of Tupperware, he spit into a tube.

“I was just curious about my ethnicity,” he says, “where my ancestors were from.”

Miller — and his sister, Nancy Duffner, and brother, Randy — grew up in Iowa City with wanderlust parents. “Adventuresome,” says Duffner with a smile.

“They traveled, and they always traveled with their kids. It was very important to them to show us the world."

With boats and dirt bikes and snowmobiles, theirs was the house where friends gathered.

“My father had a great sense of fun and was kind of like a big kid,” she says. “I talk to people around Iowa City who say, ‘I learned to water ski from Bert Miller.’”

Generosity, in all its forms, was written on their family crest. She once saw her father take the shirt from his back and give it to a drifter type passing by their house. Literally, she stresses. The shirt. From his back.

Parents and kids differed in certain ways, of course. Bert Sr. was handy and mechanically inclined, while Bert Jay was academic with a penchant for science and a voracious reader who hung out at the public library for fun. And he had ginger hair, although the rest of his extended family had variations of light brown. People would rub his mop top and ask: Where’d you get that bright red hair?

When Miller got his Ancestry results, the listed ethnicity was different from what his family had always said. Curious.

Same thing happened to Bright, who grew up very, very German. The heritage was central to the family ethos, in fact. They traveled to Germany. They spoke German. They prayed in German. They ate German food. She even went to school in Germany for a spell.

Her results said something like “Germanic Europe” bloodline, but under that was listed a different country of origin: Belgium.

Miller also didn’t see many people he actually knew on his family tree, definitely not on his dad’s side. But maybe not many of the extended Miller clan had tested? Maybe?

That’s what Bright thought, too. Her father’s family wasn’t the type to go on this kind of website, she figured.

But, still, there should be some … right?

Donor sperm: ‘Adultery by doctor’ or miracle medicine?

The Cedar Rapids Gazette’s headline sprawled the entire width of the paper on April 4, 1954.

“Fatherhood After Death Has Now Been Proven Possible.”

The narrative’s spin, hysteria mingling with morning coffee, aligned with the moral panic dogging fertility medicine’s rapid advancements.

The first babies born from frozen sperm had been delivered, a fact the University of Iowa scientists who invented and facilitated the freezing procedure had hoped to keep quiet for a more muted reveal at a coming medical conference, according to “The Birth of the Sperm Bank,” a detailed recounting of Iowa’s role in founding this first-of-its-kind repository.

The university was a leader in fertility medicine, performing artificial insemination — both by husband and donor — for years. But this new procedure aspired to improve the chances of conception with a spouse’s sperm by letting doctors collect multiple semen specimens, then combine and select the most concentrated sample.

Doctors hoped the research meant they’d have to rely less on donor sperm, which was at that point the most fruitful technique for men with defects or low counts. But keeping a stock of fresh supply was burdensome, to say the least, because donors were so hard to recruit.

Often medical residents or interns ended up providing the samples, an ethical conundrum all on its own.

Many Americans disapproved of artificial insemination — nearly 75 percent in some polls — and the Catholic Church called the procedure “entirely illicit and immoral,” notes the sperm bank article. The infusion of science into the reproduction process was the purview of totalitarian regimes in popular fiction of the era, plot twists in dystopian books such as “1984” and “Brave New World.”

Donor sperm drew particular disdain; some clinicians even described its use as inserting a “third party” into a family.

“Doctors and lawyers alike in the 1940s and 1950s worried that donor insemination was simply adultery by doctor, a possibly illegal practice that produced bastards,” according to the sperm bank history.

But the post-war period’s baby boom and American culture’s hard turn toward domesticity drove an exponentially growing interest in fertility treatments. More newlyweds got white picket fences. More couples sought help starting families.

More doctors looked to technology for answers.

More from Courtney Crowder: After years of infertility, I was finally pregnant. Then doctors said there was a problem.

Ensuring the procedures were as clinical as possible insulated them from some social stigma. This was medical, not sexual. White-starched professionalism. Antiseptic almost.

Still, given the state of public opinion, many doctors and patients kept any sort of assistance in conception to themselves.

A secrecy that may have covered deception.

Maybe even a crime.

Into this vortex of impassioned need and equally as fervent controversy came the Iowa couples: The Steinkrauses. The Stoughtons. The Millers.

And Dr. Randall.

Three truths, one revelation and possibly hundreds impacted

Now connected through online genetic databases, the newly discovered siblings began sending messages to one another. Separately and together, they tried out theories to explain their links, grasping for any logical reason they could be related.

Bright speculated that Myers and Stoughton’s father might have been a secret sperm donor.

She found a photo of the elder Stoughton online and brought it to a get-together with her girlfriends. She held it near her face: Do I look like him?

No … Not really, her friends replied gingerly

More hypotheses bubbled: Was there an affair? One messy night?

Darker ideas, too: An assault?

Honestly, Miller wondered for a while if this whole thing wasn’t just an error. A screw-up at the lab.   

The siblings traded research, each adding pushpins on their own red string map.

Bright expanded her search, joining numerous additional genealogy sites — Family Tree DNA, GenMatch and even some European forums — hoping more databases would reveal more clues.

“We were on the computer every day, all day long,” Myers says.

And a set of truths emerged over the months, the anchor pieces to Myers’ puzzle.

More: Concerned after 23andMe bankruptcy? Here's a guide on how to download and delete your data

One: They all saw connections on their mothers’ sides, and the three family sets had different and distinct relations, as is to be expected.

Their moms were, in fact, their biological mothers.

Two: They didn’t see family names on their dads’ sides. Not even on distant branches.

Miller eventually had a paternal cousin test her DNA for comparison. Myers and Stoughton did too. Neither was a match to their respective cousins.

Their dads were not their biological fathers.

They methodically wove together the information encoded in their genes with the timeline of their births, and their moms’ pregnancies, and their mothers' fertility treatments, which some of the siblings knew about and others didn’t.

Separately, they were all coming to the same conclusion. One supported by the third truth. 

Three: They were matching to people they didn’t know. The same people. People who had or were related to one name — RANDALL.

Bright called Myers a few days after she found the connection, the one that unquestionably linked her to him. She softened her language when they spoke — He could be our biological father — an effort to cushion the blow of what she was sure was a breach of trust at the very least.

“It wasn't very long before I'm thinking, Are there tens? Tens of half siblings? Are there hundreds?" Bright says.

“How far does this go?”

headline: 'They just want to bury it': Iowans seek justice for moms violated by fertility doctor
fullText:
This is the final installment in the Register's three-part serial, "Doctor Deception."

Bert Jay Miller checked his Ancestry profile regularly in the months that followed his discovery that his biological father wasn’t the man he’d grown up calling Dad.

His network of half-siblings — the scions who all discovered late in life they shared the genes of Dr. John H. Randall, their mother’s fertility doctor — regularly checked their profiles, too.

They all understood losing your foundation in this way, losing the sense of identity molded from the personal cornerstone of “dad,” one of your first protectors, first safe harbors. The law, in its black and white wisdom, calls this crumbling “significant emotional trauma and distress.”  

Becky Myers couldn’t sleep after she found out that Randall — a beloved doctor, yet a temperamental and vindictive man — was her biological father. Liz Bright either. And she avoided mirrors; she couldn’t help but see his face superimposed over her own.

For a while, Bright disconnected, she says. Trauma is like Vaseline on the lens of life, buffing out edges. Turning down luminance. Obscuring.

“I just kind of felt dirty, not just because of what he did, but because of how I read that he treated other people,” she says.

She started to hear a soft tink, tink, tink — like metal on metal — in the background of her daily life, her imagination running wild with the sound of exam room instruments being picked up and set back down. Up and down. Over and over.    

“And I thought: Was that what was happening when my mother was …,” she lets herself drift off. “I can't explain it, but was I taken back to that time?”

Bright’s mother — an orphan who was abandoned by her father and then her stepfather before her mother died — had grown up with an aloneness so innate that the fear of abandonment coursed through her like blood. So, Bright attached herself to her dad’s family as though they were an amulet warding off the darkness of a solitary existence.

But this revelation was like having that veil of protection ripped from her neck. The aloneness she’d run from consumed.

“I started reinterpreting everything my parents said in this lens of: Could that have been true or not true? Even things my dad said to me on his deathbed,” she said. “I viewed things as through that lens of betrayal, untruth.”

“It just felt like my past was forever changed.”

Losing ownership of their histories has been the deepest pain, the siblings say, the cleaving of the family narratives that shaped them. The feeling is like a kaleidoscope’s image changing even though you didn’t twist the viewfinder.

The colors may be the same, but the shapes have shifted, the patterns has changed. And the whole picture is different.

“Now, when I look at photo albums,” says Nancy Duffner, Miller's full biological sister and another one of the Randall siblings, “those aren't my stories anymore.”

So every time a new match appeared on their online profile, their stomachs dropped. They wanted to offer a soft landing for what was a hard truth: Your mother’s OB-GYN is probably your father.

“We contacted some of them, but it’s kind of touchy,” Myers says. “You're finding out that your life has been part of a lie in some way.”

More from Courtney Crowder: After years of infertility, I was finally pregnant. Then doctors said there was a problem.

Eventually, she partnered with her brother, Ron Stoughton, on a letter they’d send when a new branch sprung up on their ad hoc tree: I see we’re related. If you’re interested in knowing how, I’d be glad to fill you in.

“Part of what's hard when you go through this is because people make you feel like you have leprosy or something, because they don't want anything to do with you,” she says. “You're just trying to get information on what happened, that's all you want to know, and nobody wants to talk to you.”

As the long humid nights of summer gave way to the crispness of fall, the discovery that Randall was their father kindled a need for action. Miller had to do something.

His raw, anxious energy had to go somewhere lest it combust.

So he called the University of Iowa.

‘They could be blaming themselves’: What is a university’s obligation?

Dr. Randall wasn’t a healthy man.

For much of his adult life, he had hypertensive heart disease, a kind of catchall for ongoing cardiac problems and long-term high blood pressure. A University of Iowa professor in addition to the OB-GYN department head, he was just 60 years old when he died, two days after being incapacitated by a stroke.

By the time Miller and Myers and the rest of the Randall half-siblings discovered their true parentage, they were on the other side of 60, older than their biological father ever became.

“That first year or two, I was worried I was going to die, to be honest,” says Bright, who's long struggled with chronic illness and pain.

They’d reached the age when medical histories mattered. They had been making decisions based on the records of the dad who raised them.

Bright, for example, had a “life-alerting” surgery before her DNA test revealed the deception coded into her genetics.

“You can’t get your parts back,” she says.

Myers and Stoughton stumbled through gallbladder issues and eventual removal despite not having any such history in their mother’s family or on the side of the dad who raised them. Stoughton’s daughters had their gallbladders removed, too, a reminder that Randall’s impact ripples through generations.    

So, while Miller was reaching out to the university for himself, for a direction to send the anxiety that hung on like a shadow on a summer afternoon, he was also reaching out for those who hadn’t yet discovered the lie, like a coiled sleeping serpent, in their DNA.

Closure, elusive though it is, could lie in easing others' journeys to the truth, Duffner thought.

“The university has to acknowledge this, and they need to make a concerted effort to find out how widespread this is to give people answers,” she says. “There could be people out there who have children with medical conditions, and they have no idea how the hell something happened. They could be blaming themselves.”

“This could be the answer for them.”

The university has sent out blanket information to patients before, such as in 2016 when the institution alerted 1,700 people that they may have been exposed to serious bacterial infections by a device used to regulate body temperature during open-heart and bypass surgery.

So when Miller called the university in September 2019, he hoped it could do something like that with Randall’s clinic list. He spoke to the then-executive chair of the OB-GYN department, who took notes and said he’d discuss with colleagues and get back in touch.

“The medical people at the University of Iowa Hospital, in that clinic, could not have been more empathetic, more caring,” Miller says.

About a week later, an administrator called, one with a particular expertise in clinical services. Some physicians and managers planned to form a team to research the Dr. Randall situation, he told Miller. At the end of their work, they’d hold a meeting with all the parties involved and present their findings, which, most importantly in Miller’s view, would eventually be made public.   

OK. Now there was a plan. And a plan seemed to satiate his raw, anxious energy.

Randall’s indiscretions and the school’s reaction should be in the open, Miller and Duffner believed. The siblings lost the thread to their own histories, but the university could claim — and learn from — the truth of its own.

“I want it to become part of the university history, because the university has done great and wonderful things,” Duffner says. “But there obviously was a period that wasn't so great.

“You can't only write the history you want the world to know.” 

A few weeks later, though, Miller’s phone rang again. This was a different administrator.

She said there’d be no team. No research. No meeting. And no further comment.

No plan.

The department’s concern, she told Miller, was “donor anonymity.”

“They finished talking to me by saying they weren't going to talk to me anymore, and that I should not even try to contact anyone there,” Miller said.

The university declined to comment on these calls or any of the siblings' other allegations.

And with the click of that call ending, Miller felt any semblance of closure slip away.

But unbeknownst to him, a different group of adults with donor surprises was lobbying for a new law.

And a empathetic legislator was already on their side.  

‘They just want to bury it’: Search for closure heads to Legislature and the bench

State Sen. Annette Sweeney, R-Iowa Falls, slid into one of the Iowa Supreme Court gallery’s benches and settled in to listen as a bill that she had spearheaded was debated and analyzed in front of Iowa’s highest judges.

For government junkies like herself, this — watching the checks and balances of democracy in action — was a big score.

The crux of the issue on the night's docket was whether Iowa’s Fraud in Assisted Reproduction Act is meant to include past crimes and should be applied retrospectively to actions before the law was enacted, as desired by the Randall siblings, the plaintiffs in the case.

Or if the law can be applied only prospectively to cases from when it was passed in 2022 forward, as the defense believes.

Similar cases regarding similar laws have recently been argued in Indiana — which allowed a fertility fraud claim to proceed against Dr. Donald Cline, accused of siring nearly 100 children using his own sperm instead of a specimen from the patient’s spouse or an otherwise agreed-upon donor — and Kentucky, which held that the law’s wording isn’t retrospective.

About a dozen states have fertility fraud statutes, but only one  — Illinois  —  included specifically retroactive language.

After more than six years of research back and forth, Miller and his siblings hired the Iowa City firm Hayes Lorenzen Biderman Lawyers to file a malpractice lawsuit against the state, Randall’s employer at the time of their mothers' treatment.

They felt like they had no other option, says Stoughton, because university officials “just want to bury it.”

“The driving force behind the lawsuit was if that's what it's going to take to get people to acknowledge it, then that's what we'll have to do,” added Myers, his sister.

In the lawsuit, the half-siblings contended that their mothers were deceived about the true nature of their fertility procedures because Randall misrepresented the identity of the sperm used. And by not instituting protocols that would have protected against this behavior, the state bore additional responsibility.

“One instance of harm may be the result of deceit,” their lawsuit said, “Multiple instances are a systemic failure.”

More from Courtney Crowder: After nearly 50 years, this Iowa man discovered his mother's doctor was his biological father

Their case was dismissed in pretrial proceedings over a combination of standing and statute of limitations concerns. The judge, however, pointed out that substantive evidentiary questions, specifically about any applicable standard of care, were too fact-intensive and could not be adequately evaluated in his ruling.

Legal proceedings had given Miller and Duffner access to some of their mother’s university records, but only in regard to her prenatal exams, for which she was seen by Randall. Same for Stoughton and Myers.

Nothing about treatments or procedures appeared in the documents they received, and nothing written said Randall informed their mother, Donna Miller, he’d be using his own sperm, or that she had agreed.

And nothing at all for Bright, which felt like yet another twist of the knife in her emotionally flayed stomach.

Any other records, the state informed the siblings’ lawyers, were damaged in a flood.

As much as they can tell, the paper trail in this case doesn’t run cold. There simply isn’t one.

So, the siblings looked for a new route to more information and, hopefully, some accountability. And they found an option in the new Fraud in Assisted Reproduction Act — Sweeney’s law.

Sweeney didn’t know about this Iowa City case when she wrote the law, but she’d become emotionally invested in stories like theirs as she researched non-paternity events and donor surprises and learned about the lack of legal remedies for victims, whether they are patient, spouse or offspring.

Some who find out about their surprise parentage aren’t bothered, sure, says Jody L. Madeira, a law professor at Indiana University and an expert in fertility fraud and bioethics. 

But many others see the circumstances of their conception “like being born the product from rape,” she says, because power was used to coerce or deceive. And, similarly, they want justice.

While general fraud laws or medical malpractice could be used in some cases to seek relief, the local advocates who reached out to Sweeney were looking to carve out new penalties to address the particularities of this kind of violation.

Sweeney spent two years crisscrossing the aisle for support, going back to the bill writers to change this or add that.

She’d put so much of herself into this work that she cried when the final vote was taken, a physical release of the spiritual connection she felt to those who suffered this harm.

More from Courtney Crowder: First-of-its-kind Iowa law criminalizes fertility fraud, labeling some deceitful doctors as sex offenders

These individuals deserve “closure on what has happened in their lives,” she says.

“And I just hurt so badly for the individuals that they’re figuring out that this has happened to them.”

‘We’re in the latter part of life’: The thought of what could have been haunts new-found siblings

Stoughton has always said he has gray eyes, and, for a while, his sister would reply that, no, they’re blue. Icy blue, maybe. But blue, like Mom's.

But during his research, Stoughton found Dr. Randall’s military card on the internet, and there it was: gray eyes.

A few answers have come to the siblings over these past years of unbraiding their DNA, whether those are somewhat minor like eye color or hair tint or more core to their beings, like why Stoughton’s dad left his mother at the airport, divorcing her after decades of what looked like happiness. Did he know … something?

Or, why Miller always felt like a bit of an outsider.

“Honestly, I kind of figured out why I like science so much,” Miller says. 

“There's nature versus nurture, and I always wondered where the more academic side of me came from, so now I have an idea of that.”

Bright recently found a childhood photo of herself and held it up to a similar one of Myers: same nose, same curly hair.

She’d once held up a picture of the man Myers knew as her dad, seeking similarities, wondering during their years of research if he was their connection, a secret sperm donor maybe. Turns out they didn't have the same dad, but they did share a biological father.   

“I would have liked to know what all these siblings were like when they were young,” Bright says.

“We're in the latter part of life. We have our own families, our own children, grandchildren,” Bright says. “It's not the same as if we had met each other years ago, and with that is kind of a grief for me.”

Of all the whys and hows that stalk the quiet moments of their days, the what could have beens may be the hardest to confront.

In the last few years, Bright has made a more concerted effort to touch base with her orphaned mother’s relatives, distant though they may be. And time has scabbed over one wound: She’s starting to think about going back to Germany, a place and an ethnicity she felt she lost when she found out her dad wasn’t her biological father.

Healing has been slow. As elusive as sleep and closure, too.

“I just creeped in” right before Randall died, she says, “and it made me feel, for a while, anyway, that my conception was just kind of like a twist of fate, that I got in before this behavior ended.

“I had to regrow my faith in God as a good God, that he intended for me to be on this Earth, even in spite of what happened. So, there's been a lot of spiritual wrestling.”

A part of Miller wishes he could have met Randall, spoken to him, got to know him — without absolving his behavior, of course.

His sister, decidedly, does not.

“Part of my history that I have to accept now is the history of this man who did this,” Duffner says. “This man — I use the word evil because I think what he did was evil — this egotistical man who did this to families over and over and over again. He is now literally a part of me.

“If I could somehow undergo a procedure where every gene that I have of his is removed from me and I only had my mother in me, I would do it.”

Early on, Myers and Stoughton wrote a letter to John Jr., Dr. Randall’s son, telling him the story of their discovery, presenting the evidence. He didn’t respond. They wrote to John Jr.’s daughter, too, and she didn’t reply either.

John Jr., who also didn't respond to the Register's requests for comment, followed his father into medicine, becoming an internist and surgeon in eastern Wisconsin.

When the elder Randall died from a stroke, John Jr. was a second-year resident. A few days after his father’s burial in his native Ohio, John Jr. graduated with high honors from the University of Iowa’s medical school, his dad’s alma mater.

In the wake of Randall’s shocking loss — an absence felt on campus as much as in his family — John Jr.’s classmates and his father’s former colleagues started a fund to sponsor lectures by top doctors. The Randall Visiting Professorship saw scientists from Harvard, Johns Hopkins and the University of Michigan travel to Iowa for speeches and hands-on clinics throughout the next decade.    

And, during graduation festivities, the elder Randall was posthumously selected as the 1959 “Outstanding Instructor” — his fourth time being chosen for the honor.

As class president, John Jr. presented the honors to his mother.

The court delivers an opinion — and a new mission emerges

When Sweeney wrote Iowa’s fertility fraud law, she intended to provide relief for those in circumstances like the Iowa City kids, she says. But the Iowa Supreme Court did not see that in the statute’s final words.

The justices sided with the state, saying the law wasn’t clear enough in its intentions to be applied to past actions, and dismissed the case. Through a spokesperson, the university said it appreciated the ruling and declined to comment further.

“I feel a bit saddened that I didn’t bring forth what we were all hoping, that it would take care of their anguish that they have suffered on this,” she says. “So that’s the part that really, for me, wants to look at this again and work over the interim to see if we can perfect this legislation.”

She’s already reached out to a couple attorney friends for advice on fixing the law and its language, she adds.

The law is still in effect prospectively, however, so couples seeking care today can expect additional rights and safeguards. Despite lots of improvements in the fertility industry, having a doctor switch samples isn’t out of the question. Madeira is aware of a physician using his own sperm in treatments in 2009, and of another using different embryos than agreed upon for donation in an effort to clean out the clinic’s freezer.

Going back to make sure the Iowa law is retroactive would ensure the largest group of victims can find justice.

“The law has a strong equitable bent, and we presume that the law can craft remedies and accountability methods for harms,” Madeira says.

“If laws like Iowa's are not found to be retroactive and therefore valid for the purposes of gaining accountability, then it's tantamount to saying that the law cannot do justice,” she adds, “and that doesn't leave us feeling too good.”

Legally, the siblings' only option is to have the law changed. So, they are left to regroup, and to find peace in knowing that the unknowns may always stay as such.

 “We spent hours and hours and hours trying to figure this out, trying to put the puzzle together,” Myers says.

“I did everything possible to find out what I could, and I feel that way now,” she adds, her voice catching in her throat. “I didn't leave anything unturned. I did as much as I could to try to get answers.”

Their network of half-siblings has grown over the years. And Myers keeps sending out the letter she and her brother wrote: I see we’re related. If you’re interested in knowing how, I’d be glad to fill you in.

She gives new family members time to process, and lets them get back to her — if they ever do.

“Everybody's in different stages of acceptance, denial, whatever,” Bright says. “Some don't want to know me. Some are probably dead.

“There are more to be found.”

The siblings hoped to use legal discovery to find additional records or witnesses. Answers, really.

Now they use their stories.

“As hard as it is, it's always, always better to speak truth to power,” Duffner says. “Whether it's Dr. Randall, whether it's the University of Iowa, whether it's something that's happening in the world that I may personally find upsetting.

“You're always going to be better not to hide in the castle, but to sally forth and speak truth to power.”

Their voices — which they lift for their parents, for their mothers especially — could provide new routes to accountability. New threads to follow in rewriting their histories.

And, maybe, new roots to a family tree just being planted.

This is the final installment in the Register's three-part serial, "Doctor Deception," which traces how five Iowans discovered their mother's fertility doctor is their biological father and details the lengths they went to for justice and accountability in their mothers' names — an effort they hope to continue.

headline: 'My mother was violated': Did a beloved Iowa fertility doctor prey on young women?
fullText:
This is the second installment in the Register's three-part serial, "Doctor Deception."

Dr. John H. Randall told the woman to come to the clinic after hours for her procedure.

When she arrived, he was alone. No nurse. No residents. No one else.

The woman was having trouble conceiving, she said in a deposition taken five decades after this appointment, and Dr. Randall was well-known in the community for helping women who hadn’t been able to get pregnant. Women like her.

He was beloved, really. Certainly respected.

Dr. Randall would be inseminating her by injecting sperm into her uterus, that much she knew, said the woman, who the Register is not identifying because she declined to be part of recent legal proceedings.

The woman believed the semen used would be a mix of her husband’s and a medical student’s, someone young, someone that resembled him — as was the predominantly agreed-upon understanding of most women seeking insemination in the 1950s.

She had no idea Dr. Randall planned to use his own sperm to impregnate her.

The children of another of Randall's patients, Marlys Stoughton, believe what happened to this woman also happened to their mother. She, too, was unaware Randall would insert his own semen, they say. 

Barbara Steinkraus didn’t know Randall would do the same to her either, her daughter says.  

Nor did Donna Miller.

In the last gasps of spring 1953, Donna made her way to the heart of downtown Iowa City to see Dr. Randall at the university hospital.

She’d been married to Bert Sr. for about seven years by then, but they hadn’t been able to conceive. She was in her mid-20s now and desperately wanted to be a mother.

They’d looked into adopting locally but found the nearby agencies wouldn’t place children in their “mixed” household. She was Catholic and he was Protestant.

So they’d started the process to adopt a child from Korea, where the war had left babies orphaned or young mothers without any other choice.

As their application came together, Bert Sr. and Donna continued to try for a biological baby. Until a bundle was in her arms, all options for motherhood were worth pursuing.  

So, she made an appointment with Dr. Randall. He was known to help women like her.

More from Courtney Crowder: After nearly 50 years, this Iowa man discovered his mother's doctor was his biological father

Donna’s fertility struggles weren’t a secret in the Miller house, says her daughter, Nancy Duffner. She talked openly with her children about how badly she and Bert Sr. wanted a family and, eventually, how they went to see a Dr. Randall for help.

“I think her intention was just to let us know how truly valued we were,” Duffner says. “That this was not an easy family that got put together, and that she and Dad wanted a family, and when that family finally came to them, she treasured us.”

At the clinic, Randall told Donna that her husband’s sperm count was low, but not too low. They should be able to conceive with his specimen. No need for donor sperm.

He told Donna the problem was her, as Duffner remembers her mother recounting. He said she needed some kind of "procedure," most likely describing a version of a intrauterine insemination that would inject sperm into her uterus.

If Donna had this "procedure," he said, everything would be fine.

So she went forward with the operation.

The couple was approaching final approval for their adoption when Donna discovered she was pregnant with Nancy.

At the tail end of 1955 and the early days of 1956, Donna visited Randall for help conceiving Bert Jay. And again in the spring of 1958, to have her last child, Randy.  

Donna was a mother three times over. A dream.

But a secret thought buried deep was growing toward the sun like a tree root planted too close to a sidewalk, lingering unseen until the concrete finally cracks.

Dr. John H. Randall: ‘One of Iowa’s beloved men of medicine,’ but vindictive and temperamental

With round wire glasses and combed-over hair, styled with enough mousse to resist a wind tunnel, Dr. Randall certainly looked the part of a professor. And with his “slow and deliberate” speech, marked by frequent repetitions always delivered in a monologue, he acted the role, too.

Think Ben Stein without the irony.

He was “phlegmatic,” unemotional and stoic, wrote a colleague in a history of the university’s OB-GYN department, and offered “little in the way of humor.”

But what he lacked in pizazz he made up for with his whip smarts and his deep interest in the field, a love that extended to his son, John Jr., who eventually followed his father’s path into medicine. 

Randall attended a small teachers college a few hours from his hometown in Ohio before matriculating to the University of Iowa’s medical program. Medicine had held Randall’s interest from an early age, but with six siblings, his parent’s couldn’t afford higher education, let alone medical school, according to the department history.

So he and his wife, his college sweetheart, spent five years saving for his tuition while teaching in Iowa and Minnesota, him focused on science and her on elementary education. Despite having to take on part-time jobs to afford school, Randall more than kept up with the rigorous academic schedule during practicums, even being elected to the national honor society.

A year abroad in Vienna during his residency exposed Randall to new innovations in gynecologic cancers, cultivating his lifelong research interest in these diseases and their treatments.

His specialty was analyzing cervix tissue cultures, lab work that made him especially adept at diagnosis and was eventually recognized for excellence by the American Cancer Society.

“When a patient was referred and brought her microscopic slides with her,” the department history reads, “he would often examine them and dictate a report himself without the slides ever being sent to the Department of Pathology.”

He also established a “tumor registry” to manage cases after treatment, an innovation that led to Iowa being one of only four institutions nationwide accredited for gynecologic cancer follow-up care at the time, notes the department history.

And, unlike other department heads or beaker-focused researchers, Randall didn’t rule from his office.

He was an active part of the hospital staff; spoke at medical conferences and continuing education seminars around the country; sat on boards and committees within the Iowa Medical Society and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, among many others; and ensured Iowa stayed on the cutting edge of the era’s rapidly changing technology by establishing a pioneering computerized system for housing and retrieving clinical records. 

And in this early Pap smear era, he toured the state advocating for more research funding and hosting meetings to inform women about new tests and surgeries for cervical and uterine cancer.

But he was a bedside doctor — and a trainer of bedside doctors — at heart.  

“His personal commitment to teaching was incredible,” Roy Pitkin, a former chair of the OB-GYN department, wrote in the unit’s history.

When Randall was especially sick with the hypertensive heart disease that had plagued his life, a resident would be dispatched to bring him in a wheelchair to the obstetric ward, where he would discuss a case with a handful of medical students.

“The man was clearly very ill — his ankles were swollen and his speaking was even more hesitant than usual because of cardiac failure — but here he was, doing what he believed his job to be,” Pitkin wrote.

As much as he was a favorite among students, Randall appears to have had an even more profound effect on his clinical patients. He returned from vacation once to find his office completely refurbished, a solid walnut desk playing centerpiece in the surprise.

So many wanted to contribute to the gift that the organizer finally capped participation at 20 colleagues and former patient families, the Iowa City Press-Citizen wrote at the time. One out-of-state woman sent a check and a note that she had been “condemned to death” before having “life and hope restored with an operation performed by Doctor Randall, one of Iowa’s beloved men of medicine.” 

“Those who contributed to the grand-scale surprise felt, of course, that they had already been paid back a thousandfold in the kindly service and ‘new lease on life’ for which Dr. Randall is famous,” the newspaper wrote.

A few years later, a different group sponsored an oil portrait of Randall — which still hangs in an administration area of the university hospital — and arranged a presentation ceremony with the artist and “former patients from all parts of Iowa.”

But Randall was known to be vindictive as well, locked in a bitter rivalry with a colleague that saw each maneuver to undercut the other and often forced residents to pick a side.

And he was known to lash out, especially at female colleagues and subordinates: “He would sometimes lose his temper and heap verbal abuse, and sometimes instruments, on scrub nurses and residents,” the department history notes.

After spending his entire professional career in Iowa, at the university hospital, Randall’s final moments were there, too. The 60-year-old died at the medical center two days after a stroke in April 1959, a result of his ongoing cardiac issues.

He took with him, it seems, any knowledge of why he used his own semen to impregnate the Steinkrauses, Stoughtons and Millers.

And the handful of other families they didn’t know about yet.

Can what happened in that exam room be known — and does it matter?

Randall is far from the only doctor to act outside of the standards of conduct in this way.

In their research, half-siblings Liz Bright, Barbara Steinkraus’ daughter, and Bert Jay Miller discovered that a presumed dad is found not to be a biological father with enough regularity that there’s a name for the phenomenon: a non-paternity event.

And there are online support groups for people who’ve found out they’re donor conceived, though apparently just one fairly dormant page specifically for the children of their mother’s gynecologists.

Within the last decade or so, in certain cities, around certain hospitals, clusters of instances involving fertility doctors using their own sperm in treatments have appeared, unearthed by readily available direct-to-consumer DNA tests.

The sheer numbers are shocking in some cases: Dr. Donald Cline, a physician in Indianapolis, has been accused of siring nearly 100 children using his own sperm instead of the patient’s spouse or an otherwise agreed-upon donor.

Norman Barwin, a fertility specialist in Ottawa, Canada, was sued by more than 200 clients whose reproductive materials he misused, including 17 children determined to be his biologically. While Dr. Cecil Jacobson of Virginia used his own semen in lieu of anonymous donors, resulting in 15 confirmed children and up to 75 more suspected.

And in Randall’s case, there are “pods of his children,” said Karen Lorenzen, one of the siblings’ lawyers. The Iowa City firm Hayes Lorenzen Biderman Lawyers represented the siblings in both a malpractice suit against Randall and, later, a suit under Iowa's new Fraud in Assisted Reproduction Act.

In all of these situations, questions of consent loom large: What may or may not have been whispered in an exam room? Who may have known and what could they have known?

No one is alive to speak to “the intent of Dr. Randall, Donna and Bert when providing and receiving reproductive health services,” the state, acting as defendant because Randall was employed by the university, pointed out in briefs.

And Iowa Chief Justice Susan Christensen noted in recent arguments that she is aware of ruses where adults insisted they were a child’s parents despite knowing full well they weren’t.

“Doesn't the record show we don't know what mom and dad knew? We don't know what the doctor said?” Christensen said. “I have a family member who dealt with infertility, and I believe she would have walked through fire to have a child. How do you know that it was abusive?”

More from Courtney Crowder: After years of infertility, I was finally pregnant. Then doctors said there was a problem.

But this vein of questioning ignores the reality that both misleading a patient and using your own sperm as a medical professional had been against the standards of care for decades before the 1950s, says Jody L. Madeira, a law professor at Indiana University and an expert in fertility fraud and bioethics. 

And that generally theft, deception and misrepresentation were all illegal under common law, she adds.

Put simply: Being honest has always been a doctor’s obligation.

“Seventy years ago, we had an understanding that you don't lie to patients,” Madeira says. The universally accepted practice was that “you explain the procedure and you get consent.”

“So even though we didn't have a specific legal written consent requirement, it still would have been thought to be unscrupulous for a doctor to inseminate somebody with their own sperm.”

And surreptitiously swapping samples or knowingly using a different specimen was more than unethical, those acts were agreed to be criminal, Madeira says. One doctor she quoted told of a husband who in the 1960s asked for donor sperm to be used in the procedure but for the physician to tell his wife the sample was his.

“Had we agreed to this ruse, we would be liable for charges of assault or rape,” the doctor writes.

Despite time and place, these situations have a consistent framework with doctors using a similar script: “Women were told that the donor would be either their husband or a person resembling their husband. Nobody was told it was the doctor,” Madeira says.

And none of the dozens of women she’s interviewed, including moms from most of the high-profile American cases of doctor donors, would have consented to the doctor using his own sperm, she says — no matter how badly she wanted to be a mother.

“Just because patients are desperate does not mean they wanted to be deceived,” Madeira says.

“Their vulnerability should never be used against them.”

‘Mom had no reason to keep this from us’

In all the conversations Donna Miller had with her children about her struggles to become pregnant and her fertility procedures and how much she desperately — desperately — wanted to be a mother, she never once indicated that anyone other than Bert Sr. was their father, Duffner stresses.

Her mother had been in the process of adoption before getting pregnant, she understood that family comes together in many ways and that love runs beyond a bloodline. Had her mother known, she just would not have kept their parentage a secret, Duffner says.  

Stoughton’s children, Ron Stoughton and Becky Myers, agree. They’re convinced their mother, had she known, would have said something in the bitterness of their parents' divorce proceedings. Or, Myers adds, when she was having her own fertility issues.

“My mom had no reason to keep this from us,” Myers says.

And the same is true for Bright, whose parents also were open about needing help to conceive, always framing their struggle as she was “an answer to prayer.”

As Bright’s research led her closer to the truth of her parentage, intuition told her that her mother had been violated. Call it a daughter’s instinct or a woman’s understanding. Deep in her bones, she sensed a breach, physically and emotionally and spiritually.

When Bright discovered the connection between her and Randall, she had a “somatic reaction.” Motion sick even though she was sitting still. Tingles and pinpricks of dizziness crawling around her brain.

Duffner sensed an offense, too.

“Almost immediately, and maybe it’s because I’m female, my thoughts went to, ‘Oh my God, my mother was a beautiful, trusting young woman,’” she says. “She was a product of an era when women didn't question a male doctor. They were God-like.”

Decades removed from that exam room, Duffner and the rest of the siblings are left to sit with the unknowns: “How did this happen? How could this happen? Was it just Dr. Randall? Was the whole university, were there other doctors and nurses in on this?”

Possible scenes play like movie trailers projected in her mind, an audience of one, even if she doesn’t want to watch. Sometimes the plot twists dark: “Was there a sheet and she was knocked out, given something so she wasn't totally coherent, and was she raped?”

Or was she a young woman alone, vulnerable in a quiet clinic after hours, placing her trust in a beloved doctor?

A trust held so faithfully that Duffner’s mother honored the clinician by naming her second son after him: Randy for Randall.

Decades later, as the nature of Randall’s deception unfolded, Randy took a DNA test, too. Unlike his brother and sister, however, his test revealed he carries Randall only in his name, not in his genes.

Bert Sr. is his biological father.

Which leaves them all to reckon with the fact that Randall was right on one account: Donna Miller was capable of conceiving children with her husband.

Donor sperm wasn’t necessary.

This is the second installment in the Register's three-part serial, "Doctor Deception," which traces how five Iowans discovered their mother's fertility doctor is their biological father and details the lengths they went to for justice and accountability in their mothers' names — an effort they hope to continue.

Read the serial from the beginning here. Or click here to continue with the final installment.
