headline: Why has respect for higher education diminished? Let's dig deeper. | Opinion
fullText:
On May 13, my term as president of the Faculty Senate of Iowa State University ended. As I reflect on the past year, one concern has weighed on me more than any other: the growing lack of faith in academia.

Each morning, I began my day reading the Chronicle of Higher Education and the Iowa State Daily. Again and again, I was struck by a rising skepticism — bordering on cynicism — toward higher education. I struggled to understand it. Then I came across a Gallup poll cited in the Chronicle showing a significant decline in public confidence in higher education over the past decade. It left me asking: How did we get here?

I’ve lived in Iowa for 35 years. I remember when education was a source of immense pride. I see former students — some from decades ago — thriving in executive roles, running successful businesses, and contributing meaningfully to society in myriad elective and volunteer roles. Ask them how they got there, and I’m confident they would point to the education they received.

So why the diminishing respect for academia?

This has been my life’s work. Since the day I graduated from college, I have been a professor. Just because this has been my only career, I feel a deep responsibility to speak — not just in defense of the profession, but in hopes of rebuilding public trust.

Let me be clear: We are not perfect. Like any large institution, we have individuals who fall short. But the vast majority of faculty and staff are dedicated professionals who chose this path not for wealth but for the love of teaching, research and service to young people and our collective future. Let me address some of the recurring criticisms I’ve encountered:

Tuition increases

The burden of rising tuition is real — and deeply concerning. But we must understand the context. Not long ago, the state funded about 70% of a student’s education, with students contributing around 20%. Today, that model has flipped: Students now bear close to 70% of the cost. This isn’t about greed — it’s about shifting public priorities and funding decisions.

DEI Initiatives

Concerns about diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) efforts are current and can run deep, but I submit that we have not tried hard enough to secure what these words as goals or values were intended to secure. These initiatives originated in the business world, where a diverse and collaborative workforce is a competitive advantage, when business leaders had serious concerns whether Iowa offered and could attract the workforce they needed, and where assurance of inclusion and equal opportunity for advancement were essential to attracting it.

Employers want graduates who can thrive in diverse environments. That said, it’s fair to ask whether some initiatives have overreached and whether they’re sufficiently available to all. We must remain open to honest assessment and recalibration.

Program proliferation

New academic programs are not created in a vacuum. Every proposal undergoes rigorous review and must demonstrate a clear, unmet need. If a program cannot sustain itself financially, it does not survive. Curriculum innovation is often a response to evolving workforce demands and societal needs.

Research grants and indirect costs

Universities take a portion of research grants as indirect costs — not to pad salaries, but to fund the infrastructure required for cutting-edge research. Labs are expensive to build and maintain. Faculty salaries typically come from the university, not the grants. Graduate students often earn modest stipends. In truth, society (state, country, and industry) is getting a huge bargain: many groundbreaking discoveries of the last century were made in university settings, subsidized by the institutions themselves, the National Science Foundation, the National Institute of Health, and other funding agencies. As one example, think of the patents that Iowa State’s College of Agriculture has generated and the contributions it's made to the agricultural industry and Iowa.

Research

Even within academia, research is sometimes criticized — often by faculty in other disciplines — as impractical or esoteric. But I’ve seen academia in many countries, and I can say with pride that American higher education is the best in the world.

Research is the key reason why.

Why do we require research?

  • To ensure faculty remain current in their disciplines.
  • To demonstrate that they not only understand existing knowledge but can contribute to it and expand upon it.

Publishing requires knowing the field, identifying gaps, and moving the work forward — even incrementally. Most research makes small contributions, but over time, these add up and move science forward. Also, more importantly, they ensure that the person teaching the class is truly an expert.

Indoctrination

Of all the accusations, this may be the most perplexing. As a parent of two daughters, I’ve spent 30 years trying to influence them — and I can tell you, indoctrination is no easy feat; I failed. I’m sure most parents would agree. The idea that a professor can indoctrinate a student in 45 hours over a semester is simply not credible. Most degree programs focus on technical or disciplinary knowledge, not ideology. More importantly, students are far more discerning than they’re often given credit for.

As I said at the outset, we are not perfect, but the broad distrust toward academia is misplaced and deeply unfair. If there are concerns, and there are, we should talk; and if we identify problems or unmet needs, surely we can work together to find solutions. If a farm has weeds, do we destroy the entire field, or do we simply pull the weeds?

Let’s all come together, bringing our Iowa Nice demeanor, to solve this problem as it is in the best interests of the student, the state, the country and the business. Let’s bring back those good old days, the ones I witnessed when I moved to Iowa 35 years ago. An Iowa that cared about education and took pride in it.

Let’s pull the weeds. Let’s not destroy the farm. Thank you.

Rahul Parsa is past president of the Faculty Senate at Iowa State University. The views in this essay are his alone.

headline: Kim Reynolds’ trust of parents is selective | Letters
fullText:
Aren’t standards for working in medicine a good thing?

From the May 26 story “Med schools won’t be judged on diversity”: “a single set of accreditation expectations with which all schools … must comply.” This seems like exactly what should be the standard for medical proficiency in order to ensure that we have the best doctors possible in our health care system. To think that this will result in a less diverse group of physicians is just another example of the soft bigotry of low expectations.   

Dan Walter, West Des Moines

Thank you for calling out elderspeak

Finally, my peeve gets a forum. As a Registered Nurse serving the long-term-care community, I saw elderspeak was pervasive. As pointed out, this happens in other settings. Restaurant servers and retail still think I’m their sweetie.

Caroline Van De Pol, Des Moines

RFK’s COVID vaccine move is wrong and traumatizing

I am very concerned about the new restriction of COVID vaccines to people over 65 or with known health risks. My husband and I are well past the age 65 cutoff, but how can we accept a vaccine when our loved ones might not be able to get one?

Especially our daughter, who lost her husband, the love of her life, to COVID in 2020? Of course their two daughters were traumatized by that loss and still suffer from nightmares and worry that something might happen to their mother, leaving them without any parents at all.

The powers that be make it sound as if this is being done out of caution regarding vaccine safety, but it is impossible to trust them, given that the secretary of health and human Services is Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a known vaccine opponent. On his watch, we have children in Texas dying needlessly of measles while he dispenses bogus advice. You can imagine how our daughter and her parents-in-law are taking this news of COVID vaccine restrictions!

Barbara Aszman Stone, Grinnell

Our attitudes toward immigration used to be more healthy

I found it very intriguing when I read two articles in the May 23 Metro & Iowa section about immigration: "Bird cheers Trump's immigration policy in southern border stop" and "CelebrAsian celebrates 50 years of life in Iowa." How things have changed in 50 years.

Not too long ago, welcoming immigrants to our communities was celebrated; helping the less fortunate to achieve a better life made folks feel good about themselves. Now immigration is a hot button issue, immigrants in our country legally or illegally have been painted with the same broad brush as criminals and have become pawns of politicians to obtain votes.

My take has always been that everyone in our country, excluding Native Americans, are descendants of immigrants or are immigrants. Most came because they were being persecuted in their homeland or were brought to America against their will. Of course, because I'm a proponent of law and order, I don't condone entering our country illegally. However, currently, it appears that, for political purposes, immigrants who have entered legally are being portrayed the same way as those who entered illegally.

My conclusion is that timing is everything and politicians are nothing.

Kevin Shawgo, Nevada

Republicans kept Biden from fixing the border

I read with great interest the story about Attorney General Brenna Bird being on the southern border giving huge attaboys to President Donald Trump about his border action plan. I read it twice to be sure. Not a single mention about how Trump killed the bipartisan bill a few years ago. Y'all remember that one, right? It would have provided more money and staff for the border, more immigration judges to expedite immigrant cases, and more money to increase drug detection incidents at the border.

But, Trump, the object of Bird's affection, called the Senate's GOP caucus and told them to kill that bill, because, wait for it, he wanted to use the border problems as a campaign issue during his run for reelection.

Interesting how that fact never is mentioned by the GOP when border issues are discussed.

Phil Armstrong, Des Moines

SNAP restrictions could hurt convenience stores

The Jan. 1 changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that will eliminate any items that are subject to state sales tax from being SNAP-eligible may prove very detrimental to the convenience store industry in Iowa. C-stores are known for selling mostly junk foods, and in some locations over half their inside sales come from customers using EBT cards for their purchases. So while this change is long overdue, the effect on these businesses will be immediate. I hope they will be prepared.

John Moore, Newton

Register’s stories of graduates were inspiring

Thank you so much for running the stories of the area high school graduating seniors. Those stories meant so much more to me than a list of top graduates determined by grades. These are young people who inspire and will continue to inspire others. What an achievement.  You have given your readers a gift, and I am grateful. 

Julie Powell-Mohr, Des Moines

More: These 28 high school graduating seniors from the Des Moines area each have a story to tell

Kim Reynolds’ trust of parents is selective

In response to Althea Cole’s opinion piece May 25, I would like to compare summer food assistance and Education Savings Accounts in a different way. Gov. Kim Reynolds wants parents to choose which school their children go to because they know their children best. However, she does not believe that these same parents can make the best decision about their child's health care (trans kids) or which books they should have access to, or, now, what food they can feed their children. 

Oh, wait a minute, these are not the same parents. These are parents who have different "family values" than the governor and her supporters have. A double standard.  

Ellen Picray, Emmetsburg

Our government does not honor the principles recognized on Memorial Day

I have to admit that this Memorial Day felt very formulaic, mostly pronouncements with no real feelings or serious intentions.

"Remember and honor," which we should, but we really do not do either. If we remembered we would not support deployments of our military abroad without our national consensus of why they are deployed, to what end, and at what cost. And if we honored, then the majority of Congress would not shamefully and consistently cut benefits and much needed services to veterans.

It is often said that "freedom is not free," meaning that American troops lost their lives so that we enjoy the freedoms we have, like freedom of speech, like due process, both of which are being ridiculed and taken away by our president while the majority of Congress sits silently and gives lip service to "honoring veterans."

Members of the U.S. armed forces have gone through a lot of training and are putting their lives on the line in defense of our nation. Our responsibility as ordinary citizens is to work our citizenship muscles a little and take the time actually understand and value the principles our troops are allegedly defending, so that we don't elect people who are dishonoring our veterans daily, and trashing the principles for which their gave their lives to.

Kamyar Enshayan, Cedar Falls

Don’t demonize the tools that feed the world

With the release of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission report, I am concerned about its potential impact on Iowa agriculture and the families who depend on it.

I wholeheartedly agree that Americans need to be healthy and well-nourished — but this is impossible without tools like glyphosate. Our farmers rely on Environmental Protection Agency-approved inputs to grow the abundant, high-quality crops that feed our nation. To keep grocery store shelves stocked, farmers need continued access to these essential tools.

Iowa is a national leader in agriculture, especially in soybeans and corn. Our farmers depend on safe, effective crop protection methods to combat invasive pests. Already, globally, nearly half of all crops are lost to weeds and pests — losses that would rise dramatically without access to pesticides. That’s a risk we simply can’t afford.

Science-based, EPA-approved pesticides also save Iowa farmers hundreds of millions of dollars each year — savings we pass along to grocery store shoppers. Farming without them will drive up food prices for Iowa families and jeopardize our food supply.

The MAHA report has stirred up a lot of unfounded concerns, and I’m genuinely worried that the tools I rely on could be taken away. I urge our leaders in Washington to listen to the people who will be most affected by this, like me, not politicians with their own agendas. If we truly want to support American health, we must begin by safeguarding the tools that keep food on our tables.

Duane Aistrope, Randolph

Kim Reynolds takes Iowa backward

I see Gov. Kim Reynolds is modernizing our unemployment system. No doubt overdue. Every bill a governor signs “modernizes” the old, some that was working just fine.

This year Reynolds has modernized the civil rights code, removing transgender people from those protections. The recently signed DEI bill has modernized that program and canceled the needs for diversity, equity, and inclusion at our state universities.

We were once a “pluralistic” democracy (or tried to be). We honored those three mainstays, a fact the next generation will never know. Of course, by then, every immigrant will have been uprooted and sent to Mars, even if they’ve been here longer than Barron Trump has been alive — and contributed more to society than his dad.

Gerald Ott, Ankeny

headline: Creatures and people get set for June’s brilliance | Opinion
fullText:
The other night, at dusk, a male deer sporting small velvet antlers grazed in my backyard, just a few feet from where I sat inside.

When his antlers are fully grown in late summer or early autumn, the velvet will be gone.

Science has shown that what looks like velvet is actually skin with hair, blood vessels, and nerve endings to nourish the growing antlers.

Many fools around the world go to great lengths to cut off deer antlers while still covered in the velvet, then use the velvet to make “natural” healing medicine.

Like many such products, there is no science to prove that any claims of healing are true.

So, deer must endure the indignity of it all, succumbing to our often far-fetched notions of what will make us healthier.

I’ve not seen the badgers in Bobbi’s Hollow for a while. My last sighting was of two cubs peering out, curious about my tractor rumbling and throbbing past their den (officially a sett).

I hope that they’ve moved on, exhausting my supply of rodents and snakes.

A friend often brings his dogs to run in the hollow, but he’ll wisely keep his dogs away until the badgers are gone. Any creature sniffing around a sett is asking for trouble.

Setts are like something out of Middle Earth, vast tunnels, sometimes very deep, with numerous chambers for sleeping, rearing their young, and so on.

I like to think that perhaps there is also a chamber with a pool table, dartboard on a wall, and maybe a chamber with a cocktail bar and comfortable leather chairs, perhaps a small stereo setup, where mom can relax after a long day, listen to Steely Dan, and enjoy a beverage.

Bushes and shrubs along the road north of my house have filled in, hiding me from civilization. There is one spot where, if you’re driving past and glance quickly, you can catch a glimpse of my house.

Everything around it is green, no color of annual flowers.

My wife loved her flowers in the spring, and I kept up the practice during the final couple years of her journey, but stopped after she passed. I’m happy that planting flowers every spring brings satisfaction for so many. However, I’m much too cynical, seeing the floral industry as, well, not like you see it, probably.

Recently, I wrote about my senior cat, Pippa. This week, she is limping, her right front leg or paw causing her some pain.

I need to find a vet who makes house calls, as putting my cats into carriers has become agonizing and fraught, for all of us. And, selfishly, I want the girls to outlive me.

The anniversary of my wedding, a very long time ago, is in spring. I don’t recall a lot about the day, just snippets.

Private. Only family in attendance. Two ministers. String quartet for the reception. Vivaldi and Handel humming along. Food gone by the time I got to it.

A gorgeous, brilliant, constantly smiling woman at my side.

I was never one to smile much. On more than one occasion, my mother would say to me, “We spent a lot of money on those teeth. The least you can do is smile once in a while.”

That’s about all I remember about that late May day, and maybe that’s enough. There were countless more days to come that proved to be just as meaningful and beautiful.

I hope you all have many such days, and I hope you will recall and appreciate them with clarity and acuity.

Having said that, know that if I rise up just a little, and crane my crepey neck a bit I can see June, and it looks to be brilliant.

Kurt Ullrich lives in rural Jackson County. His book “The Iowa State Fair” is available from the University of Iowa Press.

headline: Stand up for international students, for free speech, and Iowa's universities | Opinion
fullText:
It’s been possible to imagine that the Trump administration's drumbeat of heavy-handed executive orders was, with some notable exceptions, wreaking mayhem outside our state.

Yes, the Department of Government Efficiency devastated social services agencies and their ability to serve refugees and other vulnerable people. And tariffs affect everybody, particularly threatening farmers' livelihoods. But Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins promised Iowa producers they would be taken care of — and even before courts held that Trump’s tariff orders were illegal, they’d been implemented so mercurially that the deepest consequences weren’t taking hold.

In other areas, Iowa was already a laboratory for versions of some conservative policies the White House and Congress are now spreading, so new federal guidance couldn’t produce as much whiplash.

One of Trump's post-Memorial Day moves threatens more lasting damage to Iowa. The president’s vendetta against foreign-born people now could jeopardize the future of higher education throughout the country. Iowa’s six Republicans in Congress — who have supported almost everything Trump has done, even when it was bad for Iowans — should stand up for the health of our public universities and demand consistency in how the White House advocates for freedom of thought and speech.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced May 27 that State Department staff should stop scheduling interviews for new visas while the administration works on a new plan for vetting applicants’ social media. This came on the heels of weeks of headlines about assertions from Trump and his Cabinet about their authority to set policy at private colleges (Harvard, mostly) as a condition of providing federal money, including funding for research that benefits us all. By May 29, administration officials were trying or pledging to remove all international students from Harvard and “aggressively revoke” Chinese student visas more broadly.

International students at U.S. schools are a good thing

If schools are unable to enroll new international students — or, as is already likely, they and future prospective students are discouraged from even bothering — the effects will be severe.

Rubio’s visa-interview pause “is bound to unsettle one of America’s most successful export industries — selling undergraduate and graduate degrees to intelligent foreigners — and disrupt the considerable scientific and technological research that overseas students enable at major universities,” Rose Horowitch wrote in the Atlantic magazine.

International enrollment at the three Iowa public universities peaked in the mid-2010s and has been sliding since. In fall 2024, the University of Iowa enrolled 3,775 international students; Iowa State University 3,061; and the University of Northern Iowa 202. Iowa and Iowa State were both over 4,000 as recently as 2015, and UNI’s total is down by over two-thirds from its peak. A further nose-dive would bring both immediate and long-term consequences:

  • Thousands fewer people paying full freight tuition.
  • A gash in enrollment, compounding problems posed by Iowa’s aging population that can’t be fixed simply by laying off university employees.
  • For remaining students, less diversity and connection to other cultures.
  • Less American influence on young adults around the world. Fewer future titans of culture and business would even get a choice about whether to stay in the country.

To be clear, the biggest problem here is the indiscriminate breadth of the White House’s actions. Some visa revocations are defensible. Four University of Iowa students have won a temporary reprieve in the courts after they were targeted for removal because of criminal records that include drunken driving and domestic violence. Dismissing such foreign students might not be the best use of discretion, but it’s also true that entering our country to study is a privilege, not a right.

But we deny that privilege haphazardly at our own peril.

Do Grassley and Ernst care more about Iowans, or about Trump?

The White House has been savaged by critics and the federal judiciary for its apparent position that any visa holder who voices any criticism of Israel’s government is no longer welcome in the United States. Whether or not that standard is ultimately found to be legal, it is plainly contrary to the principle that free expression should be defended.

Trump and his Cabinet secretaries have dug in their heels in their war against higher education. But the six Iowa Republicans in Congress are positioned as well as anybody to demand better.

To date, regrettably, the delegation has mostly waved Trump’s banner. All four representatives voted for the president’s “Big Beautiful Bill” to slash taxes for the wealthiest Americans and hugely reduce government assistance. Sen. Chuck Grassley has nodded toward independence a handful of times, including May 26 when he called for Trump to sanction Russian leader Vladimir Putin (alas, he invoked, approvingly, the president’s vigor against Harvard).

Grassley, Sen. Joni Ernst and the rest have shown no appetite so far to dispute Trump’s apparent belief that he can treat non-citizens however he likes for any reason. But if they stand for anything besides the proposition that Trump is always right, they need to try to stop this particular crusade.

Grassley and Ernst, whose votes could be vital for the tax-cut bill’s future, can start with these demands:

Let Iowa, ISU and UNI continue to enroll international students as they always have. Restore confidence that our country’s existing guests will be treated fairly. Make it clear that the United States will not loudly trumpet the virtue of free expression with one hand and demand fealty to specific political viewpoints with the other.

Our senators’ next moves will show us whose concerns matter more: Iowans’, or Trump’s.

Lucas Grundmeier, on behalf of the Register’s editorial board

headline: Why some towns lose local news, and others don’t | Opinion
fullText:
Why did your hometown newspaper vanish while the next town over kept theirs?

This isn’t bad luck — it’s a systemic pattern. Since 2005, the United States has lost over one-third of its local newspapers, creating “news deserts” where corruption is more likely to spread and communities may become politically polarized.

My research, published in Journalism & Mass Communication Quarterly, analyzes the factors behind the decline of local newspapers between 2004 and 2018. It identifies five key drivers — ranging from racial disparity to market forces − that determine which towns lose their papers and which ones beat the odds.

1. Newspapers follow the money, not community needs

You might expect news media to gravitate toward areas where their work is needed most — communities experiencing population growth or facing systemic challenges. But in reality, newspapers, like any business, tend to thrive where the financial resources are greatest.

My analyses suggest that local newspapers survive where affluent subscribers and deep-pocketed advertisers cluster. That means wealthy white suburbs keep their watchdogs, while low-income and diverse communities lose theirs.When police brutality spikes, when welfare offices deny claims, when local officials divert funds — these are the moments when communities need their journalists the most.

Poor and racially diverse communities often face the harshest policing and interact more with street-level bureaucrats than wealthier citizens. That makes them more vulnerable to government corruption and misconduct. Yet, these same communities are the first to lose their newspapers, because there are no luxury real estate agencies buying ads, and few residents can afford the monthly subscriptions.

Without journalistic scrutiny, scholars find that mismanagement flourishes, corruption costs balloon, and the communities most vulnerable to abuse receive the least accountability. This is how news deserts exacerbate inequality.

2. Newspapers don’t adequately serve diverse communities

Picture this: A newsroom sends its reporters, most of whom are white, to a Black neighborhood — but only after reports of gunshots or building fires. Residents, still in shock, don’t want to talk. So journalists call the same three community leaders they always quote, run the tragic story and disappear until the next crisis. This approach, often referred to as “parachute journalism,” results in shallow coverage that paints the community in a negative light while overlooking its complexities.

Year after year, the pattern repeats. The only time residents see their neighborhood in the paper is when something terrible happens. No feature story of the family-owned restaurant celebrating its 20-year anniversary, no reporter at the town hall when the new police chief gets grilled about stop-and-frisk — just the constant drumbeat of crime and crisis.

Is it any wonder racially diverse communities stop trusting and paying for that paper? Not when many working-class families of color can barely afford to add a newspaper subscription to their bills.

Diverse neighborhoods get hit twice. First, their local papers inadequately represent them. Then, when people understandably turn away, subscriptions drop, advertisers pull back and the outlets shut down, leaving whole communities without a voice.

Only in recent years have more media outlets begun to make a concerted effort to engage with and reflect the communities they serve. However, such efforts are often led by newer media organizations with fresh ideologies, while many long-standing media outlets remain stuck in traditional reporting practices, as illustrated in Jacob Nelson’s “Imagined Audiences.” Although my analyses of local newspaper decline from 2004 to 2018 paints a frustrating picture, the emerging trend of community-oriented journalism holds promise for positive changes in diverse communities.

3. Population growth doesn’t always save newspapers

It’s easy to assume that more people = more readers = healthier news organizations. But my research tells a different story: Counties with larger population growth actually saw greater declines in local newspapers.

The catch lies in who is moving in: Population growth saves papers only when it comes with wealth. Affluent newcomers bring subscriptions and advertisers’ attention. But growth driven by high birth rates, typically seen in less developed areas with more racial and ethnic minorities, doesn’t translate to revenue. In short, growth alone isn’t enough − it’s the type of growth, and the economic power behind it, that matters.

This highlights the fragility of market-dependent journalism. The news gap experienced by fast-growing communities may persist where local journalism depends primarily on traditional advertising and subscription revenues rather than diversified revenue sources such as grants and philanthropic donations. The latter, which often focus on community needs rather than profit potential, are more likely to help sustain journalism in areas with significant population growth.

4. Neighbors’ newspapers can save yours

You’d think that competition between newspapers would be a cutthroat affair. But in an era of decline, my analyses reveal a counterintuitive truth: Your town’s paper actually has better odds when nearby communities keep theirs.

Rather than competing, neighboring papers often become allies, sharing breaking news, splitting investigative costs and attracting advertisers who want regional reach. While this collaboration can sometimes cause papers to lose their local identity, having some local journalism is still better than none. It ensures some level of accountability, even if the news isn’t as focused on each town’s unique needs.

Resilient local journalism clusters together. When one paper invests in original reporting, its neighbors often benefit too. When regional businesses support multiple outlets, the entire news ecosystem becomes more sustainable.

5. Left or right? Local papers die either way

In this highly polarized era, it turns out that there’s no significant link between a county’s partisan makeup and its ability to keep newspapers.

Urban hubs such as Chicago keep robust media thanks to dense populations and corporate advertisers, not because they vote for Democrats. Meanwhile, newspapers in conservative rural areas can survive by cultivating loyal readerships within their communities.

In contrast, communities with lower income and a diverse population lose outlets no matter whether they are red, blue or purple.

Partisan battles might dominate national headlines, but local journalism’s survival hinges on practical factors such as money and market size. Saving local news isn’t a left vs. right debate − it’s a community issue that requires nonpartisan solutions.

Abby Youran Qin is a Ph.D. candidate at the School of Journalism & Mass Communication at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. This essay is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

headline: Regeneron is trying to buy 23andMe – and by extension, your DNA information | Opinion
fullText:
Did you spit in a tube for 23andMe? If so, your genetic data may soon be handed over to a new company — Regeneron.

Just four years ago, when 23andMe went public, the company was valued at $6 billion. Earlier this year, it filed for bankruptcy. While its business model — selling DNA tests to consumers, then turning around and monetizing that data — seemed full of promise, the company has struggled to turn a profit. Its most valuable remaining asset is the genetic and personal information of its customers.

Regeneron is now poised to step in and purchase this customer data, for $256 million. The sale includes 23andMe’s customer-facing genomics service arm, as well as its health and research arm.

HIPAA doesn't apply to 23andMe. So what's next?

When the bankruptcy was first announced, the realization that these data could now be sold caused understandable alarm. At least eight state attorneys general urged consumers to delete their data, citing privacy concerns. These fears were understandable. Federal health privacy laws, like HIPAA, do not apply to companies like 23andMe. And, in the absence of a comprehensive federal privacy law, what happens to customer data is largely governed by the company’s own privacy policy.

That policy is clear: “If we are involved in a bankruptcy, merger, acquisition, reorganization, or sale of assets, your Personal Information may be accessed, sold or transferred as part of that transaction.” Before the potential sale to Regeneron was announced, some consumers were uncomfortable with the prospect of a new, unknown owner gaining access to their DNA. Many took advantage of the option to log into their 23andMe account, download their results, and request that their account and biospecimen be deleted.

But with more than 15 million individuals in the database, many of whom signed up years ago, it’s likely that many failed to delete their data prior to the announcement.

Thus, the genomics and personal information of most of the consumers will likely be handed over to Regeneron as part of the sale. The sale, however, is "court-mediated," which means the bankruptcy system itself will carefully watch how this vast trove of sensitive genetic data is managed and will have the final say over whether the sale can proceed.

Letters: Kim Reynolds’ trust of parents is selective

Bankruptcy courts are designed to sort out the financial affairs of struggling companies. Traditionally, that meant auctioning off tangible assets — real estate, inventory, equipment — to satisfy debts.

But in today’s economy, intangible assets like data can be far more valuable. And genetic data is not just another marketing list. It’s immutable, uniquely identifying, and predictive — not only of an individual’s health risks, but potentially those of their family members as well.

23andMe's bankruptcy goes to court. Here's what that means.

When a company files for bankruptcy, all its assets become part of the “bankruptcy estate,” which can be sold off to maximize returns for creditors. Under Section 363 of the Bankruptcy Code, judges can approve such sales with minimal delay. Courts have routinely approved the sale of customer data in bankruptcy, provided certain protections are in place.

Still, courts don’t operate in a vacuum. While they generally prioritize maximizing value, they can also consider the risks to consumers — especially when it comes to deeply personal information. Courts have the discretion to reject a bidder whose proposed use of data is incompatible with the company’s privacy policy, or whose practices pose a threat to consumer trust. In this way, the “highest bidder wins” rule has limits.

In this case, the bankruptcy court appointed a neutral third party, called a privacy ombudsman, to consider consumers’ sensitive data. The appointment of the ombudsman was notable because it was not required by bankruptcy law.

In cases where a company’s privacy policy is silent on bankruptcy-related data transfers, courts are required to appoint a “consumer privacy ombudsman” to evaluate the risks and advise the court. But because 23andMe’s privacy policy explicitly allows for data to be transferred in bankruptcy, the court could have skipped over this safeguard.

Opinion: Why has respect for higher education diminished? Let's dig deeper.

To offer further privacy protections, courts usually require buyers to honor the original privacy policy. Indeed, as part of the sale, Regeneron says it will comply with 23andMe’s existing privacy policies and plans to further lay out their privacy and security policies for the bankruptcy court.

But here's the catch: a new owner can often revise that policy, provided they give notice. Indeed, 23andMe’s current privacy policy says that it can be changed “from time to time.” So even if data is sold with protections in place, Regeneron would also take over the right to change those protections in the future.

What protections exist for 23andMe users?

What can be done to further protect consumers now?

23andMe’s sale to Regeneron is not yet a done deal. The privacy ombudsman is scheduled to report on the privacy aspects of the sale by mid-June — a short time before the bankruptcy court hearing on whether to approve the sale. Thus, there is still time for privacy advocates to ensure strong protections of consumer data.

There’s precedent for public pressure influencing data sales. When RadioShack went bankrupt in 2015, it initially planned to sell its customer data without restriction. But after pushback from the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general, the terms of the sale were revised to limit how that data could be used.

Overall, the sale of 23andMe to a pharmaceutical company that has announced its desire to continue the customer genomics services while also respecting genetic privacy is probably a best-case scenario for this bankruptcy.

However, 23andMe’s bankruptcy is by no means a one off. We need to confront larger legal gaps: both bankruptcy law and privacy law need to play catch-up to the reality that more and more companies are widely collecting consumers’ sensitive health and genetic data. Our bankruptcy system was never designed to safeguard personal privacy and, federally, sensitive health information outside the health care setting is not well protected.

The assumption that all corporate assets are fair game for liquidation fails to account for the unique sensitivity of biometric and genetic data. Courts, regulators, and lawmakers must do more to align bankruptcy practices and privacy protections with modern data realities.

At a minimum, bankruptcy judges should, as the judge did in this case, consider appointing privacy ombudsmen even in cases where the law does not require it — especially when the asset at issue is a massive trove of health-related data. Regulators should proactively monitor the case and be prepared to intervene if the sale poses consumer risks. And Congress should move quickly to enact baseline privacy protections for biometric and genetic information — protections that don’t vanish the moment a company files for bankruptcy.

You might have thought that by mailing in a DNA sample to learn about your ancestry or health risks, you were engaging in a personal, one-time transaction. But genetic data doesn’t expire — and neither do its implications. As 23andMe’s sale proceeds, the public must remain vigilant. Because once our most intimate information is up for sale, there may be no getting it back.

Diane Lourdes Dick and Anya Prince are University of Iowa law professors. Lourdes Dick specializes in bankruptcy law; Prince specializes in genetic privacy law.

headline: Pesticides: What a mother and farmer wants you to know | Opinion
fullText:
When I became a mom, it came with a whole list of concerns. I often question if I am providing my children with the tools they need to thrive in an ever-changing world.

 In addition to the title of mom, I also have the title of farmer, giving me firsthand experiences and understanding of why farmers utilize tools like pesticides when growing their crops.

Pesticide use is a science, backed up by years of research, that allows farmers to protect their crops, preserve yields and keep food prices stable. Farmers take special care to ensure they calculate accurate application rates; this not only protects the land and water, but also ensures no product is wasted, keeping more money in the farmer's pocket and your food prices low.

Pesticides are not something to fear; they are tools that farmers use to protect corn plants, minimizing the risk of pest damage. These crops are crucial to farmers as they provide feed for livestock, fuel for vehicles and 4,000 other everyday products used by my family and yours.

Farmers are parents, and we want the same things every other parent wants. For our children to grow up happy, healthy and with the tools they need to be successful. The worries never really go away, but the joy of knowing one day I will pass this land on to my children, leaving it better than when I started, is the reason I farm.

I know that when that day comes, I will be able to say with confidence that I am proud of the choices that I am making now and look forward to the future choices that must be made to continue this farming legacy that started four generations ago. I look forward to seeing the next generation build their future on this farm, utilizing the same tools I use today as they create their own legacy.

Jolene Riessen farms alongside her two sons in Ida and Sac counties in northwest Iowa. Their operation consists of corn, soybeans, alfalfa, custom cattle feeding and cow/calf. Jolene serves as the Iowa Corn Growers Association Chair and is on the Exports & The Grain Trade Committee.

headline: Joni Ernst's not-quite-apology
fullText:
Good morning, Iowa.

Over the weekend, U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst posted a not-quite-apology video following her viral town hall comments that "we are all going to die."

The original comments came at a town hall in Parkersburg Friday while she was answering a question about cuts to Medicaid in President Donald Trump's tax package that the Senate is poised to consider. During Ernst's answer, someone in the audience interrupted her to shout, "people will die!"

Ernst replied by saying, "People are not — well, we all are going to die. For heaven’s sakes, folks."

The comment drew instant condemnation from Democrats. And Ernst responded by posting a video to her Instagram story Saturday where she spoke directly to camera, apparently from a cemetery.

"I made an incorrect assumption that everyone in the auditorium understood that yes, we are all going to perish from this Earth," she said. "So I apologize. And I’m really, really glad that I did not have to bring up the subject of the tooth fairy as well.

That post has drawn a fresh round of outrage. Stephen has more in his story.

Randy Feenstra touts ties to President Donald Trump as he explores gubernatorial bid

U.S. Rep. Randy Feenstra touted his work on the federal tax and spending policy bill moving through Congress, saying he was a “key author” of the legislation.

“I was very close to the administration on helping write this bill, not only the tax portion of it, but also the (agricultural) portion of it,” he said at his annual Feenstra Family Picnic in Sioux Center Friday.

Feenstra sits on the House Agriculture Committee, which oversaw changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, including about $300 billion in spending cuts over the next ten years. He also serves on the tax-writing Ways and Means Committee.

During his speech, Feenstra worked to align himself with Republican President Donald Trump, who remains deeply popular among Iowa Republicans. It comes as he gears up for an expected gubernatorial run, during which he’ll need to appeal to the deep-red voters expected to make up the Republican primary electorate.

headline: How Texas finally solved its OU softball 'mental hurdle' at the WCWS | Mussatto
fullText:
The seventh time was the charm for Texas softball. 

Having never beaten OU in six tries at the Women’s College World Series before Saturday, the Longhorns finally solved their Sooners problem. 

Texas outlasted OU 4-2 to draw a win away from the championship series, but for the Longhorns, the victory seemed to carry more weight than a single result. Ghosts of the past were vanquished. The crimson curse was broken. 

OU’s big-game ownage of Texas — including a pair of national championship series sweeps in two of the past three years — had become an issue for Texas that seemed to extend beyond balls and strikes. It was an intangible edge, seeped into the Devon Park dirt and suspended in the steamy Oklahoma City air. 

“We have talked about that for sure, being a little bit of a mental hurdle,” Texas coach Mike White said. “It's tough. There's a lot of pressure out there. They always have great teams. If you make a hiccup, they make the most of it.”

More: OU softball 'timing was off' vs Teagan Kavan, Texas in falling to WCWS loser's bracket

Just ask Tennessee. The Vols had the Sooners beat Thursday until Ella Parker concocted some Sooner Magic with a walk-off, three-run blast. 

“That’s in the back of your mind,” White admitted. 

Sure enough, the Sooners had the go-ahead run at the plate in the top of the seventh inning. 

Texas ace Teagan Kavan, who gutted out a complete game on the day her grandmother died, recorded all three outs in the seventh inning via strikeout. 

It was Texas’ first win against OU on Oklahoma soil since 2014. 

“We have a mental edge at home for sure,” Sooner coach Patty Gasso said. “I can feel that. I think (Texas) has it when they’re in their environment as well.” 

Before Saturday, OU wasn’t just undefeated in six Women’s College World Series games against Texas — no, the Sooners had blanked the ‘Horns and run up the score in doing so. 

All six Sooner wins, including four in the 2022 and 2024 national championship series, were by at least four runs. OU smacked Texas 16-0 in Game 1 of the ‘22 championship series. 

More: Why OU softball's Ella Parker's walk-off home run vs. Tennessee in WCWS was emotional

The narrowing talent gap between OU and Texas wasn’t reflected on the scoreboard. Until Saturday. 

“They're too good, their team is too good for us to walk in and think, ‘Well, we're just going to shut them down,’” Gasso said. “They're too good. They've proven it … They're definitely a team that can win this whole thing, I know that.”

Not getting spellbound by the Sooners’ mystique was no small thing for Texas. 

“Today was just about playing a ball game,” Texas senior first baseman Joley Mitchell said. “I think we did a great job focusing on us. We weren’t focused on the crowd or what Oklahoma was doing. We were focusing on what Texas softball was doing. We went out there and played ball.” 

Center fielder Kayden Henry and Mitchell hit solo home runs in the fifth and sixth innings off Sooner ace Sam Landry to give the ‘Horns a two-run cushion. A cushion that never felt comfortable until Kavan struck out the last Sooner of the night. 

And all of Longhorn Nation exhaled. 

“So exciting,” White said, “to be able to finally beat the Sooners in Oklahoma.”

headline: OKC Thunder vs. Indiana Pacers: Which team has the edge in 2025 NBA Finals?
fullText:
It's Shai Gilgeous-Alexander vs. Tyrese Haliburton. It's Jalen Williams vs. Pascal Siakam. It's Mark Daigneault vs. Rick Carlisle.

The OKC Thunder will face the Indiana Pacers in the 2025 NBA Finals.

No. 1-seeded OKC advanced with a 4-1 series win over the No. 6 Minnesota Timberwolves. Meanwhile, No. 4 Indiana advanced with a 4-2 series win over the No. 3 New York Knicks.

OKC won both regular-season games against Indiana by an average of 13.5 points. Both teams are searching for their first NBA championship.

But the weight of these games is much bigger.

Both teams are looking for their first NBA championship. And that magnifies everything even more for two small-market teams.

Here's a complete breakdown of the Thunder-Pacers matchup:

More: How Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Thunder 'put it all together' to punch ticket for NBA Finals

OKC Thunder vs Indiana Pacers matchup breakdown

NBA Finals 2025: OKC Thunder vs Indiana Pacers matchup breakdown, predictions

Thunder vs. Pacers: Backcourt starters

Tyrese Haliburton is playing some of his best basketball right now.

The 25-year-old guard is averaging 18.8 points and 9.8 this postseason, and he continues to deliver in big moments. He's the engine of Indiana's high-octane offense.

But OKC will make life difficult for Haliburton. From Lu Dort to Alex Caruso to Jalen Williams to Cason Wallace, the Thunder will apply constant pressure from start to finish.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander should have an easier time getting into a rhythm, though. Aaron Nesmith and Andrew Nembhard are good defenders, but they'll have their hands full when guarding the league's Most Valuable Player.

I expect Gilgeous-Alexander to be the best player in this series. Give the point to OKC.

Edge: Thunder

More: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander reflects on emotional rise to Thunder cornerstone and NBA MVP

Thunder vs. Pacers: Frontcourt starters

After a shaky second-round series against Denver, Williams bounced back in the Western Conference finals.

The 24-year-old forward showed why he landed on the All-NBA third team. Williams averaged 22.2. points and 6.6 rebounds on 49.4% shooting from the field and 46.2% shooting from deep.

OKC also has Chet Holmgren and Isaiah Hartenstein in the frontcourt. The 7-foot duo can space the floor, pass and protect the rim.

Indiana has a strong frontcourt of its own. Nesmith has become a two-way threat, Pascal Siakam is a reliable scorer with championship experience and Myles Turner is a strong shot blocker.

But I'm giving the slight edge to OKC. From shot creation to defensive versatility to size, the Thunder checks off all the boxes.

Edge: Thunder

More: OKC Thunder vs Indiana Pacers predictions, odds: Who wins 2025 NBA Finals?

Thunder vs. Pacers: Bench production

Both teams have relied on their depth to get to this stage.

OKC's second unit is led by Caruso. The one-time champion is playing elite defense this postseason, per usual, but he's also shooting a blistering 41.5% from deep.

Then there's Wallace, another stout defender who can swing the momentum of a game. And if OKC finds itself in a shootout this series, players such as Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe can catch fire.

The Pacers also have plenty of options off the bench. T.J. McConnell is a veteran floor general, Obi Toppin is electric in transition and Bennedict Mathurin is a microwave scorer.

I'm giving the point to OKC, though. While the Pacers' bench mostly provides a spark with its offense, the Thunder's bench is more capable of impacting the game on both ends of the floor.

Edge: Thunder

More: Alex Caruso and the Thunder defense did it again, carrying OKC to NBA Finals | Mussatto

Thunder vs. Pacers: Coaching

This series will be a chess match between two of the top coaches in the NBA.

Mark Daigneault led OKC to franchise-best record of 68-14 during the regular season, and he found success with various lineup combinations while key players such as Holmgren and Hartenstein missed time. He's an excellent defensive strategist, which has helped the Thunder slow down the likes of Nikola Jokic and Anthony Edwards this postseason.

Rick Carlisle was also known for his stingy defenses going all the way back to his time with Detroit in the early 2000s. But he has shown an ability to adjust to his personnel throughout the years, and he has now helped create Indiana's elite offense.

Deciding the winner of this category is tough, but I'm going with Carlisle because of his experience. He has won 83 playoff games throughout his 23 seasons as a head coach, which ranks 10th in NBA history.

Carlisle also won a championship with Dallas in 2010-11. And while that was over a decade ago, he's more familiar with this stage than Daigneault.

Edge: Pacers

More: Mark Daigneault had respect from NBA coaching peers even before OKC Thunder's rise

Thunder vs. Pacers: Intangibles

OKC is the better team on paper, but Indiana is on a special run right now.

The Pacers have completed four 17-point comebacks this postseason. That's the most by any team in a single playoff run since 1998.

Indiana has also pulled off three seven-point comebacks in the final minute this postseason. There have only been four other comebacks of that nature in the NBA since 1998.

The Pacers can't be counted out. Not when they're playing like this.

Edge: Pacers

headline: A 1935 Elgin bank heist ended in a hail of bullets and arrests: Oklahoma history
fullText:
Bank robbers Leon Siler and Charles Sands were on the run in 1935 with $600 from the Bank of Elgin in southwestern Oklahoma near Lawton.

The 20-year-olds had escaped in an automobile but eventually ditched the car when airplanes circling above spooked them. They then fled on foot into a heavily wooded area, waded into Little Beaver Creek and walked across a wheat field, ending up at a farmhouse where they planned to hide out. Inside, they took A.J. Medrano, his wife and their 18-month-old son captive.

But the hostage count would increase throughout the day.

A neighbor, C.L. Ambrose, along with his 20-year-old son, Hank, had gone to the Medrano home to borrow a shotgun, so he could join a posse searching for the bandits. Father and son were captured as they walked into the house. After Ambrose and his son didn't return home, his wife and their two younger children went to the Medrano home to find out what had happened. They were also taken hostage.

Five separate visits by officers to the Medrano home occurred before law enforcement realized the bank robbers must be at the farmhouse, according to a story on June 1, 1935, in The Daily Oklahoman. Law enforcement had trailed the fugitives' footprints to the home but had not found any trail beyond the property.

Fifty officers from seven counties and two airplanes were involved in the search and the ultimate gunfight. Unfortunately, Grady County sheriff's Deputy J.E. "Pete" Wilson, a father of six, was shot multiple times and killed when he burst into the farmhouse to try to save the hostages. Those shots spurred other law enforcement officers to begin pelting the home with gunfire.

After a hail of 200 bullets from pistols and machine guns had ended, the wounded pair were arrested. Also arrested after the battle were two of the robbers' companions, reported as Mrs. Leon Siler and Ruby Moore.

A story that had published just one month earlier on May 6, 1935, in The Daily Oklahoman, reported bank robbers were not getting rich through their crimes:

The loot taken by 19 bandits from Oklahoma banks in 1935 has averaged $390 per bandit ― and 16 of the 19 have been captured, many before they got a chance to spend a cent of the loot.

... Bank institutions no longer serve as roadside filling stations for the pockets of roving brigands.

When the state's bank robberies drop from a high of 62 holdups and burglaries in 1932 to only six the first four months of 1935, there must be a reason.

And when the loot taken from state banks drops from $127,868 in 1932 to a mere $7,427.30 the first four months of 1935, there must be a reason.

Leon Siler, of Seminole, and Charles Sands, of Fletcher, were executed June 11, 1937, both dying by electric chair at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.

headline: 'Wads of money': Oklahoma marijuana industry causing property values to skyrocket
fullText:
Housing prices, particularly in rural areas, are up significantly since Oklahoma legalized medical marijuana, according to a new study. 

The study, published in Cambridge University’s Journal of Agricultural and Applied Economics, attributes rising property values to a real estate buying spree from marijuana growers. 

Researchers examined people’s perceived impacts of medical marijuana legalization and also tried to measure the effects of the industry on the state.

Brian Whitacre, one of the paper’s authors and a professor of agricultural economics at Oklahoma State University, told The Frontier that the issue of increased home prices was not on the researchers’ radar until people at a community meeting in Okemah brought it up.

“We didn’t expect to see a big impact on the housing values, but when we went to Okemah, people were telling us they can’t afford to buy a house in the place where they grew up,” Whitacre said. “We heard stories of cash offers for places when they weren’t even for sale.”

The marijuana boom after voters approved legalization in 2018 fostered hundreds of new businesses and millions of dollars in new tax revenue.

By 2021, marijuana grows in the state outnumbered traditional wheat and cotton farms. Oklahoma ranked first in the nation in 2024 for the number of marijuana dispensaries per capita.

The researchers began their study by holding a community meeting in Okemah in September 2023 that drew 25 people. Participants voted on their top concerns about the industry, including health, safety and misinformation. The group’s discussion on property largely centered around land and houses being purchased by “outside speculators” and driving up local prices and property taxes.

Most focus group participants were generally supportive of the industry.

“We thought most of the comments were gonna be negative and that was not the case at all,” Whitacre said. “A lot of people saw the positive impacts of the dispensaries, they were pretty well thought of. Dispensary owners actually came to our meeting, and people had pretty high opinions of them, so it wasn’t as negative as we thought it would be.”

The researchers then analyzed county-level property value data in Oklahoma and compared that with similar values in neighboring states.

The analysis showed that counties with the highest number of marijuana grows per capita had an increase in housing values of 20% to 25% over five years. The increase was higher than in comparable counties in Kansas and Texas, where marijuana is not legal. Counties with high numbers of dispensaries, however, did not show a similar trend to those counties with a high number of grows.

The upward trend in housing values began about 20 months after voters approved the measure making medical marijuana legal, the study found. The authors stated they thought the increase was driven by a surge in growers coming into the state between late 2020 and early 2022 and continued over time.

The analysis validated the Okemahs residents’ perceptions that they were being priced out of the market, the study found. Home values in Okfuskee County grew from $72,500 at the time of legalization to $120,158 by June 2023, according to Zillow’s inflation-adjusted home value index.

Okemah Mayor Ron Gott said the area indeed saw a broader housing and land price increase because buyers seeking land for marijuana grows often paid far more than the market value for those properties. The buyers included marijuana growers from China, he said.

“We’ve seen an increase due to the fact that some of the Chinese came in with just wads of money and paid big amounts for land that wasn’t really worth what they paid for,” Gott said.

And those increased housing and land prices have made it more difficult for some Okemah residents to purchase property, he said. Gott said he has seen properties purchased by growers that should have sold for around $3,000 an acre sell for closer to $10,000 an acre.

“For a young person that’s going to actually purchase land, to go out and pay an exorbitant price like they paid for these grow facilities acreages, they just can’t afford it,” Gott said.

Carl Alls, a longtime Okemah real estate agent, said he did notice property prices going up during the boom, and while the number of properties marijuana growers paid a premium for likely did have an impact on housing prices, other factors, such as high lumber and building material prices, likely played a role in increased home prices as well. Property prices were already on the rise before the arrival of the marijuana growers, he said.

“The prices were going up anyhow, because in our area we’ve had relatively really cheap land here for a long time,” Alls said. “I’m seeing homes selling for more than they did, and all of that has more to do with the price of lumber than these grows.”

Gott, Alls and other real estate agents in Okemah who spoke with The Frontier said several of the smaller marijuana cultivators in Okfuskee County are now no longer in business and the county is seeing a decline in the number of grows after the state has cracked down on illegal operations.

headline: How did OKC Thunder get back to NBA Finals? Timeline from Paul George trade to now
fullText:
Six years ago this summer, the Thunder took its first step in what’s been a methodical march to the NBA Finals. 

It was a step Sam Presti and the Thunder were shoved into making, but once on the rebuilding road, Presti and Co. navigated it with nary a misstep. 

The Thunder is back in the NBA Finals for the second time in team history. 

How did the Thunder get here? A series of moves that started in 2019.

Pre-order book on the Thunder's journey to the NBA Finals

More: NBA Finals 2025: OKC Thunder vs Indiana Pacers matchup breakdown. Who has the edge?

July 6, 2019: The Paul George Trade 

The transaction that started it all. 

After a third-place MVP finish in his second season with the Thunder — and coming off back-to-back first-round playoff exits — George asked out of OKC with the intention of teaming up with Kawhi Leonard on the Clippers. The Clippers had to make it happen, though. 

Only Presti had the codes to unlocking the LA combination, and he leveraged not only the value of George, but also the chance to pair him with Leonard — a player Presti didn’t even have. 

The price was exorbitant. 

Thunder traded George to the Clippers for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Danilo Gallinari, five first-round picks and two pick swaps. 

The trove of picks headlined the return. In time, it was revealed that Gilgeous-Alexander was the real prize. 

More: How Mark Daigneault, OKC Thunder are managing another lengthy break during NBA Playoffs

July 11, 2019: The Russell Westbrook Trade

With George out and the reset button pushed, it was time for Westbrook — the star who stayed — to leave. 

The Thunder dealt Westbrook to the Rockets for Chris Paul, two first-round picks and two pick swaps. 

The fact that the Thunder received picks for Westbrook instead of having to attach them was a win that only grew more lopsided in hindsight. 

More: Thunder home-court advantage is real. Another reason why OKC is NBA Finals favorite.

July 25, 2019: ‘Looking back, thinking forward’

The headline of Sam Presti’s op-ed in The Oklahoman. 

“This summer, the story of the Oklahoma City Thunder is transitioning to a new phase,” Presti wrote. “Over the last few weeks, we have parted ways with foundational players — people who have represented our city to the world, who have sacrificed for us and flourished on our behalf. Although this has been painful, I also believe that — given the circumstances — it was necessary. 

“In saying goodbye to the past, we have begun to chart our future. The next great Thunder team is out there somewhere, but it will take time to seize and discipline to ultimately sustain.” 

More: Why Queen's 'Don't Stop Me Now' is the OKC Thunder's victory anthem at Paycom Center

Jan. 13, 2020: SGA flashes star potential 

Gilgeous-Alexander recorded a 20-point, 20-rebound, 10-assist triple-double in a win at Minnesota. 

SGA averaged 19 points, 5.9 rebounds and 3.3 assists in his first season with the Thunder. The Thunder’s three-guard lineup of Gilgeous-Alexander, Paul and Dennis Schröder was a revelation. 

More: OKC Thunder might be 'idiots' but strength is their youth entering 2025 NBA Finals

March 11, 2020: COVID stoppage

Isolated in an Oklahoma City hotel room, then-Jazz center Rudy Gobert became the first NBA player to test positive for COVID-19. Gobert’s test results came back just before the Thunder and Jazz were about to tip off in Oklahoma City. The game was delayed and then postponed. Basketball would resume five months later in the Orlando bubble. 

Sept. 2, 2020: Thunder loses first-round Game 7 to Rockets

Lu Dort, an undrafted free agent who joined the team on a two-way contract, scored 30 points in the Thunder’s Game 7 loss. Dort’s scoring output was an outlier, but his defensive hounding of Rockets star James Harden would prove to be Dort’s carrying skill. 

Rather than run things back with what had been a feel-good team, the 2019-20 Thunder would prove to be a transitional one. The rebuild had yet to begin in earnest. 

Sept. 8, 2020: Billy Donovan, Thunder agree to part ways 

Donovan knew the direction the Thunder was heading. Not eager to head a rebuild, Donovan and the Thunder agreed to part ways. 

Nov. 11, 2020: Thunder hires Mark Daigneault as head coach 

The Thunder’s coaching search dragged on. Turns out, there was no rush. Presti’s man was already in the building. 

Daigneault had spent one season as a Thunder assistant under Donovan and the five before that as head coach of the G League Oklahoma City Blue. 

“As we reposition our franchise for future sustainable success, we want to remain cutting edge, forward thinking, asking tough questions of ourselves and pushing ourselves forward, and I can't think of someone better than Mark to be the person leading that charge…” Presti said. 

More: Former OKC Thunder star Kendrick Perkins says SGA will be best player in franchise history

Nov. 21, 2020: Thunder trades Steven Adams to Pelicans

Adams was a fan favorite. The rebuild had gotten real. 

Among the throw-ins the Thunder received from the Pelicans: Kenrich Williams, now the third-longest-tenured Thunder player behind SGA and Dort. 

The Thunder traded Adams, Schroder and Gallinari — three key players from a playoff team — within a 10-day stretch. 

March 27, 2021: Al Horford shut down for season 

The Thunder acquired Horford from the 76ers on draft night before the season. Horford played in 28 games for the Thunder, providing a template of what it would look like for Gilgeous-Alexander to play alongside a pick-and-pop big. 

However, when Gilgeous-Alexander suffered a season-ending plantar fascia tear, the Thunder opted to shut down Horford — both preserving Horford’s trade value while positioning itself for a better lottery standing. 

The Thunder finished the season 22-50. No fans were allowed at Paycom Center all season due to COVID precautions. OKC was the only team to bar fan entry for the entire season. 

May 20, 2021: ‘We want it to be an arrival’ 

Among Presti’s most memorable quotes during the rebuild. 

“When we do get back to the postseason, we want it to be an arrival and not an appearance,” Presti said in his exit interview. 

June 22, 2021: Thunder gets rotten lottery luck

The Thunder had an 11.5% chance at landing the No. 1 pick in the 2021 draft, a 25% chance at two top-five picks (thanks to a Houston swap) and a 75% chance at getting at least one top-five pick. 

All of those hopes were dashed on lottery night. Houston kept its top-four protected pick and OKC’s pick fell to No. 6. 

The Thunder selected Australian guard Josh Giddey with the No. 6 pick. Giddey played three seasons in Oklahoma City. The Thunder now has Alex Caruso to show for the Giddey pick. 

Of OKC’s four 2021 draft picks — Giddey, Tre Mann, Jeremiah Robinson-Earl and Aaron Wiggins — only Wiggins, the 55th pick in that draft, remains. 

More: How Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Thunder 'put it all together' to punch ticket for NBA Finals

Aug. 3, 2021: SGA signs extension 

Gilgeous-Alexander agreed to a five-year, $172 million rookie max extension. That contract takes him through the 2026-27 season. Next summer, the MVP will be in line to sign a five-year, $380 million deal. 

May 17, 2022: Thunder lands No. 2 pick 

The Thunder went 24-58 in Year 2 of the rebuild. And this time, lottery luck was on its side. 

Orlando won the lottery and drafted Paolo Banchero with the No. 1 pick. OKC was awarded the No. 2 pick, which it used to select Chet Holmgren. 

Holmgren is the only top-five pick of the rebuild.

June 23, 2022: OKC rounds out Big Three 

A defining night of the rebuild. 

The Thunder got its guy in Holmgren with the No. 2 pick. OKC traded up with New York to draft Ousmane Dieng with the No. 11 pick, and then the Thunder used the No. 12 pick — acquired in the original Clippers trade — to select Santa Clara’s Jalen Williams. 

Williams is already an All-Star. Holmgren would’ve been had he not gotten hurt. Alongside SGA, they’ve formed a homegrown Big Three. 

Aug. 25, 2022: Holmgren injures foot 

Holmgren sustained a Lisfranc injury in his right foot while defending LeBron James in a pro-am event in Seattle. The Thunder announced that Holmgren would undergo surgery and miss the entire 2022-23 season. Holmgren’s rookie season was delayed by a year. 

April 14, 2023: Thunder falls game short of playoffs

After back-to-back 20-something win seasons, the Thunder went 40-42 to make the play-in tournament. OKC beat New Orleans in the first play-in game before losing at Minnesota. 

April 20, 2023: Thunder closes in on second mountain

The first iteration of the Thunder had an extended stay atop the mountain. Then came the valley of the rebuild. By this time, the second mountain had come into view. 

“We're staring that sucker down,” Presti said. “We're seeing it, and we're trying to figure out how we're going to find a way to the top of that. I mentioned we have a ton of work to do. No one knows that more than us.” 

June 22, 2023: Thunder drafts Cason Wallace 

OKC traded up to the No. 10 pick, which it used on Kentucky guard Cason Wallace — another draft pick Presti nailed. 

Sept. 27, 2023: Presti cools hype 

The Thunder hadn’t yet made it back to the postseason, but everyone could tell something was cooking. 

“We have to finish our breakfast before we start acting like we’re on the cusp of something,” Presti said. 

The Thunder finished the season 57-25, going from a play-in elimination to the No. 1 seed in the West. 

May 18, 2024: Thunder eliminated by Mavericks

After sweeping the Pelicans in Round 1, the Thunder fell to the Mavericks in six games in the Western Conference semifinals. 

A couple of the Thunder’s flaws were highlighted in the Dallas series. The Thunder needed more size. And Josh Giddey, benched against the Mavs, no longer fit in the starting lineup. Both issues would soon be resolved. 

June 21, 2024: Thunder swaps Giddey for Caruso 

Sam Presti didn’t want to trade Josh Giddey. But when the Thunder broached the idea of Giddey coming off the bench, the Aussie guard asked the team to explore trades for him. 

Presti found a fit with Chicago. The two teams finalized a Giddey for Alex Caruso one-for-one swap. 

Caruso has been among OKC’s most valuable players in these playoffs. 

July 1, 2024: Isaiah Hartenstein signs with Thunder 

The biggest free-agent signee in Thunder history. 

Hartenstein, following a breakout year with the Knicks, signed a three-year, $87 million deal with the Thunder. Hartenstein fortified the Thunder’s frontcourt. 

April 13, 2025: Thunder wins 68th game 

OKC put the finishing touches on a 68-14 campaign — good enough to win the West by 16 games. 

The Thunder’s 12.86 average margin of victory set an NBA record. 

May 21, 2025: SGA wins MVP

Gilgeous-Alexander joined Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook as the third Thunder player to win the award. 

SGA led the league in scoring at 32.7 points per game on 52% shooting. 

May 28, 2025: Thunder wins West 

Six years after the Paul George trade, three years removed from a 24-win season, the Thunder is in the NBA Finals.
