headline: Revenue at OKC airports is expected to decrease slightly, but projects are only going up
fullText:
Amid several ongoing projects, OKC Airports is proposing a slight decrease in its budget for the upcoming fiscal year due to an expected loss of revenue from reduced airline ticket purchases.

Technically, the decrease in the proposed FY 2026 budget, set at $27.04 million, for the city's Department of Airports is so minor in comparison to the previous fiscal year's (only 0.4%, or $103,000) that it is essentially flat, officials said. The same 149 positions from last year will be authorized for the FY 2026 budget, with 38% of the budget meant for administration, while 27% will go toward commercial aviation and 20% toward maintenance.

“We did some add/delete with our positions, but no new positions for this next year,” said Jeff Mulder, airports director. “We’re seeing the benefit of some risk chargeback reductions, some insurance costs that we’re seeing a decrease in, and that’s helping us maintain essentially this flat portion of the budget for this next fiscal year.” 

The city’s airports department, which operates OKC Will Rogers International Airport, Wiley Post Airport and Clarence E. Page Airport, is funded through a combination of sources, but largely through the Oklahoma City Airport Trust, or OCAT. The trust manages the airports, and revenue generated from airport operations, like landing fees, parking and concessions, goes to the trust. 

More: OKC Will Rogers Airport to offer direct flights to Cancun this winter in 'historic' move

A closer look at the OCAT budget for the upcoming year shows an expected $8 million reduction in revenue, which Mulder said is due to a reduction in flight passengers that airlines have been forecasting. 

In 2024, OKC Airports provided services to a record-breaking 4.6 million passengers, but Mulder expects to fall slightly short of that number this upcoming fiscal year due to constrained consumer spending amid economic pressures.

“A lot of that has to do with consumer confidence, and you’ve seen that on the national level go down,” Mulder said. “Airline tickets are something that’s discretionary, so they expect to see a reduction. For this calendar year, we’re tracking about a 2% reduction in passengers compared to last year, so we’re basing our budget plans on that.”  

Airlines also are struggling to expand their fleets and retire older aircraft because of delays on new airplane deliveries from manufacturing companies like Boeing. 

More: How understaffed is air traffic control at your airport? Map of FAA data shows shortfalls

Multiple airport infrastructure plans still underway

But Mulder said the city's airports department can still tap into unused carryover resources from FY 2025, including capital projects meant to improve the infrastructure that were previously budgeted but haven’t been completed. 

“A lot of that capital funding comes from federal grants," Mulder said. “It’s a timing issue, generally. We haven’t been able to get the grants in a timely manner, and so sometimes it’s a timing issue where projects roll from one year to the next.”

Examples include an ongoing project to replace passenger boarding bridges at Will Rogers International Airport. Seventeen of the bridges are more than 25 years of age, and the airports department is planning to use $9 million of federal grant funding to replace some of them in FY 2026. 

Another project is the current construction of a 3-bay, 80,000-square-foot hangar at Will Rogers airport, a collaboration with the state and airport tenant AAR Corp. that is costing $39 million.  

“We are probably about two-thirds of the way through that project, and this next fiscal year we expect to spend about $13 million,” Mulder said. “The tenant hopes to then have it complete and start using it January of ‘26.”

Related: OKC's airport is applying for $4.3 million in federal grant funding. Here's why.

A new, multi-story parking garage at the same airport also currently is being designed to help deal with parking issues during peak hours. Mulder said that in the past few years, since airline travel rebounded from the pandemic, the airport has seen the parking garage exceed 85% of its capacity for half of each year. 

According to airport staff, more than 40,000 people passed through security checkpoints to catch their flights for the recent Memorial Day holiday, one of the busiest times of the year for travel.

“One of the ways we’re addressing this in the last year is we constructed a surface parking lot that has canopy covers on it, about 600 spaces, and that’s now available to our customers,” Mulder said. “We feel that’s a good move (because) it gives our customers some cover during this time of year when they’re traveling and they don’t want their car parked outside and subject to the weather.”

An additional project currently in the design phase is a new air control tower at Wiley Post Airport. The aging tower isn’t tall enough to see all of the airfield services, Mulder said, and the airport department is pursuing Federal Aviation Administration grant funding to help with its construction. 

Overall, $135.2 million will go towards capital improvement plans for FY 2026. Of that, $86.4 million will be allocated toward Will Rogers, $20.6 million to Wiley Post, $27.4 million toward the Mike Monroney Aeronautical Center, and $885,000 toward Clarence E. Page Airport. 

A five-year capital improvement plan, as required by the FAA, is expected to cost about $588 million through the end of the decade.

headline: Thunder fans around the world see Oklahoma City's transformation on live TV
fullText:
David Holt, more than just Oklahoma City’s mayor, is also a social media influencer, so it’s of no surprise that he got thousands of “likes” and responses to a post about the city’s appearance on national television following the first Thunder playoff game against the Minnesota Timberwolves. 

The post, featuring a view of downtown Oklahoma City shown on ESPN, noted the significant changes to the skyline, including Scissortail Park, Devon Energy Center, BOK Park Plaza Tower, the Omni Hotel and the Oklahoma City Convention Center, all built or completed since the last time the Thunder made the NBA Finals in 2012. 

“When I’m talking to someone outside OKC, I invariably ask if they have been to OKC,” Holt wrote. “Even if they have, if they haven’t been in the last decade, I might observe that they really haven’t been to OKC. The list of attractions that have opened in the last 15 years is very long. Even our skyline is dramatically different.” 

Followers of Holt’s social media agreed the images shown on the May 20 ESPN/ABC broadcast of the Western Conference Finals were far different than images they found online of the 2012 season playoffs. 

“I was struck by how virtually everything in the image did not exist when we hosted the NBA Finals in 2012,” Holt said. “However long this journey lasts, we are very excited to welcome the eyes of the world once again to OKC. We have a lot to catch you up on.” 

Oklahoma City has recorded a rapid growth in population since the last time the Thunder made the NBA Finals; the population in 2012 was 601,040, compared to 709,330 reported in the latest U.S. Census estimate. 

More: OKC Thunder might be 'idiots' but strength is their youth entering 2025 NBA Finals

The Oklahoman obtained footage of the 2012 playoff series and the changes are indeed dramatic, with downtown looking dull and lifeless and Chesapeake Energy Arena (now Paycom Center) surrounded to the south and west by blighted industrial blocks and surface parking lots. 

The view in 2025 is far different and thanks to the use of drones the footage aired during the 2025 NBA Playoffs include a sweeping view through Scissortail Park, it’s lake, play areas, and walkways leading up to the new convention center, the Omni and Paycom Center

Much of the footage is created by the Thunder for use on national broadcasts. Dan Mahoney, director of communications for the Thunder, said the organization is equally interested in promoting the team and their city. 

“Every time we’re on national television, which truly is international television, it’s an opportunity not just for our team and organization, but for the city and the state,” Mahoney said. “It’s a great opportunity to showcase Oklahoma City in whatever way we can.” 

Mahoney said the same footage will be provided next season to NBC and Amazon when they replace TNT as a broadcasting partner. Keeping track of the rapid transformation of downtown Oklahoma City, Mahoney said, is a constant challenge. The team is not just promoting the city, but also documenting its transformation. 

“The one thing that has truly changed is the technology and the drone footage that makes us able to provide these really vibrant images,” Mahoney said. “We’re really pleased with what the partners use, how they tell our story with the images and put Oklahoma City in the best light possible. And that’s always been our goal.” 

Mahoney said ESPN is a great partner in that they want to showcase the city and they shoot their own footage in addition to what is provided by the Thunder. Much of the footage showcases downtown Oklahoma City, the arena and Scissortail Park. The Wheeler Ferris Wheel and the large OKC letter sculpture along the Oklahoma River are also frequently featured during the game broadcasts. 

Fans across the country are noticing the city’s transformation and following it. James Jewel, living in Dallas, last visited Oklahoma City in 2018, before the opening of Scissortail Park, the Omni and the new convention center. 

“It looks busier,” Jewel said. “I remember in the past, 2012, when we had the first good team, seeing the B-roll shots where the footage was sped up. You could count the individual cars. I remember thinking, it sure is slow there. It looks like it has gotten busier since then.” 

Another fan, Kyle Lee, moved from Tulsa to St. Louis in 2022 and hasn’t attended a Thunder game since 2017, though he has been a fan of NBA play in Oklahoma City since it was the temporary home of the Hornets in 2005. 

“I work in the casino industry and I’ve moved around working at different casinos,” Lee said. “I’ve lived in Florida, St. Louis also, and at a previous time at Riverwind in Norman. My son (Camden) who is 7, has become a massive Thunder fan and it’s been fun seeing the team grow with him.” 

Lee said he is struck by the footage of Scissortail Park and how much the city has changed in a few short years. He made a return trip when the park opened, stayed at the Skirvin Hilton Hotel and walked around downtown visiting restaurants and attractions. 

Some of the fans watching the games have no ties to Oklahoma City but fell in love with a team from a smaller market making a big splash in the NBA. 

Evan Weaver, a school psychologist in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania, grew up loving basketball and was a “big sports fan.” But growing up in Pittsburgh, he had no NBA team to follow. 

“There was never a team I could truly root for,” Weaver said. “I was 11 years old and going into sixth grade when the Thunder started rising up with KD (Kevin Durant), Russell Westbrook and James Harden. I saw the crowd on TV and thought this was a special environment. It was a cool team to latch onto. I began consuming all the content I could, watching the team play and listening to podcasts. I grew up with that first squad.” 

Weaver closely follows the team and read The Oklahoman’s recent coverage of former Thunder star Russell Westbrook investing in development of a stadium district east of the arena, prompting more excitement for Oklahoma City's future. On New Year's Eve of 2021, Weaver flew to Oklahoma City to catch a Thunder game featuring future MVP star Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. He, like Holt, was impressed with the footage of the city shown in this year’s playoffs. 

“I definitely noticed they have drone footage that went over Scissortail Park,” Weaver said. “I remember thinking how green the grass looked and how it contrasted to those early years.” 

Holt said whenever he travels, he hears excitement about the growth of Oklahoma City, a perception he credits to the national Thunder broadcasts. 

“It’s difficult to really wrap your mind around the sheer number of eyeballs that pay attention to the NBA, especially when you get to this stage,” Holt said. “There are literally billions of people around the globe who will pay at least a passing glance to the scores of the NBA finals games. That has an impact that we will capitalize on for years to come.”

headline: Renovators uncovered an OKC mystery: What were the tunnels at a building downtown used for?
fullText:
What was the purpose of mysterious passageways just discovered during renovation of the 115-year-old Investors Capital Building in downtown Oklahoma City? Tunnels to an underground Chinese city of local lore?

Hidden passageways to a speakeasy? Oklahoma was dry from statehood in 1907 until lawmakers OK'd 3.2%-alcohol beer in 1933, and the law prohibited hard liquor sales until 1959. Prohibition didn't keep people from hiding and sneaking drinks.

Were they holes for drainage because of the high downtown water table, when the building was under construction circa 1906-1909? Maybe shafts for train cars or carts loaded with newsprint coming in and "patent insides" — pre-printed pages of news and ads — heading out, on a spur from the nearby rail yard?

More: Oklahoma County DA asks for more space and gets a whole downtown OKC building

Early Louis L'Amour work published in what is now Oklahoma County-owned ICB Building in downtown Oklahoma City

One of OKC history's mysteries has been uncovered in the future home of the Oklahoma County District Attorney's Office: the five-story, 50,000-square-foot Investors Capital Building, originally the Oklahoma City home of Western Newspapers Union. It does have an interesting background.

The building was also the location of several publishing companies including Lusk Publishing, which printed at least one book of poetry by Louis L'Amour, the western novelist, when he lived near Choctaw in the 1930s, and the offices of regionally influential Harlow's Weekly, according to The Chronicles of Oklahoma.

Several filled-in, arched openings underneath the basement floor of the county-owned office building at 217 N. Harvey Ave. have officials wondering what they might have been. The county acquired the building decades ago. The discovery "warrants investigation," said Keith Monroe, director of county facilities management.

"In our discovery and review of the basement, we found some — Keith refers to them as catacombs — we have some hallways or small crawl spaces. I don't know what we want to do with them. We discovered them last week," consultant Bill White told the county Public Building Advisory Committee Tuesday, May 27.

More: Whose rules? Oklahoma County finally formalizes the way it conducts business

What passageways were for is 'all speculation,' OK County official says

What they might have been is "all speculation," said committee Chairman Paul Foster, chief of staff for District 3 Commissioner Myles Davidson. He later said four to six of the filled-in spaces are along the north and east walls of the building, which is on the southwest corner of Harvey and Robert S. Kerr avenues.

"Do we know they're crawl spaces?" Foster wondered. "I went down there after Keith told me about this, and it looks like there might have been, at one time, pathways to somewhere. But then they were all blocked up."

The uncovered apparent passageways don't seem to affect the building's structural integrity, said White, owner of OKC consulting firm White and Associates.

"This is just to let you know they're there and (to discuss) whether we need to fill them with flowable fill or what we need to do. I don't know. I just think leave them alone," he said.

Foster said later, "It’s definitely interesting to imagine what, if anything, they were used for."

Monroe said the discovery of architectural details below grade was a surprise.

"I don’t have any information, but after seeing the bricked archways I believe it at least warrants investigation," he said.

More: Extra energy: OG&E power plant upgrade tests roads and bridges with heavy 'superloads'

headline: Mental health belongs at the center of Oklahoma justice reform efforts | Opinion
fullText:
I have worked in the criminal justice system my entire career. As a federal prosecutor and now as Oklahoma County district attorney, I’ve seen firsthand how untreated mental illness fuels the revolving door of arrest, incarceration, release, rearrest, incarceration and release. I’ve spent decades navigating the complexities of our justice system, and I can confidently say that there is a direct correlation between the investment in intervention and treatment programs and crime in our community.

More: You can't say we're not a Top 10 state in wacky government performances | Opinion

Too often, our jails act as mental health holding facilities, with some people landing behind bars not because they’re dangerous, but because they’re mentally ill and don’t have access to a continuum of care. This approach is neither just nor effective. It strains our legal system, burdens law enforcement and taxpayers, and fails to address the root causes of why a mentally ill person continues to enter the criminal justice system.

In Oklahoma County, we’re witnessing the consequences of this misalignment. The Oklahoma County jail has long grappled with overcrowding and inadequate conditions. Many inmates suffer from mental health issues that go untreated for years, exacerbating their conditions and increasing the likelihood of reoffending upon release.

Treating mental health helps lower crime rates

Programs like ReMerge and DREAMS courts (Mental Health Court) offer a more compassionate and sensible alternative. By diverting individuals with mental health and substance use disorders away from incarceration and into treatment, these initiatives not only help keep people from cycling back through the system but can also restore families and the dignity of those suffering with mental illness.

The result is a lower crime rate and safer communities. In Oklahoma City alone, the crime rate has significantly declined over the last six years. 

Opinion: 1 in 4 Oklahomans face a mental illness. We deserve access to affordable care.

Providing community-based treatment options and intervention programs enhances public safety and ensures that our justice system upholds the dignity of every individual.

As someone who has prosecuted high-profile cases, I understand the importance of a justice system that is both fair and effective. By placing mental health care at the center of justice reform, we can create a system that truly serves and protects our community.

To break the cycle, we must prioritize mental health care as a cornerstone of justice reform.

Vicki Behenna is the district attorney for Oklahoma County. She previously served as executive director of the Innocence Project and as an assistant U.S. attorney, where she helped prosecute Timothy McVeigh after the Oklahoma City bombing.

headline: Patty Gasso vs Melyssa Lombardi: Former OU softball allies in WCWS win-or-go-home showdown
fullText:
For Paige Parker and countless OU softball alums from 1997 to 2018, Sunday night’s Women’s College World Series win-or-go-home showdown in Oklahoma City will be painful to watch.

The loser’s bracket elimination game pits Sooners coach Patty Gasso against her longtime assistant and associate head coach, Melyssa Lombardi and the Oregon Ducks. On the one hand, there’s an excitement factor in seeing the two lead their respective clubs to this point of the greatest show on dirt. 

On the other, one will survive to see another day while the other feels the ache of defeat.

“You want to root for both,” Parker, who won back-to-back national titles under Gasso and Lombardi at OU, told The Oklahoman. “Throughout this world series, I've been a Duck fan and I’ve been a Sooner fan. One's going to go home at the end of it. It’s a special thing to see. … They’re two of the most competitive people I've ever met in my life.”

Lombardi was responsible for the Sooners’ pitchers and catchers throughout her 21-season stint under Gasso. The two won four national championships and 15 Big 12 regular season or postseason tournament titles together. Twelve of Gasso and Lombardi’s 21 seasons in Norman ended with WCWS appearances. 

For the first time, the two will share the Devon Park field as opponents on Sunday. Additionally, former Sooner All-American and graduate assistant Sydney Romero is a Ducks assistant coach and former OU volunteer analyst Sam Marder is Lombardi’s associate head coach.

MUSSATTO: How Texas finally solved its OU softball 'mental hurdle' at the WCWS

Of course, the two programs battled in last season’s Norman Regional at Love’s Field. This will be different, however, with the stakes elevated on a stage Gasso and Lombardi owned as partners for two-plus decades. 

“It's a celebration. She has been with me for over 20 years,” Gasso said. “She’s like a sister to me.”

Lombardi, who is in her seventh season as Oregon’s coach, has the Ducks in their first WCWS since 2018, when Longhorns coach Mike White led the program. Oregon surrendered a walk-off home run to UCLA Thursday to open the WCWS before walking off Mississippi Friday night to keep its season alive. 

The numerous similarities between the two programs have been a hot topic in OKC this week. Lombardi has built her program by bringing in like-minded coaches who carry championship mindsets. Both teams play a high-speed game. You can go down the list.

Parker, an assistant coach at Utah, knows both Gasso and Lombardi as well as anyone and has seen the similarities firsthand, having faced Lombardi and the Ducks with the Utes 11 times, including once earlier this season.

“Oregon is very hard working, very blue collar, which is similar to how things are at OU,” Parker said. “They are competitive and get after it. It’s a lot of offense with runners in motion and speed. I saw a lot of similarities. Lockdown defense and lockdown pitching, especially this year’s Oregon with their offensive production, home runs and runs they score per game. 

“The past few years, when we've played against Oregon, it's felt very similar. In the back of my head, always, when we would prepare to play against them, it felt like we were preparing to play against Oklahoma.”

More: OU softball 'timing was off' vs Teagan Kavan, Texas in falling to WCWS loser's bracket

It wasn’t easy for Lombardi to get the proud softball program back to OKC.

When she took over the Ducks ahead of the 2019 season, the program endured a mass exodus of players transferring out. Then came the COVID-19 pandemic. Oregon reached the NCAA Tournament each of the past four seasons but failed to advance as one of the final eight. 

“I'm proud of her,” Gasso said during WCWS media day on Wednesday. “I love watching her. I love her staff. I have worked with all of them. And to see what she's putting forth, she understands winning. She understands what you need to do to win. She's been working hard to get the right team. 

“And the one thing that she told me was how much she knows this is the team. She's got the right team. She's got the right chemistry. She's got everything covered. And a coach knows when you're missing a piece here and there, and to hear her say that, I'm not surprised at all that they're here. So I'm excited for her.”

Parker considers Lombardi her “biggest mentor” when it comes to pitching. When teaching at Utah, she finds herself uttering phrases Lombardi used to say to her daily or catching herself sounding like her former pitching coach.

Parker’s favorite memory as a Sooner was in the 2016 WCWS championship series, where she was named the event’s Most Outstanding Player after defeating Auburn in three games. OU leaned on Parker to throw the bulk of the innings that season and Gasso and Lombardi helped her endure when the going got tough.

“They would look at me in my eye, and I knew that they had the confidence in me,” Parker said. “Just knowing how much they cared for me during that time, they were with me hand in hand the whole way. It was hard on my body. It was hard mentally too and knowing how much both of them cared for me during that run was special to me.”

More: Who are top OU softball players in 50 years of program history? Meet 50 greatest Sooners

While Sunday night will undoubtedly be full of moments remembering past experiences when they were side-by-side, after Gasso and Lombardi exchange lineup cards at home plate, Parker says it’s going to be “a dogfight.”

OU aims to keep its quest for five consecutive national titles afloat. Oregon is looking to add title No. 1 to the program’s record books.

If it’s not the Sooners that keep going, Gasso wants it to be her longtime companion and the Ducks.

“It's going to be done professionally and the right way. And that means a lot to me. If it's not going to be us,” Gasso said, “I want it to be them. I'll say that very clearly and out loud because they've lived in our program and their program might mimic us a little bit by the way she's coaching. I take that as a complete honor.”

headline: OU baseball eliminates Nebraska with 17-1 beatdown in NCAA Chapel Hill Regional
fullText:
Follow The Oklahoman's coverage of the OU-North Carolina NCAA baseball tournament game in the Chapel Hill Regional final.

CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — Staring elimination in the face Sunday, maybe Oklahoma was riding the momentum of their late-game revival from one night earlier.

Powered by two home runs from junior catcher Easton Carmichael, the Sooners made quick work of former conference rival Nebraska, striking for three runs in the first and six more in the third en route to a 17-1 elimination of the Big Ten champions.

The win sent Oklahoma (37-21) into a rematch with North Carolina (44-12), and the Sooners needed to win that game and another Monday with the Tar Heels to claim the Chapel Hill Regional of the NCAA baseball tournament and advance to a super regional.

UNC coach Scott Forbes has announced that senior right-hander and No. 3 starter Aidan Haugh (5-4, 3.74 ERA) will be on the mound for the Tar Heels. OU coach Skip Johnson said he would have to meet with his staff before deciding on his pitching plans.

More: OU baseball falls to North Carolina as Tar Heels send Sooners to NCAA elimination game

On Saturday night, the Sooners had fallen behind North Carolina 9-0 after five innings but got their offense untracked late to make the final count a more respectable 11-5.

Johnson praised the never-say-die attitude then, and maybe he was onto something. Over the last four innings against UNC and the first six against Nebraska, the Sooners exploded for 20 runs.

“Absolutely, there’s no doubt about it,” Johnson said after the rout of the Huskers. “Once we broke that and stopped trying so hard and just started competing, it was a big difference. And I thought it was a great example of it today when those guys got big hits in big moments and just kind of sustained the rallies.

“Even though we forced some mistakes on them, we kind of sustained the rally and ran the bases really well.”

On a day when the Sooners banged out 18 hits, including eight for extra bases, defensive shortcomings by the Cornhuskers (33-29) set the tone early. Nebraska committed five errors, three of them in the first inning that helped OU to 3-0 lead.

“Obviously, we didn’t play very well, especially in that first inning,” Nebraska coach Will Bolt said. “We didn’t get off to a good start, didn’t pick each other up. And give credit to Oklahoma. They capitalized on our mistakes.”

Bolt admitted he was surprised by the defensive meltdown.

“We’ve played at such a high level, especially defensively, it’s very uncharacteristic of our team to play that kind of defense," he said. "So, yeah, there was no indication that was coming. … And it just snowballed from there.”

There were plenty of offensive standouts for the Sooners, but the biggest was Carmichael, a second-team All-SEC pick this season and a third-team All-American a year ago.

Carmichael ignited the six-run rally in the third when he blasted the first pitch of the inning from left-hander Will Walsh (4-8) into the screen behind the left-field wall for his 16th home run.

He bettered that effort in the sixth as the first batter that reliever Jalen Worthley faced, launching a towering three-homer over the scoreboard in left center. The blast traveled an estimated 413 feet and capped a five-run rally that made it 15-0 at the time. His two homers gave him three for the regional and 17 on the season.

“He’s a good offensive player, and he’s gotten better and better and been a leader,” Johnson said of Carmichael. “It showed today. He had some really great swings on some good pitches.”

Sam Christiansen, who sparked the OU offense Saturday night with an RBI pinch-hit double in the loss to UNC, went 3 for 5 with two doubles and a triple, worth two RBIs.

Jaxon Willits, who had had a quiet regional to this point, was 2 for 5 with three RBIs and contributed a key two-run, bases-loaded single in the first. Drew Dickerson, Kyle Branch, Trey Gambill and Dawson Gillis also had two hits each, with Branch adding two RBIs.

The beneficiary of all of the offense was junior left-hander Cade Crossland (5-5), who threw seven solid innings before freshman Michael Catalano finished up. Crossland struck out nine, walked two and scattered five hits before an infield error helped the Huskers break through for an unearned run in the sixth on a bases-loaded infield single by Dylan Carey.

“You really don’t realize how tough it is when you’re sitting in the dugout for 15, 20 minutes at a time to go out and stay focused on throwing strike one,” Johnson said of the junior left-hander. “I think that he showed a great example of doing that (today).”

For his part, Crossland said he didn’t mind watching his teammates hammering balls into the gaps and circling the bases.

“It’s fun to watch those guys just play with everything they’ve got out there,” Crossland said. “And it makes it easy to pitch because you know they’re working hard behind you, just rallying the whole team in the dugout. It makes it fun.”

Despite relegation into the losers’ bracket following their loss to UNC on Saturday night, the Sooners still have a way forward to win the regional and even host a super regional.

The Chapel Hill Regional is paired with the Eugene Regional, where host Oregon, the No. 12 national seed, has already been eliminated. No. 2 regional seed Arizona is in the driver’s seat in Eugene, unbeaten after two games. But if the Sooners, also a No. 2 regional seed, can pull off two more wins with their backs to the wall, they could earn host privileges over Arizona.

headline: Oklahoma State baseball stuns Georgia with 4-run ninth to reach NCAA regional final
fullText:
Follow The Oklahoman's coverage of the OSU-Duke NCAA baseball tournament game in the Athens Regional final.

ATHENS, GA —  Down to its last breath of the 2025 season, Oklahoma State baseball is still alive. 

The Cowboys trailed 9-7 in the bottom of the ninth of Sunday afternoon’s elimination game at the NCAA Athens Regional, but cleanup hitter Kollin Ritchie crushed a game-tying two-run home run out to right field off Georgia reliever Tyler McLoughlin, and Brock Thompson hit a walk-off two-run home run off Zach Harris to secure an improbable 11-9 win to reach the regional final.

“That ending is a reflection of our team and our season,” Oklahoma State head coach Josh Holliday said. “The kids continue to compete and fight their tails off, even when things go against you a little bit.”

More: Oklahoma State baseball's Harrison Bodendorf is 'stabilizing force' entering Athens Regional

Oklahoma State (30-24) has now survived two of its four required elimination games to win the regional after Friday’s loss, but will have to turn around and beat a rested Duke squad twice. 

To even reach the bottom of the ninth in striking distance, Oklahoma State had to battle. The Cowboys gave staff ace Harrison Bodendorf a 3-0 lead after two innings, but Georgia (43-17) responded with seven runs over the next three frames to take a 7-3 advantage. The Bulldogs scored five runs in the third off the back of a pair of two-run homers from Slate Alford and Christian Adams, and both players homered again their next time at the plate in the fourth and fifth innings, respectively. 

Oklahoma State tied the game with four runs in the fifth, but fell behind 9-7 after lone Bulldog tallies in the seventh and eighth. 

Georgia also put runners on second and third with nobody out in the top of the ninth with a golden opportunity to put the game out of reach, but reliever Matthew Brown came in and saved the day. Brown struck out three consecutive batters to strand the two runners in scoring position, getting Oklahoma State back to the plate down just two with the heart of the order due up. 

“We had a freshman in Matthew Brown come in and keep it right there where it was at,” Holliday said. “He gave us a chance to do something special.” 

Nolan Schubart drew a lead-off walk to bring Ritchie to the plate for his game-tying heroics. After Ritchie tied the game, Colin Brueggeman singled to put the winning run on base. With one out Georgia appeared to have an inning-ending double play on a ground ball to the right side, but Harris — covering the bag in place of first baseman Tre Phelps after he started the double play — did not step on the bag at first base. 

It was a fielder’s choice, not an inning-ending double play, and it gave the Cowboys one final chance to avoid extra innings. 

Thompson took advantage with a shot out to left field, Oklahoma State’s 15th home run of the regional and by far the most crucial.

“It’s awesome,” Thompson said. “We knew it was going to be a big battle. Georgia is a great ballclub. We were down a little bit. Ritchie got the party started early, and kind of got the vibes going high.”

Duke beat Oklahoma State 12-5 on Friday, and advanced to the final out of the winner’s bracket by beating Georgia 6-3 on Saturday night. 

“Just toughness, grit, fight, care, all the things that you want to see in your kids, they put on display for us today,” Holliday said. “We earned a chance to get to play here again in an hour and a half, and that’s what we’re looking forward to doing.” 

Freshman Noah Wech will make his second career start on the mound for the Cowboys, opposing Duke freshman Henry Zatkowski.

headline: Karlyn Pickens, Tennessee oust UCLA softball in extra innings to reach WCWS semifinals
fullText:
Laura Mealer didn’t feel much pressure as she stepped into the batter’s box. 

With the bases loaded and one out in the bottom of the ninth inning against UCLA, the Tennessee senior shortstop had the chance to keep the Volunteers’ season alive with one swing. 

And for Mealer, it’s exactly where she wanted to be. 

“I worked my whole life in that moment,” she said. “But in that moment, it felt like 25 of us against the pitcher. (Coach) Karen (Weekly) even kept walking over to me and was like, ‘The pressure is not on you in this moment.’”

Mealer stayed calm in the situation and went on to deliver just what Tennessee needed. 

Mealer hit a walk-off single to lift the seventh-seeded Volunteers to a 5-4 win over No. 9 UCLA in a Women’s College World Series elimination game Sunday at Devon Park and will play No. 6 Texas at 11 a.m. Monday. 

It was far from an easy victory for Tennessee (47-16). 

The Volunteers led 4-2 against UCLA (55-13) heading into the seventh before Megan Grant launched a two-run homer off Tennessee starting pitcher Karlyn Pickens with two outs, reminiscent of Tennessee's WCWS opener Thursday against OU when Ella Parker hit a three-run walk-off bomb off Pickens with two outs to give the Sooners a 4-3 win.

After Grant's homer, one of the most bizarre situations in recent WCWS memory happened. 

More: UCLA softball game-tying home run vs Tennessee stands after play ruled not reviewable

Grant missed home plate before being met and touched by teammates before going back several steps and landing on home plate. 

Weekly and Tennessee’s side saw it and notified umpires. 

After a lengthy review, the umpire said that type of play is actually not reviewable, so Grant was ruled as safe. 

“That was one of the most exciting, intense, emotional games I have ever been part of in all my years of coaching, and I couldn't be more proud of our young women hanging in there, not letting what happened in the seventh inning costing us the game,” Weekly said.

“That's a real battle, and I have to give a ton of credit to the young ladies in our dugout, the young ladies on our bench pouring energy into the team that entire game. They're the MVP that nobody knows about.” 

Pickens pitched the whole game for Tennessee, allowing 11 hits.  

She gave up three homers, two solo shots in the second inning off the bats of Alexis Ramirez and Sofia Mujica that tied it at 2-2 and the seventh-inning blast by Grant. 

Pickens improved to 25-10 and finished with a pitch count of 148. 

“I'm feeling pretty good,” she said. “Yeah, I'll do whatever it takes. I'll get as much in the tank as I need to be. So I'm good to go.” 

Tennessee’s offense had success against UCLA starter Kaitlyn Terry as it scored four runs in the first five innings but struggled against reliever Taylor Tinsley, who tossed the final 3⅓ frames and allowed just three hits. 

But Tennessee got going in the 10th, and Mealer — who finished 2 for 5 with three RBIs — was the hero as she drove in Taylor Pannell. 

“When I was standing on third, I had full faith in her,” said Pannell, who went 3 for 4 with a homer and two RBIs. “No matter how it's going to get done, it's going to get done right here.”

headline: OU baseball roars past North Carolina to force final game in NCAA Tournament regional
fullText:
CHAPEL HILL, NC — When the Oklahoma Sooners woke up Sunday morning, they no doubt embraced the old Ernie Banks line, “Let’s play two!” 

That’s because OU baseball team would have to win two elimination games in one day to stay alive in the Chapel Hill Regional of the NCAA Tournament. 

Now, having routed Nebraska 17-1 in the afternoon game and rallying past North Carolina 9-5 in the nightcap, maybe their new slogan should be, “Let’s win three!” 

The Sooners exploded for five runs in a decisive sixth-inning against UNC, getting a two-run homer from Drew Dickerson and a two-run double from Jaxon Willits, to upend the No. 5 national seed and force a winner-take-all game at 2 p.m. CDT Monday for the regional championship and a berth in a super regional. 

The Chapel Hill Regional is paired with the Eugene Regional, where host Oregon, the No. 12 national seed, has already been eliminated. No. 2 regional seed Arizona is in the driver’s seat in Eugene, unbeaten after two games. But if Oklahoma, also a No. 2 regional seed, can pull off one more win, it could earn host privileges over Arizona. 

The Sooners (38-21), as they were Sunday night, have been designated the home team Monday. 

More: Who's in super regionals? Updated bracket, schedule for NCAA baseball tournament

UNC coach Scott Forbes said he would start freshman right-hander Ryan Lynch (4-1, 2.92 ERA) for UNC, with freshman right-hander Walker McDuffie probably in reserve. Lynch’s most recent start was a four-inning shutout effort with seven strikeouts in the ACC championship win over Clemson on May 25. 

OU coach Skip Johnson said he would meet with his staff before determining his pitching plans for Monday. 

Bullpen ace Dylan Crooks nailed down the win for OU with two shutout innings of hitless relief for his 15th save. 

Willits said the Sooners knew Sunday would be a marathon day, but they were ready for it. 

“It was a long day, but I feel we bring that energy and focus every day in practice,” he said. “And when you do that every day in practice in the fall and then all spring leading up to the season, it gets easy to stay locked in.” 

The OU offense is certainly locked in. Over the past 22 innings, beginning with the sixth Saturday night of the 11-5 loss to UNC that tumbled them into the losers’ bracket, the Sooners have scored 30 runs. 

“I want to give credit to Oklahoma,” Forbes said. “They have a really good team. 

“They had traffic (on the bases) the whole night. I don’t think we had a 1-2-3 inning. We didn’t make our usual plays defensively. (When) you don’t pitch at a high level and defend at a high level, it’s hard to win those games against a really good team.” 

In fact, two UNC errors paved the way to five unearned runs for the Sooners, who also benefited from nine walks by UNC pitchers to go with three home runs and 11 hits overall. 

More: OU baseball eliminates Nebraska with 17-1 beatdown in NCAA Chapel Hill Regional

Dawson Willis and Dasan Harris hit solo homers for OU. Willis belted his sixth in the third for a 1-0 lead, and Harris’ second of the season made it 9-5 in the eighth. 

UNC (44-13) had overcome a 2-1 deficit to go up 3-2 on Gavin Gallaher’s two-run double in the fifth. Gallaher was the hitting star for the Tar Heels, blasting his 15th homer in the fourth to momentarily tie the score at 1-1. He added an RBI double in the seventh during a two-run rally that narrowed the OU lead to 7-5 and finished 3-for-5 with four RBIs. 

But the Sooners had turned the tide with their big rally in the sixth.  

Harris singled to open the inning against reliever Olin Johnson (2-1), who had come on in the fifth for UNC. Dickerson delivered his second homer of the regional and fourth of the season to put the Sooners on top 4-3. 

Folger Boaz relieved Johnson, but OU put together a two-out rally against the left-hander. Carmichael reached on a two-out throwing error, and Sam Christensen hit a hard comebacker that knocked the glove off Boaz and went for a single. 

Willits doubled to left center for two runs, and another run would score on a single by Kyle Branch before Trey Gambill was cut down at the plate trying to score on the hit. 

Willits celebrated by giving the “shush” sign to the crowd of 4,001 in Boshamer Stadium while standing at second base. The UNC fans had been on him since an incident in the third inning when he waved at a ground ball while running from first in an attempt to obscure the vision of UNC second baseman Jackson Van De Brake, who confronted Willits after the play. Teammates and umpires intervened, and both dugouts got a warning. 

The crowd booed Willits at every subsequent appearance and cheered loudly when he was caught stealing in the fifth, the first time he was thrown out in 15 attempts this season. 

“We’re just having fun out there playing the game of baseball,” Willits said. “They booed me, and y’all saw what I did.” 

He added, “I just want to say I wasn’t trying to be a dirty player. I was just trying to help my team get a run, and he took exception to that. He came at me, and I went back to him, but there was nothing personal. We were just competing out on the baseball field.” 

The Sooners added an insurance run in the seventh on Carmichael’s single to right following three walks to load the bases. Carmichael also swung a hot bat against Nebraska earlier Sunday, hitting his 16th and 17th homers while collecting four RBIs. 

The win went to Jamie Hitt (3-0), the second of four OU pitchers. He worked two innings behind freshman left-hander Jaden Barfield, who matched his season high with four innings before leaving with a 2-1 lead. 

Hitt ran into trouble in the eighth, giving up a leadoff walk and a single to Tyson Bass, and OU coach Skip Johnson called on his closer, Crooks, to face a dangerous hitter in Sam Angelo.  

Angelo had homered twice Saturday night off OU All-American Kyson Witherspoon, and he narrowly missed a game-tying homer against Crooks when he hooked a drive just foul down the right-field line. 

Angelo ended up walking, but Crooks rallied to strike out Carter French and get Kane Kepley and Van De Brake on shallow fly balls. He retired the side without incident in the ninth. 

“When I went out there to visit him, we had bases loaded,” Johnson said he told Crooks. “I reminded him of that, told him to throw the ball to the target, and whatever happens, happens. He’s a tough kid, and he went through a lot, and I’m really proud of him.”

The Sooners kept their hopes for a fifth consecutive Women's College World Series title alive, defeating former OU assistant Melyssa Lombardi and the Oregon Ducks 4-1 Sunday night at Devon Park.

headline: Oklahoma State baseball's season ends with late-inning loss to Duke in Athens Regional
fullText:
ATHENS, GA — One run short.

Oklahoma State baseball pulled off one ninth-inning rally to extend its season on Sunday at the NCAA Athens Regional, but could not turn the trick twice as Duke squeaked out a 3-2 win to complete the regional sweep and eliminate the Cowboys. 

The loss confirms this as the fifth year in a row Oklahoma State (30-25) has lost in a regional,  although the Cowboys went down with a fight. After losing Saturday, Josh Holliday’s squad beat Binghamton on Saturday, scored four runs in the ninth inning to stun Georgia in Sunday’s early game and had a 2-0 lead over Duke (40-19) in the nightcap, but could not hold on. 

“We had a big swing in the first game, they had a big swing in the second game,” Holliday said. “And you don't minimize the results down to that, but the kids emptied the tank.”

More: Oklahoma State baseball stuns Georgia with 4-run ninth to reach NCAA regional final

The Blue Devils scored three runs in the eighth to take their first lead of the game. AJ Gracia started the rally with a solo home run, and after putting two more runners on base with one out, Holliday brought in Friday starting pitcher Mario Pesca out of the bullpen for the jam. 

Pesca retired the first batter he faced, but Duke designated hitter Sam Harris laced a two-out, two-strike two-run single into the gap in right center to flip the score. 

The final out of the game happened in somewhat controversial fashion. Oklahoma State’s Garrett Shull struck out on a breaking ball in the dirt, but it bounced away from Duke catcher Macon Winslow. Shull briefly appeared to reach base on a dropped third strike as the throw down got away, but the umpires reviewed it and deemed Shull ran outside the baseline and interfered with the throw. 

"The game was celebrated and the umpires walked off, which they should,” Holliday said. “There's no point in arguing. You don't argue calls that are reviewed on by the people in our review booth. The umpires on the field had no say in that."

It was a bitter end to an outstanding final month of 2025 for the Cowboys. Oklahoma State won 10 of its final 12 games in the regular season to sneak into the regional and secured one of the iconic moments in the program’s storied history with the walk-off home run to eliminate Georgia early on Sunday.

“Anybody that played against us this weekend or played against us in the last month will tell you that we had a really good baseball team,” Holliday said. “Do we strive for more and do we want more? Absolutely. But if you're unable to see the big picture and appreciate kids and their effort and the growth of a team by simply the final result of the last game, then that's a position that someone could certainly take.

“But if you're asking me as their coach, a person that is with them every single day, I couldn't be more proud of them.”

Freshman starting pitcher Noah Wech was the unsung hero of the losing effort. In just his second career start, he threw six shutout innings with just five hits allowed, five strikeouts and no walks. Wech ended up hastily in the starting role as the Cowboys battled all weekend without usual No. 2 starter Sam Youngerman, and gave his team every opportunity to make it to Monday. 

“Everything,” Holliday said when asked what he liked about Wech’s performance. “I think it'll provide him with a tremendous amount of confidence and a great launching point going forward.”

It was a fitting end to the year for the Cowboys. A tough start to the weekend, a courageous battle to get to the regional final, an outstanding effort from a true freshman and another close game in the weekend decider. 

“I appreciate their effort, and I'm proud as hell of this team,” Holliday said. “And anyone that's got a problem with that didn't watch close enough to see what these kids did in the Oklahoma State uniform this last month."

Duke advanced to its fourth Super Regional in program history, looking to reach its first College World Series since 1961.

headline: UCLA game-tying home run vs Tennessee stands in WCWS thanks to NCAA softball Appendix G
fullText:
UCLA softball's Megan Grant smacked a two-run home run to tie Tennessee 4-4 with two outs in the top of the seventh inning during the Women's College World Series Sunday at Devon Park.

The dramatic game-changing play was in doubt for several minutes as umpires got together to discuss if Grant missed home plate.

After a lengthy review, it was determined assisting her to go back and touch is not reviewable. Since the play was not reviewable, Tennessee couldn't file a protest.

As a result, the Bruins and the Volunteers are tied 4-4 in extra innings. The winner plays Texas in the semifinals on Monday.

If the play was reviewable and it was deemed Grant missed home plate, the Bruins' season would've been over.

More: Patty Gasso vs Melyssa Lombardi: Former OU softball allies in WCWS win-or-go-home showdown

Here's the Q&A with a pool reporter and Vickie Van Kleeck, Secretary-Rules Editor, NCAA softball rules committee and Steve McCowan, national coordinator of softball umpires.

Question: What transpired following the home run hit by UCLA’s Megan Grant?

Following the celebration at home plate the umpires got together to determine whether the runner touched home plate. The umpires observed that the runner returned to touch home plate, but it wasn’t clear if the runner was assisted by a teammate. In an effort to get the call right, the umpires decided to initiate video review to help determined what occurred.

Question: What made the play not reviewable?

A runner being assisted on the basepaths by a teammate is not on the list of reviewable plays in the NCAA Softball Rule Book.

Appendix G of the NCAA Softball rules book does not allow for the challenge of rule 12.17.3.4.1, which states that no offensive team personnel other than the base coaches and base runner(s) shall touch a runner until the runner contacts home plate.

Question: What would the outcome have been if the play was reviewable?

Because a home run is considered a dead ball, per Rule 12.17.3.4, on an initial offense, a warning would have been issued to the offending team, and it would not have affected the score of the game.

fullText:
OKLAHOMA CITY – Tennessee softball is playing to live another day in the Women's College World Series.

The No. 7 seed Lady Vols (46-16) run-ruled No. 3 seed Florida in an elimination game to advance, and they'll face No. 9 seed UCLA (55-12) at Devon Park on June 1 (3 p.m. ET, ABC). The Bruins lost 3-1 to No. 12 seed Texas Tech on May 31.

Tennessee scored seven runs in the first inning against the Gators, going through its entire lineup before Florida stopped the bleeding. The Lady Vols went up 10-0 in the third inning before Florida scored three runs. But Tennessee scored another run in the bottom of the fourth to make it 11-3, and UT won in five innings.

UCLA battled against Texas Tech ace NiJaree Canady, who struck out the Bruins seven times.

Tennessee faced UCLA in nonconference play, and it lost 4-3 after the Bruins scored four times in the fifth inning.

Junior ace Karlyn Pickens (24-10) started against UCLA and threw four innings with one strikeout, four hits allowed, one walk, two hit by pitch and three earned runs. Pickens was pulled after giving up three runs, and sophomore pitcher Sage Mardjetko finished the game.

headline: How Tennessee baseball, Marcus Phillips beat Cincinnati to reach Knoxville Regional final
fullText:
Marcus Phillips peered down the right-field line, scanning from the corner to behind home plate.

The Tennessee baseball pitcher took his time on the walk from the mound to the dugout after a sweet postseason start to keep the Vols pressing onward in the Knoxville Regional.

The No. 14 overall seed Vols topped Cincinnati 10-6 on May 31 and moved within a win of a fifth straight super regional. Tennessee is 11-0 in home regional games under coach Tony Vitello and has won four straight home regionals.

Wake Forest (37-21) and Cincinnati (33-25) play an elimination game June 1 (noon ET) with the winner advancing to play Tennessee (45-16) for the regional title at 6 p.m.

The Bearcats scored two unearned runs in the ninth and had two in scoring position before Brandon Arvidson came in to get a strikeout to end the game.

Marcus Phillips gave Tennessee a quality start

Marcus Phillips had one of his best starts of the season to follow Liam Doyle with a quality start to open the Knoxville Regional.

Phillips threw six-plus innings, allowing three runs on four hits and four walks. He matched a career-high eight strikeouts.

The junior had a rocky first inning and a dicey third inning. But he retired long strings of batters in a row outside of those two up-and-down frames. He set down 12 of 14 batters from the back half of the third through the sixth inning.

Tennessee baseball's infield did damage against Cincinnati

Dean Curley smacked a two-run single in the first inning to get Tennessee rolling early as the infield got it done at the plate.

The starting infield combined for nine hits, nine RBIs and six runs.

Curley had two hits with a solo homer off the batter's eye. Fischer had a pair of doubles to drive in three runs, including a two-run double in the four-run sixth. Kilen went 4-for-5 with three runs.

Manny Marin drove in two with an 0-2 single up the middle in the ninth.

DOYLE: How Liam Doyle flipped Tennessee baseball's win in Knoxville Regional opener vs Miami (Ohio)

Gavin Kilen is on a tear in the Knoxville Regional

Kilen has been rolling to open the Knoxville Regional.

Kilen smashed a single up the middle in the first and another single to right in the second. He tripled to shallow left in the fourth as three Bearcats could not make the catch as Kilen sprinted around the bases. He crushed another single to right in the sixth.

The Louisville transfer was 2-for-4 with a walk, two runs and RBI against Miami (Ohio) in his first NCAA tournament game.

headline: Tennessee baseball hitting, starting pitching have clicked in both regional wins | Adams
fullText:
Tennessee baseball began the season by reeling off 22 consecutive games. Now, it would gladly settle for a three-game winning streak.

After beating Cincinnati in its second game of the Knoxville Regional on May 31, the Vols are one victory away from qualifying for another NCAA super regional, which has become routine for a program that once served as little more than a pushover for the SEC’s upper class.

The defending national champion Vols also have reached the College World Series in three of the past four seasons under coach Tony Vitello. Their first two performances in the Knoxville Regional suggested they’re rising to the postseason challenge once more.

Next challenge: win a third consecutive game for the first time since April 18.

Maybe, Tennessee just needs postseason motivation to string together more than two victories.

Hitting and starting pitching have both clicked in UT’s back-to-back NCAA tournament victories. So have its fans.

The Vols defeated Cincinnati 10-6 in the winner's bracket, the night after they had their way with Miami (Ohio) 9-2 before a standing-room only crowd at Lindsey Nelson Stadium.

Tennessee fans have done more than fill up their stadium. They have raised their voices while sensing the significance of this weekend.

I had a firsthand view from Porch 13 in left field when the Vols began their latest postseason venture. During the regular season, that vantage point qualified as a social event. There was as much interest in what’s on the grill as who’s at-bat.

But the porch populace was screaming from the get-go in the NCAA tournament. And the large state flag that normally swings into motion only on home runs was activated every time a UT player crossed the plate.

As the Vols mounted momentum for a successful postseason run, Porch 13’s DFW (designated flag waver) Kim Conley laid the groundwork for a case of tendinitis halfway through Game 1.

Liam Doyle, who hadn’t been at his best in his previous two outings, regained the form that made him one of college baseball’s preeminent pitchers against Miami. He struck out 11 and allowed just four hits in 6.2 innings that advanced the Vols into the winner’s side of the bracket.

Tennessee also proved resourceful on offense, which wasn’t always the case during the SEC’s regular season. The Vols converted nine hits into nine runs despite hitting only one home run. Aside from a throwing error to first by Doyle, the defense was uncharacteristically airtight.

Game 2 was more difficult.

ADAMS: Barring surprises, Tennessee baseball could pitch way through Knoxville Regional

Starting pitcher Marcus Phillips did his part. He allowed two runs and three hits while striking out eight through his first six innings. Vitello replaced him with reliever AJ Russell after Cincinnati led off the seventh inning with a home run.

Russell struck out six batters but couldn't close out the Bearcats, who tacked on two runs with two out in the ninth. Reliever Brandon Arvidson got the last out.

And set the Vols up for a possible three-game winning streak and fifth consecutive super regional.

headline: How Drew Gilbert's celebration has returned to Tennessee baseball through Cannon Peebles
fullText:
Cannon Peebles slashed the second pitch he saw against Miami (Ohio) into the right field corner.

The Tennessee baseball catcher scampered to second base, where he stood and brought back a celebration from the 2022 Vols and outfielder Drew Gilbert.

“It just popped up on my phone one day and I thought it was cool and it was something that I think a lot of the young guys on this team and even everybody grew up kind of watching," Peebles said.

He vowed then that he would deploy the celebration the next time he hit a double in the NCAA tournament, which he did in the second inning of Tennessee's 9-2 win against the Redhawks on May 30, and again in the fifth inning.

The next day, he doubled twice more in UT's 10-6 win against Cincinnati.

"I just ended up doing it for fun," Peebles said. "Luckily, the team said that they loved it. I was just like might as well keep it going.”

For the celebration, a player who hits an extra-base hit stands on the base and spreads their arms parallel to the ground before dropping to a knee, leaning back and raising their hands in front of their face.

Peebles had four doubles in 47 games entering the Knoxville Regional and had not hit one since May 3 against Auburn. He has four in the past two games as the No. 1 Vols (45-16) rolled to a pair of wins to move into the regional final

Wake Forest (37-21) and Cincinnati (33-25) play an elimination game June 1 (noon ET) with the winner advancing to play Tennessee (45-16) for the regional title at 6 p.m.

Gilbert is with the Syracuse Mets, the New York Mets' Triple-A affiliate. He was taken No. 28 overall by the Houston Astros in the 2022 MLB Draft.

The 5-foot-9, 185-pound Gilbert hit .314 with 22 homers and 140 RBIs in 141 career games as a three-year starter.

Gilbert cemented himself in Tennessee history in the 2021 postseason with a walk-off grand slam against Wright State. The homer, which lifted UT to a 9-8 win in its opener in the Knoxville Regional, got the Vols started on their roll to the program's first College World Series berth since 2001.

ALBERTO: How Alberto Osuna made the most of his season with Tennessee baseball

The Stillwater, Minnesota, native was a consistent performer for the Vols in 2022 and garnered multiple All-America honors. He hit a team-best .362 with 11 homers and 70 RBIs. He had 33 walks to 32 strikeouts, posting an on-base percentage of .455.

headline: Smokies come up short in extra innings of doubleheader sweep of Birmingham
fullText:
The Knoxville Smokies fell just shy of a sweep May 31, dropping a 2-1 extra-inning nail-biter to the Birmingham Barons in the second game of a twin bill at Covenant Health Park.

Following a game one victory behind a shutout from Nick Dean, the Smokies (24-25) were unable to capitalize on the momentum or the number of scoring opportunities in the nightcap, stranding nine base runners and an opportunity to pull within a game of first place in the Southern League North Division Barons (27-22)

Antonio Santos had a quality start for the Smokies, allowing just one run in five innings pitched. He held off the Barons for the majority of his start, striking out three and throwing three flawless innings.

The Smokies took an early 1-0 advantage in the first when Pedro Ramirez doubled on a line drive to right field and later scored on a Corey Joyce deep RBI double to left center. Birmingham tied it in the top of the second on a groundout after Jacob Gonzalez's leadoff double to make it 1-1 at the end of the frame.

Knoxville had scoring opportunities in all but the fifth inning, including a wild sixth in which Parker Chavers made it to second base with two outs, only to see the rally extinguished on a strikeout.

The Smokies' best chance to walk it off in the seventh and final inning of the doubleheader was when Brett Bateman singled and was in scoring position on second base with one out, but Pedro Ramirez and BJ Murray Jr. were unable to drive him in, and the game headed to extra innings. Doubleheaders are seven innings under Minor League Baseball rules.

William Bergolla lined a go-ahead RBI single to right field, scoring the placed runner and putting Birmingham up one. The Smokies were unable to answer in the bottom of the inning despite starting with the tying run in scoring position. Garrett Schoenle struck out two and stranded Murray at third to give the Barons a 2-1 win and preserve their three-game advantage in the standings.

Knox News reporter Gabriel Jackson covers the Knoxville Smokies and One Knox SC.

headline: What to know about Tennessee, Karlyn Pickens vs UCLA in Women's College World Series
fullText:
OKLAHOMA CITY – Tennessee softball has a rematch in its second elimination game of the Women's College World Series.

The No. 7 seed Lady Vols (46-16) will play No. 9 seed UCLA (55-12) at Devon Park on June 1 (3 p.m. ET, ABC) to stay alive in the WCWS.

The Bruins lost 3-1 to No. 12 seed Texas Tech on May 31, falling to the loser's bracket. Tennessee run-ruled No. 3 seed Florida in five innings, eliminating the Gators with a 11-3 win on May 30.

Here's what you need to know about Tennessee's rematch with UCLA.

Buy tickets for Tennessee softball vs. UCLA in WCWS

How UCLA beat Tennessee in February

Tennessee took a 3-0 lead over UCLA in the first inning on Feb. 21, and it held that lead until the fifth.

Tennessee ace Karlyn Pickens (24-10) gave up a leadoff single followed by a walk. Pickens gave up another single to load the bases. Then Tennessee coach Karen Weekly did something she learned to never do again – she pulled Pickens out of a jam.

Weekly sent sophomore Sage Mardjetko into the circle, and the Bruins scored one run in the next at-bat before Jordan Woolery hit a three-run home run to take a 4-3 lead.

"I learned my lesson back at UCLA – you don't take Karlyn Pickens out of a jam," Weekly said during the NCAA regional on May 16. "Karlyn believes, if I got us in this jam, I'm getting us out of this jam. And 999,999,999 times out of whatever that number is, she's going to do it."

UCLA struggles to hit off Texas Tech ace NiJaree Canady

UCLA wasn't able to generate any offense against Texas Tech ace NiJaree Canady outside of a solo home run in the fifth inning by Kaniya Bragg.

Canady, who leads the nation with a 0.86 ERA, struck out seven and only walked two. UCLA only logged four hits and left five on base.

That's a good sign for Tennessee, which will be able to start Pickens with almost two full days of rest. Pickens started against Florida, but Weekly pulled her after the first inning when UT took a 7-0 lead.

Pickens wasn't her typical self the first matchup with the Bruins – she only had one strikeout with one walk and two hit by pitch with four hits allowed. She has been at her best in the NCAA tournament, throwing 59 strikeouts in 37⅓ innings with only 23 hits allowed.

UCLA has All-American hitters in its infield

Even though UCLA struggled offensively against Canady, three of the Bruins' infielders were named NFCA All-Americans this season for a reason.

Third baseman Jordan Woolery and first baseman Megan Grant were named to the first team, and second baseman Savannah Pola was named to the third team.

Pola leads UCLA in batting average at .439, and Woolery is right behind her at .418. Woolery leads the Bruins with 86 RBIs along with 23 home runs. The junior hit a walkoff two-run homer to force Game 3 of the super regional at South Carolina.

Grant has hit 79 RBIs and a team-high 25 home runs this season. Pola leads the team with 73 runs scored and 20 doubles.

Tennessee softball vs UCLA WCWS prediction

Tennessee 5, UCLA 2: The Lady Vols have gotten better with every game of the NCAA tournament, and they're more than capable of avenging themselves with a win over UCLA. The Bruins will struggle against Pickens like they did against Canady, and Tennessee's offensive momentum will carry over.

Tennessee softball vs UCLA: Series history

Tennessee is 4-10 all time against UCLA. The Lady Vols have lost the last four matchups with the Bruins, three of them within two runs.

Tennessee played UCLA in 2024 and 2022, but before that UT hadn't faced off with the Bruins since 2013. The Lady Vols are 1-1 against UCLA in the WCWS. Tennessee lost 3-1 in 2005 and then won in 4-3 in 2006.

headline: How Marcus Phillips mastered controlling the base paths in Tennessee baseball vs Cincinnati
fullText:
Andrew Fischer pumped his fist before the umpire signaled out.

The Tennessee baseball first baseman knew Cincinnati’s Kerrington Cross had hopped toward second base. He knew Marcus Phillips’ snap throw was perfectly timed with Cross' step. He knew that Phillips reaped a tangible reward of weeks of work on controlling the base paths in a gratifying fifth-inning moment.

“I have been working on it a little bit every week,” Phillips said. "It is something I never really put a lot of attention towards. As I have been working on it, I feel like I have been making some pretty good progress on it — and it has been showing.”

Phillips pitched 6⅔ innings with eight strikeouts in No. 1 seed Tennessee’s 10-6 win against No. 3 seed Cincinnati on May 31 at Lindsey Nelson Stadium. He allowed three runs on four hits and four walks.

He allowed one stolen base to the Bearcats, who led the Big 12 with 128 steals entering the Knoxville Regional.

“I give him a lot of credit,” Bearcats coach Jordan Bischel said. “He has worked really, really hard over the last probably three, four weeks on stopping the running game.”

Phillips allowed 36 stolen bases in 40 attempts in 63⅓ innings after his start against Vanderbilt on May 10. Vols coach Tony Vitello swore then that Phillips “needs to get better at it or he's not going to pitch.”

He has allowed one steal in 14⅓ innings in his past three starts.

Bischel’s assessment was accurate. Phillips has gotten quicker to the plate, cutting down the time opposing runners have to steal a base. He is mixing up his timing in delivering pitches, how many times he looks at runners and how often he throws over.

“The learning process is just every day you can learn something new, whether it is on the mound or in catch play or bullpens — which is what helped me a lot,” Phillips said. “Just working on a quicker step to home plate and just progressing week by week.”

CELLY: How Drew Gilbert's celebration has returned to Tennessee baseball through Cannon Peebles

SEC teams ran freely on Phillips in April. Ole Miss stole seven bases. Kentucky stole eight a week later. Auburn stole two the next week before Vanderbilt had four.

Phillips noted SEC teams are built to attack both hitters and pitchers. Teams attacked him on the base paths, which challenged him to do what Vitello says he does best. He had to progress and he did.

“There’s been significant progress and that was an area he’s improving at, and has improved at, and has made progress,” Vitello said.

Fischer went nuts when first-base umpire Mark Wagers called Cross out for a successful pickoff attempt for Phillips, whose showing propelled UT (45-16) into another regional final against the winner of No. 2 seed Wake Forest (37-21) and Cincinnati (33-25) play an elimination game June 1 (6 p.m. ET).

Phillips had a mellow response. He got the ball back from Fischer and said, “Let’s go, baby.” He was cool and in control.

headline: A year ending in 5 has been eventful for Tennessee football and 2025 won't be exception | Adams
fullText:
Longtime Tennessee football fans know the significance of seasons ending in five. For 60 years from 1965 through 2015, those seasons have been eventful.

And with a couple of exceptions, those seasons have been favorable for the Vols. You don’t have to be a numerologist to see that.

Just check the track record. It tells us that the 2025 season will be memorable.

1965: That’s the season in which second-year coach Doug Dickey turned Tennessee from a loser into a winner.

After going 4-5-1 in 1964 when Dickey orchestrated the transition from the single wing to the wing T, the Vols went 8-1-2 in 1965 and finished 10th nationally. Moreover, only a 14-13 loss to Ole Miss separated them from an unbeaten season. They also tied Auburn and Alabama.

1975: That season told you Bill Battle’s time as coach was nearing an end. For the third consecutive season under Battle, UT’s record spiraled in the wrong direction (7-5). It even lost to Vanderbilt for the first time in 11 years.

Battle was fired the following season.

1985: Few Tennessee teams have surprised their fan base in such a good way.

The Vols seemed in serious trouble after losing star quarterback Tony Robinson to a season-ending injury. But unheralded backup quarterback Daryl Dickey led Tennessee to six consecutive victories and the SEC championship.

The Vols capped a 9-1-2 season by pulling off a historical 35-7 victory over second-ranked Miami in the Sugar Bowl.

1995: This season began a glorious four-year run for Tennessee and future hall of fame quarterback Peyton Manning.

Manning had become the starter a year earlier as a freshman. He closed out the 1994 season by leading the Vols to five consecutive victories, which gave them an 8-4 record after a 3-4 start.

Their momentum carried over into the 1995 season when they went 11-1 and finished third nationally. From 1995 through 1998, they lost only five games − a stretch culminated by a 13-0 record and national championship in 1998.

2005: Big things were expected of Tennessee that season. But bad things happened.

UT’s talent-laden, experienced team began the season ranked No. 3. It finished with a 5-6 record, including a loss to Vanderbilt.

That was the beginning of the end for coach Phillip Fulmer. Although Tennessee won 19 games over the next two seasons, the program was far removed from its 1990s success.

Fulmer was fired after Tennessee went 5-7 in 2008.

2015: The Vols appeared headed for a disaster in coach Butch Jones’ third season. They won only three of their first seven games.

But the four losses were by only 17 points combined. Just when the Jones era seemed to be moving in the wrong direction, Tennessee finished the season with a 9-4 record and a six-game winning streak.

ADAMS: Tennessee football lost more than Nico Iamaleava in the transfer portal

They followed that stretch run with five consecutive victories, including back-to-back wins over Florida and Georgia, in 2006. But that proved as misleading as the strong finish in 2015. Tennessee ended the 2016 season with another 9-4 record.

Jones was fired a year later after UT went 4-8.
