headline: Things to do in Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg: Summer fun for kids and grown-ups alike
fullText:
School is out, and summer vacation is here − which means the kids are ready to play! Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, along with the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, are a just short drive away and full of fun activities that allow family members of all ages to enjoy a much-needed break.

Whether it's at the aquarium or onboard a go-kart, these East Tennessee spots will keep you engaged on breezy, sun-filled mornings or even summer afternoon thunderstorms.

With over 100 attractions between Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, there are plenty of activities to choose from, but don't be overwhelmed. Knox News has narrowed down some options that are sure to be a hit with the kids for any season or budget.

Indoor things to do on hot or rainy days in Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg

At the peak of summer heat or on a rainy day, sometimes it's just easier to keep the fun indoors.

Ripley's Aquarium of the Smokies

  • Stop by to see an assortment of ocean critters ranging from cute to totally bizarre. Catch the curious axolotl and zebra moray eel, or watch African penguins jump and dive at the Penguin Playhouse.
  • Tickets prices range from $14.99 for ages 2-5 to $39.99 for ages 12 and older. For an additional fee, visitors can explore the aquarium on a glass-bottom boat tour. Ticket combos also are available, allowing visitors to visit multiple Ripley's attractions − including the mountain coaster and mirror maze − at reduced prices.
  • Location: 88 River Road, Gatlinburg

WonderWorks

  • The eye-catching upside-down attraction along the Parkway offers a hands-on approach to discovery and is made up of "Wonder Zones," each with a different scientific theme. The Extreme Weather Zone allows you to feel the power of an earthquake or hurricane, and the Physical Challenge Zone lets you rest on a bed of nails.
  • Ticket prices range from $25.99 for ages 4-12 to $34.99 for teens and adults.
  • Location: 100 Music Road, Pigeon Forge

MagiQuest

  • Kids can take an interactive journey, armed with a magic wand and clue book as they encounter fairies, princesses, the Goblin King and a dragon. For $27.99, kids are admitted to play for 90 minutes, plus they can keep their wand as a souvenir.
  • Location: 2491 Parkway, Gatlinburg

TopJump Trampoline & Extreme Arena

  • For more active indoor activities, TopJump offers a chance to run, jump and play.
  • Location: 3735 Parkway, Pigeon Forge

Pigeon Forge Snow

  • Have snow day fun indoors - snow tubing and building snowmen and forts - any month of the year, no coat required.
  • Location: 2533 Teaster Lane, Pigeon Forge

Crayola Experience Pigeon Forge

  • Slated to open in 2025, the Crayola Experience Pigeon Forge will provide visitors with more than 20 hands-on attractions, including naming their own Crayon and making art with melted wax, plus a chance to shop the world's largest selection of Crayola products, according to a media release.

Fun things to do outdoors in Pigeon Forge and Gatlinburg

Goat Coaster at Goats on the Roof

  • Keep things exciting with twists and turns, plus riders get the chance to see goats as they whoosh their way down 4,875 feet of track. Kids must be age 3 or older and at least 38 inches tall to ride, and must ride with a driver who is at least 16. Those 54-84 inches tall can ride alone.
  • Tickets cost $12 per person.
  • Location: 1341 Wears Valley Road, Pigeon Forge

Dollywood

  • If one roller coaster isn't enough, try everyone's favorite theme park, Dollywood, with rides galore plus live shows and more. Dolly Parton's park is celebrating its 40th season, which runs through Jan. 4, 2026.
  • Ticket prices for adults are $92, so you'll want to plan this as an all-day excursion.
  • Location: 2700 Dollywood Parks Blvd., Pigeon Forge

Water parks

  • Interested in splashing around this summer? You can take your pick of Dollywood's adjoining water park, Splash Country, or Soaky Mountain Waterpark just outside Pigeon Forge in Sevierville.
  • Ticket prices are around $50 for either water park. The Splash Country season runs daily through Aug. 9, and weekend operation through Sept. 21. Soaky Mountain Waterpark's daily season lasts until Sept. 1, and then continues on the weekends through the end of that month.
  • Locations: Splash Country, 2700 Dollywood Parks Blvd., Pigeon Forge; Soaky Mountain Waterpark, 175 Gists Creek Road, Sevierville

Mini golf or go karts

  • Ride the incline to the top to play some mini golf at Hillbilly Golf, or check out the 45-hole course at Gatlin's Mini Golf.
  • Or head off to the races in a go kart at Xtreme Racing Center. Riders age 11 and older and 56 inches or taller can hit the course solo. For double karts, drivers will need to be at least 16 and 56 inches or taller, and riders must be at least 3.
  • Locations: Hillbilly Golf, 340 Parkway, Gatlinburg; Gatlin's Mini Golf, 716 Parkway # 219, Gatlinburg; Xtreme Racing Center, 3144 Parkway, Pigeon Forge

Parrot Mountain and Garden of Eden

  • At Parrot Mountain in Pigeon Forge, kids can "see, touch and feed" hundreds of exotic birds, according to its website.
  • Location: 1471 McCarter Hollow Road, Pigeon Forge

Free and inexpensive activities in the Great Smoky Mountains

Great Smoky Mountains National Park

  • At the country's most popular national park, the only fee is for parking, which costs $5 for a one-day parking pass. Take a family hike on a shorter, kid-friendly trail like the Sugarlands Valley Nature Trail, a paved, half-mile loop. For a completely free choice − unless you plan on parking for over 15 minutes − drive the scenic Roaring Fork Motor Nature Trail or the Cades Cove Loop and see some of the park's streams, forests and historic buildings. If you'd like to walk or bike it, the Cades Cove Loop is vehicle-free on Wednesdays between June 18 and Sept. 24 in 2025.
  • Kids ages 5-12 can work on becoming junior rangers. Purchase the Junior Ranger Activity Guide online or at one of the visitor centers − Sugarlands is closest to Gatlinburg − for $4.50, then complete at least five activities and five experiences to be sworn in as a junior ranger at one of the park's visitor centers.
  • Locations: Sugarlands Visitor Center, 1420 Fighting Creek Gap Road, Gatlinburg; Roaring Fork Motor Nature Trail, 117 Historic Nature Trail, Gatlinburg

Gatlinburg Trolley

  • Back in town, tour the city aboard the Gatlinburg Trolley for free, hopping on and off to view sites as you please. The hub is the Mass Transit Center outside Ripley's Aquarium. More information about routes is available on the Gatlinburg website.
  • Location: Mass Transit Center, 88 River Road #101, Gatlinburg

Gatlinburg parks

  • Looking for an easy location to let the kiddos stretch their legs? Try Mynatt Park or Herbert Holt Park, both in Gatlinburg and equipped with standard playgrounds and picnic tables.
  • Locations: Herbert Holt Park, North Park Lane, Gatlinburg; Mynatt Park, 622 Historic Nature Trail, Gatlinburg

Restaurants with game rooms and arcades

You finally get the chance to sit down for a bite to eat, and suddenly you hear those two dreaded words: "I'm bored!" These restaurants provide plenty of activities to go along with the dining, so the kids can stay occupied from apps through dessert.

Downtown Flavortown

  • "Play with your food" is the philosophy of this arcade and dining concept by Guy Fieri. Here, kids can check out video games, arcade classics and bowling, while parents enjoy dishes like Nashville hot chicken nachos and blackened salmon, or even hit the tiki bar.
  • Location: 2655 Teaster Lane, Suite #100, Pigeon Forge

Fannie Farkle's

  • At this Gatlinburg mainstay, kids can try the "legendary Ogle Dog" before exploring the game rooms, which feature Ticket Time, Robot Storm and Sink It, according to its website.
  • Location: 656 Parkway, Gatlinburg

Big Daddy's Pizzeria

  • The Pigeon Forge location has an arcade with skee ball and air hockey and pizza options ranging from classic to more adventurous.
  • Location: 3053 Parkway, Pigeon Forge

headline: Great Smoky Mountains National Park to close lanes on these popular roads during June
fullText:
Drivers traveling through Great Smoky Mountains National Park should prepare for lane closures and traffic delays during June.

Maintenance along popular roads, including the Spur, will require temporary single-lane closures and partial road closures beginning June 3, the National Park Service announced.

From June 3 to June 12, crews will complete roadside work along the Spur and Little River Road. Maintenance includes mowing and pruning, ditch and culvert cleaning, shoulder drop off repair and hazard tree mitigation.

The temporary closures allow park staff to safely and efficiently complete the maintenance work. 

Little River Road closures

  • Townsend Wye to Metcalf Bottoms Picnic Area will be closed 7 a.m.-noon on June 3 and 4. Drivers can use Wears Valley Road (US 321) between Townsend and Line Springs Road as a detour. 
  • Metcalf Bottoms to Elkmont Junction will be closed 7 a.m.-noon on June 5. Drivers can use Wears Valley Road between Line Springs Road and Pigeon Forge as a detour. 

Popular sites including Elkmont, Metcalf Bottoms and Cades Cove will remain accessible during the closures but might require detours. Visitors should plan for increased travel time. 

Motor homes, buses and vans longer than 25 feet and any passenger vehicles towing a trailer are prohibited on Wear Cove Gap Road from the park boundary to the Metcalf Bottoms bridge, the park service noted.

The Spur closures

  • Temporary single-lane closures along the north and southbound Spur will be implemented 7 a.m.-4:30 p.m. June 9-12. Drivers might encounter some traffic delays.  

The park implemented similar closures on Little River Road for the first time last year to complete deferred road maintenance.

Crews mowed and string trimmed 24 miles along roadsides, cleaned nearly nine miles of roadside ditches, repaired 27 damaged road areas and side armed 12 miles of roadside banks.

headline: Karlyn Pickens' parents shed light on Tennessee's record-breaking pitcher, Smokey's journey
fullText:
OKLAHOMA CITY – Smokey the stuffed animal has lived inside what can only be described as Karlyn Pickens' world the last two years.

Pickens' mother, Rebecca, bought Smokey for Tennessee softball to keep in its dugout during the Women's College World Series in 2023. Rebecca heard from one of the senior's parents that teams often brought something to make their dugout at Devon Park feel more like home.

She documented their road trip from Weaverville, North Carolina, to Oklahoma City with photos of Smokey at various stops. Rebecca took photos of the stuffed animal with Lady Vols' bus driver and team moms.

"We decided it would be just silly to take pictures, kind of like a Where's Waldo kind of thing," Rebecca said. "Freshman year, we stopped everywhere. I was crazier with it that year, because Karlyn’s boyfriend was with us this year, and I think he probably thought I was nuts."

After the WCWS run ended, Rebecca stored the stuffed dog in the box with all the memorabilia from Pickens' career. T-shirts, ticket stubs, newspaper articles, photos – every keepsake from the last 12 years are stored there. And so was Smokey until May 27 when the Pickens made the road trip again to the WCWS.

Documenting the journey on social media is Rebecca's way of supporting the team and engaging with the fanbase that adores her daughter. She wants everyone to feel the excitement of the trip.

Rebecca and her husband, Phillip, have been steadying forces for Pickens as she has risen to stardom. The holder of the fastest pitch thrown in a softball game has already found peace of mind with her parents in her second WCWS run.

How Karlyn Pickens' parents keep pressure off Tennessee's ace

The Pickens family didn't make it far on their walk before Karlyn was spotted. They were heading to the Myriad Botanical Gardens after Tennessee's heartbreaking 4-3 loss earlier in the day against Oklahoma, which ended with Pickens giving up a two-out, three-run home run.

"Somebody yelled, 'That’s Karlyn Pickens!' " Rebecca recalled. 

They laughed about Pickens getting recognized immediately after leaving the team hotel. She wasn't even wearing Tennessee gear, but her 6-foot-1 frame and long blonde hair were a dead giveaway for one of her biggest fans.

After Pickens took a picture with the young fan, it was obvious she had made her day.

It was exactly the kind of moment Pickens needed. Rebecca even broke her rule to point it out – she and Phillip never talk about games with Pickens unless she initiates the conversation. But Rebecca made an exception that evening.

"Karlyn, that little girl doesn't care that you won or lost. She sees how you inspire her to be a better softball player," Rebecca said. "In that moment, she didn’t care about what the score was of the ball game. She just wanted to have a picture with you because you’re her idol."

Eventually they made their way to the beautiful pond full of koi fish and ducks. They took Pickens' mind off softball as they waded through the flowers and enjoyed the cooler-than-normal weather.

Pickens' parents do everything they can to take pressure off their daughter. They draw a firm line with their roles, and they don't cross it. Phillip asked Rebecca how practice was after she got off the phone with Karlyn once. Rebecca responded, "I don't know, she went to Ulta. We talked about makeup."

Rebecca joked that Karen Weekly of the Lady Vols is the one getting paid the big bucks to coach, so they leave it to her.

"Through all these years, I think it saved her from burnout," Rebecca said. "Knowing that she can come off the field, and if things didn’t go their way, she can come to her parents and we can support her."

How it felt to watch Karlyn Pickens break her own record

Rebecca's phone started buzzing five minutes after Pickens threw a 79.4 mph pitch, breaking her own record during the NCAA super regionals.

Rebecca usually ignores her phone during games, but eventually she couldn't ignore the flood of texts.

"I was like, 'Oh my gosh, she broke her own record,' " Rebecca said. "When we realized it was against Jordy (Bahl), I was like, that explains it. She wanted that out ... she just never ceases to amaze me, because there's always just a little bit more."

It felt exactly like the first time Pickens threw the fastest softball pitch ever recorded on March 24. That time she threw 78.2 mph against USA Softball Player of the Year Bri Ellis. The stadium got quiet before everyone's phones started blowing up.

The Pickens befriended season ticket holders near them, and Phillip caught their daughter's eye. She was holding her phone with a huge smile on her face. Phillip knew something happened, and then Rebecca's phone exploded.

The record-breaking pitches are the epitome of one of Phillip's sayings from high school.

"He would always yell, 'There’s more in the tank!' " Rebecca said. "And people laugh, we’re like, how much more is in the tank?"

It seems Pickens' tank is bottomless when Rebecca watches her power through entire games, still hitting her top velocity into the fifth and sixth innings. It's a credit to Tennessee strength and conditioning coach Dan Wirth, who transformed Pickens from a lanky high schooler to a workout junkie.

When Rebecca watches her daughter at Devon Park this year, she looks powerful.

headline: What happened between Lady Vols softball, UCLA in Women's College World Series
fullText:
UCLA's Megan Grant missed home plate after hitting a game-tying two-run home run against Lady Vols softball, which prompted a 13-minute review in the Women's College World Series.

Officials indicated that Grant did miss home plate and was assisted back to touch it by a teammate, but it did not matter.

"The play is not reviewable according to Appendix G," umpire Chris Neighbors announced, referencing the section of the NCAA rule book that pertains to reviewable plays.

The Lady Vols won 5-4 in the ninth inning on a Laura Mealer walk-off single to left field, advancing to the WCWS semifinals after Grant's homer forced extra innings.

Grant's homer with two outs in the seventh inning tied the elimination game 4-4 on June 1 at Devon Park in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. Alexis Ramirez, the on-deck hitter, pulled Grant back to touch home plate after she stepped over it celebrating the home run with her teammates waiting in a half-circle at home plate.

Lady Vols coach Karen Weekly was irate with the decision following the review. Weekly attempted to file a protest but could not due to the play not being reviewable, according to ESPN.

Tennessee led 4-2 going into the seventh inning and Lady Vols ace Karlyn Pickens got the first two outs in order. Jordan Woolery singled with two outs before Grant homered to right center on the first pitch she saw from Pickens.

Pickens got Ramirez to ground out after the review to end the top of the seventh. UT threatened in the bottom of the seventh against UCLA (55-13) before the game headed for extra innings.

headline: Smokies rally silenced by grand slam as Knoxville shifts focus to Chattanooga homestand
fullText:
All hopes of a series-ending comeback were undone by a ninth-inning grand slam as the Knoxville Smokies fell 8-4 to the Birmingham Barons on June 1 at Covenant Health Park.

The Smokies were down 4-0 for most of the game before rallying to erase a four-run deficit, tying Birmingham in the bottom of the seventh. A series of costly walks in the ninth, however, opened up the window for Barons slugger Ryan Galanie to deliver the decisive blow.

Birmingham (28-22) capitalized on Smokies starter Sam Armstrong immediately. He gave up a three-run homer to Wilfred Veras for three of the four runs the Barons scored in the opening frame.

Ethan Hearn provided Knoxville (24-26) with a spark of life with a solo homer in the second, and the Smokies bullpen stalled the Barons over the next five innings to give the offense a chance to get going.

In spite of several threats, the Smokies stranded the bases loaded in the sixth and were down 4-1 going into the bottom of the seventh.

That's when the bats woke up.

Hearn and Jaylen Palmer reached on a one-out single, and Jordan Nwogu scored a run with a center single. Pedro Ramirez added a two-run line drive to center to tie the game 4-4, completing a gritty comeback rally and allowing the Smokies the chance to finish it off.

But the bats cooled down just as quickly as they heated up, with neither team able to get ahead of the other in the eighth.

Smokies reliever Zac Leigh walked three consecutive hitters with two outs on the board, setting off a mound visit and bullpen call to Cayne Ueckert. Facing one opportunity to get out of the jam, Ueckert threw a first-pitch strike before the next ball sailed over the left field wall for a grand slam.

With one more chance to extend the game, the Smokies went three-and-out to finish the first of two consecutive homestands.

Following a day of rest, the Smokies will return to action June 3 at Covenant Health Park to face the Chattanooga Lookouts in another six-game series.

headline: Tennessee softball survives extra innings vs. UCLA to return to the WCWS semifinal
fullText:
OKLAHOMA CITY –  Laura Mealer was the hero for Tennessee softball with a walk-off run-scoring single in the bottom of the ninth inning to send the Lady Vols to the Women's College World Series semifinals.

No. 7 seed Tennessee beat No. 9 seed UCLA 5-4 on June 1.

The Lady Vols (47-16) will face No. 6 seed Texas (53-11) on June 2 (noon, ESPN). They have to beat the Longhorns twice to advance to the championship series.

Tennessee almost won the game 4-2 in regulation before a lengthy home-run review in the seventh inning went in UCLA's favor.

The game went to extra innings after UCLA first baseman Megan Grant's two-run homer off ace Karlyn Pickens to tie it went to review. On the replay, it appeared that Grant stepped over home plate, missing it completely. Her teammates then assisted her in touching home plate, but the call was upheld after a 13-minute review because the play was not reviewable "according to Appendix G," an umpire announced, referencing the section of the NCAA rule book that pertains to reviewable plays.

Tennessee offense keeps rolling in first innings

Mealer put Tennessee on the board in the first inning with a two-RBI single to center field. Taylor Pannell and Ella Dodge hit consecutive singles to get on base, and Sophia Nugent moved them to second and third with a fly out that was nearly a home run. The ball hit the top of the wall in left field.

UCLA (55-12) then intentionally walked McKenna Gibson to load the bases with two outs to set up Mealer's heroics.

Tennessee took a 2-0 lead quickly, the fifth straight game it has scored in the first inning. The lead didn't last long, though, with UCLA hitting two solo home runs off Pickens in the second inning. Both offenses died down after that with neither team logging a hit until the Bruins logged two hits in the fifth inning.

Pannell blasted a two-run homer in the fifth inning to give Tennessee a 4-2 lead.

Karlyn Pickens holds off UCLA for the win

Pickens (25-10) didn't have her best outing against the Bruins.

UCLA logged 11 hits and three home runs against Pickens, which is the most any team has hit against her this season. The previous highs were eight hits and two home runs. It's only the second game this season a team has homered multiple times against Pickens – the other time was Tennessee's 4-3 loss to Oklahoma in the WCWS opener.

But Pickens did enough to hold off the Bruins for a win. She even got out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning, striking out Alexis Ramirez for the final out. Ramirez hit a homer in the second inning.

The junior finished with seven strikeouts with nine hits allowed, three walks and four earned runs.

Pickens had a brief scare in the sixth inning when her foot got stuck in the dirt and she tweaked her ankle on her landing. She went down for a moment, but after a few practice pitches she was good to go.

headline: Learn about June's full moon, including how it got its name and when you can see it
fullText:
The next full moon is nearly here, and it’s the last full moon of spring.  

Here’s what’s to come this month.  

When is the next full moon?   

The next full moon, a strawberry moon, will be visible on June 11 at 3:44 a.m., according to Almanac. 

Ahead of the full moon, the first quarter moon will appear on June 2 at 11:41 p.m., followed by the last quarter moon on June 18 at 3:19 p.m. and the last quarter moon on June 25 at 6:31 a.m., according to Almanac.   

What is a strawberry moon?  

June’s full moon is the strawberry moon, named after the small wild strawberries that ripen at this time of the year, according to Almanac.  

The strawberry moon is also known as the “hot moon,” “green corn moon” and “berries ripen moon” to Native American tribes; the “horse moon,” “rose moon” and “dyan moon” in Celtic culture; and the “mead moon” to Anglo-Saxons, a nod to the moon occurring during a time of year meant for mowing the meads, or meadows, according to TimeandDate.com.  

Around every 20 years, the strawberry moon coincides with the summer solstice, occurring on either June 20, 21 or 22.

ICYMI: ChristianaCare to take on 5 Crozer Health outpatient locations with $50M bid

July full moon  

Looking ahead, July’s full moon is called the “buck moon” and will be visible on July 10 at 4:36 p.m. It signifies the new antlers that emerge on a deer buck’s forehead around this time of year after they shed their previous pair, Farmers Almanac reports.  

Embody your favorite Blue Hen at home: Want to play as a Blue Hen? Delaware added to EA Sports 'College Football 26' video game

The buck moon is also known as the “raspberry moon,” “claiming moon,” “salmon moon,” “wyrt moon” and “herb moon,” among other names, according to Native American and Celtic tradition, according to TimeandDate.com.  

Some refer to July’s full moon as the thunder moon, due to the frequent thunderstorms during the summer, or the hay moon, in honor of the hay harvest in July.

headline: Arden Shakespeare Gild brings rich history to annual summer production
fullText:
(This story has been updated to correct an inaccuracy. The Arden Shakespeare Gild's annual summer festival takes place June 13 to 21. In addition, William Shakespeare authored 38 plays. Incorrect information was initially supplied by the theater company.)

Nestled in a leafy space next to the main Arden Green is a tiny theater, the Frank Stephen’s Memorial theater, popularly known as the Field Theater.  

Quiet most of the year except for a rare concert or wedding celebration, it comes alive each June with the Arden Shakespeare Gild’s annual Shakespeare production.

Performances spaces abound in the three Arden Villages. There are two more outdoor venues: The Shady Grove stage next to the Arden Gild Hall, and the Moonlight  Amphitheater adjacent to the Hall. 

Inside the Gild Hall is a fully appointed theater and another smaller stage in the Buzz Ware Center in Arden.

Ardentown hosts the professional Candlelight Theater in the converted Harvey Barn. However, the Field Theater was built specifically for the performance of Shakespeare’s plays and is the home of the Arden Shakespeare Gild.

When the  Village of Arden was founded in 1900 by Georgist philosophers Frank Stevens and William Lightfoot Price, the Field Theater was one of the first dedicated spaces created, even before many of the houses were built. The founders believed that it would be necessary to hone the oratorical skills of the community members to help them share the message of Single-Tax community on which the village was founded.

The performance of Shakespeare was thought to be a good means of supporting that goal. The huge boulder on the back of the stage was intentionally incorporated into the design to create a useful backdrop for Shakespearian productions.  

There have been Shakespearian productions in the Ardens for the last 125 years. The Shakespeare Gild is responsible for these productions, usually performed in the spring, as well as a Young Actor’s Workshop of Shakespearian scenes and compilations from December into February. Some of the Young Shakespeare Actors perform at the annual Shakespeare dinner, scheduled around Shakespeare’s birthday, (April 23) and prepared by the Shakespeare Gild members and hosted by the Arden Dinner Gild.

The Shakespeare Gild also lends its talents to many other Arden community events such as the Arden Fair and the Arden Community Recreation Association.

The Gild has a large costume collection that they share with another Gild, the Arden Singers. Those costumes are frequently loaned to other theaters and performance organizations in the area. 

The name Arden actually comes from Shakespeare’s comedy, "As You Like It,'' which takes place in The Forest of Arden. Since 1900, this comedy has been performed every 10 years to celebrate the origins of the villages. 

Shakespeare wrote 38 plays. The group tries to alternate each year between Shakespeare’s comedies, histories and tragedies. The Gild has performed almost all of them. 

Festival frenzy: 17 Delaware events this spring & summer 2025

While there are more frequent repeats of the more popular plays, such as "A Midsummer Night’s Dream," "Henry V," "Twelfth Night" and "Much Ado About Nothing'' and "Hamlet,'' each rendition will have a different interpretation, setting and costuming.

The universal nature of Shakespeare’s work allows for much flexibility. For the last 100 years, each performance has begun with the cast strolling across the Arden Green singing “Or the Hills and Far Away.” 

While the reasons for using this particular folk song are lost in the mist of history, Arden loves tradition and everyone enjoys preparing this piece. The harmonies and tempo each year depend of who is doing the singing,, so it never gets old.

The production this year is "The Winter’s Tale.'' It is one of the few the Gild has not performed in the past and director, John K Baxter is excited to correct that oversight. First performed in 1609, it is a tragicomedy (someone dies, someone misbehaves, loves conquers all.) It returns to some of the Bard’s favorite themes: jealousy, revenge, bucolic charm and redemption. It also contains one of Shakespeare’s most famous stage directions, “Exit, chased by a bear.” John has put the piece in a modern setting with a ‘70s vibe.

Aubrey Plaza update: Aubrey Plaza is back on red carpet at Cannes promoting 'Honey, Don't' summer film

Performances are June 13, 14 19, 20 and 21 at 7:30 p.m., and June 15 at 2 p.m. at The Field Theatre. In case of rain, performances will be at the Gild Hall except for June 14, which would take place at the Buzz Ware Center.

Tickets can be purchased at the door or at the Arden Club website Ardenclub.org.  There is ample parking at both locations.

Kathryn Donovan is co-chair of Arden Shakespeare Gild.

headline: These Delaware restaurants, food businesses closed permanently in 2025
fullText:
It's been a good year for lots of diverse, promising new restaurants to open their doors around the First State.

But, sadly, not all restaurants make it. So far, we've said goodbye to these restaurants and other food establishments, which closed for good in 2025:

Ruby Tuesday

Ruby Tuesday in the Pike Creek Shopping Center, at 4700 Limestone Road, closed its doors to the public on Jan. 7, according to Regency Centers, the shopping center’s commercial developer.

The chain filed for Chapter 11 Bankruptcy in 2020 after struggling from years of increased competition and in the face of the pandemic, but kept its four Delaware locations open. The casual dining chain emerged from bankruptcy a year later as a much smaller company.

Two Ruby Tuesday locations remain in the First State: in Milford at 945 N. DuPont Blvd. and in Middletown at 474 W. Main St.

The 8,000-square-foot space has remained vacant and, according to the Regency Centers website, is still available.

Rasa Sayang

The owners of the 17-year-old restaurant in the Concord Mall, which formerly had been located in the Independence Mall shopping center near Fairfax, said it would close its doors on Jan. 19.

Rasa Sayang, which loosely translates to "Feel the Love," opened in 2008 in the Independence Mall shopping center. It moved into a larger space next to Boscov's in the Concord Mall in June 2020.

Rasa Sayang was known for its roti canai, a Southeast Asian pancake, as well as soups, noodle dishes and spicy curries. It also served sushi.

No reason was given for Rasa Sayang's closing, announced on Jan. 8, in a message posted on its Facebook page. The restaurant thanked customers for their support.

Concord Diner

Located about 2½ miles away, at 2530 Concord Pike in Fairfax, Concord Diner posted on Thursday, Jan. 16 to its Facebook page that it was permanently closing. No date was given. Messages left at the diner were not immediately returned.

In July 2023, the Concord Diner popped open at the site of the former Touch of Italy. The Italian restaurant operated at 2530 Concord Pike from 2018 until closing in April 2020 due to the pandemic, according to a post that Touch of Italy founder Bob Cipretti posted on its Facebook page. It never reopened for business.

The building, next to the Charcoal Pit, had operated before that for about four years as a Big Fish Restaurant Group restaurant known as Bella Coast Italian Kitchen & Market. The sprawling space had 150 seats.

Concord Diner touted that it was open for 24 hours soon after opening.

A farewell note on Jan. 16, on the restaurant's Facebook page reads: "After careful consideration, we have made the difficult decision to close our doors permanently. We want to express our sincere gratitude for your support. It has been our pleasure to serve you, and we will cherish the memories made here. Thank you."

A restaurant called La Fête is moving into the space, according to social media posts.

We got word that the site will be reconfigured this summer as a French-themed restaurant under new ownership.

Red Robin, Dover

Dover’s Red Robin, located at 40 N. DuPont Highway, quietly closed down on New Year’s Eve, to the surprise of community members and employees alike. 

Al Fresco guide: Dine outdoors at these restaurants in and around Delaware

R&R Realty, the site’s commercial developer, confirmed that another tenant had been signed on to the building, but could not confirm what tenant that was. 

The location initially opened up during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. There are four remaining Red Robin locations in Delaware. 

Hardee's, Bear

The Hardee’s restaurant located at 1801 Pulaski Highway in Bear closed early in January. 

Its franchisee, Summit Restaurant Holdings, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023 and has since closed dozens of stores around the country, including one in Elkton, Maryland. 

Delaware still has eight Hardee’s locations around the state.

The Wandering Chef Cart

The Wandering Chef cart, which has operated around the University of Delaware's Newark campus for 13 years selling soup, sandwiches and dumplings, called it quits in early February.

The cart was known by several names including the Dumpling Cart and The Cart at UD. It was founded by Culinary Institute of America-trained chefs Michael Blovad and John Pudil in 2011. Blovad's wife, Lauren, also worked the cart.

A post on Feb. 2 said, "thank you all for your support. We have closed the cart. We are enjoying our family, friends and new opportunities." 

For more information, visit the website wandering-chef.com

Alaska Stand

821 N. Atlantic Ave., Ocean City, Maryland

Ocean City, Maryland, locals and tourists will be sad to hear Alaska Stand, a part of the town since 1933, has closed for good, according to a recent Facebook post.

For more than 90 years, the seasonal Ninth Street location on the boardwalk served breakfast, milkshakes, burgers, split hot dogs, and other food to generations of Ocean City visitors.

Owners said they have entered into an agreement with Thrasher's French Fries, which will take over the corner site.

Colbie's Southern Kissed Chicken

481 Stanton Christiana Road, Stanton

It's been a moment, but in case you missed it, Colbie's Southern Kissed Chicken, a chain of restaurants selling fried and grilled chicken sandwiches and wraps created by Craig and Mike Colby, and former Philadelphia Phillies first basemen and slugger Ryan Howard, closed its Delaware operation several months ago.

New dining options: 7 new Delaware restaurants include a reboot of an old favorite in Fenwick Island

Signs on the doors read: "We are sorry for the inconvenience. This location is permanently closed. Colbie's Southern Kissed Chicken."

The drive-thru, dine-in restaurant off Del. 7 between Border Cafe and Royal Farms opened in September 2021. It was initially slated to be called Dixie's Southern Kissed Chicken when the concept was first announced in 2019. The name was later changed.

According to its website, Colbie's still has locations at Citizens Bank Park and the Philadelphia Zoo, in Mount Holly, New Jersey, and Trenton Thunder Park in Trenton, New Jersey.

The Colbys run the Colby Restaurant Group, which owns Chuck Lager-America's Tavern in Pike Creek.

Atlantic Social

19340 Lighthouse Blvd., Rehoboth Beach

Atlantic Social opened off Coastal Highway in Rehoboth Beach in 2020, taking over the Ruby Tuesday space with an all-over layer of white paint and serving modern mid-Atlantic cuisine.

It's owned by Derek Fink and Zach Diogo; Fink also owns Blackwall Hitch in downtown Rehoboth.

When Atlantic Social closed in January, a Facebook post said it was for renovations, but a few weeks later, SoHo Slice signs started going up on the building.

More food news: 10 best Delaware-area restaurants we wish made USA TODAY's Restaurants of the Year list

"We're going through some major renovations, so it was, 'Do I want to stay with (Atlantic Social) or go with something completely different?' And we voted to go with something completely different," Fink said.

SoHo Slice, a New York-style pizzeria, is now open.

MAY

Fuego Peri Peri Grill, Stanton

Fuego Peri Peri Grill in the Churchmans Plaza shopping center near Christiana Hospital has closed after operating for three years.

It celebrated flame-grilled Halal chicken flavored with the Portuguese Peri-Peri Pepper.

A sign posted on the door of the restaurant read: "We are permanently closing from Monday, 4/21/25." Messages left with the restaurant were not returned.

In 2022, Fuego Peri Peri Grill took over the location of the former Viva Chicken, a fast-casual restaurant concept that specialized in rotisserie chicken marinated for 24 hours in Peruvian spices and spun in a charcoal oven.

Viva Chicken operated from 2018 until closing shortly after the pandemic began in 2020.

322 BBQ, Newark

322 BBQ and its co-located business, Hill Donut Co., which took over the former space of the Stone Balloon, a restaurant that endured in one form or another for 50 years, has closed its doors.

A post on the Open Table reservations site for 322 BBQ/Hill Donut Co. in Newark reads: "This restaurant is permanently closed."

The 115 E. Main St. restaurant, which served barbecue, burgers, beers, doughnuts and pancakes, had been open for less than a year. It opened in late summer 2024.

The Newark business, no longer listed on the 322 BBQ website, was not accepting phone calls, the sign was removed from the exterior of the building, and the interior was dark during a visit on April 23. Two messages left via social media to the 322 BBQ Newark site were not immediately returned.

The Wilmington restaurant on Marsh Road and the site in Mullica Hill, New Jersey, remain open.

Bob Evans Restaurant, near Lewes

The family-style restaurant at 18492 Coastal Highway near Lewes in operation for nearly 27 years has shut for good in April, according to the company.

"The Delaware store is permanently closed," read an email sent to Delaware Online/The News Journal on April 30 from Bob Evans guest relations.

No other information was provided.

The other Bob Evans locations in Delaware are still operating.

The Bob Evans chain was founded in Rio Grande, Ohio. Bob Evans Restaurants are in 18 states.

Ciro Forty Acres, Wilmington 

The Wilmington breakfast/lunch cafe closed its doors permanently on April 6, after nearly five years in business.

Reader's choice: This retro-style Delaware diner has been named one of the country's best roadside diners

The 3,746-square-foot business was inside a building at 1836 Lovering Ave. that dates back to 1925. The cafe business had been listed for sale on commercial real estate websites.

Venu Gaddamini, who owned Ciro Forty Acres with chef Michael DiBianca, said brunch is now offered on Saturdays and Sundays at Ciro Food & Drink, a restaurant the pair have operated at 321 Justison St. at the Wilmington Riverfront since 2019. The first brunch service, from about 10 a.m. until 2 p.m., was on April 19.

Ciro Food & Drink's new brunch menu includes shrimp & grits, Croque Madame, bacon and egg pizza, and a roasted tomato frittata.

Before Ciro, the space housed De La Coeur Café et Pâtisserie and Fresh Thymes Cafe.

Midnight Oil Brewing Co., Glasgow

The Glasgow craft brewery announced it was pouring its final brew on April 19. It joins a string of First State breweries that have shuttered in recent years.

When Midnight Oil opened on Feb. 3, 2018, at 674 Pencader Drive, it was the only brewery in Glasgow.

A year after Midnight Oil opened, another craft brewery joined them in Glasgow with the smaller Autumn Arch Beer Project launching just a few feet down the road.

In the years since, the state's craft brewing world has grown, now boasting about 40 breweries. But in an interview with Delaware Online/The News Journal, managing partner and brewer Mike Dunlap said Midnight Oil's model with a small tasting room and a 15,000-square-foot production brewery – one of the biggest brew houses in the state – just didn't work in the long run.

Delaware beer historian John Medkeff Jr. agreed with Dunlap that Midnight Oil's 15-barrel brew house became a liability as competition increased for shelf space at retailers as the craft beer industry grew.

Kaisy's Delights, Lewes

Kaisy's Delights in Lewes is closed and the property has been sold, owner Thierry Langer said. He is focusing on Kaisy's Millsboro location at 303 Main St., which is open daily from 8 a.m. until 3 p.m.

"Your grandma from Europe is in the kitchen, that's the concept," Langer said.

Langer is French and has family members from Poland and Austria. Kaisy's menu was based on his aunt's recipe book, he said, with breakfast, lunch, and Kaiserschmarrn, a traditional Austrian dish of shredded pancakes.

The Coffee House Powered by Schell, Rehoboth Beach

Ubiquitous homebuilding company Schell Brothers' downtown Rehoboth Beach coffee spot, at 18 Rehoboth Ave., is closed. The decision was a tough one, Schell Brothers' spokesperson Alyssa Titus said.

"We thoroughly enjoyed serving coffee and smiles to our customers, but with so much expansion into other divisions as a company, we needed to focus on our core business operations," Titus said.

A new store called Sugar & Thread took over the space.

You can learn more about both Sugar & Thread locations here.

Pizzeria Maki, Glen Mills, Pennsylvania

Pizzeria Maki, which has its flagship location in Greenville, announced on Wednesday, March 19, that it would be closing its Glen Mills, Pennsylvania, location at 45 W. Baltimore Pike.

Owners wrote in social media posts that the space, which opened in 2023, will soon be home to The Salty Cow, a homemade ice cream shop. The Salty Cow has a shop in West Chester, Pennsylvania.

Pizzeria Maki, which serves sushi and pizza, continues its "thriving" Greenville location, owners said. Plans are in the works to expand to new locations, they added.

Cromwell's American Tavern & Taqueria, Greenville

The longtime Greenville restaurant in the Powder Mill Square shopping center permanently closed after three decades of service.

Owner Pat Nilon closed the site off Kennett Pike (Route 52) on March 15. It had been a part of the shopping center since November 1991.

Nilon took over a space formerly occupied by Schoonover's restaurant and Cromwell's soon became a locals' favorite. It carved out a comfortable niche for its casual fare and laidback atmosphere.

SIW Vegetables

Owner H.G. Haskell III, who ran the Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania, farmstand since 1986, announced on March 19, that he would not be reopening the business for the 2025 season.

Haskell said he was retiring and that SIW Vegetables off South Creek Road, just over the Delaware state line, was closed permanently. The stand usually operates from April to early November.

SIW, which stands for "Stepped in What?," has been a staple of the community. It's been a kind of hidden gem tucked off the winding South Creek Road on a shady patch of land next to railroad tracks. Customers came from Delaware and Pennsylvania to purchase sweet white and yellow corn, eggplants, cucumbers, lima beans known as Doc Martins, and a wide variety of heirloom tomatoes that Haskell has grown on his nearby historic Hill Girt Farm for almost 40 years.

The stand also sold cheeses, homemade tomato sauce, local eggs and honey, ice cream, salsa and chips made by local businesses along with flowers, plants, pumpkins and gourds.

Over the years, SIW Vegetables has provided pumpkins for the annual Great Pumpkin Carve in Chadds Ford and has held "Field to Fork" dinners prepared by regional chefs in its barn.

H.G. Haskell's father, Hal Haskell, who had purchased the farm from the Pyle family and operated it as a dairy farm until 1972, was a Delaware congressman from 1957 to 1959 and later served as mayor of Wilmington from 1969 to 1973. He died at age 98 in 2020.

Haskell has said on videos on Instagram that a new vendor will be running the stand beginning in early June. He has not yet named the farmer. Haskell said he will not be growing the produce that will be sold at the market.

headline: Pennies are going away. What to do with the ones in your coin jar?
fullText:
It's just sitting there collecting dust.

It takes many forms – glass milk bottles, coffee cups, ceramic or glass pigs – and it's holding a small fortune.

It's the container of coins sitting on your nightstand, desk or kitchen counter.

Sure, it might not seem like much, but you'd be surprised at how those coins add up – especially if you have a rare coin in your container.

Here's what to know about your coins as the U.S. Treasury stops minting pennies.

Is my jar of coins worth anything?

American consumers made only 16% of their payments in cash in 2023, according to the Federal Reserve. A 2022 Pew survey found that two-fifths of consumers never use cash at all.

President Donald Trump has ordered the Treasury to stop minting pennies because their production cost exceeds their value. (Intriguingly, the same is true of nickels.)

Many Americans regard both nickels and pennies as more of a nuisance than currency. The typical household is sitting on $60 to $90 in neglected coins, enough to fill one or two pint-size beer mugs, according to the Federal Reserve. Americans throw away millions of dollars in coins every year, literally treating them like trash.

To state the obvious, coins are worth money. The average jar yields $58 in buying power.

Most of us don’t realize how much our coins are worth. Thus, a trip to a coin-exchange kiosk or a bank, or a credit union can yield a pleasant surprise.

“People underestimate the value of their jar by about half,” Kevin McColly, CEO of Coinstar, the company behind those coin-cashing machines you see in supermarkets, said. “It’s a wonderfully pleasurable experience. People have this sensation of found money.”

Certain groups of Americans – lower-income households, and those over 55 – still use plenty of cash, the Fed found, along with people who prefer to shop in person.

What's next for the penny? The details on US decision to end penny production

Coins aren't clutter, they're currency

As for the rest of us, McColly thinks it is time for a paradigm shift. Don’t think of your coins as clutter. Think of them as recyclables.

“They’re metal,” he said, in case we needed a reminder. “And they have a long and useful life.”

The Treasury still mints more than 5 billion coins a year, although the figure is dropping, according to the journal CoinNews.

“Those are just natural resources coming out of the Earth,” McColly said: Copper-plated zinc for pennies, copper-nickel alloys for nickels, dimes and quarters.

His point: If Americans got serious about gathering up their idle coins and “recycling” them into the monetary system, the Mint wouldn’t have to make so many new ones.

Granted, McColly has a vested interest. His company collects a small cut of the coins that consumers deposit. Coinstar generally waives its fee if the depositor chooses to trade in coins for a retail gift card, rather than cash.

However, there are places you can exchange your coins for no cost.

“You can go to your own bank or credit union and not pay any fee,” said Kimberly Palmer, personal finance expert at NerdWallet. Both NerdWallet and Bankrate offer tip sheets on exchanging coins for cash. Most banks will take an account holder's coins for free, Bankrate reports, but not all, and you may need to roll the coins yourself.

“I think that a lot of people probably do have hidden coins stashed around their home, and it can be worth their time to go and collect them,” Palmer said.

Retiring coins: Where does it end?

But what is the future for the penny, the nickel, and their more profitable kin.

“We’ve been much slower than parts of Europe and Asia to adopt mobile payments and contactless credit cards,” said Ted Rossman, a senior industry analyst at Bankrate.

The pandemic delivered a timely reminder of how much we still rely on cash: Consumers and business owners sat on their coins amid a global shutdown, seeding an actual coin shortage.

“It kind of froze the whole system,” Rossman said.

While Trump has only instructed the Mint to stop making pennies, some voices have urged America to stop using them.

The Common Cents Act, introduced on April 30 by a bipartisan group of lawmakers, would round cash transactions to the nearest five cents.

“The penny is outdated and inefficient and no longer serves the needs of our economy,” said Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the New York Democrat.

But the bill could push the nation down a slippery slope.

“So, You Want to Get Rid of the Penny,” the New York Times mused in a recent headline. “Do You Have a Plan for the Nickel?”

As it turns out, nixing the penny creates new problems. If America rids itself of pennies, the Times reported, the nation will soon find itself flooded with nickels.

The government loses nearly three cents on every penny it mints. On a nickel, it loses nearly nine cents. More nickels would mean steeper losses.

America could kill both the penny and the nickel, the two money-losers on its roster of coins.

But without pennies or nickels, how would a consumer pay a 15-cent tab?

You could round every price to the nearest 10 cents, taking the Common Cents Act a step further. But then, what becomes of the quarter?

And so on.

Is an old penny worth as much as a million dollars?

Experts say it's highly unlikely.

You may have seen one of many headlines blasted online lately about valuable pennies in circulation, "Lincoln Wheat Penny Worth $124M You Could Have at Home" reads one, but the reality is most pennies are worth one cent or possibly a bit more.

Reality does not meet the hype, according to one expert.

"There are million-dollar pennies, but there are no $100 million pennies," said Donn Pearlman, spokesman for the Professional Numismatists Guild, a nonprofit organization composed of many of the nation's rare coin experts. "Only a few Lincoln cents dated 1909 to 1958 with the wheat stalks design on the back ("wheat pennies") have sold for $1 million or more."

The most valuable U.S. coin ever, a $20 gold piece, a 1933 "Double Eagle" coin, sold for $18.9 million at auction in 2021. The most valuable pennies, which are rare but possibly still in circulation, are 1943 copper Lincoln wheat pennies, a few of which were produced accidentally as the U.S. mints were supposed to use zinc to save copper for the World War II effort, said John Feigenbaum, publisher of rare coin price guide Greysheet.

In rare cases, some 1943 pennies have sold for $1 million, while one went for more than $200,000 at an auction in 2019.

Depending on their condition, those 1943 Lincoln wheat pennies would be worth at most between $100,000 and $250,000, Feigenbaum told USA TODAY.

But the likelihood of having a near-priceless penny is similar to "saying your lottery ticket might be worth $100,000. Of course, anything is possible, right? But not likely," said Feigenbaum, who is also the PNG's executive director.

What are wheat pennies worth?

So-called "wheat pennies" get their name from the back of the coin having stalks of wheat encircling the "One Cent" text. They were produced from 1909 to 1958. After that, the wheat stalks were shorn and pennies began displaying an engraving of the Lincoln Memorial.

Most Lincoln wheat pennies are not super-valuable and are worth just a few cents more than one cent. However, some may escalate into the hundreds of dollars, depending on the condition and when minted. Certain vintages, especially with minting errors, may be worth thousands. You can see the NGC price guide here.

But headlines about super-valuable "Lincoln wheat pennies" stretch the imagination. Most likely, the headlines are created by artificial intelligence to drive traffic to a website, Feigenbaum said.

"These coins are improbably in people's change," he said.

Still, all the online-stirred interest has resulted in "coin shops being inundated with these folks who believe they have something rare, but they don't," according to Feigenbaum.

Increased interest in coins has led to overvalued coins being sold on eBay and Etsy, plus there are counterfeit Lincoln wheat pennies made in China being hawked.

"If I've seen these coins ... somebody is every now and again being taken advantage of," Feigenbaum said.

What should I do if I have some pennies or other coins I think are valuable?

Even though the most valuable coins are usually in collections and have very publicly been "sold and resold," Feigenbaum said, sometimes people may inherit a cache of well-preserved coins or purchase some at an estate sale.

  • Read up on your coins. While there are apps you can use to check on your coins, they aren't always accurate. But you can check the value of coins in "The 2026 Red Book: A Guide Book of United States Coins," available in book stores and online on Amazon.com and Barnes and Noble. "It answers all kinds of questions, like, 'Oh, if I'm thinking about collecting Lincoln cents, what can I expect to pay?" said Feigenbaum, one of the book's editors. "You'll see in that book there's no million-dollar cents."
  • Go get your coins graded. You can have your coins authenticated at their value, just as jewelry is, from several services, including CAC, Numismatic Guaranty Company, and Professional Coin Grading Service.

headline: Biggest-ever Delaware Pride Festival, plus 19 more First State Pride Month 2025 events
fullText:
At a time when Delaware's LGBTQ+ community feels under attack from federal anti-DEI actions and restrictions against transgender Americans, the 28th annual Delaware Pride Festival undoubtedly will be unlike any other in recent memory.

"This year hits a little different," says Zach Workman, president of festival organizer Delaware Pride Inc. "It's as important as ever to have this festival this year because a lot of queer spaces are losing funding and disappearing. Also to show solidarity among queer folks and show they aren't backing down to bigotry or keyboard warriors."

Attendance for the free festival, set to be held June 7 on The Green in downtown Dover, has grown year over year and 2025 is expected to be the biggest yet, possibly drawing up to 7,000 people.

Workman hopes the range of anti-LGBTQ+ pressures that have surfaced nationally in recent months will spur a big show of public support at Delaware's largest annual LGBTQ+ event by both queer people and allies.

Not only is it possible that the festival will draw its largest-ever crowd, it will be the biggest in terms of participants with about 40 performers across eight hours, more than 180 vendors and sponsors and at least 10 food trucks and food vendors on-site.

Even with the pressures on the community, Workman says it's also important to celebrate and find joy. And Delaware Pride Festival is custom-made for it as the all-day, all-ages party takes over the four streets that frame The Green near Legislative Hall.

"This year is going back to the origins of Pride, focusing on community, advocacy and creating safer spaces. It's much closer to the original meaning rather than just a festival for fun," Workman says. "However, it shouldn't only be about combating negatives. It's important to focus on the positives and fun.

"I think what queer people can do is show up, have a great time at a larger event based around them with support of their allies, and perform what is probably the the most rebellious act of all right now: existing and being themselves."

Here is a full rundown of some of the major Pride Month-themed events happening across Delaware in June, celebrating LGBTQ+ Pride.

Sunday, June 1: Pride Market, Old New Castle

The pop-up Pride Market organized by the Delaware Sexuality & Gender Collective is back for a second year, running from noon to 5 p.m.

The market, the first of its kind in Delaware, debuted in November and is returning to kick off Pride Month with 56 LGBTQ+-aligned vendors on The Green at 211 Delaware Street in Old New Castle.

Originally conceived as a fall event, it was expanded to include a June date due to the success of its inaugural run.

"I think what queer people can do is show up, have a great time at a larger event based around them with support of their allies, and perform what is probably the the most rebellious act of all right now: existing and being themselves." ~ Zach Workman, Delaware Pride Inc.

It returns to the same site Saturday, Nov. 1.

Sunday, June 1: LGBTQ+ flag raising, Rehoboth Beach

Rehoboth Beach will raise the LGBTQ+ flag at Rehoboth Beach City Hall (229 Rehoboth Ave.) at noon in celebration of Pride Month.

It will be flown throughout the month.

“Rehoboth Beach is home to a vibrant LGBTQ+ community, which greatly contributes to the social and economic vitality as well as the character of our city,” Mayor Stan Mills said. “The City of Rehoboth Beach strives to foster diversity among its residents and visitors and to be a welcoming community to all.”

Friday, June 6: Delaware Pride Pre-Party, Dover

Dover's Rail Haus (92 N. West St.) will host "high-energy, feel-good" pre-party for the Delaware Pride Festival at 5 p.m.

It starts with a 45-minute Zumba class with Kyle at 5:30 p.m. with all proceeds from the class donated to local LGBTQ+ organizations followed by karaoke with Diva DJ with LGBTQ+ fundraising all night long.

Saturday, June 7: Delaware Pride Festival, Dover

The 28th annual Delaware Pride Festival will be the biggest ever, running from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. across The Green (43 The Green, Dover).

Each year it draws thousands of LGBTQ+ people and their families, along with allies, for a day of fun with live musical performances, shopping and plenty of food with a beer garden. All ages are welcome.

It will be hosted by Delaware drag queen Scarlet Masters and will feature family-friendly performances by Maddelynn Hatter and Louisiana Purchase, both of "The Boulet Brothers' Dragula" reality television program.

First State Brewing Co. of Middletown and Rehoboth Beach will brew a special Pride beer called Inclusive Solution, which will be sold at both of its locations. The beer is a 7% ABV rainbow sherbet hazy IPA with notes of tart raspberry, sweet orange and pineapple. A portion of sales from the beer and the brewery's new Pride shorts will go to Delaware Pride Inc.

Saturday, June 7: Delaware Pride After Dark, Wilmington

If you're looking for adults-only Pride fun, the official afterparty, Delaware Pride After Dark, is the place to be at Theatre N (221 W. 10th St., Wilmington).

Like the Pride festival, Scarlet Masters will host and the headliners will be "The Boulet Brothers' Dragula" contestants Maddelynn Hatter and Louisiana Purchase.

Doors open at 7:30 p.m. and the 21-and-older show starts at 8 p.m. Tickets are $30 in advance at delawarepride.org. Day-of tickets are $35 on-site. VIP meet-and-greet tickets also are available for $45 with early entry at 7 p.m.

An all-Black queer lineup is slated for Pride at the Loft at 7:30 p.m., taking over the monthly listening room music series at The Loft (701 N. Shipley St., Wilmington) organized by Wilmington soul singer Darnell Miller.

The $10 live music show will be hosted by "Queue Points" podcast co-host Jay Ray and feature performances by Pennsylvania-based R&B/soul singer Janay Keys and Philadelphia rapper Big Grizz.

Passcode 101# gains entry to the show, which is open to all.

It may be the morning after the Delaware Pride Festival, but the celebration doesn't have to end.

Docklands Riverfront (110 West St., Wilmington), which regularly hosts drag performances, will welcome the Pride Drag Brunch & Afterparty for an eight-hour bash with doors opening at noon.

It starts with brunch from 1 to 3 p.m., DJ Shadylady playing on the patio from 3 to 6 p.m. before finishing with a drag show from 6 to 8 p.m. featuring Elektra Ryan, Onyx Black, Zephyra Rivers and Stefani Steel.

For 16 years, Our Night Out Wilmington has been hosting LGBTQ+ happy hours across the city.

Each year, its annual Our Night Our Pride Party draws the biggest crowd of the year, usually around 300 people. This year organizers are hoping to draw up to 500.

headline: Salesianum comes from behind to win Delaware boys lacrosse state championship
fullText:
CAMDEN – Salesianum only led for seven minutes and 34 seconds in its latest championship test against Cape Henlopen.

But it was the Sals who at the end of 48 minutes of play tossed their gloves and helmets as high as they could and piled on each other in jubilation after a 12-9 victory on May 31 at Caesar Rodney's Rider Stadium.

The newest entry in the rivalry between Delaware's top two boys lacrosse powers of the 21st century had a bit of everything: crafty shots, remarkable saves, clobbering checks and critical penalties. Cape Henlopen led 8-4 at halftime, looking to become the first Delaware school to beat Salesianum in any game – regular season or playoffs – since Cape won its last state championship on June 6, 2019.

Salesianum, which has now won the last five boys lacrosse state titles and 14 of the last 18, rallied in the second half, outscoring Cape 8-1.

"Cape played a great game," Maryland-bound senior Luca Pompeii said. "They had us nervous at times, but we dug deep."

Salesianum took its first lead of the second half on a leaping shot by sophomore Drew Motta with 10 minutes and 59 seconds to play. Cape's Grant Conway tied the game a minute later. Then both teams spoiled multiple scoring chances for their opponent before Salesianum broke through with a fastbreak goal with 5:44 remaining.

Tate Fontanazza gained possession of the ball near the Salesianum goal and passed to Tyler Stukis. The freshman ran more than three-quarters of the length of the field before dishing to Pompeii. After he caught the pass, Pompeii paused for a moment, shuffled his feet and coiled, then released a fastball from the left side for the definitive goal.

Pompeii scored again about four minutes later, crashing inside as the Cape goalie vacated the net. His shot somehow found the net as contact from multiple defenders forced Pompeii to the turf and his helmet off. Pompeii added another goal – he had six in the game – on an open net with 38 seconds remaining.

"I was amped," Salesianum goalkeeper Cameron Taylor said. "When Luca gets hot, you know that the tide is going to change."

GIRLS LACROSSE: Claire Lopez, Macy Steinwedel lead Cape Henlopen girls past Tower Hill for lacrosse title

Momentum in the first half belonged to Cape Henlopen. Both teams were scoreless until the first of three Motta goals at the 3:52 mark of the first quarter. The Vikings then scored the game's next five goals.

Remarkably, Cape added a score in the twilight of each of the first two quarters.

At the end of the first quarter, Brenner Short scored off a pass from Evan Burris with 1.8 seconds on the clock. In the second quarter, the Vikings scored with seven tenths of a second remaining when Burke Healy capitalized on a pass from behind the net by Conway.

In the second half, Salesianum controlled the game at the X, where Cape freshman Channing Smith had been hot in the first half. Sals senior Brayden Lasensky won the majority of the late face-offs with sophomore Luca Joseph mixing in.

Chris Cobb scored twice for Salesianum in the third quarter. Pompeii and Motta each scored once, tying the game at eight with 1:57 left in the quarter.

Taylor made several saves in the second half as Salesianum did a better job keeping Cape from point-blank range, he said.

"We were a little bit antsy," Taylor said. "We were kind of getting in our heads a little bit. Halftime gave us a minute just to calm down and collect ourselves and start working as a team again."

"In the first half, we gave up a couple of cheap ones on the inside. The two that came at the end of the quarters were really unfortunate. So we just really put an emphasis on locking down the middle and giving up the outside shots and giving me a chance."

Salesianum and Cape have faced off in the last six state championship games and 11 overall since the first official championship in 1993 (Sallies has won eight of the matchups). No other pairing has been featured more than three times.

Conway and Short led Cape with three goals each. Burke Healy had two and freshman Alan Grapski scored one.

"They're a special group of young men," Cape Henlopen head coach Geoff Shupard said. "They worked extremely hard to get here. I'm very, very proud of them. ... I thought our defense played spectacular all game long."

Salesianum led Cape 5-4 at halftime in their April 14 matchup at Abessinio Stadium. Salesianum won 15-5.

It was the only in-state loss for second-seeded Cape Henlopen (17-3), which also fell to Bullis (Maryland) in its season opener. Salesianum, the top seed in the tournament, finished the season 16-2 with losses to Chaminade (New York) and Malvern Prep (Pennsylvania), the sixth- and twelfth-ranked teams in the country by USA Lacrosse.

headline: Why are white numbers painted on I-95 lanes in Delaware? We have the answer
fullText:
Brake lights, swerving vehicles and unrelenting chaos.

It's a picture we've come to expect with the ever-present construction on I-95, Delaware's largest highway. But, the Delaware Transportation Department has a new initiative to improve the confusion.

You may have noticed white single-digit numbers, 1-5 in the north lanes and 6-10 in the south lanes, painted on the highway near and south of Wilmington.

The lane numbers are a way to better guide drivers through construction and emergency lane closures and shifts, according to DelDOT spokesman Charles "C.R." McLeod.

"We can better inform the public of construction, through labeling which lanes are going to be closed," explained McLeod, "Rather than describing something as the 'far-most lane' for example, we could use the numbered lane."

McLeod pointed to the current construction project at Churchmans Marsh as one that was benefiting directly from the new numbers.

"We're closing two lanes at a time because of the bridge [construction]," McLeod said. "So being able to bring more clarity to the public in describing those two lanes, and the ones that are open, is very important."

McLeod says the numbers will also aid first responders responding to accidents by making lane identification easier.

"911 callers will be able to easily identify which lane they're in during an accident," McLeod said.

The hope is that the plan leads to a more comprehensible highway for everyone, from construction workers to emergency personnel to the drivers themselves.

"Everything should make communication better," McLeod said. "Things should be a lot easier for everyone."

headline: Delaware City Refinery continues toxic chemical release. Here's what we know
fullText:
(This story has been updated to include information provided by the Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control after the story was first published, and to correct a typo in a photo caption.)

The Delaware City Refinery has been continuously releasing more than permitted amounts of toxic sulfur dioxide into the air for a week now, but air quality in the area remains safe, according to the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control.

Here's what we know.

What is the Delaware City Refinery?

The Delaware City Refinery is located on 5,000 acres just north of Delaware City, along the Delaware River, with a New Castle address.

It's owned by PBF Energy, "one of the largest independent petroleum refiners and suppliers of unbranded transportation fuels, heating oil, petrochemical feedstocks, lubricants and other petroleum products in the United States," according to the company's website.

The Delaware City Refinery is "one of the largest and most complex refineries on the East Coast," the website says, and can process up to 180,000 barrels of oil per day.

Historically, the Delaware City Refinery has been the state’s biggest polluter, frequently cited for air pollution violations. In October 2024, the Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control found that the refinery had deviated from its permit standards nine times between September 2022 and August 2023 and fined the refinery $75,000.

More than 86,000 people live within a 5-mile radius of the refinery, over half of whom are people of color and 20% of whom are lower-income, according to EPA data. Due to federal rules regarding diversity, equity and inclusion, earlier this year, the EPA canceled a $500,000 grant that would have allowed the nonprofit Clean Air Council to monitor air pollution in the area of the refinery.

What is sulfur dioxide?

Sulfur dioxide is a gas composed of sulfur and oxygen. It forms when fuel such as oil is burned, such as it is at like at the Delaware City Refinery.

Background: Air monitor shows pollutant from Delaware City Refinery in acceptable range: DNREC

Sulfur dioxide can make it hard to breathe and harm the human respiratory system, according to the Environmental Protection Agency. It also can harm animals and plants.

Delaware Environmental Release Notification System, which reports on the Delaware City Refinery releases, says sulfur dioxide "may cause death or permanent injury after very short exposure to small quantities."

Signs of acute sulfur dioxide exposure include symptoms such as coughing, shortness of breath, wheezing, fatigue, chest discomfort, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain and cyanosis, the reports say. People with asthma, subnormal pulmonary functions or cardiovascular disease are at a greater risk than others.

The fossil fuel industry is the largest contributor of sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere, according to the EPA. Refineries like the Delaware City Refinery typically are allowed to emit certain amounts of pollutants into the air and water through state and federal permits.

How much sulfur dioxide has been released in this incident and how much is unsafe?

The release of sulfur dioxide is ongoing and will continue "until the repairs are made," a May 31 Delaware Environmental Release Notification System report says.

While the refinery's air quality permit is available online, how much sulfur dioxide the company is normally permitted to emit is unclear. One Delaware Environmental Release Notification System report says the refinery "reported an exceedance of their permit by releasing greater than 500 pounds of sulfur dioxide."

According to reports publicly posted on the Delaware Environmental Release Notification System website, the following amounts of sulfur dioxide were released by the Delaware City Refinery since May 25.

  • 11:30 p.m., May 25: "over 100 pounds"
  • 12:01 a.m., May 26: "greater than 500 pounds"
  • 9:55 a.m., May 28: 500 pounds per hour
  • 11:16 a.m., May 29: 1,450 pounds per hour
  • 10:05 a.m., May 30: 1,450 pounds per hour
  • 9 p.m., May 31: "greater than 500 pounds"

The Delaware Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control issued a news release related to these incidents on May 31. It noted information from an air monitoring station east of the refinery on Route 9, but didn't state the direction in which the wind was blowing at the time the information was recorded.

"The Route 9 monitor is located downwind of the refinery under generally prevailing wind conditions," DNREC spokesperson Nikki LaVoie said. "And its location was chosen for that purpose and because it is between the refinery and the residential area of Delaware City."

Related: Delaware City Refinery 'deviated' from its permit 7 times in 2024 with no violations

The "health standard" for sulfur dioxide, according to the news release, is 75 parts per billion. The highest hourly measurement during "this incident" was 25 parts per billion for 6 a.m. on May 31, the release said. The highest-recorded daily average sulfur dioxide level was 2.5 parts per billion on May 26. When the news release was issued on May 31, the average was 7.33 parts per billion.

Since the news release was issued, more data has become available on the department's Air Quality Monitoring Network website. It shows a new highest hourly measurement of 29 parts per billion at midnight on June 1.

What is causing the release?

Some Delaware Environmental Release Notification System reports cite "a boiler failure."

"The cause of the emissions is a mechanical issue with a primary air pollution control device at the refinery," Lavoie said. "The facility switched to a secondary control device that does not manage sulfur dioxide emissions, resulting in excess sulfur dioxide. The facility is currently diagnosing and working to repair the primary device."

PBF representatives did not immediately respond to questions.

Why haven't nearby citizens been notified?

Delaware Environmental Release Notification System sends out notifications of chemical releases, but only to people who have signed up. Related to a past chemical release, DNREC spokesman Michael Globetti said DERNS is "not intended to be an emergency notification system, but rather a system to allow citizens to stay informed."

"We understand the public’s concerns and questions about ongoing emissions at the Delaware City Refinery and take any exceedance seriously," LaVoie said. "Based on known quantities released along with real-time air quality data, there has been no indication of a public health threat from this incident that would require a broader emergency response."

Why hasn't the refinery shut down operations?

"DNREC evaluates whether emissions during continued operation pose a greater risk than those associated with a shutdown," Lavoie said. "In this case, safely shutting down the emission unit is complex and takes several days, and the current SO2 emissions would continue through the shutdown."

Shutdown emissions often are higher than operation emissions, she added.

"Based on the incident emission levels and air monitoring data, the Department has not demanded a shutdown," Lavoie said.

DNREC is investigating the sulfur dioxide releases and enforcement actions will follow as appropriate, according to Lavoie.

Molly McVety contributed to this story. Shannon Marvel McNaught reports on southern Delaware and beyond. Reach her at smcnaught@gannett.com or on Facebook.

headline: Police ID Dover man killed in Cheswold motorcycle crash
fullText:
Delaware State Police have identified the motorcyclist killed in a car crash in Cheswold May 30 as 22-year-old Jordan Cuffee.

Around 7:50 p.m. that night, Cuffee was traveling south in the left lane of North Dupont Highway, approaching Rose Bowl Road, police said. At the same time, a Toyota Sienna was traveling east on Rose Bowl Road, stopped at a stop sign at North Dupont Highway.

A preliminary investigation found the Sienna crossed the southbound lanes and entered into the motorcycle's path, police said, resulting in the motorcycle striking the Sienna and ejecting Cuffee.

Cuffee, of Dover, was taken to a hospital and later died. The driver of the Toyota, a 74-year-old Smyrna man, sustained a minor injury and refused transport to a hospital, police said.

The Delaware State Police Troop 3 Collision Reconstruction Unit continues to investigate the crash. Anyone who witnessed this collision should contact Master Cpl. J. Lane at 302-698-8457, send a Facebook message to Delaware State Police or contact Delaware Crime Stoppers at 1-800-847-3333.

headline: Caravel repeats as DIAA DII girls soccer champs as Hood scores decisive goal in OT
fullText:
There were goals and there were opportunities in the 80 minutes of scoreless regulation that comprised the DIAA Division II Girls Soccer Tournament title game.

But somebody just needed one of those goals to actually count.

Maci Hood made that happen in the third minute of sudden-death overtime, deflecting a teammate’s try off a cornerkick and scoring to give Caravel a 1-0 win over Saint Mark’s on June 1 at Caravel’s Bob Peoples Stadium.

“Teammate Sydney [Hayden] kind of hit it across,” Hood said. “I guess I was just standing there and I just put my foot out and I guess it went in.”

Caravel had two goals nullified by offsides in regulation and Saint Mark’s had one.

There were also near misses galore that each would lament before Hood ensured the game’s only goal would be golden.

“It was a little bit frustrating at first,” said fellow senior Lillian O’Brien, who had a couple close shots and also took the cornerkick. “But I think we just used it as like a confidence booster and I feel like we were in their half a majority of the time.

FIRST STATE'S FINEST: Coaches' preseason Top 36 players in Delaware high school girls soccer

“Our game plan going out to halftime and before overtime,” she added, “was just to use that as momentum and confidence. We're in their half. We can finish. We just have to keep going forward and shooting and shooting, and eventually it goes in, so it's great.”

That finish eventually came and it gave top-seeded Caravel (13-1-1) its second straight state title and eighth in nine tries since 2014.

“Going out senior year, your home field, nothing better,” Hood said.

Hood and O’Brien had also been freshmen on the Caravel team that lost to Saint Mark’s 2-1 in the 2022 state final and were quite aware of the challenge the Bucs faced, especially after a 2-1 regular-season win over the Spartans on April 3 that could have gone either way.

No. 2-seeded Saint Mark’s (13-3) was shut out for the first time this year.

Caravel goalie Taylor Fitzgerald made the key stops, and the defense fronting her did enough to thwart a skilled and creative slew of Saint Mark’s goal hunters led by Lily Phillips, who’d scored as a freshman in the Spartans’ 2022 title win over Caravel, and Whitney Evancho.  

“It really is a full circle moment,” O’Brien said, “because it started against them, tough opponent, freshman year, and we lost. So it feels great to finish out senior year on your home field, an opportunity not many people get.”

headline: Fear factor: The poll results are in for most feared wildlife in Southwest Florida
fullText:
People who voted in our poll "What Southwest Florida wildlife do you fear the most?" were definitely channeling their inner-Indiana Jones.

The famous movie character, an archeologist who travels the world searching for iconic artifacts like the Ark of the Covenant, famously encountered challenges from man and beast.

There is a scene in "Raiders of the Lost Ark" where Jones finds himself in a cave surrounded by thousands of snakes.

"Snakes,'' Jones said. "Why did it have to be snakes?"

Exactly. Our audience agrees. Snakes were the No. 1 most feared wildlife in Southwest Florida based on the votes in our poll.

More: Deep in the woods: Remote camera leads to stunning photos of SWFL wildlife

Snakes (pythons, cottonmouths, eastern diamondbacks, rattlesnakes, etc.) received 42% of the votes. Coming in second, not surprisingly, were alligators with 15% of the votes cast. Spiders, mosquitoes and sharks all got more than 5% of the votes.

Here are the full results:

Most don’t want to be bothered by humans. Most will leave you alone if you don’t bother them. Wild boar is only one I fear that will attack just because.

Instagram

ahe1015x said: Cane toads! My poor puppies!

sharronclayton said: Definitely cane toads.
